lessons.title: Campaign Strategy
lessons.description:
Campaigns are your one-off sends at a specific date & Time
Send between 2x - 4x per week
Content: Stay TOP of mind
Who are you going to call when your power goes out? The electrician who's knocking at your door
Send frequency will vary based on different factors, primarily on store revenue & site traffic
Find a good balance of Graphic & Text-Based Emails
Educate the customer on a problem, position yourself as the solution. Don't throw around discounts like candy... Dilutes & cheapens the brandLink to document in video: https://gamma.app/docs/Email-Marketing-Campaigns-uefllw8w707qptn

lessons.title: Segmentation
lessons.description:
Dynamic customer cohorts (groups) determined by meeting certain conditions

Better deliverability
More sales

Personalization

lessons.title: Text Based Email Masterclass
lessons.description:
See what makes a great text based email, why they're effective, and how to build a great one yourself!

Plain text emails are a highly effective, underrated e-commerce marketing strategy that can generate significant revenue. These emails, without any design or graphics, stand out and connect with customers on a personal level.
Key Pointers for Success:
Why they work:
Stand out from graphic-heavy emails (0:47).
Feel personal, like a friend sent them (1:02).
Build trust by appearing human, not corporate (2:47).
Best practices:
Keep it short: under 250 words (6:43).
Use 1-2 clear calls to action (7:00).
Send from a real person (or created persona) (7:25).
Include a "PS" section for key messages (7:37).
When to use them:
In key email flows (welcome, abandonment, post-purchase, win-back) (13:08).
Mix with graphic emails; aim for a 4:1 graphic to plain text ratio (13:18).
Send at least two plain text emails per month (one educational, one promotional) (13:26).
Test different senders and content (13:37).

lessons.title: ChatGPT Copywriting
lessons.description:
AI isn't perfect, but capitalize on Chat GPT for the ideation, guides, frameworks
Any LLM is an iterative process. Embrace the back and forth.
Email Marketing Brain >>>
Your prompts are everything. Lazy prompts = Lazy results. Good prompts = Good (not perfect) Results
Copy Template >>>
Simple and Effective Copywriting Prompt
You're an expert copywriter trained to write ecommerce email marketing copy.
Your mission is to write punchy, direct-response friendly email marketing copy tailored for ecommerce brands. The copy must be short, skimmable, and optimized for mobile inboxes, while aligned with brand tone and the customer's journey stage.
Write 3 short and punchy email campaign variations displayed in table format for this consumer product brand.
Each variation must include the following fields in this exact order:
Subject Line
Preview Text
Headline
Subheadline
First CTA (text only, no button styling)
Body Copy (2-4 sentences, short, scroll-stopping, mobile-first)
Bridge Section (Example: “Graphic: Side-by-side results” or “Visual: 5-star review snapshot”)
Product Section (Highlight 1 product with background info if appropriate such as 3 feature bullets OR 3–6 products with 1-line benefit/feature per product + CTA)Important Notes:
Built for image-based layout (e.g. Figma, Canva)
Designed for mobile-first consumption
Bold, no fluff, attention-grabbing
Optimized for engagement and clicks
Must include social proof, direct response copy principles, and objection handling when applicable
No discounting unless strategically required
Tone and language should reflect the brand as described aboveHere’s what you need to know about the brand and email you are writing about:
Brand Website: [INSERT LINK]
Brand Overview (2-3 sentences): [Briefly explain who you are, your tone/voice, and what differentiates you]
Customer Insights: [Describe your customer—what they want, pain points, desired outcomes, and what motivates them to buy]
Email Topic or Campaign Angle: [e.g. “New product launch,” “FAQ Myth Bust,” “Founder story,” “Us vs. Them,” etc.]Link to document in video: https://gamma.app/docs/Email-Copywriting-3kadzcmu0ixjepr?mode=doc

lessons.title: Subject Lines & Preview Texts
lessons.description:
Not about your open rates. About the frame of the email & quality of the customer you're attracting
Guidelines:
Short & punchy: aim for curiosity, urgency, and specificity. Avoid generic “Newsletter” subject lines
Invoke curiosity
Personalization: using names, segments, and past behavior to make the subject feel relevant.
Complementarity with preview text: preview text expands or reinforces the subject line; use wisely (not just filler).
Testing & optimization: A/B test subject lines; track open rates; tweak based on what works.Remember: people should open your emails based off your sender name, NOT your Subject line.
Don't overthink it
Link to document in video: https://gamma.app/docs/Email-Copywriting-3kadzcmu0ixjepr?mode=doc

lessons.title: MX Email Expert Claude Skill
lessons.description:
👉 Download MX Email Expert Claude Skill
This module walks you through installing and using the Claude skill file... the most advanced AI tool in the space. Where the custom GPT is built for speed, this is built for depth: it's trained on the full 2026 Well Copy methodology and everything we run internally for clients. It writes copy, builds strategy, reviews emails, and answers questions using our exact process and it won't move forward without proper context, plus it quality-checks its own work to catch anything it might have made up.
Installing the skill (one time): Download the skill zip attached to this module (linked above). In Claude, go to Customize → Skills → + → Create skill → Upload skill, then drag in the zip. Done. Inside the file you'll find the base skill plus all the rule files (brand research, calendar builder, campaign briefs), brand examples, and references — everything that powers it.
Accessing the skill and knowledge in Claude: Simply type /mx in any Claude chat (mx = "max" without the a). That tells Claude to reference the skill. Then you can ask it to do any task for you!
PROPERLY ONBOARD YOUR BRAND(S)
Don't run this in plain chat. Create a separate Project for each brand you work with. A Project is a private space in Claude that only remembers what happens inside it, so each brand's memory, chats, and files stay clean and organized.
The onboarding flow (do this once per brand):
Create a project for your brand.
In the brand's Project, type /mx then "onboard this brand [name]."
It runs deep research, flags gaps, and asks you to fill them in. Tell it it's inside a Project so it saves everything there.
It builds your brand files such as profile, voice, products, memories.
Answer all of it's questions and ask when it is done with onboarding before you start with having it create calendars and strategy.Once onboarding is complete, you can ask it to plan next month's calendar, build flows, write copy, etc and it gets better the more real data you give it.
Same rule as always: don't outsource your brain. Double-check it, push back, workshop the output. It's the best AI strategist you'll find — but you're still the operator.

lessons.title: [July 30th] Email Marketing Tools + Reviews
lessons.description:
Call Summary — Top Email Marketing Tools Stack, August Challenge & Live Email Reviews


---
Opening & Community Wins (0:00–5:00)
Max opened with wins from the community — highlights included a flash sale hitting its biggest hour ever, a new top performing campaign angle discovered internally, a member's first 25 sales with zero ad spend six days after launch, and a member joining and immediately generating $3K in email revenue using the free content.
Max's win: finding a new killer campaign angle for one of Well Copy's brands that outperformed everything they'd built themselves. Details in the daily insights post.

---
August Email Design Challenge Announcement (5:00–10:00)
Well Copy is running an email of the month challenge throughout August. Three winners selected at the end of the month.
Prizes:
Private 1-on-1 call with Max
Featured across all of Max's social channels
Additional bonuses TBCRequirements:
Post at least one email design per week in the community
Respond to at least one other person's submission per week
More submissions = more chances to winMax will review every submission live on the weekly calls. The last time a challenge like this ran, Tristan won — Max noted that the private call ended up going for 90 minutes and directly led to Tristan now co-hosting the agency calls. Winners announced live on a call at the end of August.

---
Weekly Insights Roundup (10:00–15:00)
Max highlighted a few recent insights from his daily posts worth actioning:
Alia Smart Trigger:
A feature inside Alia pop-up forms that uses AI to predict when to re-show the pop-up to someone who initially closed it. One brand added 2,400 extra email submits and $95,000 in attributed sales in a single week just by enabling this. Worth turning on immediately if you're on Alia.
Klaviyo analysis with Claude:
If you use Hyros, you can connect it to Claude and run prompts directly on your account data. Covered in a recent insight post — highly recommended for anyone doing deep campaign analysis.
Stealing angles from the Meta Ads Library:
Max is pushing his team hard on this. The principle: if an ad has been running for more than a few weeks, the brand is putting money behind it because it's working. Find long-running ads in your client's niche and steal the angle for email. Recent examples from Mars Men that Max flagged as direct email fodder: "Man boobs gone or your money back," "I just tired isn't a personality trait," and a divorce angle — all strong emotional hooks that work even better on a warm email list.

---
Email Marketing Tools Stack (15:00–42:00)
Max walked through the full stack Well Copy uses internally, broken into categories.
Ideation — finding campaign angles:
Meta Ads Library (facebook.com/ads/library) — look at own brand, direct competitors, and top brands in the niche. Filter for ads that have been running the longest — longevity = budget spend = winning ad.
Milled — follow brands and see every email they've ever sent. Best ongoing reference for email design and campaign strategy.
Email Donut — curated email inspiration. Couldn't load in Max's location during the call but confirmed it works.
Trendtrack — recently added email functionality alongside its ads library. Worth checking.
Claude MX Skill — the primary internal tool for campaign ideation and copy. The Well Copy copywriting system is literally built around this skill — what community members have access to is the exact same thing the internal team uses, just with a different UI wrapper. Access via the classroom under Templates & Resources → MX Expert Claude Skill. Type /MX to activate within Claude Projects.
Past winners in Klaviyo — Max is relentlessly pushing his team on resending proven past winners. One brand couldn't crack campaigns for weeks. Resent an email the client's internal team had made pre-Well Copy and it tripled everything they'd built themselves. Don't underestimate what you already have.Email creation:
Figma — all email design is done in Figma.
Magnific — AI image generation and stock image tool used alongside Figma. Connected to major AI image models (Midjourney, ChatGPT image generation) in a cleaner UI with better prompting. Well Copy recently bought a large team plan. Recommended as the go-to for AI creative for email.
Figma plugins — Giffy Canvas for creating GIFs directly in Figma. GIF Export plugin for downloading. Also worth exploring the Figma plugin marketplace for UI generators and other tools.
Community email templates — the monthly template packs and Figma template files shared in the community.Analytics:
Hyros (Hiro Analytics) — preferred analytics platform for deeper reporting beyond what Klaviyo natively shows. Used for monthly client reports (auto-generated, brandable), deep audits, and identifying anomalies. Recent example: a brand's results declined and Max dug into Hyros to find first-time customer revenue was down 25% month over month while returning customer revenue was up. Traced it back to a new acquisition landing page the client hadn't told them about — the pop-up wasn't firing on that page. That diagnosis came directly from Hyros visibility. Mention Max for a discount when signing up.Inbox optimisation:
Maverick — adds a snippet to your emails that helps them land in the main inbox rather than Promotions. A/B test data from Maverick's own site: 0.25% click rate without snippet vs 0.68% with. $2K vs $3.6K revenue. Significant uplift just from adding the snippet. Typically gate-kept — Max is opening it up. Use the link trymaverick.com/deliverabilityoptimizer and mention Max for a free trial setup call.Third-party data and abandonment recovery:
OpenSend — captures emails from people who abandon on a different device or who don't opt into the pop-up form. Connects abandoned sessions to real email addresses and fires flows in Klaviyo. A recent Well Copy case study showed $200K additional revenue added in a couple of months for a single brand. Best suited for brands spending $30K–$50K+ per month on ads (roughly $1K/day ad spend minimum).
Alternatives: Customers.ai and Retention.com exist but Max finds OpenSend gives better quality profiles with more filtering capability to protect deliverability.
Legal note: technically legal through cookie consent agreements users accepted. Works particularly well for high-traffic, high-spend brands.Interactive email features:
Zemo — allows customers to take actions directly inside the email: leave reviews, edit subscriptions, delay or skip orders, complete one-click upsells, fill in forms, and interact with animated elements (flip to reveal discount codes, open animations, find the hidden shade games). Particularly powerful for subscription brands — editing subscriptions without going to a portal dramatically reduces churn. Used for almost all Well Copy's subscription clients.AI customer segmentation:
Arena — AI-powered segmentation tool that goes beyond native Klaviyo segmentation. Creates win-back and engagement segments automatically based on set goals. Only recommended for 8-figure+ brands where the complexity justifies the additional tool. Well Copy has rolled it out for a few brands.Pop-up forms:
Alia — the best pop-up platform available. Max's unequivocal recommendation. If you're not on Alia, moving to it will get better results. Period. Smart Trigger alone (mentioned above) justifies it.Cashback / offers:
Fondue — instead of "10% off," you offer "20% cashback." Cashback is sent post-purchase via email as a digital Visa card. The key: very few people actually claim cashback, so the effective discount rate ends up being around 4–6% despite advertising 20%. Fondue cites 52% growth in one brand's revenue, 43% more orders. Redeemable for 90 days. Works because of the psychological appeal of a higher advertised number with low real cost.SMS platforms:
Klaviyo — preferred for brands that want email and SMS in one place. Approximately 60–70% of Well Copy's SMS-running brands are on Klaviyo for SMS.
Postscript and Attentive — both are solid alternatives, split roughly evenly among brands not using Klaviyo SMS. They offer similar features and will each try to sell you on AI conversation features — Max advises against using conversational SMS flows because every back-and-forth message costs 1–2 cents and ROI rarely justifies it versus standard broadcast SMS.
For peptide and telehealth brands: Klaviyo and Omnisend are actively kicking these brands off. The only platform Max has found consistently lenient for this category is Attentive. If you're running peptides or telehealth, go directly to Attentive.
One Text — a platform that allows customers to buy directly by replying to an SMS. Customer receives a text about a new product, replies "buy," and the order is placed using their stored card details. Interesting for brands with high SMS engagement but requires the customer to have placed a prior order through the platform.
SMS inspo: Attentive's "Texts We Love" swipe file — Max dropped the link in the community chat.Summary of the core stack per brand:
Alia for pop-ups, Klaviyo for email and SMS (or Attentive/Postscript for SMS), Hyros for analytics, Maverick for inbox optimisation, OpenSend for abandonment recovery at scale, Zemo for subscription brands.

---
Live Email Reviews (42:00–55:00)
Social proof / testimonial welcome email:
Design is solid and testimonial layout is strong — Max liked the concept of FAQ objections being handled by testimonials specifically
Missing: discount code. Every single welcome flow email must have the discount code visible, ideally in a bar at the top and again before the bottom CTA. Without it, people forget
Add the number of reviews and potentially the Trustpilot logo if reviews are from Trustpilot — adds credibility weight
Category buttons in the footer always — give people somewhere to go if they didn't find what they wanted in the emailMango word search engagement email (Tyler):
Max loved this concept — a word search where customers find the three product ingredients and get a reward for completing it
Suggested making it a reply mechanic rather than "post and tag" — replies are far easier to get than social shares
Recommended keeping only three hidden words to make it achievable
Creative, original, high engagement potential — strong concept to stealButt-focused welcome flow email:
Good structure overall
Move the discount code above the first CTA — front and centre
Discount code already looks random which is correct
Add category navigation buttons in the footer — universal ruleFree gift flow email:
Strong framing — "your free gift is waiting" makes the customer feel like they already own it
Step-by-step visual is clear and effective
Add urgency — "last chance" on its own isn't enough. Frame it as "your access is being revoked" or "your free gift expires in X hours" — specificity and threat of loss adds meaningful uplift
Show what the free gifts actually are — don't just tease them, reveal the options so people are motivated to hit the threshold
PS section with upsell is present and correct — keep itNew in / product launch email:
Spacing is too tight throughout — compare side by side with a well-designed brand email and match the spacing and text sizes
Recommend showing both lifestyle photography and flat product photography together for new product reveals — lifestyle gets attention, flat product shows the actual item clearly
Add shop buttons underneath each product
"Available in four colours" without showing the colours is a missed opportunity — display themCampaign and clothing brand emails:
Text size consistently too small — minimum 20pt for body copy in email
A/B test Klaviyo dynamic product blocks instead of manually curated product sections — Max has seen this beat custom designed sections repeatedly for high-SKU brands
More photo galleries — for clothing specifically, volume of imagery drives clicks more than almost anything else. Max referenced Comfort as a brand doing photo galleries well in their hero sections.
Flash sale emails: keep design clean, text bigger, and lean into Klaviyo dynamic product feeds
---
Q&A (Throughout)
Nasal tanner brand / peptide-adjacent products on Klaviyo:
Likely to get kicked off Klaviyo with 30 days notice if the product is flagged. If the brand isn't already on Klaviyo, Max wouldn't even attempt onboarding them there. Attentive is more lenient with this category. Go straight to Attentive.
SMS platform for peptide brands:
Attentive only. Klaviyo and Omnisend are actively removing peptide brands.
Running SMS and email on separate platforms:
Completely fine. No technical issues with having Klaviyo for email and Postscript or Attentive for SMS running in parallel.
OpenSend minimum size requirement:
$1K/day in ad spend as a rough baseline (approximately $3M/year in revenue). Below that, the traffic volume is too low to justify the cost.

---
Closing (~55:00)
Max jumped to another call. Reminded the community that DMs and Skool posts are always open for follow-up questions. August challenge details to be posted in the community shortly — everyone encouraged to start preparing submissions.

Recent examples from Mars Men that Max flagged as direct email fodder: "Man boobs gone or your money back," "I just tired isn't a personality trait," and a divorce angle — all strong emotional hooks that work even better on a warm email list.
Email Marketing Tools Stack (15:00–42:00)
Max walked through the full stack Well Copy uses internally, broken into categories.
Ideation — finding campaign angles:
Meta Ads Library
facebook.com/ads/library
) — look at own brand, direct competitors, and top brands in the niche. Filter for ads that have been running the longest — longevity = budget spend = winning ad.
Milled
— follow brands and see every email they've ever sent. Best ongoing reference for email design and campaign strategy.
Email Donut
— curated email inspiration. Couldn't load in Max's location during the call but confirmed it works.
Trendtrack
— recently added email functionality alongside its ads library. Worth checking.
Claude MX Skill

— the primary internal tool for campaign ideation and copy. The Well Copy copywriting system is literally built around this skill — what community members have access to is the exact same thing the internal team uses, just with a different UI wrapper. Access via the classroom under Templates & Resources → MX Expert Claude Skill. Type /MX to activate within Claude Projects.
Past winners in Klaviyo

— Max is relentlessly pushing his team on resending proven past winners. One brand couldn't crack campaigns for weeks. Resent an email the client's internal team had made pre-Well Copy and it tripled everything they'd built themselves. Don't underestimate what you already have.
Email creation:
Figma
— all email design is done in Figma.
Magnific

— AI image generation and stock image tool used alongside Figma. Connected to major AI image models (Midjourney, ChatGPT image generation) in a cleaner UI with better prompting. Well Copy recently bought a large team plan. Recommended as the go-to for AI creative for email.
Figma plugins
— Giffy Canvas for creating GIFs directly in Figma. GIF Export plugin for downloading. Also worth exploring the Figma plugin marketplace for UI generators and other tools.
Community email templates
— the monthly template packs and Figma template files shared in the community.
Analytics:
Hyros (Hiro Analytics)

— preferred analytics platform for deeper reporting beyond what Klaviyo natively shows. Used for monthly client reports (auto-generated, brandable), deep audits, and identifying anomalies. Recent example: a brand's results declined and Max dug into Hyros to find first-time customer revenue was down 25% month over month while returning customer revenue was up. Traced it back to a new acquisition landing page the client hadn't told them about — the pop-up wasn't firing on that page. That diagnosis came directly from Hyros visibility. Mention Max for a discount when signing up.
Inbox optimisation:
Maverick

— adds a snippet to your emails that helps them land in the main inbox rather than Promotions. A/B test data from Maverick's own site: 0.25% click rate without snippet vs 0.68% with. $2K vs $3.6K revenue. Significant uplift just from adding the snippet. Typically gate-kept — Max is opening it up. Use the link
trymaverick.com/deliverabilityoptimizer
and mention Max for a free trial setup call.
Third-party data and abandonment recovery:
OpenSend

— captures emails from people who abandon on a different device or who don't opt into the pop-up form. Connects abandoned sessions to real email addresses and fires flows in Klaviyo. A recent Well Copy case study showed $200K additional revenue added in a couple of months for a single brand. Best suited for brands spending $30K–$50K+ per month on ads (roughly $1K/day ad spend minimum).
Alternatives:
Customers.ai
and
Retention.com
exist but Max finds OpenSend gives better quality profiles with more filtering capability to protect deliverability.
Legal note:
technically legal through cookie consent agreements users accepted. Works particularly well for high-traffic, high-spend brands.
Interactive email features:
Zemo

— allows customers to take actions directly inside the email: leave reviews, edit subscriptions, delay or skip orders, complete one-click upsells, fill in forms, and interact with animated elements (flip to reveal discount codes, open animations, find the hidden shade games). — AI-powered segmentation tool that goes beyond native Klaviyo segmentation. Creates win-back and engagement segments automatically based on set goals. Only recommended for 8-figure+ brands where the complexity justifies the additional tool. Well Copy has rolled it out for a few brands.
Pop-up forms:
Alia
— the best pop-up platform available. Max's unequivocal recommendation. If you're not on Alia, moving to it will get better results. Period. Smart Trigger alone (mentioned above) justifies it.

— instead of "10% off," you offer "20% cashback." Cashback is sent post-purchase via email as a digital Visa card. Klaviyo
— preferred for brands that want email and SMS in one place. Approximately 60–70% of Well Copy's SMS-running brands are on Klaviyo for SMS.

Klaviyo and Omnisend are actively kicking these brands off. The only platform Max has found consistently lenient for this category is Attentive. If you're running peptides or telehealth, go directly to Attentive.
One Text

— a platform that allows customers to buy directly by replying to an SMS. Customer receives a text about a new product, replies "buy," and the order is placed using their stored card details. SMS inspo:
Attentive's "Texts We Love" swipe file — Max dropped the link in the community chat.
Summary of the core stack per brand:

Alia for pop-ups, Klaviyo for email and SMS (or Attentive/Postscript for SMS), Hyros for analytics, Maverick for inbox optimisation, OpenSend for abandonment recovery at scale, Zemo for subscription brands.
Live Email Reviews (42:00–55:00)
Social proof / testimonial welcome email:
Design is solid and testimonial layout is strong — Max liked the concept of FAQ objections being handled by testimonials specifically
Missing: discount code. Every single welcome flow email must have the discount code visible, ideally in a bar at the top and again before the bottom CTA. Without it, people forget
Add the number of reviews and potentially the Trustpilot logo if reviews are from Trustpilot — adds credibility weight
Category buttons in the footer always — give people somewhere to go if they didn't find what they wanted in the email
Mango word search engagement email (Tyler):
Max loved this concept — a word search where customers find the three product ingredients and get a reward for completing it
Suggested making it a reply mechanic rather than "post and tag" — replies are far easier to get than social shares
Recommended keeping only three hidden words to make it achievable
Creative, original, high engagement potential — strong concept to steal
Butt-focused welcome flow email:
Good structure overall
Move the discount code above the first CTA — front and centre
Discount code already looks random which is correct
Add category navigation buttons in the footer — universal rule
Free gift flow email:
Strong framing — "your free gift is waiting" makes the customer feel like they already own it
Step-by-step visual is clear and effective
Add urgency — "last chance" on its own isn't enough. Frame it as "your access is being revoked" or "your free gift expires in X hours" — specificity and threat of loss adds meaningful uplift
Show what the free gifts actually are — don't just tease them, reveal the options so people are motivated to hit the threshold
PS section with upsell is present and correct — keep it
New in / product launch email:
Spacing is too tight throughout — compare side by side with a well-designed brand email and match the spacing and text sizes
Recommend showing both lifestyle photography and flat product photography together for new product reveals — lifestyle gets attention, flat product shows the actual item clearly
Add shop buttons underneath each product
"Available in four colours" without showing the colours is a missed opportunity — display them
Campaign and clothing brand emails:
Text size consistently too small — minimum 20pt for body copy in email
A/B test Klaviyo dynamic product blocks instead of manually curated product sections — Max has seen this beat custom designed sections repeatedly for high-SKU brands
More photo galleries — for clothing specifically, volume of imagery drives clicks more than almost anything else. Max referenced Comfort as a brand doing photo galleries well in their hero sections.
Flash sale emails: keep design clean, text bigger, and lean into Klaviyo dynamic product feeds
Q&A (Throughout)
Nasal tanner brand / peptide-adjacent products on Klaviyo:

Likely to get kicked off Klaviyo with 30 days notice if the product is flagged. If the brand isn't already on Klaviyo, Max wouldn't even attempt onboarding them there. Attentive is more lenient with this category. Go straight to Attentive.
SMS platform for peptide brands:
Attentive only. Klaviyo and Omnisend are actively removing peptide brands.
Running SMS and email on separate platforms:
Completely fine. No technical issues with having Klaviyo for email and Postscript or Attentive for SMS running in parallel.

$1K/day in ad spend as a rough baseline (approximately $3M/year in revenue). Below that, the traffic volume is too low to justify the cost.
Closing (~55:00)

Max jumped to another call. Reminded the community that DMs and Skool posts are always open for follow-up questions. August challenge details to be posted in the community shortly — everyone encouraged to start preparing submissions.

lessons.title: [July 23rd] Post Purchase Strategy + LIVE Reviews
lessons.description:
Call Summary — Post Purchase Strategy by Niche, Live Klaviyo Audit & Live Email Reviews


---
Opening & Community Wins (0:00–5:00)
Max opened from San Diego with a personal win (back home for the month) and a business win — a new senior IAM hire with both in-house and agency experience, which Max flagged as the cream of the crop combination. In-house only tends to lack speed and multi-brand juggling. Agency only tends to be more execution-heavy and less strategic. Both together is the ideal.
Community wins included a member graduating from Canva to Figma, email revenue up 850% in a month, a pop-up submit rate jumping from 7% to 20%, and multiple members completing first welcome flow rebuilds and full flow builds.

---
Post Purchase Philosophy Shift — Clothing, Accessories & CPG (5:00–28:00)
Max opened with a core strategic update being rolled out across Well Copy's client base — a fundamental shift in post purchase flow timing and aggression, based on repeat order data pulled from their internal analytics platform.
The problem it's solving:
Two clients — an eight-figure jewelry brand (12–15% repeat order rate, targeting 20%) and a nine-figure clothing brand (20% repeat order rate, targeting 30%) — were doing everything right: sending every other day, correct segmentation, all core flows in place. But the repeat order rate wasn't moving.
The data discovery:
By pulling repeat order timing data from the Well Copy analytics platform (and cross-referencing in Hyros), Max found that when customers who placed a first order come back to place a second, the timing is dramatically different by niche.
Clothing and accessories:
The repeat order curve is heavily front-loaded. The majority of second orders happen before or right around when the customer receives the product — day 3 to day 10. Customers are in a honeymoon phase: they're excited about the brand, they just bought, they're already looking at other products. By the time day 30 or 45 arrives — when most agencies fire replenishment reminders and post purchase upsell sequences — the excitement has already faded significantly.
Current standard approach across the industry: exclude past 21–30 day purchasers from campaigns and fire post purchase upsells at days 30–45.
The new approach for clothing and accessories:
Stop excluding recent purchasers from campaigns (or at minimum, exclude for only 7 days)
Send daily or every-other-day post purchase emails immediately after purchase
Front-load offers and upsells into the first 10 days
Test an "automated customer holiday" sequence — starting on day 7, create a hype sequence that feels like a live brand event but is fully automated: a "coming soon" teaser, then 7 days of daily deals, each with a new offer. Creates forward momentum and repeat engagement in the exact window when customers are most primed.The philosophy: take what's already working (people are naturally buying again early) and add fuel to that fire rather than trying to re-engage people at day 45 when interest has already dropped.
CPG and supplements:
The curve is completely different. Very few purchases happen in the first five days — customers haven't received the product yet and don't know if they'll like it. The rebuy window for CPG is roughly day 10 to day 35 after the first order, once the customer has tried the product, enjoyed it, and started thinking about getting more.
Standard approach: replenishment reminder on day 30–45. This is actually quite well timed for CPG — but only if you're also capitalising on the active window at days 10–35.
The new approach for CPG:
Pre-delivery focus is purely education: get them to use the product correctly and prime them on new flavours or variations
From around day 10 onwards, start sending consistent emails about trying new flavours, upgrading to a larger supply, or bundling
Move replenishment reminder and offer testing to day 15–21, not day 30–45 — this is where the action is happening in the data
Insert a harder offer around day 30–35 when the tail-off begins to try to catch any stragglers before they go coldKey philosophical shift:
Most agencies and brands look at where the drop-off happens and try to intervene there. Max's approach is the opposite — look at where things are already working naturally and add fuel to that period. The drop-off intervention is a harder problem. Amplifying existing momentum is a much easier win.
How to pull your own repeat order data:
Export all orders from Shopify for customers who have placed at least two orders in the past 365 days. Make sure the spreadsheet has the first order date and second order date as columns. Upload the CSV to Claude or ChatGPT and ask it to generate a histogram showing which day number (after first order) repeat orders are being placed. Look at the curve and adjust your post purchase timing accordingly.
Note: Klaviyo doesn't have this view natively. Hyros does. Well Copy's internal analytics platform does. For everyone else, Shopify CSV export plus Claude is the workaround.
On peptide brands:
A completely different model. The entire game is getting someone to their first subscription order as fast as possible. Once they subscribe, you've won — move to a light educational sequence and check-ins only. For prospects who haven't subscribed yet, go as aggressive as possible: two emails and one text message per day is standard for Well Copy's 30M/month peptide client. The opt-in to purchase timing graph makes this obvious — 80% of purchases happen on day zero. The fall-off is dramatic and fast after that. Every day of hesitation loses you buyers.

---
Live Klaviyo Audit — Hair Removal Subscription Brand (28:00–42:00)
Max walked through a live audit for a subscription-forward hair removal brand.
Initial context:
Subscription is the majority of the business but subscribe-and-save is a relatively small visible option on the PDP
Custom placed order metric already set up (excluding rebuilds) — showing 14% attribution, compared to a higher standard placed order figure
Main product driving first purchases is a pink 3-tube bundle, with everything else positioned as an upsellPop-up form:
Running a mystery offer through Alia — good
32% open rate on the first welcome email is low for a brand telling people to check email for the offer. If the discount is being revealed in the pop-up form itself, some people will skip the email — fix this firstDeliverability:
The main bottleneck across this account. Low engagement across flows and campaigns signals the emails are landing in promotions or spam for a meaningful portion of the list.
Recommended fix: install Maverick (try maverick.com/deliverabilityoptimizer) — an inbox optimisation tool that helps emails land in the main inbox rather than promotions. Max offered to hook the brand up via his referral.
Also recommended running a GlockApps test to see exactly where the emails are landing across different inbox providers, and what changes GlockApps recommends.
Welcome flow:
Only three emails — extend to five or six
No text-based emails — add at least one
No raised offer or store credit at the end — add this
Discount code should be in the hero section of every email
Overall content and structure is solid — deliverability is the blocker, not the strategyAbandonment flows:
Generally set up correctly
Add an offer at the end
Low engagement is again deliverability, not contentCampaigns:
Sending every other day — good cadence
Need to make sure active subscribers are being excluded correctly and the custom placed order metric (without subscription rebuilds) is being used as the primary attribution viewOn attribution for subscription brands:
Standard placed order metric shows all revenue including rebuilds. Custom metric strips those out, showing only one-time orders and first-time subscription placements. For this brand: €568K on the standard metric vs €357K on the custom metric — the difference of ~€200K is all rebuilds. Using the clean metric gives a true picture of what email is actually driving in new revenue.
On the 15% attributed revenue: not atypical for a subscription-first brand, but there's room to grow. Deliverability fix should move the needle significantly.

---
Live Email Reviews (42:00–58:00)
Peptide brand (Omnisend):
Welcome email is strong — good structure and education
Make the discount code look random and custom (e.g. GX47HY rather than a branded code)
Add "click here to activate your offer" text near the CTA — even if it's not required, it drives extra clicks which improves inbox placement signals for future sends
Abandonment email: strong. Add a welcome discount reminder bar at the top for non-buyers
Overall metrics are solid. Minor tweaks only.Gospel board game brand:
Creative concept and strong educational content throughout the flow
Offer framing needs clarification — "shop 10% off" without a visible code or activation mechanism is confusing
If the site already has a standing discount (e.g. 30%), frame the email offer as the total (40% off) rather than just the incremental amount
Add a text-based founder email to the flow — the brand story is strong and a personal founder email would fit well here
The "$22 off" mechanic (dollar amount rather than percentage) could outperform the mystery percentage offer — worth testing as the lead offerUpside Down Kingdom brand:
Gamified pop-up revealing discount at end — this is fine, but worth A/B testing against gating the code in the welcome email to improve email open signals
Always send email first, then SMS with a 5-minute delay — if both send simultaneously, people open SMS and ignore email, which hurts future deliverability
Click to activate your discount in the hero section — good, keep this
Mystery offer framing is solid — make the code look random
Strong content throughout. Offer framing and SMS delay are the main changes.Jacob's supplement brand:
Designs are bangers — clean, professional, myths vs facts format executed really well
Subscription confirmation email is exactly right — order information front and centre, clear structure
No comments from Max beyond genuine praise for the design quality and strategyClaude-designed welcome flow (various brands):
Recurring feedback across multiple submitted flows:
Text size is too small — minimum 20pt on mobile, ideally 24pt for body copy
Hero section text needs to be readable without zooming — if copy is hard to read, people won't click
Add a dark overlay to hero images with text on top if the text is getting lost in the image
Align all elements — misaligned blocks look amateurish even in otherwise good designs
Discount code should always appear in the body text as well as the header bar — say "click here to activate your discount" in both places
If a standing discount already exists on the website, make sure email framing stacks the offers clearly — "you already have 30% off, here's an extra 10% = 40% total"
Mystery discount at checkout works well for abandonment — test showing vs not showing for welcome
---
Closing (~58:00)
Max jumped to his next call. Reminded the community that Skool DMs are open for follow-up questions, flow reviews, and anything else — "you guys pay for access to me, so use me."

lessons.title: [July 16th] Live Email Design Reviews + Q&A
lessons.description:
Call Summary — July Template Pack, Design Tips & Live Email Reviews


---
Opening & Community Wins (0:00–5:00)
Max opened with community wins — highlights included a nine-figure brand pitching a higher price than planned and landing it, gamification pop-up hitting 7% opt-in rate, and a member scheduling two weeks of campaigns ahead after being inactive for two months.
Max's own win: a nine-figure brand Well Copy works with referred three other fast-growing brands off the back of loving the work. All the strategies being used for those brands are shared in this community.

---
July Template Pack & Quick Wins (5:00–15:00)
Max dropped the July monthly template pack — 15 new Figma creative templates available in the classroom under new monthly templates. A walkthrough video is being recorded and uploaded the following day.
Templates included:
Viral video with comments feature (highlight a video that went viral and screenshot the comments)
iMessage-style text layout with exact iMessage fonts
"Other people vs you" phone call meme format
Phone notification style for back-in-stock or new product drops
Instagram frame product highlight
Instagram and Facebook comment-style testimonials
Myths vs facts email layout
Us versus them — clean clipboard aesthetic
Airdrop and search bar graphic
Simple review email
Sale layout highlighting a percentage off deal
Additional Instagram feature and testimonial optionsQuick wins shared from recent insights posts:
"Click below to activate your discount" on any discount email — put the discount code at the end of the URL so it auto-applies at checkout. Adds a meaningful lift to click rates on welcome and abandonment emails.
Gamified CTAs that drive clicks: "click for good luck," "click to reveal," "magic button" (link to anywhere on the site — people click out of curiosity), "click for early access."
Free always outperforms percent off. If you're running a 25–33% off discount, reframe it as a buy-to-get-one-free bundle instead. Visualising what someone gets for free converts far better than a percentage.
Free gift tiers. A section on the website where spending $100+ unlocks a selection of free gifts to choose from, and spending $175+ unlocks a higher tier — particularly strong for Black Friday/Cyber Monday.
Use characters in your emails. Named senders from the team (Alex from the warehouse team, Austin from the product team, someone from customer success) consistently outperform generic brand sends. The dog accessories brand example: an email sent from the owner's dog — "my dad and I are working as fast as our paws and hands can allow" — performs extremely well.
Use more female senders. Statistically, emails sent from or featuring females get higher open rates and engagement. If you can use a female character or sender identity, do it.
---
Live Email Review — Clothing Brand Welcome Flow (15:00–25:00)
Max reviewed a welcome flow built by his own team for a clothing brand, showing exactly the feedback he would give internally.
Email 1 — Welcome email:
Structure is correct: discount code prominently at the top, founder bridge section, product discovery below. This is the template everyone should be following.
Add "click to activate your discount" CTA so the link auto-applies the code at checkout
Make the discount code look custom and random (e.g. HGB68HG) rather than something generic like WELCOME10. Generic codes signal the offer is always available — random-looking codes make urgency feel more believable
Remind of the discount again mid-email — don't make people scroll back up to find it
Swap static product sections for Klaviyo dynamic product blocks. A live A/B test on this brand showed 26 placed orders vs 9 for the same email using dynamic blocks vs a manually designed product section. Klaviyo dynamic blocks pull bestsellers from the past 72 hours and any products the specific customer has viewed recently — particularly powerful for high-SKU fashion brands where styles go in and out quickly
Add "shop all" button at the bottom as a fallback for anyone who didn't find what they were looking for in the product sectionEmail 2:
"Move with confidence" headline doesn't add much — a more specific value proposition or bridge section point would serve better
Remind of discount early in this email tooEmail 3 (urgency email):
Use "access to your discount code" framing rather than "don't forget your welcome code" — the former creates more urgency
Discount code should look random/custom so expiry messaging lands with convictionFinal text-based founder email:
Change "code still active but expires tonight" to "I extended your welcome discount" — feels personal and generous rather than transactional
Always add a PS section linking to a bestseller. Scientifically proven that PS sections get read more than the body of the email. This is free revenue on every text-based email.
Add a magic button (curiosity CTA linking to something on site)
Add two additional emails at the end of the welcome flow with a raised offer. 80–90% of purchases happen within the first week of someone opting in — if someone hasn't bought after five days, it becomes very hard to convert them without sweetening the deal
---
Email File Size & Technical Q&A (25:00–30:00)
Email size vs image file size — two separate things:
Email size (KB): visible in Klaviyo's preview section. Keep under 85KB where possible. Going over occasionally won't dramatically impact results but risks email clipping — where some images or sections get cut off in the recipient's inbox.
Image file size (KB/MB): affects load speed in the inbox, not deliverability. Aim for images under 500KB each. Over that, images will visibly load slowly which hurts user experience.
GIFs: fine to use as long as they're under 2MB per file.Slicing emails into smaller sections (rather than one large image) keeps individual image file sizes lower and prevents awkward loading moments where the top loads but the bottom takes a second to appear.
On compressing images: Klaviyo offers compression on upload. For brands where compression visibly distorts colours, use an image compressor tool with a sliding scale (look up "image compressor" — most have adjustable quality settings). You don't have to compress — it's purely a load speed consideration.
On uploading images vs HTML/CSS emails: Well Copy uploads designed emails as sliced images. Buttons included in the images are fine. This approach has been tested across 100+ brands including nine-figure clients — it works.

---
Live Email Review — Holo Socks (30:00–36:00)
Design quality is strong and clean. Specific feedback:
Visualise the offer. "Buy 2 get 2 free" is a great offer but showing it converts far better than stating it. Add a section showing two pairs being bought and two pairs coming for free — let people see exactly what they're getting. Max referenced a current A/B test where the version showing the free gift has significantly higher pop-up conversion than the version that just states the offer.
Move the main CTA button higher — it should be visible without scrolling, ideally right after the offer is revealed
Add urgency copy near the button ("expiring soon")
Use Klaviyo dynamic product blocks at the bottom. Holo Socks has a wide range of customer personas — tradesmen, marathon runners, snow sports, everyday wear — making it very difficult to manually select products that will resonate with each individual. Dynamic blocks solve this by showing products the specific customer has viewed or that Klaviyo predicts they'll like.
Add "shop now" buttons to every product in the feed — statistically increases click rate on every email
---
Live Email Review — Additional Emails (36:00–45:00)
Minimalist aesthetic brand:
Increase text size significantly. Minimum 20pt, ideally 24pt for body copy — 13pt is unreadable on mobile.
Use lowercase text in body copy — all-caps is harder to read.
CTA needs to be more direct — "book now" or "shop now" rather than an abstract or unclear action.
Use Klaviyo dynamic blocks for product sections.Faithful Grace (daily Christian devotionals, $40 AOV):
Test a buy-to-get-one-free bundle offer rather than a flat 15% off — for a product this emotionally driven, a free bundle feels far more compelling than a percentage discount.
Add a discount code bar at the very top of every welcome email — a slim banner above the header reminding subscribers their code is active.
Swap generic short testimonials for long-form ones. Long testimonials with specific detail and emotion convert significantly better than short placeholder quotes. Facebook comments, TikTok comments, and DM screenshots also work extremely well as testimonial formats.
Add a store credit email at the end of the welcome flow ("you have $7.14 of store credit waiting — use code [X]"). Text-based, personal-feeling, sent 2–3 weeks after opt-in.
Add a PS section to every text-based email and sign off with the founder's name.High-ticket diamonds made from pet ashes (~$2,500–$4,000 AOV):
Long-form education is exactly right for a product this high-ticket and emotionally charged. Don't cut it.
Add a "reply to this email" CTA on every email — and even auto-populate the subject line and recipient when they hit reply so the barrier to reach out is as low as possible. This brand especially needs a direct line to the founder for people with questions.
Add a CTA above the logo: "feel free to reply with any questions — I personally respond within 48 hours."
Mix in plain text emails that look like they're coming directly from the founder — no branding, just an honest personal message. For a product like this, trust is everything.
Add a "book a call with the owner" CTA inside the reactivation and welcome flows — for a $4K average order, many people will want to speak to a human before buying.
Explain what the welcome kit is — it's being referenced without making clear what it actually contains.Skincare brand with free gift tier and new spa line launch:
Spend $65, get a free gift — this is the right idea. Make the hero section with this offer the first thing people see, big and unmissable.
Make all buttons significantly larger — the bigger the button, the higher the click rate.
Add body copy to the spa line teaser — there's no context for what the spa line is. "Introducing our spa line" without any description gives people no reason to click.
Add small product images or circles showing what's in the spa line alongside the teaser headline.
For the product drop teaser: consider blurring the products so people have to click through to a landing page to see them — creates curiosity and drives traffic before launch.
Split product categories clearly (shampoos, sprays, cleansers) with a "shop all" button as a clear fallback.
---
Post Purchase Strategy (45:00–48:00)
Don't exclude recent purchasers from campaigns.
Data from a nine-figure clothing brand shows that the highest repeat purchase rate happens within the first 30 days of someone's first order — they're in the honeymoon phase and more likely to buy again than at any other point. Excluding them from sale campaigns means missing out on your warmest audience.
Post purchase email structure for fashion and multi-SKU brands:
Email 1 (immediate): personal thank you from the founder. PS section with an upsell — PS upsells get read and convert. People read PS sections more reliably than the main body.
Emails 2–4 (daily or every other day): dedicated upsells and cross-sells using Klaviyo dynamic product blocks. Don't try to manually predict cross-sells — data consistently shows most repeat buyers purchase more of the same product or a variant of it. Use dynamic blocks to show them more of what they bought.
After day 7: pull them back into standard campaigns. Exclude 7-day purchasers while the post purchase flow is running, then reintroduce them.On cross-selling: A nine-figure brand was focused on cross-selling buyers of one product to bags. Max pulled the data — the vast majority of repeat purchasers just bought more of the same product in a different style. Stop trying to predict cross-sells and show people more of what already worked.

---
Closing (~49:00)
Max jumped off to a team call. Any emails that weren't reviewed live — DM Max on Skool and he'll review them within 24 hours. All questions welcome in the community feed for broader feedback from the group.

lessons.title: [July 9th] SMS Marketing Full Playbook + Q&A
lessons.description:
Call Summary — SMS Collection, Legal Compliance, Flow Strategy, MMS Best Practices & Q&A

---
Opening & Community Wins (0:00–5:00)
Max opened with a shoutout to Ben's onboarding calls — now available for all new community members. The goal is to reduce the overwhelm of joining and point people in the right direction with a custom roadmap and weekly goals. Early feedback has been strong.
Community wins roundup included a pop-up form submit rate up 21%, biggest revenue day on July 4th, triple revenue from a pop-up A/B test, a brand's emails selling a product out of stock mid-week, and Max auditing four nine-figure subscription brands simultaneously.

---
SMS Collection — What You Need to Do First (5:00–12:00)
Collect SMS even if you're not sending it yet.
The single biggest mistake brands make is not collecting SMS because they haven't launched an SMS programme. Start gathering consent now. When Black Friday comes around and sales need a boost, having 5,000 phone numbers already collected is a meaningful lever. You can't go back and collect it retroactively.
How to frame the SMS opt-in step:
The default Klaviyo copy asking for SMS sounds like charity — "get exclusive updates via text." Nobody wants that. The framing that dramatically increases SMS opt-ins:
"Finish signing up with text to activate your discount."
This works because of commitment bias — once someone has already entered their email, they're primed to follow through. Framing the SMS step as the activation mechanism for the discount they already started claiming removes friction and increases follow-through significantly.
Don't give an extra discount for SMS.
A lot of brands offer 10% for email and 15% for SMS opt-in. This has been shown to actively harm results — people get to that step, decide they're fine with 10%, and exit. It also creates confusion in your flows when SMS is sending a different discount to email. Don't do it.
SMS pop-up for existing email subscribers:
For brands with high site traffic, run a separate SMS-only pop-up form targeting email subscribers who haven't provided a phone number yet. Set it to display to "email only subscribers" in Klaviyo or Alia, and trigger it after around 50 seconds on site. Clean, simple way to recover missing SMS consent from your existing list.

---
SMS Legal Compliance (12:00–18:00)
Quiet hours law — this is serious.
It is illegal in the US to send SMS before 8am or after 9pm in the recipient's local time. Law firms are actively running ads targeting consumers, encouraging them to check their text history for brands that sent outside these hours and claim settlements of up to $20,000 per violation.
Max shared a live example — a client requested SMS sends outside 9pm, the team complied, and they are now facing a potential $20,000 settlement from someone who received those messages months ago. Even if it was the client's request, the liability can still land on the agency.
How to stay compliant:
Flows: quiet hours are automatically enabled in Klaviyo — leave the checkbox on and don't touch it
Campaigns: always send at recipient local time, not a fixed timezone. A 7pm PST send hits East Coast recipients at 10pm, which is illegal.Gray areas:
Someone who moved states but kept their old area code is technically in a gray area — the platform uses area code to determine timezone. This is part of the current legal dispute Max referenced. As long as you've collected proper consent and are sending at recipient local time, you're in the strongest defensible position. But be careful.
Going forward: Max is updating client contracts to include clauses that shift liability to the client if they explicitly request sends outside compliant hours.

---
SMS Flow Strategy (18:00–38:00)
Core SMS flows every brand needs:
Welcome
Site abandoned
Browse abandoned
Cart abandoned
Checkout abandoned
Post purchase
Replenishment reminder
Win backMost brands only run SMS for pre-purchase flows. Post purchase, replenishment, and win back SMS are consistently overlooked and consistently generate meaningful revenue.
Abandonment flows — the one-SMS rule:
You can only legally send one SMS per abandonment instance in the US. TCPA guidelines require a single message sent within 48 hours of the abandonment event. Attentive and Postscript enforce this at the platform level. Klaviyo technically allows more but sending additional messages exposes you to legal risk.
Workaround for a second abandonment touchpoint:
Build a separate flow triggered by a segment — "abandoned cart 24+ hours ago and has not placed an order." This functions as a second abandonment message without being a second SMS within the same flow. Whether this is fully compliant is legally ambiguous — but it's what some brands do.
Flow setup — avoid this common mistake:
Don't create a conditional split where SMS subscribers only receive SMS and everyone else only receives email. If someone abandons at 9pm and their SMS is blocked by quiet hours, they get nothing at all. Instead, run SMS in parallel with email — everyone receives email, and SMS subscribers also receive the SMS with a short delay. If someone converts from email, the flow filter catches it before SMS sends.
Abandonment SMS copy — what actually works:
Stop using "did you forget something?" That framing implies the person abandoned on purpose. Use the same principle as the email subject line: make it sound like something is already in motion.
"Your order is ready to ship."
This framing drives a 50% increase in click rates and 50% improvement in overall performance compared to passive abandonment copy. The same principle that works in email works in SMS — make it feel like forward momentum, not a reminder.
Split buyers vs non-buyers in all abandonment flows.
For non-buyers: include their welcome discount in the SMS. For past buyers: a simple "welcome back, did you find what you need?" framing. This alone is one of the highest-leverage changes you can make across your abandonment setup.
Recommended welcome SMS flow:
SMS 1 (Day 1): discount code + welcome
SMS 2 (Day 2–3): brand info + discount expiring reminder
SMS 3 (Day 4–5): last chanceFor aggressive brands, send every day. Data from Well Copy's internal analytics platform shows 77% of email subscribers who convert do so on day zero — and the drop-off after that is steep. Every day you wait, the window closes further.
Store credit in SMS:
Works identically to email. Send 2–3 weeks after someone opts in but hasn't purchased. Give a specific, non-round number: "You have $13.47 in store credit." The specificity signals it's real and personal. Consistently one of the best performing messages in the welcome sequence.
Post purchase SMS — the data:
For a nine-figure brand with no post purchase SMS, 50% of all second orders placed within 90 days of the first purchase happened before day 21. The honeymoon phase is the highest-converting period — hit people while they're excited, because customer loyalty is at its lowest when a brand is new to them.
Post purchase SMS structure:
Day 2: upsell or cross-sell
Day 8: product tip plus cross-sell
Day 21: upsell or cross-sellWin back:
Fire at around day 90 after last purchase. Don't send "we miss you" — by that point the person has received months of campaigns, sale emails, and product drops and still hasn't bought. A sentimental text won't move them. Hit them with your strongest offer. No-holds-barred.
Espresso Shop flow (SMS version):
Same segment trigger as the email version — active on site 3+ times in past 30 days, zero orders in past 30 days, clicked email or SMS at least once. Fire 15 minutes after segment entry with a 2-hour offer. In Q2 this year, this flow generated $115K for one brand from SMS alone.

---
MMS — When to Use It (38:00–44:00)
MMS (multimedia send — includes an image) costs approximately 3x more than a standard SMS. Most people hear this and never send MMS. That's wrong.
The right question isn't cost — it's gross profit.
Live example from Max: an A/B test on a brand — SMS with no image generated $321 revenue, MMS with image generated $694 revenue. ROI was worse on MMS (3x cost, 2x revenue), but gross profit was $658 vs $309. The MMS was the better business decision despite the worse ROI ratio.
A second example: showing a free gift in MMS generated $2,000 vs $534 for the plain SMS version — a $1,500 revenue difference for roughly a $200 cost difference. After stripping out product cost, the MMS won easily.
When to use MMS:
Welcome flow — one infographic showing what the product does or what's inside it
New product drops — always use MMS, showing the product
Bundle or BOGO offers — helps people visualise what they're getting
Occasional branding play — a well-placed meme or lifestyle image once in a while
Educational infographic — once a month at most; SMS isn't primarily an education channelGeneral rule of thumb: around 25% of total SMS sends should be MMS. For campaigns, MMS is rare. For welcome flows, MMS makes sense for one or two messages.
Emojis: avoid them. Each emoji eats 35–50 characters from your 160-character limit. With only 160 characters per message before costs double, every character counts.

---
SMS Campaign Frequency (44:00–47:00)
Subscription brands: can send SMS every day. Your entire goal is getting someone to place that first subscription order — be aggressive. Once they subscribe, pull back.
High-frequency replenishable brands: 1–2 per day if you always have new product and content to share. Otherwise 2 per week.
Most brands: minimum 1 per week, no matter what. Even in the off-season, stopping sends entirely will kill your domain reputation and inbox placement by the time peak season returns. Keep the list warm.
Best performing campaign type: SMS exclusive offers once a month consistently outperform standard sale messages. If you don't know what to send, a bestseller highlight or restock works — "restock" is one of the highest-performing single words in SMS marketing.Resource: Attentive's SMS inspiration library is one of the best free tools for SMS copy ideas — link dropped in the Skool community.

---
Q&A (47:00–58:30)
Brands that won't offer a discount (auto parts brand, 50,000+ SKUs)
Not every brand can or will offer a percentage discount — especially those with huge catalogues and thin margins.
Reframe the offer around something the brand already gives — free shipping, a free PDF guide, a value-add rather than a straight discount
If free shipping applies above a threshold, make that the pop-up hook: "get free shipping on your order"
Gate whatever the brand already provides behind the pop-up so there's a tangible reason to opt inCustom checkout abandonment copy for made-to-order products (Kate — custom jewellery, ~$200 AOV)
"Your order is ready to ship" doesn't work when the product is made to order. The principle still applies — make it feel like something is already in motion — but the copy needs to be adapted.
Suggestions from Max:
"We've reserved your custom stone for the next 24 hours"
"Your order is ready to be customised"

content.text: Call Summary — SMS Collection, Legal Compliance, Flow Strategy, MMS Best Practices & Q&A
Opening & Community Wins (0:00–5:00)

Max opened with a shoutout to Ben's onboarding calls — now available for all new community members. The goal is to reduce the overwhelm of joining and point people in the right direction with a custom roadmap and weekly goals. Early feedback has been strong.

Community wins roundup included a pop-up form submit rate up 21%, biggest revenue day on July 4th, triple revenue from a pop-up A/B test, a brand's emails selling a product out of stock mid-week, and Max auditing four nine-figure subscription brands simultaneously.
SMS Collection — What You Need to Do First (5:00–12:00)
Collect SMS even if you're not sending it yet.

The single biggest mistake brands make is not collecting SMS because they haven't launched an SMS programme. Start gathering consent now. When Black Friday comes around and sales need a boost, having 5,000 phone numbers already collected is a meaningful lever. You can't go back and collect it retroactively.
How to frame the SMS opt-in step:
The default Klaviyo copy asking for SMS sounds like charity — "get exclusive updates via text." Nobody wants that. The framing that dramatically increases SMS opt-ins:
"Finish signing up with text to activate your discount."

This works because of commitment bias — once someone has already entered their email, they're primed to follow through. Framing the SMS step as the activation mechanism for the discount they already started claiming removes friction and increases follow-through significantly.
Don't give an extra discount for SMS.

A lot of brands offer 10% for email and 15% for SMS opt-in. This has been shown to actively harm results — people get to that step, decide they're fine with 10%, and exit. It also creates confusion in your flows when SMS is sending a different discount to email. Don't do it.
SMS pop-up for existing email subscribers:

For brands with high site traffic, run a separate SMS-only pop-up form targeting email subscribers who haven't provided a phone number yet. Set it to display to "email only subscribers" in Klaviyo or Alia, and trigger it after around 50 seconds on site. Clean, simple way to recover missing SMS consent from your existing list.
SMS Legal Compliance (12:00–18:00)
Quiet hours law — this is serious.

It is illegal in the US to send SMS before 8am or after 9pm in the recipient's local time. Law firms are actively running ads targeting consumers, encouraging them to check their text history for brands that sent outside these hours and claim settlements of up to $20,000 per violation.

Max shared a live example — a client requested SMS sends outside 9pm, the team complied, and they are now facing a potential $20,000 settlement from someone who received those messages months ago. Even if it was the client's request, the liability can still land on the agency.
How to stay compliant:
Flows: quiet hours are automatically enabled in Klaviyo — leave the checkbox on and don't touch it
Campaigns: always send at recipient local time, not a fixed timezone. A 7pm PST send hits East Coast recipients at 10pm, which is illegal.
Gray areas:

Someone who moved states but kept their old area code is technically in a gray area — the platform uses area code to determine timezone. This is part of the current legal dispute Max referenced. As long as you've collected proper consent and are sending at recipient local time, you're in the strongest defensible position. But be careful.
Going forward:
Max is updating client contracts to include clauses that shift liability to the client if they explicitly request sends outside compliant hours.
SMS Flow Strategy (18:00–38:00)
Core SMS flows every brand needs:
Welcome
Site abandoned
Browse abandoned
Cart abandoned
Checkout abandoned
Post purchase
Replenishment reminder
Win back
Most brands only run SMS for pre-purchase flows. Post purchase, replenishment, and win back SMS are consistently overlooked and consistently generate meaningful revenue.
Abandonment flows — the one-SMS rule:

You can only legally send one SMS per abandonment instance in the US. TCPA guidelines require a single message sent within 48 hours of the abandonment event. Attentive and Postscript enforce this at the platform level. Klaviyo technically allows more but sending additional messages exposes you to legal risk.
Workaround for a second abandonment touchpoint:

Build a separate flow triggered by a segment — "abandoned cart 24+ hours ago and has not placed an order." This functions as a second abandonment message without being a second SMS within the same flow. Whether this is fully compliant is legally ambiguous — but it's what some brands do.
Flow setup — avoid this common mistake:

Don't create a conditional split where SMS subscribers only receive SMS and everyone else only receives email. If someone abandons at 9pm and their SMS is blocked by quiet hours, they get nothing at all. Instead, run SMS in parallel with email — everyone receives email, and SMS subscribers also receive the SMS with a short delay. If someone converts from email, the flow filter catches it before SMS sends.
Abandonment SMS copy — what actually works:
Stop using "did you forget something?" That framing implies the person abandoned on purpose. Use the same principle as the email subject line: make it sound like something is already in motion.
"Your order is ready to ship."

This framing drives a 50% increase in click rates and 50% improvement in overall performance compared to passive abandonment copy. The same principle that works in email works in SMS — make it feel like forward momentum, not a reminder.
Split buyers vs non-buyers in all abandonment flows.

For non-buyers: include their welcome discount in the SMS. For past buyers: a simple "welcome back, did you find what you need?" framing. This alone is one of the highest-leverage changes you can make across your abandonment setup.
Recommended welcome SMS flow:
SMS 1 (Day 1): discount code + welcome
SMS 2 (Day 2–3): brand info + discount expiring reminder
SMS 3 (Day 4–5): last chance

For aggressive brands, send every day. Data from Well Copy's internal analytics platform shows 77% of email subscribers who convert do so on day zero — and the drop-off after that is steep. Every day you wait, the window closes further.
Store credit in SMS:

Works identically to email. Send 2–3 weeks after someone opts in but hasn't purchased. Give a specific, non-round number: "You have $13.47 in store credit." The specificity signals it's real and personal. Consistently one of the best performing messages in the welcome sequence.
Post purchase SMS — the data:

For a nine-figure brand with no post purchase SMS, 50% of all second orders placed within 90 days of the first purchase happened before day 21. The honeymoon phase is the highest-converting period — hit people while they're excited, because customer loyalty is at its lowest when a brand is new to them.
Post purchase SMS structure:
Day 2: upsell or cross-sell
Day 8: product tip plus cross-sell
Day 21: upsell or cross-sell
Win back:

Fire at around day 90 after last purchase. Don't send "we miss you" — by that point the person has received months of campaigns, sale emails, and product drops and still hasn't bought. A sentimental text won't move them. Hit them with your strongest offer. No-holds-barred.
Espresso Shop flow (SMS version):

Same segment trigger as the email version — active on site 3+ times in past 30 days, zero orders in past 30 days, clicked email or SMS at least once. Fire 15 minutes after segment entry with a 2-hour offer. In Q2 this year, this flow generated $115K for one brand from SMS alone.
MMS — When to Use It (38:00–44:00)
MMS (multimedia send — includes an image) costs approximately 3x more than a standard SMS. Most people hear this and never send MMS. That's wrong.
The right question isn't cost — it's gross profit.

Live example from Max: an A/B test on a brand — SMS with no image generated $321 revenue, MMS with image generated $694 revenue. ROI was worse on MMS (3x cost, 2x revenue), but gross profit was $658 vs $309. The MMS was the better business decision despite the worse ROI ratio.

A second example: showing a free gift in MMS generated $2,000 vs $534 for the plain SMS version — a $1,500 revenue difference for roughly a $200 cost difference. After stripping out product cost, the MMS won easily.
When to use MMS:
Welcome flow — one infographic showing what the product does or what's inside it
New product drops — always use MMS, showing the product
Bundle or BOGO offers — helps people visualise what they're getting
Occasional branding play — a well-placed meme or lifestyle image once in a while
Educational infographic — once a month at most; SMS isn't primarily an education channel
General rule of thumb:
around 25% of total SMS sends should be MMS. For campaigns, MMS is rare. For welcome flows, MMS makes sense for one or two messages.
Emojis:
avoid them. Each emoji eats 35–50 characters from your 160-character limit. With only 160 characters per message before costs double, every character counts.
SMS Campaign Frequency (44:00–47:00)
Subscription brands:
can send SMS every day. Your entire goal is getting someone to place that first subscription order — be aggressive. Once they subscribe, pull back.
High-frequency replenishable brands:
1–2 per day if you always have new product and content to share. Otherwise 2 per week.

minimum 1 per week, no matter what. Even in the off-season, stopping sends entirely will kill your domain reputation and inbox placement by the time peak season returns. Keep the list warm.

SMS exclusive offers once a month consistently outperform standard sale messages. If you don't know what to send, a bestseller highlight or restock works — "restock" is one of the highest-performing single words in SMS marketing.

Attentive's SMS inspiration library is one of the best free tools for SMS copy ideas — link dropped in the Skool community.
Brands that won't offer a discount (auto parts brand, 50,000+ SKUs)
Not every brand can or will offer a percentage discount — especially those with huge catalogues and thin margins.
Reframe the offer around something the brand already gives — free shipping, a free PDF guide, a value-add rather than a straight discount
If free shipping applies above a threshold, make that the pop-up hook: "get free shipping on your order"
Gate whatever the brand already provides behind the pop-up so there's a tangible reason to opt in

"Your order is ready to ship" doesn't work when the product is made to order. The principle still applies — make it feel like something is already in motion — but the copy needs to be adapted.
