lessons.title: [July 2nd] Live Campaign Calendar Build + Q&A
lessons.description:
Call Summary — Live Campaign Calendar Build, Claude Skill Walkthrough & Q&A

---
Context & Brand Overview (0:00–4:00)
Max opened with a live walkthrough using Chronic Australia (hemp and magnesium pain cream, Australia-based) as the example brand — the same brand from the previous week's flow audit. This session focused entirely on campaign calendar strategy, which wasn't covered last time.
Quick context on the brand:
Drives all acquisition traffic towards a hero bundle at 15% off
Email consistently bringing in ~30% of total revenue
Subscription was just added to the brand — noted by Max but set aside for this session as it was only just implemented
---
Campaign Calendar Build Process (4:00–30:00)
Max walked through the exact campaign calendar process used internally at Well Copy. The hierarchy of inputs, in order:
Step 1. Past Winners
Pull up campaigns filtered by placed order rate or revenue, and identify the top non-sale performers to repurpose or riff on.
Skip sales emails when looking for past winners — focus on educational, brand, and community content
If you have Hyros or a similar analytics platform, filter specifically by first-time buyer revenue to find what's converting new customers
You can go back as far as a year — don't limit to recent sends
For this brand, two past winners identified: a "5 Questions, 5 Answers" FAQ-style email and "The Chronicles" founder newsletter series
Don't worry about repeating a format too soon — repurposing proven concepts with fresh content is one of the most reliable ways to generate campaign revenueStep 2. Winning Ad & LP Angles
Identify what's currently working in paid acquisition and bring those angles into email.
Best source: ask the founder or ads team directly what angles are converting on Meta
If no direct access: go to the Meta Ads Library, look up the brand, and scan for ads that have been running a long time (longevity = it's working) or that appear in multiple variations (repetition = it's working)
For Chronic Australia: two angles pulled from the ads library — founder story and "most magnesium creams stop at magnesium" (the product's unique multi-ingredient angle)Step 3. Competitor Swipes & Inspo
Pull inspiration from competitor emails (Milled is a strong resource), the Skool community, Max's Instagram posts, and an internal best-performing emails bank.
Look for new concepts that haven't been tested on this account yet
For this brand: long-form testimonial and a myths vs. facts style email ("turn the page on magnesium myths") pulled from a competitor account
How-to content also identified as a strong fit for a product like this ("how to use the product properly")On long-form testimonials:
Works across virtually every niche — not just consumables. For fashion brands specifically, the angle shifts to emotional outcomes rather than functional results. Best performing fashion testimonials tend to focus on confidence, compliments received, and how the product made someone feel in a social moment. Always prioritise long, detailed testimonials over short ones — length signals authenticity and drives conversions.
Step 4. AI Ideation — Claude Skill + MX Tool
Once past winners, ad angles, and competitor swipes are locked in, use AI to fill the remaining calendar gaps.
Claude Skill setup:
In Claude, go to Projects → create a new project per brand
Type /MX to activate the skill, then say "onboard [brand name]" and paste the website URL
Claude scrapes the site, builds a brand profile (voice, products, key messaging, memory index), and asks for email examples to refine the brand voice document
Once onboarded, you can say "plan July 2026 campaign calendar" and it will pull the campaign calendar protocol, brand knowledge, and best practices to generate a full month of campaign ideas
Feed it all the manually planned emails first ("include these campaigns") and it will slot them in and fill remaining dates around themMX Tool (internal Well Copy platform — community access being explored):
Max showed a preview of an internal AI-powered campaign writing tool the Well Copy team uses
Brands are organised by client, with past flows and campaigns all stored and searchable
You can brief a new campaign in a few words ("summer sale, 10% off, focus on cabin season"), generate the full copy, then refine inline — ask for headline alternatives, change an element to an infographic, adjust CTA copy, all in real time
Output goes straight to the designer as a brief
Also includes flow map generation, calendar planning, and copywriting — trained on Well Copy's frameworks and best practices
Max is working on making this accessible to community members as a bonus to staying in the community — not confirmed yet but actively in progressLive calendar output for Chronic Australia (July 2026):
Every-other-day send cadence, 3–4 emails per week. Key placements included:
Winter warm-up seasonal email (Australia is in winter — the tool caught this automatically)
Founder story email
3 Questions, 3 Answers FAQ
"Most magnesium creams stop at magnesium" — us vs. them angle on the multi-ingredient formula
What's inside educational breakdown
Founder newsletter (Chronicles)
"Straight to the source — rub it in" — topical vs. other intake methods angle
Long-form testimonial
Sale sequence in late July: designed launch email → value pack bundle → urgency email → whole-list final send
---
Q&A (30:00–51:00)
Sale campaign segmentation — who to send to
Don't just send sale campaigns to your engaged list. For a multi-email sale sequence, Max's segmentation approach:
Launch email: blast to the whole list — everyone, including cold subscribers
Middle emails: 90-day engaged + anyone active on site at least once in the past 90 days
Final urgency email: blast to the whole list againSome cold subscribers who receive the launch email will re-engage, pulling them back into the 90-day engaged window for future sends. Most people in the space have over-corrected towards only sending to engaged lists — for sale moments specifically, wider sends are the right call.
Inbox optimisation tools — Mailmen & Maverick
Certain tools add snippets to your emails that improve inbox placement (moving emails from Promotions to the main Gmail inbox).
Maverick is Max's preferred tool — better payment terms, free trial available, and in his experience it outperforms alternatives. Mention Max's name when signing up for access.
Confirmed as a meaningful lever for deliverability — Max described it as something he typically gate-keepsSubscription flows — what you actually need (Jacob)
Max outlined the core subscription email infrastructure, in order of customer journey:
Confirmation email — transactional, sent from Shopify. If on Shopify Plus, move this into Klaviyo for more control.
Post-purchase onboarding — 4–6 emails covering the first two weeks. Go hard on education: how to use the product, what results to expect, habit formation. This is the number one driver of long-term retention — customers churn when they don't know how to use the product or when to expect results.
Billing reminder — fires around day 27, before the next charge. Ideally customised by order number (first rebill message is different from third, fifth, etc.). One of the highest-leverage emails in the entire subscription setup.
Custom campaigns — 1–2 per month for active subscribers. Nothing more than this is needed for people actively receiving the product.
Immediate cancel flow — triggered on cancellation, customised by cancel reason. One email to attempt recovery.
Cancel win-back — 60 days after cancellation, special offer, 2–3 emails.
Transactional notifications — order skipped confirmation, order paused, order delayed, order unpaused. Keep these simple and functional.Upcoming resource: Max has a YouTube video dropping Tuesday specifically on subscription flows, plus a community-exclusive document for members only.
14-day check-in flow (Luca)
Luca shared a flow where subscribers receive a check-in 14 days after their first order — clicking "I'm loving it" or "I need more time." Anyone who clicks "I need more time" enters a secondary flow that re-educates, sets expectations, and pushes them to commit to at least 4 weeks before judging the product.
Max's reaction: strong concept — gets people to actively recommit rather than passively churn
Engagement signals in Klaviyo are strong so far, retention impact still being measured (~60 days to see cohort data)
Max flagged the Thomas Lawless podcast on retention marketing as must-watch for any subscription-focused operatorA/B testing frequency
Well Copy runs a minimum of 6–8 A/B tests per month across campaigns
Most campaigns get a test — some account managers prefer to run the same variable across every campaign for a week before moving to the next test (e.g. dynamic sections vs. no dynamic sections), others test different things each time
Flows: set up and optimise tests during quarterly roadmap reviews rather than on an ad hoc basisFlow revamp process
Well Copy runs quarterly roadmaps with brands — at the end of each quarter, review all flow performance, identify low performers and high-priority optimisations, and set a 3-month roadmap covering campaign events and flow updates.
Not a rigid "full overhaul every quarter" process — it's fluid, driven by performance signals and account changes (new products, seasonal shifts, campaign learnings to implement into flows)
Senior strategists review on feel and expertise — "this seems low, let's revise this" — and then prioritise by impactCampaign frequency for seasonal products (Brooke — Mosquito Beads)
Send a minimum of once per week through the off-season, no matter what. If you stop sending entirely during quiet periods, domain reputation decays, and you'll land in spam when the season picks back up and you actually need to send.
For mosquito repellent specifically: Max's view is there are always regions and climates where mosquitoes are present year-round, so the off-season argument is weaker than it might seem
Recommendation: still send twice a week even in quieter periodsWelcome offer alternatives for premium fashion brands
Brand owner not keen on mystery discount — feels off-brand. Testing dollar-amount-off as an alternative.
Dollar-off on higher AOV products is generally stronger than percentage off — Max agreed and confirmed this as the right direction
Also worth testing: free gift with purchase (e.g. free accessory, free socks — whatever fits the brand). Free gift offers can outperform discounts for premium brands because they don't undermine perceived value
If no free gift is viable: high-AOV bundle play (buy X get one free) can work as an alternative incentive
Max offered to strategise a specific offer if the brand's website link is sent via Skool DMFlow performance benchmarks
Max doesn't use internal benchmarks for flow conversion rates — every brand is too different for that to be meaningful.
Assessment is based purely on experience and feel ("this feels low") built from auditing a large number of accounts
The only way to confirm whether something is underperforming is to A/B test
One exception: open rates do have reliable macro benchmarks:
Welcome email 1: 50%+ opens minimum
Abandoned cart email 1: 50%+ opens minimum
If below these thresholds, deliverability is the problem, not the content
---
Closing (~51:00)
Max wrapped up and jumped off. Reminded the community to post questions in the Skool feed rather than DMs where possible — Matthias, Tristan, Avon, and other experienced members are active and responsive. Signed off with a 4th of July shoutout.

Upcoming resource: Max has a YouTube video dropping Tuesday specifically on subscription flows, plus a community-exclusive document for members only.
14-day check-in flow (Luca)

Luca shared a flow where subscribers receive a check-in 14 days after their first order — clicking "I'm loving it" or "I need more time." Anyone who clicks "I need more time" enters a secondary flow that re-educates, sets expectations, and pushes them to commit to at least 4 weeks before judging the product.
Max's reaction: strong concept — gets people to actively recommit rather than passively churn
Engagement signals in Klaviyo are strong so far, retention impact still being measured (~60 days to see cohort data)
Max flagged the Thomas Lawless podcast on retention marketing as must-watch for any subscription-focused operator
A/B testing frequency
Well Copy runs a minimum of 6–8 A/B tests per month across campaigns

Most campaigns get a test — some account managers prefer to run the same variable across every campaign for a week before moving to the next test (e.g. dynamic sections vs. no dynamic sections), others test different things each time
Flows: set up and optimise tests during quarterly roadmap reviews rather than on an ad hoc basis
Flow revamp process

Well Copy runs quarterly roadmaps with brands — at the end of each quarter, review all flow performance, identify low performers and high-priority optimisations, and set a 3-month roadmap covering campaign events and flow updates.
Not a rigid "full overhaul every quarter" process — it's fluid, driven by performance signals and account changes (new products, seasonal shifts, campaign learnings to implement into flows)
Senior strategists review on feel and expertise — "this seems low, let's revise this" — and then prioritise by impact
Campaign frequency for seasonal products (Brooke — Mosquito Beads)

Send a minimum of once per week through the off-season, no matter what. If you stop sending entirely during quiet periods, domain reputation decays, and you'll land in spam when the season picks back up and you actually need to send.
For mosquito repellent specifically: Max's view is there are always regions and climates where mosquitoes are present year-round, so the off-season argument is weaker than it might seem
Recommendation: still send twice a week even in quieter periods
Welcome offer alternatives for premium fashion brands
Brand owner not keen on mystery discount — feels off-brand. Testing dollar-amount-off as an alternative.
Dollar-off on higher AOV products is generally stronger than percentage off — Max agreed and confirmed this as the right direction

Also worth testing: free gift with purchase (e.g. free accessory, free socks — whatever fits the brand). Free gift offers can outperform discounts for premium brands because they don't undermine perceived value
If no free gift is viable: high-AOV bundle play (buy X get one free) can work as an alternative incentive
Max offered to strategise a specific offer if the brand's website link is sent via Skool DM
Flow performance benchmarks
Max doesn't use internal benchmarks for flow conversion rates — every brand is too different for that to be meaningful.
Assessment is based purely on experience and feel ("this feels low") built from auditing a large number of accounts
The only way to confirm whether something is underperforming is to A/B test
One exception:
open rates do have reliable macro benchmarks:
Welcome email 1: 50%+ opens minimum
Abandoned cart email 1: 50%+ opens minimum
If below these thresholds, deliverability is the problem, not the content
Closing (~51:00)

Max wrapped up and jumped off. Reminded the community to post questions in the Skool feed rather than DMs where possible — Matthias, Tristan, Avon, and other experienced members are active and responsive. Signed off with a 4th of July shoutout.

lessons.description:
Call Summary — Community Wins, Analytics Tool Launch, Zemo Demo & Live Klaviyo Audit

---
Community Wins Roundup (0:00–10:00)
Max opened by collecting wins from the community. Highlights from the chat:
Chelsea. Deployed a long-form testimonial from a customer who'd been buying since 2020 — performed well across the board. Max noted it should be repurposed into the welcome flow and post purchase flow.
Matthias. Started posting on Instagram. Max dropped a follow live on the call and encouraged the community to do the same.
Jonathan. Unused promo credit email performed strongly — Max reinforced this as one of the best performing email types and encouraged everyone to use it across accounts.
4th of July sale (community member). Already pulled $15K in the first send of the campaign — easy win.
Curtis. Store credit emails working well.
Community member. Klaviyo opt-in rate jumped from 5% to 29% — significant uplift.
Tristan. A business reel hit 29K views, generating a wave of inbound leads. Max's advice: find what works and post the same format at least once a week. Don't overcomplicate it — find a winner and repeat it.Max's content habit: Every single morning, posting content is the first item on his to-do list before checking any devices. His advice — whatever the most important thing for your business is, make it the first task of the day, no exceptions.

---
Well Copy Analytics Tool Launch & Zemo Demo (10:00–22:00)
Well Copy Internal Analytics Tool
Max shared a live demo of an internal retention analytics tool the Well Copy team has built out with their dev and data engineering team.
Key features:
Retention metrics, cohort analysis, repeat purchase breakdowns, and time between orders — all in one view
Ability to split data by subscription vs non-subscription (organic only)
Campaign and flow level audience split — showing how many first-time buyers vs returning buyers each send is driving, something Klaviyo doesn't natively provide
Campaigns can be sorted by first-time buyer revenue vs returning buyer revenue — helping identify which campaigns work best in welcome flows or for acquisition
AI chat feature. Ask questions like "what products drive the most repeat purchases?" or "how does average time to second order differ across our top products?" — returns graph-based answers in 20–30 secondsThe tool is kept internal and is not for sale — it's used as an aura play during the sales process and shared with clients for their own reporting access.
Alternative for the community: Flaunt offers a very similar AI chat experience connected to Shopify, Klaviyo, and subscription data. Max recommends it — mention his name for a bonus.
How to view first-time vs returning buyers in Hiro:
Go to Campaign Deep Dive
Toggle on "show first time vs returning" — instantly shows returning vs first purchase revenue per campaign
Filter by first purchase revenue to identify your best acquisition campaignsZemo
Zemo is an interactive in-email editing and order management tool — particularly powerful for subscription brands.
Key features:
Customers can edit subscriptions, delay billing, or trigger orders directly within an email — no need to visit the portal
In-email reviews — customers leave a review without leaving the email
One-click upsells directly in email
Billing reminder emails where subscribers can click "send now" or "delay" in one tapMax recommends Zemo for every subscription brand, specifically for billing reminder flows and upsell campaigns.

---
Ben's Introduction (22:00–24:00)
Max introduced Ben as the new community manager for the Email Marketerz Skool group. As the community continues to grow, Max wanted to make sure members are getting the time and attention they deserve.
Ben's role:
Available in the community to answer questions and respond to DMs
Conducting onboarding calls for new members
Helping members build personalised roadmaps — identifying the best course content to start with based on where each person is in their agency journey
General support for anyone who needs direction or just wants to chat through their situation
---
Live Klaviyo Audit: Context & Benchmarking (24:00–32:00)
Brand: Chronic Australia — a CBD and magnesium cream brand for chronic pain, running ads primarily to their hero product. Purely ad-driven acquisition. Brand has been scaling since around January this year.
Max's audit framework — four pillars:
Acquisition (pop-up form and list growth)
Flows
Campaigns
DeliverabilityInitial context check:
Email attributed revenue sitting at 30% of total store revenue (~$295K past 30 days) — consistent but has room to grow
No SMS set up — a quick win that could push attributed revenue towards 40%
Business review dashboard (Klaviyo): use this view to see total store revenue vs attributed email revenue over 12 months — gives a true picture of how email is tracking against overall business growth
Outlier months worth investigating — if email attribution spikes or drops sharply, go to campaigns for that period and identify what drove it (big sale, product launch, ads turned off, etc.)
Flow/campaign revenue split: 65% flows, 35% campaigns — this range is fine. A heavily flow-weighted split (80/20) typically signals a low repeat purchase rate brand or high AOV brand. For a replenishable brand like this, campaign revenue should ideally be higher — inconsistency in campaign frequency is the likely cause here.
Returning customer benchmark: for a replenishable brand, aim for 40%+. For non-replenishable (planners, one-time purchases), 20–30% is more realistic. It's always brand-dependent.
---
Live Klaviyo Audit: List Growth & Pop-Up Form (32:00–40:00)
List Growth
To view this in Klaviyo: go to Overview Dashboard → Add Card → List Growth view. Shows new subscribers vs exclusions over time.
This brand: 8,100 new subscribers vs 1,200 exclusions — roughly 8:1 ratio
Max's benchmark: aim for at least 2–3x new subscribers vs exclusions at minimum for a scaling brand
At 8:1 with a solid pop-up form already in place, the signal is: send more emails. If the list growth ratio were only 2:1, the first priority would be fixing the pop-up form before increasing frequency. Since the form is already strong, the lever is volume.Pop-Up Form Audit
The brand was running a mystery discount form — 7.5% submit rate. Max had already duplicated a new form template into their account.
Issues with the original form:
Included an image — images can slow load time and typically reduce conversion. Removing it usually improves results.
No X button on the first page — no way for users to close it. The new form added an "I don't want a discount" option for accessibility.
Five quiz options stacked horizontally — too many. Max prefers 3–4 options, stacked vertically for clarity.
Triggering after 8 seconds — too long. Should fire at 2–6 seconds.
Not collecting SMS — significant missed opportunity. Always ask for SMS alongside email.
Discount revealed inside the form itself — removes the incentive to open the welcome email. If deliverability is a concern, gate the code inside the welcome email to drive opens and clicks.Projected improvement: Max estimated a 25–50% increase in list growth from these fixes alone — moving from 7.5% to 10–12% submit rate.
Alia recommended as the best pop-up form platform — Max said he'll likely move this brand to Alia for better form performance and testing capability.

---
Live Klaviyo Audit: Flows (40:00–50:00)
Core flows check — Welcome ✓, Site Abandoned ✓, Browse Abandoned ✓, Cart Abandoned ✓, Checkout Abandoned ✓, Post Purchase ✓. No win back flow identified — flagged as a gap.
Welcome Flow
Offer: mystery discount to $10 off. Given the brand also runs 15% on their three-pack, the effective total discount is closer to 20%. Recommendation: consolidate and lead with "$20 off the three-pack" — cleaner, more compelling, higher AOV push.
Offer to test: buy one get one free. The margins are already close to supporting it — well worth pitching to the brand.
Discount not revealed until checkout — this forces people into the purchase funnel. Worth A/B testing showing vs not showing the offer upfront.
Open rates at 44% — a bit low. Likely landing in promotions or spam. Healthy deliverability benchmark is 55%+.
Every email does remind of the discount — correct. But the actual code and how to claim it should be explicitly stated in each email.
No store credit email in the sequence — add one. "You have $14.17 in store credit waiting" is one of the best performing email formats across accounts.
Recommendation: split welcome flow based on quiz responses from the pop-up form. Personalising the first 1–2 emails to the specific pain point the subscriber selected typically lifts conversions 15–25%.
Scratch-to-reveal vs quiz pop-up: scratch-to-reveal converts at 16–17%, quiz-style at 10–11%. Higher volume wins more than better data. For getting more opt-ins, keep the scratch-to-reveal. If you want segmentation data, add a follow-up question after the SMS opt-in step rather than replacing the form.Abandonment Flows
Across all abandonment flows, the single biggest lever is splitting by buyers vs non-buyers. Non-buyers abandoned checkout within seven days of signing up 75% of the time — they still have their welcome discount. Surface it front and centre.
Checkout abandoned: subject line "your order is almost ready to ship" — best performing subject line for this flow. Split by buyers and non-buyers. Add a text-based email. Remove cross-selling from checkout abandoned — the person already made their decision, showing other products is wasted space. Save cross-selling for browse abandoned where the person hasn't committed to a product yet.
Cart abandoned: currently firing after 2 hours — change to 30 minutes. 1% place order rate is low. Add text-based email. Test mystery discount vs a stated dollar-off offer at the end of the flow.
Browse abandoned: 45-minute trigger is fine. Only 2 emails — extend to 4 and add a discount later in the sequence.
Site abandoned: brand had built this flow right after a prior audit with Max. Already split by buyers and non-buyers, giving the welcome offer. Performing well — strong example of what this split looks like when done right.Deliverability in flows: flows themselves rarely cause deliverability issues — they're high-engagement by nature. If open rates are low on flows, the problem is almost always campaign deliverability. Fix campaign segmentation and engagement first, and flow metrics will improve accordingly.
Post Purchase Flow
The brand runs a trial pack with a quiz — the post purchase flow for this upsells to the full product using a founder VSL email (video sales letter). 2.9% place order rate on this — excellent. Generating ~$1.49K in additional revenue per send.
The brand delays fulfilment by one day so any upsell purchases from the VSL email get added to the same order — a clever operational trick worth noting.
Missing: onboarding education. The number one reason customers churn is not knowing how to use the product or what results to expect. Add 3–4 educational emails covering product usage and what to expect in the first 30 days.
Missing: replenishment reminder flow. For single product buyers, fire this at around day 27 (just before the 30-day supply runs out). For three-pack buyers, extend to around day 75. 2–3 emails, with offer testing — this is where buy one get one free would work well as a win-back offer.
Win back: send 3 months after last purchase for non-repurchasers.
Overall flow conversion upside: Max estimated 25–50% improvement in conversion rates is achievable with these changes.
---
Live Klaviyo Audit: Campaigns & Deliverability (50:00–57:00)
Deliverability
Open rates slightly low — likely hitting promotions and spam for some subscribers
Spam rate at 0.02% — slightly elevated but not critical
Fix: add a reply-back email in the welcome sequence (around email 3) — prompts subscribers to reply, which signals to inbox providers that the sender is legitimate and boosts deliverability across the board
Unsubscribes are elevated but not a deliverability concern — people who don't want emails should unsubscribe. It doesn't hurt sender reputation.Campaigns
Current send cadence: roughly every 5 days — not enough. Move to every other day to a 60-day engaged segment.
Current segment window is 90 days — tighten to 60 days to protect open rates and maintain 55–60% open benchmarks.
Campaign revenue has been inconsistent month to month — this is almost entirely a frequency issue. Being consistent at every-other-day sends will smooth this out and add meaningful revenue on its own.
Creatives are packed and could be significantly cleaned up — but creative quality isn't the bottleneck. List size is. The brand has only recently started scaling, so campaign revenue is naturally capped by audience size. The priority is growing the list and maintaining frequency.
10–20% of campaign sends should be plays on proven winners — not exact repeats, but same format and angle with refreshed creative.
Open send recommended for recovering people who abandon cart or checkout without opting into the email list — captures emails even without a form submission. Max's preferred tool for this use case.Audit summary and pitch framing
Max's overall conclusion: this brand is doing the fundamentals well but has clear, actionable gaps.
Pop-up form improvement: 25–50% more subscribers
Flow optimisation: 25% uplift in conversions is conservative and achievable
Campaigns: increase to every-other-day cadence, tighten to 60-day segment
SMS: set up immediately — could add 5–10% attributed revenue on its ownIf pitching this brand: "I'm confident we can get you from 30% to 35% attributed revenue fast, and to 40% within 3–6 months." That's the honest, data-backed pitch.
Max's audit workflow for pitching:
Record a 10–15 minute screen share of the live audit walkthrough
Transcribe it
Paste transcript into Gamma with a 2-sentence prompt: "I'm an email marketer auditing a brand I want to pitch. Break this into these pillars and create a 10-slide presentation."
Review, clean up, and send
---
Closing (~57:00)
Max wrapped up and directed any follow-up questions to Skool DMs. Encouraged everyone to watch the recording back and take notes — the audit format is directly reusable for any pitch or account review.

lessons.title: [June 18th] Additional Flows + Q&A
lessons.description:
Call Summary — Additional Flows, Welcome Flow Optimisation, Post Purchase Segmentation & Live Klaviyo Audit

---
Context & Intro (0:00–3:00)
Max opened with a shoutout to Matthias as community MVP — consistently answering questions, leading agency calls, and never missing a session. Max then introduced the focus of the call: flows that sit outside the five core flows (welcome, site/browse abandoned, checkout abandoned, post purchase, win back) — what to layer on once the fundamentals are locked in.

---
The Espresso Shot Flow (3:00–16:00)
Concept: catch a prospect at their peak engagement moment and fire a fast, punchy offer before intent fades. Quick, strong, no padding.
Segment trigger setup in Klaviyo:
Subscribed to marketing
Active on site at least 3 times in the past 30 days
Clicked an email at least once in the past 48 hours
Placed zero orders in the past 30 days
First email fires 10–15 minutes after segment entry — short, high urgency, with a specific offer valid for 3–4 hours only. No education, no brand story, just the offer.
Subject line: "quick question" — consistently drives very high open rates.
Live example: $118K revenue year-to-date from this single flow for one brand, outperforming both browse and site abandoned flows.

Campaigns: sale, educational, comparison, promotional, social proof, occasion, urgency

Alia's visitor count was showing ~2x Shopify's figures, and tracking was resetting to zero when new team members were added.

Max wrapped up and moved to another call. Any follow-up questions can be sent via Skool DMs.

lessons.title: [June 11th] Email Design Principles
lessons.description:
Call Summary — Email Design Principles, Quick Win Tactics & Deliverability Warm-Up
Wins Round (0:00–3:00) DNS records sorted for a client brand ("rite of passage"). MX skill is being used and crushing. Barbie wrote a song on top of flying planes and doing calculus. Florian set up a Carrd redesign. Max is launching a quiz funnel and testing landing pages across client brands.

---
Quick Wins Review (3:00–20:00) Max walked through the insights he posts daily and sends to his internal team — stuff he's actively executing for clients.
Elite Subscription Checklist (3:00–6:00): Full subscription journey from acquisition to retention. Don't default to 10% off — use free gifts tied to consumption. Get Shopify confirmation emails out of Shopify and into Klaviyo. Optimize your PDP for first-order subscription take rate. Packaging and unboxing is underrated but drives repeat purchase intent directly, especially at higher AOV. Add handwritten cards optionally. Send 1–2 campaigns per month max. Give new products to subscribers who churn.
Klaviyo AB Test Size Distribution (6:00–9:00): On campaign AB tests, set size distribution to 25% total (12.5% per variation). Klaviyo waits 4 hours, picks the winner by open rate, then auto-sends to the remaining 75%. Max is considering rolling this out on every campaign — always running two variations and always pushing the winner.
Founder Email (9:00–11:00): Plain-text email from the founder sent to non-buyers as a campaign or inside the welcome flow. Opens with "hey quick thought…", shares the brand origin briefly, frames a discount code as store credit ("I just activated $5 store credit to your account"), 24-hour urgency, links to bestsellers, ends with "PS — if you have questions, just hit reply. I actually read these myself."
Mystery vs. Surprise Discount in Abandonment (11:00–15:00): Mystery discount in cart abandonment lifted click rate from 3.2% to 6.7% and placed orders from 2.4% to 3.5%. It works in abandonment because friction is low — one click to reveal. It doesn't work as well in welcome flows because the customer still has to find a product, go to checkout, and apply it. "Surprise" is now outperforming "mystery" on some brands as the mystery framing gets more saturated — get in now before that one gets picked up widely too.
Four-Step Campaign Creative Process (15:00–18:00): Start with past winners → steal winning ad and landing page angles (Meta Ads Library, Forplay for competitor swiping) → look at what competitors are spending on repeatedly since that signals it's working → only then use AI for ideation. Never start with AI.
Resending Past Winners (18:00–20:00): Resend past winning campaigns. You can change the subject line.
---
Email Design — Three Principles (20:00–28:00) Pretty does not equal profit. One job: get the click.
Ease of Click (20:00–24:00): Buttons above the fold in most cases. Make them large and centered. Repeat CTAs — not just top and bottom but mid-email too. Every individual product needs its own "Shop Now." Always finish with a general "Shop All" CTA for people who scrolled through and didn't like what they saw but are still browsable. Side buttons are fine as long as they cover the center — a button stuck in the top-left corner kills click rate because most people hold their phone in their right hand and have to stretch. Exception: education-heavy brands sometimes see better conversion with no hero button, forcing the customer to read before clicking, since an early click without context has no intent behind it.
Skimmability (24:00–27:00): Use a smooth singular background instead of blocky color sections — it creates depth and flow rather than harsh visual breaks. An email with a smooth background 4x'd placed orders for one brand vs. a basic product launch. Use infographics, icons, and visual breaks rather than walls of copy. Clear separated sections. Avoid visually overwhelming layouts with competing colors and hard-to-read fonts.
Branding (27:00–28:00): Stay on brand. Not elaborated deeply — the other two principles are where the active work lives.
---
Email Anatomy — Hero Section (28:00–40:00) The above-the-fold section should contain a clear headline, supporting body copy, a clear button, and a strong graphic in 80% of emails.
Call-Out Bar (28:00–30:00): Optional but highly recommended — a bar at the very top screaming urgency or an offer. Free shipping threshold, promo code, countdown, presale deadline. Max loves these and his team uses them constantly.
Imagery (30:00–33:00): Most underrated lever and most important thing you're probably not thinking hard enough about. Be intentional. Skincare → before/afters. Fashion → people wearing the product in real life. Cologne → evoke lifestyle and scent through visuals. Plain product shots don't convert on their own — show transformation or lifestyle context.
Clean Background Behind Text (33:00–36:00): If the hero image is busy behind your headline, you're adding friction. Use AI image extenders to add clean space at the top of the image, then layer a dark contrast overlay so the text is effortless to read. Most of their fluid hero sections use AI image extending — the original image never actually fit the layout.
Text Layout (36:00–38:00): Avoid orphan words — one or two words sitting alone on a line looks awkward. Manipulate line breaks to form a visual triangle that guides the eye naturally down to the button.
Making the Hero Pop (38:00–40:00): Add floating visual elements — snowflakes, leaves, stars, small product images, flowers — to bring depth to what would otherwise be a flat background. The bigger lever: use different font weights, sizes, and colors within the hero. Two designers given identical copy — a boring designer outputs flat uniform text; a great designer uses a thin all-caps variant on one line, a bold variant on the next, repositions the logo into dead space, and creates visual energy that grabs attention without changing a single word. Don't reuse the same hero layout send after send — vary it monthly to keep the list engaged.
---
Email Anatomy — Bridge, Product Section & Footer (40:00–48:00)
Bridge Section (40:00–43:00): One infographic-heavy section per email in most cases. No blocks of copy. Before/afters, feature breakdowns, us-vs-them charts, numbered lists, comparison charts, photo galleries with testimonials. If a designer gets handed a block of copy, the job is to break it up with icons and images. Skool community has the mix-and-match template file with pre-built bridge section options to steal from.
Product Section (43:00–45:00): Mix layouts — lifestyle images, category groupings, tips alongside products, testimonials next to products. Every product listed gets its own individual "Shop Now" button. Always finish the product section with a general "Shop All."
Footer (45:00–48:00): The most consistently clicked section in every email — Max estimates 20% of total clicks typically come from the footer, sometimes as high as 50%. Must-haves: category navigation buttons (for customers who scrolled through everything and didn't find what they wanted), social proof (star rating, review count), and an Instagram/social CTA. This is the catch-all for the customer who's still open but didn't bite on anything featured in the body.
---
Q&A — Cohort LTV & Retention Analytics (48:00–51:00) Matias asked whether the advanced course will cover cohort/LTV data analysis.
Max walked through the cohort LTV dashboard he uses internally (Shopify-connected, not High Road which is Klaviyo-only). Read it like this: January cohort acquired 2,600 new customers. By month two (March), average spend across that cohort is $89. The value is in spotting anomalies — why was month-three LTV $128 in June but only $100 now? What changed? The real edge: split cohorts by first product purchased, first discount code used, or acquisition funnel. Identify which entry point produces the highest LTV customer, then acquire more of those.

---
Q&A — Migrating ~70K Subscribers to a New Klaviyo Account (51:00–54:00) A member is spinning a child brand off a parent brand's Klaviyo account onto its own new account.
Migration mechanics: Create a segment in the parent account filtered to people who engaged with that specific child brand's products. Export directly from the segment as a CSV (you can export segments, not just lists). Import into the new account, upload contacts, mark as subscribed.
Deliverability warm-up: Set core flows live immediately — welcome, browse abandon, cart abandon, checkout abandon, post-purchase — one email per flow only. First emails in flows get the highest engagement, which passively warms the domain without any blasting.
Campaign warm-up sequence: Start with the 2,000 most engaged subscribers (placed order + opened at least once). Send every other day using Klaviyo's batch send feature (spread over 4 hours so it's not a spike). After every 2 sends, expand the audience by 50–100%. Real example: started at 1K people, grew to 5K at two weeks, 10K at three weeks, consistently hitting 5%+ opens and 2%+ clicks throughout. It feels scarier than it is — deliverability is hard to permanently damage if you ramp methodically.
---
Closing — Claude/AI & Community Updates (54:00–55:00) Claude skill is being used for copy and context-loading before generation. Max gave up on Claude for design — finds it faster to design manually than to wait on prompts loading. New hire incoming with agency and email experience. 15-minute onboarding calls launching for all new community members. Advanced course in progress — this live session's design doc is being shared with attendees only.

Don't reuse the same hero layout send after send — vary it monthly to keep the list engaged.
Email Anatomy — Bridge, Product Section & Footer (40:00–48:00)
Bridge Section (40:00–43:00):

One infographic-heavy section per email in most cases. No blocks of copy. Before/afters, feature breakdowns, us-vs-them charts, numbered lists, comparison charts, photo galleries with testimonials. If a designer gets handed a block of copy, the job is to break it up with icons and images. Skool community has the mix-and-match template file with pre-built bridge section options to steal from.
Product Section (43:00–45:00):

Mix layouts — lifestyle images, category groupings, tips alongside products, testimonials next to products. Every product listed gets its own individual "Shop Now" button. Always finish the product section with a general "Shop All."

The most consistently clicked section in every email — Max estimates 20% of total clicks typically come from the footer, sometimes as high as 50%. Must-haves: category navigation buttons (for customers who scrolled through everything and didn't find what they wanted), social proof (star rating, review count), and an Instagram/social CTA. This is the catch-all for the customer who's still open but didn't bite on anything featured in the body.
Q&A — Cohort LTV & Retention Analytics (48:00–51:00)
Matias asked whether the advanced course will cover cohort/LTV data analysis.

Max walked through the cohort LTV dashboard he uses internally (Shopify-connected, not High Road which is Klaviyo-only). Read it like this: January cohort acquired 2,600 new customers. By month two (March), average spend across that cohort is $89. The value is in spotting anomalies — why was month-three LTV $128 in June but only $100 now? What changed? The real edge: split cohorts by first product purchased, first discount code used, or acquisition funnel. Identify which entry point produces the highest LTV customer, then acquire more of those.
Q&A — Migrating ~70K Subscribers to a New Klaviyo Account (51:00–54:00)
A member is spinning a child brand off a parent brand's Klaviyo account onto its own new account.
Migration mechanics:

Create a segment in the parent account filtered to people who engaged with that specific child brand's products. Export directly from the segment as a CSV (you can export segments, not just lists). Import into the new account, upload contacts, mark as subscribed.
Deliverability warm-up:

Set core flows live immediately — welcome, browse abandon, cart abandon, checkout abandon, post-purchase — one email per flow only. First emails in flows get the highest engagement, which passively warms the domain without any blasting.
Campaign warm-up sequence:

Start with the 2,000 most engaged subscribers (placed order + opened at least once). Send every other day using Klaviyo's batch send feature (spread over 4 hours so it's not a spike). After every 2 sends, expand the audience by 50–100%. Real example: started at 1K people, grew to 5K at two weeks, 10K at three weeks, consistently hitting 5%+ opens and 2%+ clicks throughout. It feels scarier than it is — deliverability is hard to permanently damage if you ramp methodically.
Closing — Claude/AI & Community Updates (54:00–55:00)

Claude skill is being used for copy and context-loading before generation. Max gave up on Claude for design — finds it faster to design manually than to wait on prompts loading. New hire incoming with agency and email experience. 15-minute onboarding calls launching for all new community members. Advanced course in progress — this live session's design doc is being shared with attendees only.

lessons.title: [June 4th] Copy Strategy, Banger Angles & Audit
lessons.description:
Opening & Wins (0:00–2:00)
Max kicked off with a win from the group — someone getting strong engagement from warm-up campaigns during a Klaviyo migration. He talked briefly about how migrations are underrated as a learning experience: you bring an account over with no reputation, watch engagement climb as flows go live and campaigns tighten up, and you really start to understand how deliverability works under the hood.
Max shared his personal W: heading to Marbella the next day for two weeks, then Greece for four weeks, then back to the US.

---
Call Structure & Community Reminders (2:00–4:30)
Max reminded everyone how the calls work: a mastermind training/presentation first, then open Q&A. He encouraged people to interrupt with questions during the presentation.
He also reminded the group about two resources in the classroom: the Custom GPT (good for quick strategy questions, quick copy drafts) and the Claude MX Skill (the real sauce — exclusive to the community, same system Well Copy uses internally). If you onboard your brand correctly into the Claude skill, it rips. He encouraged everyone to use it.
The group voted to cover copy over design, and Max agreed — copy has a bigger impact on conversions than design in his experience. He's seen copy changes triple conversions. Design improvements are incremental by comparison.

---
Training: Email Copy Strategy
1. The Banger Angle (4:30–14:00)
The single most important element of any email is the angle — the core emotional hook the entire email is built around. Not body copy, not product descriptions. The headline, the one idea that hits the customer in the chest.
Framework for finding banger angles:
Start with the generic benefit (e.g., "helps with sleep"), then ask four questions:
What's the specific emotional version? → "This is why you keep waking up at 3 a.m."
What's the tension? → "Your sleep supplement might be keeping you awake."
Would someone screenshot this and send it to a friend?
Does it reframe something the customer hasn't considered before?Examples Max walked through:
Dog food brand — Weak: "Help your dog live longer with our product." Banger: "You want your dog to live forever. Feed them like it."
Dog food brand — Weak: "Give your dog the best quality ingredients." Banger: "If you wouldn't eat it yourself, why are you feeding it to your dog?"
Ingredient transparency — Weak: "Here are our ingredients." Banger: "What's NOT on our label is just as important as what's inside."
Bite (toothpaste brand) — "The average person will toss out 137 plastic toothpaste tubes in their life" with a visual showing the pile. Makes you feel guilty. Then: "This kit can change it all."
Supplement brand — "What we left out matters just as much as what we put in. Zero sugar, zero cacao, zero carbs."Weak angles are factual and forgettable. Banger angles create an emotional reaction — guilt, curiosity, reframing — and make the customer see something they hadn't considered.
Brands to study for angle inspo: Bite, Maev (meetmaev.com), Sundays for Dogs, Seed.
Max also pointed out you can literally tell Claude "here's the framework for banger angles, come up with some for this product" and it'll generate strong options.

---
2. More Copy in the Hero Section (14:00–20:00)
A major mistake Max sees (including internally at Well Copy): hero sections with just a headline and a button. That gets clicks without intent. Someone taps a button with no context and bounces.
Max's push: add more copy before your first CTA. Give the customer a reason to click, not just a button to click.
Example he broke down — Magic Mind:
Instead of just "Your calmest morning yet" + a button, the full hero section reads: "Morning shouldn't start with anxiety, but coffee jitters, racing thoughts, and energy crashes became normal somewhere along the way. Magic Mind helps you start calm and stay focused." Then supporting points, then the CTA.
All of that information lives above the fold. People absorb it in the hero section. Remove it and conversions drop.
Another example — a THC/mushroom brand:
"Keep the feeling, leave the fallout. The only thing that should carry over from a night out are the core memories and social connections you made. Hold the drunk text to your ex or the puking session at 2 a.m." That's everything someone needs to make a purchase decision, right in the hero.
Max recommended Milled.com as a tool for following brands and studying their emails — you can see every email any brand sends and steal inspiration.

---
3. The SCE Copy Framework (20:00–28:00)
Three questions to run every email through:
S — Skimmable
The 2026 customer doesn't read emails, they skim. You have roughly three seconds of attention. So: bold your main points, split into clear sections, eliminate large copy blocks. Squint test: blur your eyes and see if you can still identify the structure, the key points, and the sections.
C — Clear and Concise
One clear takeaway per email. Don't try to educate on every benefit and every ingredient. Pick one angle and go deep. Every sentence earns its place. Cut all filler — "we're so excited to share this with you," "as you already may know," "without further ado" — all of that gets deleted.
E — Engaging
Two ways to be engaging: be educational or be entertaining. Numbers are extremely engaging. "This product helps with sleep" vs. "91% of users reported better sleep after 90 days of consistent use" — the second one converts dramatically better.
Example Max loved: a gut health brand with the angle "Don't just buy shit. Invest in yours." Then: "You will spend 92 days — or 2,200 hours — of your life on the toilet. Do you want to make that time feel smoother?" Numbers, humor, specificity, and an emotional hook all at once.
The Claude MX skill is trained on this framework — you can ask it to run any copy through the SCE checklist after drafting.

---
4. Infographics in Email (28:00–32:00)
Email copy and design are intertwined — at Well Copy, copywriters don't just write in a plain doc. They structure how the email should visually flow, section by section.
The key insight: customers don't want to read blocks of copy. Infographics solve this by making copy skimmable, clear and concise, and engaging all at once. Checkboxes, tables, timelines, icon features, us-vs-them comparisons, numbered lists, testimonial blocks, photo galleries, feature callouts — all of these break up text and make information digestible.
Max pointed the group to the Mix and Match Templates in the classroom (under Email Templates and Resources) for a massive library of infographic section templates to pull from. The Claude MX skill is also trained on these.
He also briefly showed the internal Well Copy copywriting tool — custom-built UI but powered by logic similar to the Claude MX skill the community has access to.

---
5. Text-Based Emails (32:00–38:00)
Text-based emails (the plain ones that look like they're from a friend) are the secret weapon. They stand out because everyone else has gone graphic-heavy. They show up in the inbox like a personal message.
Max recommends sending them about 25% of the time for most brands. For brands where they crush, up to 50%.
Three formats:
Medium form (most common, ~50%) — Intro, body, CTA, and always a PS section. The PS gets read more than almost anything else in the email.
Short form / SMS style (~25%) — Stupid simple. "Hey, you've been looking at this. Buy it now." Max said he hates it but it works.
Long form / direct response (~25%) — He cited a brand doing hundreds of millions monthly using nothing but long-form text-based direct response emails. Pure copy, no design.Why not go 100% text-based? Diminishing returns over time. Text-based emails work best as a pattern interrupt. You also lose infographics, which build up education and trust that makes the text-based emails hit harder when they land.
Formatting rules for text-based emails:
Bold main points
Tons of line breaks — no more than one to three sentences per line
Use bullet points
No large copy blocks
Include a PS in every one
Don't overload with CTAs — keep it dead simple, one clear actionCheat code — the Magic Button: A button at the bottom that just says something like "Magic Button" and links to the homepage or a landing page. People are curious, they click. It drives extra clicks and revenue. One major brand includes it in every single text-based email.
When full text-based makes sense: Supplement brands, info products, anything where the product itself isn't visually compelling and you're selling an invisible benefit. For fashion or equipment brands where people need to see the product, graphic emails are essential.

---
6. Product Launch Email Strategy (38:00–42:00)
A question came up about copy for new product category launches. Max shared his framework:
2–3 weeks out: Subtle mentions in regular campaigns. Tease something's coming. Blur out the product image. Add a teaser line in the footer of existing emails.
1 week out: Show the product. Offer early access signup to build a separate list. Also run a deliverability booster email: "We're dropping something — move this email to your primary, click the star, reply with a heart so we know you're in."
Day of launch: Send SMS early access first, then email. Daily emails on launch day.
Max pulled up a creatine brand as a live example of this done right — they started with a founder's note hinting at something new, then a sneak peek linking to a short-form video (driving tons of clicks from email), then multiple teaser emails, then the hard launch with full product info.

---
Q&A
Multi-Country Flow Filtering for Supplement Brand
Question: Expanding a supplement brand from a local market to English-speaking countries and Germany. Running into issues where the welcome flow is getting mixed up — customers from different regions ending up in the wrong flows. One Shopify store, one Klaviyo account.
Max's answer:
Create separate pop-up forms for each region, targeted by location in Klaviyo (show to visitors in certain locations based on IP).
Use conditional splits in the welcome flow based on location.
As an extra fallback: on each region-specific pop-up, add a profile property on the submit button (e.g., "region" = "UK"). This tags every subscriber with their region at the point of signup regardless of IP accuracy later.
If things are already messed up for existing profiles, physically click into individual profiles, look at activity, and trace where the routing went wrong. Unfun but necessary for debugging.
---
Live Klaviyo Account Review — Seed/Gardening Brand
Question: One member shared their Klaviyo account for a live review.
Max's feedback:
Pop-up form:
Good submit rate but way too crowded — too many offers stacked (18 premium seeds, $10 off, plus $10 off, plus $60 in bonus seeds). Compress it down. Something like "You've got a mystery discount + $60 in bonus gifts" and leave it at that.
Set a 2-second trigger instead of firing immediately.
Consider converting to a quiz-style pop-up for better micro-commitment and conversion.Campaigns:
Text-based approach is fine and performing well.
Would simplify segmentation — use a base engaged list and send every other day.
Would mix in some designed emails alongside the text-based ones.Abandonment flows:
Big win available immediately: change the first abandoned cart and abandoned checkout subject line to "Your order is ready to ship." Max said this subject line consistently crushes and he guarantees better conversions.
Switch from a flat discount to a mystery discount in abandonment emails. He's seen 50% increases in placed orders and double the clicks from this change alone because curiosity drives people back to their cart.
The bonuses mentioned on the site (the $300 in free seeds value) should be front and center in abandonment emails, not buried.
Placed order rate on the last abandonment email is above 0.8%, which means there's room to add 1–2 more emails to the flow.Welcome flow:
3.7% placed order rate is a bit low. Lead harder with the big value prop ($300 in free seeds) instead of just 10% off.
Mix in text-based emails in the flows — campaigns are text-based and working great but the flows have none.
Test making the discount code look random instead of "WELCOME10" — a predictable code kills urgency because people know they can come back anytime. A random-looking code creates scarcity even if it's technically the same offer.Other flow tweaks:
Cart abandonment: cut the 1-hour trigger to 30 minutes.
Browse abandonment: only 2 emails — add a raised discount at the end with the offer in people's faces.Max estimated stacking all of these small wins could compound into meaningful lifts across the board.

---
Tracking Subscription Revenue Accurately in Klaviyo + Recharge
Question: If Klaviyo is integrated with Recharge, is there a cleaner way to track revenue from email that excludes automatic subscription rebills?
Max's answer:
Create a custom metric in Klaviyo called "Placed Order Without Subscription Renewals." The filter: Placed Order → Revenue Source Name → does not start with subscription_contract.
This metric shows only one-time orders and first subscription orders. It strips out automatic rebills that would otherwise inflate email revenue numbers. Most subscription brands have inflated revenue attribution because they don't use this metric. Max said for subscription brands, this is the only placed order metric they look at.

---
Attribution for Service-Based / Call-Only Businesses
Question: Working with a floral event design service where all bookings happen over the phone. How do you attribute revenue to email?
Max's answer:
You can't — not in the traditional sense. If there's no e-commerce conversion tracked through Shopify or an ESP, there's no placed order metric to tie to email.
Instead, change the gold star metric to booked calls. Build or pay someone to build a custom integration that tracks how many calls were booked from email campaigns. That becomes the attribution metric: how many booked calls did this campaign generate? How many booked calls are we getting per month from email? That's the number you optimize around.

---
Closing
Max shared the copy training slides directly in the community for attendees on the live call (noted this won't be shared publicly — it pays to show up live). He mentioned all of this content will eventually be re-recorded and added to an advanced DTC marketing course inside the community.

Charlie confirmed he was traveling and being "a bit lazy" but it kept working. Max: "We have one peptide brand A/B testing literally the same email ten times and we cannot beat it with our custom concept. Just repeat the fuck out of your winners."
Action Item: If you have a past winning email angle, resend it. Adjust the graphic slightly, tweak the headline — don't reinvent. The angle is the asset.

---
Announcements & Community Updates (~8:00–~18:00)
May Template Pack
Updated templates pinned inside the classroom. Highlight: Mix & Match Template Library — rather than full email templates, this gives modular sections (hero, bridge, testimonial, product, photo gallery, transitions, footers) that can be combined. Max: "I don't like getting full email design templates. I like mixing and matching sections because sometimes a full email you can't use."
YouTube Summary Docs
New community feature: every YouTube video now has an in-depth written summary doc, gated to community members. Includes all examples Max references in the video, key points, and graphics. Max noted he plans to start gatekeeping some content to these docs that won't be available publicly.
MX Claude Skill Pack (Community Exclusive Release)
Max announced and live-dropped the MX Skill Pack — a custom Claude skill file trained on Well Copy's full email marketing methodology.
What it is:
A zip file of MD skill files that installs directly into Claude under Settings > Skills
Trained on Well Copy's procedures for campaign calendars, copy, flow strategy, QA, store credit, and segmentation
Mirrors the internal platform Well Copy's copywriters useHow to install:
Download the MX skill pack zip
Go to Claude > Customize > Skills > Add/Upload a Skill
Drag and drop the zip folder in — Claude uploads all files automaticallyHow to use:
Type /MX to invoke the skill in any chat
To use per brand: create a separate Claude Project per brand (so memory stays isolated and doesn't bleed between accounts)
Inside the brand project, type /MX then: onboard [brand name]
It will ask for the website, pull all brand research, and create a persistent brand memory/skill file
From there: ask it to build campaign calendars, write copy, create flow briefs, etc.Key design principle: The skill will not produce output unless it has all required context. Max: "AI output was fucking ass internally — not because the model sucked, but because people weren't giving it proper context or the context was wrong. So we literally had to gatekeep it where it will not answer you unless you give it everything it needs."
MX vs. Custom GPT (Email Brain 2.0):
Use Case Tool Quick questions, email strategy advice, email feedback/audit Custom GPT (Email Brain 2.0) Polished output — campaign calendars, copy, flow briefs Claude MX Skill Brainstorming, ideation, fast back-and-forth Custom GPT Operational execution with no corners cut Claude MX Skill
Max also dropped a live look at Well Copy's internal platform (not publicly available) — a custom-built tool where all copywriters write and all campaign/calendar work is managed per brand. The MX skill is the community version of the same methodology.
Action Item: Download the MX zip from the community, install it into Claude, create a project per brand you manage, and run /MX onboard [brand name] as the first step.

---
Campaign Calendar Planning — The Exact Process (~18:00–~42:00)
Max's core teaching segment. Framing: "I'm sick and tired of people just throwing their brand into a custom GPT and getting a shitty fucking calendar. You need to think for yourself first."
The Five Pillar Content Flywheel
Starting framework for calendar balance:
Educational emails
Social proof / community emails
Product-focused emails
Story / brand narrative emails
Sales / offer emailsNot a rigid formula — use it as a balance check, not a strict quota.
Campaign Calendar Build Order of Operations
Step 1: Past Winners Before touching AI, pull your data. Look at your last 30–60 days of campaign performance. Identify your 2–3 best-performing angles.
Pull those angles forward — same concept, slightly adjusted graphic, maybe a tweaked headline
These go directly into next month's calendar as locked slots
Max: "You can literally send the same email over and over once a week. People won't really notice and they'll buy."Step 2: Winning Ad & Landing Page Angles Ask your client (or check your own ads): what's crushing right now in paid?
Identify the 1–2 top ad angles currently running
Translate those directly into email angles
Example from call: ad angle "most supplements focus on one thing — your body doesn't work that way" → email concept built around that
Max: "Why are we not looking at that data and implementing it into our systems?"Step 3: Competitor Swipe (Milled) Go into the community's Best Performing Emails file. Find angles from top-performing brand emails that fit your client's positioning.
Don't copy design — steal the angle/concept
Examples pulled live: long-form testimonial highlight, "every system needs a foundation" angle, "rituals build results" conceptStep 4: Sale/Offer Slot Lock in at least one sale email per calendar, timed to a relevant moment.
Max's preferred sale mechanic: Store Credit, First 100 Orders Only
Why: removes the "I have 72 hours" mental delay — creates genuine urgency because it's quantity-limited, not time-limited
Tie it to an upcoming moment (holiday, seasonal event, product drop)Step 5: AI Ideation (Last, Not First) Only after Steps 1–4 are defined, bring in AI.
Feed it everything you've already decided: winners, ad angles, competitor swipes, sale concept
Ask it to generate additional ideas — don't ask it to build the calendar
Review options, pick your favorites, then ask it to fill the full calendar around what you've already chosen
Ask for ideas first, then approve, then build — never one-shot "build me a calendar"Max's demo used the custom GPT (Email Brain 2.0) for the live walkthrough since the community has access. The Claude MX skill follows the same protocol but with tighter guardrails.
Action Item: Before creating next month's calendar — run your Klaviyo data, pull 2–3 past winners, ask your client for their top ad angles, and do a 15-min Milled swipe session. Come to AI with those inputs, not a blank prompt.

---
Q&A (~42:00–End)
Claude Cowork — Is It Worth Building Automated Systems? (Q: Unnamed)
Max's take: proceed with caution.
He attempted to build a recurring content performance dashboard using Claude Cowork — spent weeks on it, didn't get to a quality he was happy with, abandoned it
General principle: "I spend more time building the system and trying to upkeep it and make sure the quality is good compared to me just doing it myself"
Where he does see Cowork value: automated Klaviyo flow performance reports (weekly QC — flag any flows with major drop in recipients, catch broken flows, quick summary of results)
Can set up: "Every Monday, send me a performance report on last week's email campaigns" — works because it's a consistent, defined task with clear dataCaveat on AI + Klaviyo campaign insights: AI can read campaign names and subject lines, but cannot read the actual email creative. So "insight" reports on why something performed are partially guessing. Max trusts it more for flow QC than for deep campaign analysis.
One community member (unnamed) confirmed they've been connecting Claude to their Klaviyo accounts per brand via the connector feature and using it to pull top performers for the past 30/60/90 days as part of their calendar process — Max endorsed this as a valid use.
Note: When using Claude with multiple Klaviyo accounts, you must uncheck other brand connectors before pulling data for a specific brand to prevent cross-account bleed.
Action Item: If you manage multiple brands, set up individual Claude Projects per brand with the Klaviyo connector attached per project. Use it for flow QC reports on a weekly cadence.

---
Scheduling Separate Campaigns for Sub-Segments (Winbacks, New Subscribers, VIPs) (Q: Aiden)
Max's answer: not until you've hit your baseline.
If you're not sending 3–4 campaigns per week to your full engaged list, you have no business worrying about winback segments or new-subscriber-specific sends
"You might get $2,000 on a winback segment send when you could get $15,000 sending to your whole engaged list. You got no business talking about that."
Winback and new-subscriber logic should live in flows — that's the point of a winback flow and a welcome flow
Once baseline cadence is locked (6+ months in, flows optimized, send volume consistent), then you can layer in segmented campaign sends for incremental lift
Max: "It's not a core part of our calendar strategy until we've been working with a brand for six-ish months"Action Item: If you're under 3–4 campaigns/week to your engaged list, prioritize volume before segmentation.

---
How Much Do Your Copywriters Use AI? How Good Is Claude at Copy? (Q: Unnamed)
Max: "A fuck ton. And it's as good as how it's trained."
Well Copy's internal platform is where all copywriters work — AI-assisted, but human-reviewed
The output from Claude MX (skill-trained) is significantly better than base Claude or base ChatGPT
Some brands they still can't get AI to crack — "sometimes just doing it yourself and not going back and forth with AI ends up being better"
Target: AI gets them 80% of the way there. Copywriters close the last 20%.Action Item: If AI copy feels generic or off-brand, the problem is almost always context — not the model. Run the full MX onboarding for that brand before generating any copy.

---
Pop-Up Optimization Review (Q: Unnamed — skincare brand, currently 10% off offer)
Max's live feedback:
Offer is the biggest lever — 10% off is weak. If the brand already has site-wide discounts (e.g., up to 65% off), lead with that on the pop-up. Don't add extra discount — highlight the discount that already exists. "That's what iM8 does. That's what Groons does. They're not giving extra discount — they're highlighting the evergreen discount already on their website."
If you must offer a discount: test a mystery discount vs. a stated percentage
Segmentation buttons (face acne / body acne / both) — make them bigger. Add a "just browsing" option — some people won't answer and will close the pop-up; giving them an out keeps them in the flow
Test full-page form vs. partial
Test background image vs. none
Add a small social proof element near the CTA
Charlie's add-on: for acne/skincare specifically, the avatar isn't primarily price-motivated — result-driven headline may outperform discount-driven ("Cleared my acne in 10 days" style) paired with a mystery credit or offerAction Item: If your pop-up is stuck, audit in this order: (1) offer, (2) form size, (3) CTA button size, (4) social proof, (5) background image. Offer is always the biggest lever.

---
Well Copy Internal Analytics Dashboard (Sneak Peek)
Max showed a preview of a custom internal analytics tool built by a developer he found on Twitter — built in approximately 10 days.
What it does:
Pulls and combines Shopify, Klaviyo, and subscription platform (Recharge) data into one dashboard
Cohort analysis by product: which product a customer first bought, their retention over 6/12 months, LTV by cohort
Gross margin and CAC integration in progress
Customer health segmentation: winback, re-engage, nurture, lost cause, reward — with projected revenue from each segment
Time-between-orders analysis (subscription excluded/included toggle)
Product journey mapping (what products do customers buy in sequence)
LTV drivers breakdownAI layer (Flaunt-style):
Chat interface that connects to all the data
Ask it questions it can't answer in Shopify or Klaviyo natively — e.g., "Compare 6-month LTV for customers acquired with a discount vs. full price, which group is more valuable long-term?"
Returns charts and analysis, not just data tables
Max: "Shopify dashboards suck. Klaviyo dashboards suck. Subscription platforms suck. This answers all these questions and actually pulls up graphs."Note: Max flagged that no analytics tool is 100% accurate — always cross-check against Shopify and ultimately against bank/credit card statements for true revenue.

---
Tool Mention: Manus AI (Community Discussion)
A community member flagged Manus (Chinese AI) as a strong tool for:
Scraping and analyzing video content (including YouTube videos and competitor ad libraries)
Ad angle identification and copy generation from video/ad analysis
Website and app buildingMax co-signed it: "It's freaky. It's a lot more freaky than the others." Also noted Meta acquired Manus and it now has deeper ad library integration. Less relevant for email production but strong for competitive research and ad angle mining.

lessons.title: [May 21st] Welcome Flows + Q&A
lessons.description:
Watch Recording >>
Summary below 👇

---
Opening & Wins (0:00–3:30)
Max dropped the W requirement in chat before getting started.
Wins from the room:
Matthias: #1 on the Skool leaderboard with 99 aura points
$18K on a single back-in-stock email
About to sign a new client
Tyler: two new product versions landing in ~2 weeks, getting all the user guides shot
Chelsea: redesigned bundles + loyalty page + built a new post-purchase email for new customers (flex — Max called it three wins, not one)
Florian: pop-up submit rate up by 1 point (huge on high-traffic brand); A/B test with no X button beating standard 10% lift, 0.71 controlMax's win: A big brand inbound on custom landing pages — specifically email-exclusive landing pages. Walked through Happy Being's /pages/first-sip-gift example (used only in email, never in ads), and Breeze's "email subscriber exclusive" banner play. Max is building out a small team (one person to start) to do these for clients — drive welcome flows and abandonment flows for non-buyers to a custom email-only LP. With AI shipping speed, he's bullish this becomes a real lever.

---
Welcome Flow Masterclass — Foundations (3:30–10:00)
Max teed up the welcome flow as the most-asked-about flow he gets. Pulled up his Commerce Roundtable deck and walked through the foundations.
Why the welcome flow matters:
First impressions: 58% don't change (human psychology)
Engaging the welcome flow = 33% higher future brand engagement + 33% higher list engagement
CAC has risen ~40% over the past 2 years; a properly optimized welcome flow drops CAC ~15% (e.g., $100 CAC → $85; at 1,000 first-time purchases/month, that's $15K/month back)
Retention starts at acquisition — biggest lever nobody talks about. Framing the customer's relationship to your product on the front end determines their LTV.AG1 example: Their entire messaging is built around "use this every day, make it a ritual, customers since 2012, since 2021." That framing makes the buyer commit long-term before they buy. Contrast with an AG1 alternative promising "life-changing benefits in 2 weeks" — if it doesn't deliver in 2 weeks, the customer churns and hates the brand. AG1 wins on LTV because of the framing, not the product.
Biggest lever = the offer. You cannot CRO your way to a 2x — moving buttons and tweaking copy won't get you there. Offer testing will. Max showed a 4-part offer test from an 8-fig legacy brand running a free-gift offer for years at 3.3% placed order rate. The winner: $25 off at 10.7% placed order rate, with 3x the people entering the pop-up. They gave up a few dollars of margin per order and printed.

---
Welcome Flow Non-Negotiables (10:00–14:00)
Every welcome flow, every brand, no exceptions:
Double opt-in OFF. Go into list → consent → switch to single opt-in. Double opt-in massively increases churn.
First email fires immediately. No 1-minute or 10-minute delays. Max's biggest pet peeve — train them to open your emails now.
Minimum 3 emails. Standard is 4–5. Some brands can push more, but past a point, just send campaigns.
Emails 1 day apart. Aggressive brands can send 2–3 in a day. Never wait multiple days between emails.
Welcome discount in the hero of every email. Biggest miss Max sees. If the discount isn't up top in every email, it's just a campaign.
At least one plain-text email from the founder or support team. Ideally one early, one at the end.
Urgency. People buy from urgency. The discount code is expiring — say it.
---
Core Welcome Flow Template (14:00–19:00)
Max walked through the templated structure (all available in Skool community):
Email 1 — Welcome email: Deliver the incentive. Discount + button way up top.
Emails 2–3 (sometimes 4–5 for high-AOV/educational brands): Filler emails — story, ingredient breakdown, FAQ, how it works, social proof. Every one reminds of the discount.
Second-to-last email — Last chance: Discount expiring, timer.
Final email — Plain-text support email from founder/support.
Bonus — Store credit email sent ~2 weeks after the flow ends. Most people who buy do so within 3 days; almost nobody buys after 28 days. Send from rewards@brand, two-decimal dollar amount, make it look like a real account credit. Best-performing email Well Copy sends.
---
Brand Examples Walkthrough (19:00–32:00)
Marsmen (single-SKU testosterone supplement) — extreme frequency play:
3 emails/day for the first 3 days, then 1/day
Welcome offer reinforced relentlessly
Plain-text founder story positioned email 2
Social proof emails 3 and 4
Month-by-month framing pushing daily long-term use (LTV framing)
Layered extra $10 off on day 3
Then medical advisory board, most potent stack, etc.
A/B testing priorities: offer first, then timing (2x/day vs 1x), then text vs graphicMax's A/B testing philosophy for flows:
Stop A/B testing button colors. Flow attribution is messy and you'll forget the tests are even live.
Best lever: take winning campaign concepts and port them into the welcome flow.
Example: Gainsinbulk "our creatine isn't cheap" email — top campaign ever, then ran as welcome flow email 3 vs the existing science email. Doubled conversions.Klaviyo Experiments tab tip: Most people don't know it exists. Shows every active and ended A/B test across campaigns and flows with win probability. Find it under Experiments.
Jewelry (Ice Cartel — men's): Minimal aesthetic, discount auto-applied at checkout, founder text-based email, celebrity highlight (they convert off celebrity association), bestsellers, social proof, last chance. For jewelry: just show product pictures — people want to see the product worn.

---
Welcome Flow Reviews
Merlijn — Women's Red Light Belts (32:36–40:00)
Single-product brand, women-focused.
Max's feedback:

Every button should remind of the discount in its copy (e.g., "Use code XYZ"). Nitpicky but worth it.
Kill the 12-hour and 36-hour time delays. If someone signs up at 9am, a 1-day delay sends the next email at 9am — that's their proven active time. Don't fight it. Max never goes longer than a 4-hour micro-delay, and prefers 24-hour for everything else.
A/B test single long testimonial vs the short testimonial grid — long usually wins.

Add the store credit email at the end.

Aggressive brand, aggressive cadence works.Action item logged: Align with founder on welcome offer + LP routing, then rebuild flow: B&A-led creative, plain-text founder email, Marsmen cadence, route CTAs to advertorial, A/B test code style.

Niccolo — Barefoot running shoes (40 SKUs, 60 with accessories): Wants to ask experience-level + gender on the pop-up to segment by sole thickness.
Max pushed back: gender is a higher-impact segmentation question than experience. If anything, ask why (performance vs. foot health) — Velocity Running does this well.
Two-question pop-ups will reduce opt-in rate. If doing it, ask for email/SMS first, then ask the secondary question (multi-step). Lower completion on Q2, but the data is still useful.
