lessons.title: [May 14th] Post-Purchase Flow + Q&A
lessons.description:
Watch Call Recording >>
Full Summary Below 👇

---
Holdout Test: The Real Value of Email [0:05:30]
Ran a holdout test on a post-purchase replenishment flow — split into recipients vs. non-recipients, then cross-referenced Shopify data.
Klaviyo attributed hundreds of thousands in revenue to the flow
True incremental lift: 7% — meaning only 7% more people bought because of the email
15% of holdout (no email) bought anyway. 15.5% of flow recipients bought. That's the real gap.
Actual incremental value: ~$30K over 4 months (~$7-8K/month)Takeaway: Klaviyo over-attributes. Know the difference between captured revenue and created revenue. Abandon/checkout flows likely have much higher true incrementality.

---
Post-Purchase Flow Framework [0:11:30]
Max's definitions:
Post-purchase: Days 0–30
Replenishment: Days 30–120
Win-back: 120+ daysPhilosophy: Relationship and retention first. Sales happen as a byproduct when done right.
Goals in order:
Make the customer feel great about their purchase
Express genuine gratitude
Educate on product use / drive consumption
Cross-sell/upsell when excitement is highest
---
Non-Negotiables [0:14:00]
Email 1 — Immediate plain-text founder thank you [0:14:20]
Split by order count (different copy for order 1, 2, 3, 4+, then stop after order 4)
Personal, conversational tone from the founder
Always link to site — people revisit this email when they want to reorder
Soft PS cross-sell optionalEmail 2 — Product education (Day 2–3) [0:17:00]
Consumables: dosage, timing, routine, how to use daily
Fashion: how to style
Skincare: routine
Core goal: drive consumption. The #1 reason for cancellations is unused product. If they don't use it, they cancel.Email 3 — Cross-sell/upsell (Day 10) [0:18:30]
Earlier than most brands think
Data shows strong rebuy intent at days 8–14, peaks days 22–28, big window is days 15–35
Don't wait for day 30 — hit them in the honeymoon phase
Don't force cross-sells that data doesn't support. Look at what customers are already buying and add fuel to that fire.Email 4 — Founder check-in (Day 21–28) [0:19:30]
"Hope you're loving it, here's what you should be experiencing by now"
Soft nudge toward next logical product
Underrated and effective — doesn't feel salesy
---
When Do People Actually Rebuy? [0:15:30]
Data from a replenishable brand on conversion to subscription by day:
Days 1–7: almost nothing
Days 8–14: 11.9% — product arrives, they try it, they're in
Days 22–28: biggest spike (approaching end of supply)
Days 36–42: less than days 8–14Implication: Push cross-sells earlier than you think. Day 10–14, not day 30.

---
Subscription-Specific Notes [0:24:00]
Go harder on education upfront — daily emails for first 5 days if needed
Don't aggressively cross-sell — you already have them, focus on keeping them
Include a "how your subscription works" email — show the portal, how to manage, pause, swap
Reinforce a 90-day challenge framing — getting past day 90 is the retention unlock. Most brands break even at month 3, everything after is profit.
Show churn spike points and build flows to address them:
Day 0: impulse cancels
Product delivery day: gets reminded they subscribed
Day 27: billing reminder spike
Day 30: actual charge spike — biggest churn moment
Month 2 charge: much smaller, then it stabilizes
---
Brand-Specific Approaches [0:26:00]
Lots of SKUs / general store [0:26:00]
Skip product-specific education, do brand education instead
Treat it like a mini welcome flow — Our Story, brand values, social proof
Cross-sell to bestsellersFashion / clothing [0:37:30]
Don't overthink it — immediate thank you, maybe community/brand email, cross-sell to bestsellers
What drives repeat purchase for fashion: newness. New drops, new styles.
Tell them how often you drop new product and prime them for it
Highlight what's hot and selling out vs. pushing old inventoryLaunch-heavy brands [0:39:00]
Don't fight the launch model — lean into it
Between launches, milk the current drop: "selling out," "still available," social proof on what just dropped
In post-purchase: thank you → cross-sell to bestsellers → tell them when next drop is coming → keep them subscribed
---
Getting UGC / Social Shares [0:43:30]
Feature the customers who do share — others will follow
Run a "Build of the Week" or similar recurring feature
Put it in the post-purchase flow: show other customers' photos, invite them to submit
Optional incentive, but social proof of others doing it is more powerful than the incentive itself
Add a footer CTA in every email: "Tag us / post us on socials"
---
Review Request Strategy [0:46:40]
Standard approach:
Two reminder emails, no incentive unless the brand is really pushing for it
Timing and friction reduction are the only levers
Zamo allows inline reviews directly inside Klaviyo emailsThe Star-Filter Hack [0:48:15] (shared by Merlijn)
In your review request email, show clickable star ratings
4–5 stars → links to your public review page (Trustpilot, Google, etc.)
1–3 stars → routes to customer support / private feedback form
Result: 4.8 average public rating even with imperfect shipping times
Works. Max confirmed his team uses this. Needs to be standardized.
---
ManyChat / Instagram DM Automations [0:50:30]
Set up a keyword trigger (e.g. "DM me the word EMAILS") in bio and every post
Flow branches: agency/freelancer → link to community + free resources. Brand owner → service info + book a call
Follow automation: when someone follows you, send a quick welcome DM, ask if they're a brand or just here for vibes
Klaviyo's DM feature exists but doesn't support follower-triggered automations — ManyChat still wins for that
Future prediction: Instagram will eventually support cart abandon and checkout abandon DM flows. Get ready.
---
Retention / Cohort Marketing [0:57:00]
Best thing you can do as a retention marketer: cohort analysis
Use Shopify cohorts or Lifetimely
Find which first-order product produces the highest 6-month LTV
Example: first order as subscription = ~$200 at month 6 vs. one-time purchase = ~$120 — 68% higher LTV
Once you find it, go after those customers harder in your marketing
Find drop-off points in the cohort and build flows/SMS/direct mail to attack them

lessons.title: [May 8th] Campaigns Strategy + Q&A
lessons.description:
Call Recording >>
Summary Below 👇

---
Opening & Wins (0:00–4:30)
Max opened by reading member wins: Matthias hit 0% churn in 2026, someone booked their first call from the Klaviyo Directory, a member restocked after months stuck in customs and immediately did 50K, and a Mother's Day campaign pulled 10K in two days. Max's win: Kim Kardashian's beverage brand booked a sales call with Well Copy — rare enough that he's personally taking it.
He reminded people to send campaign copy for review and teased that the existing GPT tool is outdated and he's planning to build a custom Claude skill file to replace it.
Magic Buttons in Footers (4:30–6:45)
Max showed how Breeze, Hormozi, and his own newsletter use clickable footer elements (mystery buttons, memes, linked images) to inflate click rates. The principle: never show content inline if you can force a click to reveal it. Hormozi shifted from embedding memes to linking them. Max does the same with his "email inspiration of the day" — forces the click instead of displaying the design. Recommended adding a small "magic button" under the founder's sign-off in any text-based email. Links to homepage or wherever — the point is the click.
Campaign Philosophy — Full Framework (6:45–28:00)
This was the bulk of the call. Max walked through the campaign philosophy he's been codifying internally for his team:
Email's real job isn't generating direct sales — it's staying top of mind so when the customer is ready to buy, your brand is first. Proof: switching Klaviyo attribution from 5-day open/click to 1-day click drops email revenue from ~40-50% down to ~8%. That gap is invisible warming work — someone gets a great educational email, doesn't buy, but converts off an ad three days later because the email pre-sold them.
Frequency is the #1 lever. More sends almost always equals more revenue. Max is running a multi-brand scatterplot study correlating campaigns sent per week against click rate, RPR, and unsub rate. Early findings: click rate dips slightly with more sends, unsub rate barely moves (one brand actually had higher unsubs at 3x/week than at higher frequency), and revenue trends up. He'd rather send one general email to 100K engaged subscribers than a hyper-targeted email to 5K. Audited a brand that day making exactly this mistake — segmenting down to 5K sends on a 50K engaged list. Segmentation is kept extremely simple. A blank email with just a logo and a shop-now button sent 4x/week would make money.
75/25 graphic to text-based mix. Text-based emails convert better on a percentage basis but work best as a pattern interrupt. Higher unsub rates if overused. Can mix in semi-designed text emails with a founder headshot. 25% of sends should be plain-text style from a real person.
Specificity is the #1 copy principle. The angle behind the email matters more than anything else. One email, one micro-topic. "How magnesium improves your REM sleep" beats "5 benefits of our greens powder." If a customer can't summarize the email in one sentence after a 3-second skim, the email failed. Max called out the classic bad example: "How our product supports your overall health" with six bullet points — customer reads all six, retains zero.
Five content pillars, kept in roughly even rotation:
Educational — micro-topic deep dives (ingredient breakdowns, how-to, FAQs, product science, use cases)
Social proof — testimonials, reviews, customer photos, before/afters, influencer mentions, awards, milestones
Community/brand — founder stories, brand mission, behind-the-scenes, team intros, text-based founder emails
Product/collection highlights — single product features, new arrivals, restocks, seasonal collections, gift guides (restocks especially rip — the implication that it sold out does the selling)
Sales — discount-driven sends with creative framingDiscounts — use them, but twist the framing. The 2026 customer is numb to standard percentage-off. Reframe as store credit (even small odd amounts like $13.42), mystery discounts, first-100-people flash sales, order lotteries ("we'll randomly refund 3 orders in 24 hours"), UUP late-night sales (send at 9-10 PM, live for 3 hours, morning email says "you snooze you lose" with a smaller code). The store credit email that looks like an automated "credit applied to your account" notification rips every single time. Big mistake: running the same % off rotation monthly and wondering why conversion drops. The offer isn't the problem — the predictability is.

Repeat Your Winners (28:00–34:00)
Major emphasis. Max is frustrated that his own team (and himself) will send a banger email, celebrate, then never send anything like it again. The mandate:
Resend winning emails at least monthly (bi-weekly is fine too)
Put them into flows — welcome, abandonment, everywhere relevant
Redesign if you want, but keep the same angle

Recurring Themes (34:00–35:30)
Recurring email themes work when not forced. Bi-weekly to monthly cadence — weekly is too much and fatigues the audience. Examples:
Build of the Month (German car accessories brand — customers submit car photos, winner gets a gift card)
Staff Picks (rotating team member each month)
Ask a Urologist (health brand with a professional on staff — issue 20+, strong engagement)
Slow Sip Sundays (Breeze — Sunday wind-down email)Calendar Building Checklist (35:30–36:00)

The existing GPT for campaign strategy is outdated. Max committed to building a Claude skill file to replace it, likely the best path forward since the internal tool isn't public. Shared the Gamma presentation with call attendees only.
Q&A — Referral Emails, Non-Opener Resends, Resend Timing (36:30–39:00)

Mapa's question: What changes for a gifting brand (wildflower gin, honey, tea) in terms of flows, frequency, and strategy?

Email flows and cross-sell sequences can get 10% incremental improvements
The big jumps in repeat purchase rates come from new product launches, new flavors, and collabs
Fashion brands are dead without constant new releases — that's the only LTV driver
Dr. Squatch runs a new collab practically every week to drive repeat purchases on a product (soap) that people rarely run out of

Max spent two weeks on a deep audit for a beverage brand trying to get churn under 18% — concluded the real unlock would be dropping new flavors, which would likely drive a 50%+ increase in repeat purchase rate
The more he's in retention, the more he sees: acquisition is driven by offers, retention is driven by productQ&A — Retargeting Ad Spend & Post-Purchase Timing (56:08–1:01:30)

Max's answer: ~10% of ad spend on retargeting is standard. Many supplement brands (especially subscription-first) don't retarget at all. The biggest lever is still product quality — for supplement brands, repeat purchase rate is the clearest signal of product-market fit.

Most brands don't start replenishment reminders until day 30-40, which is too late based on actual data.

Max's answer: Offers are the biggest lever (percent off, dollar off, different amounts, gifts, bundles). After that, form style — Plinko, spin-to-win, micro-commit questions, different quiz questions. Max cited a recent test where simply changing the quiz question on a pop-up got 25% higher opt-ins. Had to cut the answer short due to running late to his next call.

lessons.title: [May 1st] Abandonment Flows + Q&A
lessons.description:
Call recording >>
Summary below 👇

---
Part 1 — Abandonment Flow Training (0:00–20:30)
Max walked through Well Copy's current abandonment flow framework — what's working now, what's worth setting up, and where to deviate.
The four flows + base architecture
Site Abandoned, Browse Abandoned, Cart Abandoned, Checkout Abandoned
Every flow split on "placed order at least once over all time" → Buyer track vs. Non-Buyer track
Non-buyers get welcome discount reminder up front (people know they have a code but won't go searching)
Buyer side mirrors structure but no early discountWhen to add a product-level split
Example: Gains in Bulk — 20 SKUs but ~90% of revenue is creatine. Build a creatine-specific abandonment track and an "other" track. Generic "we use the best ingredients" copy converts worse than creatine-specific copy when 90% of abandons are creatine.Two non-negotiable rules for graphic abandonment emails
Dynamic product block at the very top — show the abandoned item immediately, no oversized hero
Aggressive copy — kill "forgetting something?" forever. Use "Your order is ready to ship," "We've got this reserved for you," "You're one click away." Frame the purchase as already done, just needs finishing.Discount cadence
Non-buyers: welcome reminder → welcome reminder → higher discount → higher discount + urgency
Past buyers: no discount → no discount → discount → discount + urgencyFlow-by-flow content notes
Site Abandoned — 2 emails, low intent. Email 1: bestsellers + welcome discount. Email 2: text-based founder/support note.
Browse Abandoned — Email 1: abandoned item at top, social proof. Email 2: text-based FAQ from founder. Email 3: discount + show similar items (browse intent is weaker than cart/checkout — cross-pollinating products helps). Final: text-based last chance.
Cart / Checkout Abandoned — Nearly identical content. Dynamic product block top, social proof, founder text follow-up, then discount.Mystery discount A/B test result (Cart Abandoned)
Flat 15% off: 3.2% CTR, 2.4% PO rate
"Mystery discount in your cart, click to reveal": 6.7% CTR, 3.5% PO rate
Roughly 2x click rate, ~50% lift in placed order rate
Max's directive: if you don't have this running in cart/checkout abandoned, set it up now.When to break the framework
Plush Beds case study: high-ticket mattress, near-zero repeat rate. They send 0-second-delay emails, 4 emails day 1, 3 emails day 2/3/4. When LTV is one purchase, brand fatigue doesn't matter — aggression does. Same logic applies to subscription brands (Mars Men reference).Templates — All flow templates live in Skool. Recommended workflow: pick the closest flow template, then pull section blocks from the email design template library to swap in/out (testimonial sections, etc.).

---
Part 2 — Q&A Block 1 (20:30–29:00)
Aven — text-based vs. designed for site/browse abandoned: Some brands run all text-based and it just rips, never slows down. Brand preference often drives design-heavy choice. For a designed cart abandoned, Max's structure: one email per objection, hit them sequentially. Peptide brands specifically perform better on text-based — partially deliverability (Medvi reference).
GDPR / cookies on site abandoned: Max has never seen this become a real issue. Not adjusting strategy for it.
Dynamic similar-items section (not the abandoned product):
Use Klaviyo product feeds → "Products a customer may also like" (uses view + purchase history)
Fallback: best-selling products last 3 days
Notable: a Well Copy team member just A/B'd Klaviyo dynamic sections vs. fully designed sections — dynamic won.
Caveat: no clean way to handle dark mode with Klaviyo dynamic blocks. Accept it.Mystery discount on welcome AND checkout abandoned simultaneously: Yes, runs fine on multiple brands.

---
Part 3 — Alia + Prism.ai (24:30–28:00)
Brand currently running: 33.3% email submit rate, 27% SMS submit rate.
Setup: enable Prism inside Alia, build variants (copy or imagery), Alia's AI matches variant to visitor profile. Max's recommendation — variant on images, not copy. Build 10 image variants (male-focused, female-focused, product-focused, lifestyle-focused, gaming vs. home office for relevant brands). Publish, let it learn.

---
Part 4 — Claude Design → Figma Workflow (29:30–33:30)
Max showed an email built entirely in Claude Design from one prompt. Cost: $7–$10 per campaign in tokens right now.
Mapa's question — getting it editable in Figma:
In Claude Design: Share → Download as HTML
In Figma: install plugin html.to.design (free version works)
Upload HTML → fully editable, text boxes intact, fonts preserved if installed locally (otherwise fallback to Arial — adjust manually)Action item logged: Mapa to send recording to her designers — solves the "text comes in as individual lines instead of paragraphs" problem her team was hitting.
---
Part 5 — Deliverability / Promo Tab (Jacob — Fulop Nutrition) (33:30–37:00)
No magic switch. Gmail decides based on engagement. Reality check: most brands live in promotions. Even Anthros (Well Copy client doing 40%+ of revenue from email/SMS) lands in promo tab.
Tactics if you really want to fight it:
Get above 50% open rates, maximize CTR
Critical move: in pop-up form, don't hand over the discount code. Tell people to check inbox + reply to the email. Early engagement is the single biggest signal to Gmail.Deliverability tools Max uses:
Maverick (trymaverick.com/Deliverability Optimizer) — free, snippet-based, requires ~$60K/mo email campaign revenue minimum. Max actively gatekeeps this one outside of clients.
Avoid MailMend — paid trial, 1-year lock-in, doesn't optimize the snippet.
---
Part 6 — Pixel Picasso Highlights (37:00–50:30)
Top emails from Well Copy's roster this week. Standout concepts worth stealing:
Testimonial-as-story (Instead of Flowers gifting brand) — built a narrative around a single testimonial, ripped, now being repeated and ported to other brands
Monthly featured product at top of every email — limited edition meal of the month, increased revenue, now standard placement
Newspaper-format testimonial email — long-form testimonials styled as newspaper articles
Hand-drawn Mother's Day email (perfume brand) — designer drew crayon-style art on iPad, uploaded to Figma. Max's reaction: "we need to give her more work, why does she have time for this" — but it's gorgeous
"First 100 mystery discount" welcome email — heavy urgency, works for aggressive brands
Phone-shaped sock email ("Your top drawer called")
WhatsApp-format email — products explaining themselves to each other in chat bubbles
Caged email (winner of the week vote) — clean, educational, button on every product
Comment-layout testimonial sections — performing very well right nowInspiration system at Well Copy: every team member must send one inbox inspiration email per day to a Slack channel as their clock-in. Forces constant exposure. Max: "we steal stuff, and then everybody gets inspiration from Pixel Picasso."

---
Part 7 — Q&A Block 2 (50:30–58:00)
Post-purchase flow when AfterSell already runs on thank-you page: Build alongside it. Email post-purchase isn't competing — it's not "add to your order," it's "place another order." Best post-purchase emails are data-driven: look at what customers buy next after their first product, build the cross-sell offer around that. For replenishables, day 14 is the sweet spot for cross-sell/upsell.
Mapa — other industries where text-based wins:
Health/supplement brands, especially "black hat" or aggressive direct-response health
Long-form direct response (men's health, classic infomercial-style)
Personal brands and newsletters
Emotional purchases vs. visual purchases
Reference: Rosabella ($100M faceless health brand) — almost entirely text
Rule of thumb: design wins when product needs to be seen (clothing); text wins when the purchase is emotional or educationalJacob — ChatGPT image gen 2.0 and AI email creation:
Max has shipped emails with the prompt: "Attaching brand guidelines + past emails, follow best practices, make me an email"
Claude advantage over ChatGPT: Claude can generate a full 4-email flow in one rip; ChatGPT does one email at a time
Workflow tip if hiring is too expensive: feed Claude/ChatGPT a template export and have it apply the template to your brand
Image-to-Figma plugin exists for further editing; Max prefers Canva for edits
Nano Banana — best for product imagery and renders, not for full emailsJacob — Alia format for low opt-in (currently 6% quiz, 3% scratch-off, brand running light Meta ads):
Quiz is the safest default — stick with it
Plinko works on certain brands but demographic-dependent
6% is decent but Max wants 12%+ for a brand that size
Real diagnosis: Meta's still learning the ICP (broad targeting + Website Click optimization = colder traffic). The pop-up isn't the bottleneck — the traffic quality is.Action item logged: Jacob to DM Max for a pop-up review; test quiz offer variants.

No magic switch. Gmail decides based on engagement. Reality check: most brands live in promotions. Even Anthros (Well Copy client doing 40%+ of revenue from email/SMS) lands in promo tab.
Tactics if you really want to fight it:
Get above 50% open rates, maximize CTR
Critical move: in pop-up form,
don't
hand over the discount code. Tell people to check inbox + reply to the email. Early engagement is the single biggest signal to Gmail.
Deliverability tools Max uses:
Maverick (
trymaverick.com/Deliverability
Optimizer) — free, snippet-based, requires ~$60K/mo email campaign revenue minimum. Max actively gatekeeps this one outside of clients.
Avoid MailMend — paid trial, 1-year lock-in, doesn't optimize the snippet.
Part 6 — Pixel Picasso Highlights (
Top emails from Well Copy's roster this week. Standout concepts worth stealing:
Testimonial-as-story
(Instead of Flowers gifting brand) — built a narrative around a single testimonial, ripped, now being repeated and ported to other brands
Monthly featured product at top of every email
— limited edition meal of the month, increased revenue, now standard placement
Newspaper-format testimonial email
— long-form testimonials styled as newspaper articles
Hand-drawn Mother's Day email
(perfume brand) — designer drew crayon-style art on iPad, uploaded to Figma. Max's reaction: "we need to give her more work, why does she have time for this" — but it's gorgeous
"First 100 mystery discount" welcome email
— heavy urgency, works for aggressive brands
Phone-shaped sock email
("Your top drawer called")
WhatsApp-format email
— products explaining themselves to each other in chat bubbles
Caged email
(winner of the week vote) — clean, educational, button on every product
Comment-layout testimonial sections
— performing very well right now
Inspiration system at Well Copy:

every team member must send one inbox inspiration email per day to a Slack channel as their clock-in. Forces constant exposure. Max: "we steal stuff, and then everybody gets inspiration from Pixel Picasso."
Part 7 — Q&A Block 2 (
Post-purchase flow when AfterSell already runs on thank-you page:
Build alongside it. Email post-purchase isn't competing — it's not "add to your order," it's "place another order." Best post-purchase emails are data-driven: look at what customers buy
next
after their first product, build the cross-sell offer around that. For replenishables, day 14 is the sweet spot for cross-sell/upsell.
Mapa — other industries where text-based wins:
Health/supplement brands, especially "black hat" or aggressive direct-response health
Long-form direct response (men's health, classic infomercial-style)
Personal brands and newsletters
Emotional purchases vs. visual purchases
Reference: Rosabella ($100M faceless health brand) — almost entirely text
Rule of thumb: design wins when product needs to be
seen
(clothing); text wins when the purchase is
emotional
or
educational
Jacob — ChatGPT image gen 2.0 and AI email creation:
Max has shipped emails with the prompt: "Attaching brand guidelines + past emails, follow best practices, make me an email"
Claude advantage over ChatGPT: Claude can generate a full 4-email flow in one rip; ChatGPT does one email at a time
Workflow tip if hiring is too expensive: feed Claude/ChatGPT a template export and have it apply the template to your brand
Image-to-Figma plugin exists for further editing; Max prefers Canva for edits
Nano Banana — best for product imagery and renders, not for full emails
Jacob — Alia format for low opt-in (currently 6% quiz, 3% scratch-off, brand running light Meta ads):
Quiz is the safest default — stick with it
Plinko works on certain brands but demographic-dependent
6% is decent but Max wants 12%+ for a brand that size

Jacob to DM Max for a pop-up review; test quiz offer variants.

lessons.title: [April 24th] Claude Design + Q&A
lessons.description:
Watch call recording >>
Summary below 👇

---
Opening & Housekeeping (0:00–3:30)
Max called in from Porto, Portugal — mid-travel circuit (San Diego → Vegas → Austin → Portugal, with NYC for a month coming up after). About 18 Well Copy team members were out there with him, working out of a co-working space and stacking apartments next to each other. Light banter with Barbie about her cat Jagger, with Tyler about Bosnian and Croatian food, and with Chelsea about Terry Black's BBQ in Austin (Max didn't realize they charged by the pound and dropped $60 on lunch).

---
Claude Design + Claude Code for Email Creation (3:30–19:17)
The main teaching segment of the call — Max walked through how he's using Claude Design and Claude Code to generate full marketing emails, both as standalone outputs and pushed directly into Figma.
Claude Design (web app only — not desktop):
Found under "Prototype" in the web app. Ignore the Slide deck and form template options for now.
Design Systems = custom branding. You can spin one up by giving it just a website URL — it pulls fonts, logos, colors, and the full brand identity automatically. Max has a Well Copy design system saved that he uses to convert audit Loom transcripts into branded pitch decks.
Workflow Max ran live: dropped 2–3 example emails as references, attached the Happy Being website URL, asked it to "create a marketing email about us vs. them." Claude asked clarifying questions (hero product, comparison angle, layout style, tone, headline direction, variations) and built two full email variations in a couple minutes.
You can edit directly inside Claude Design — type to adjust, leave comments on specific sections, or draw on the canvas (e.g., "I want a button up here" → it adds it).
Demo result: not perfect (some sizing/spacing issues, weak product imagery placeholders) — but Max only fed it a website and three examples. With proper brand guidelines, fonts, and a product image bank uploaded, output quality goes up significantly.Claude Code → Figma integration:
Claude Code (not Claude Design) is what currently has the Figma MCP integration. Web Claude doesn't have full Figma access yet.
Workflow: start a Claude Code chat, link an empty Figma file, prompt it to build an email and upload it to Figma. It writes the HTML, runs its own QA, and pushes the design straight into Figma as a fully editable file.
Once it's in Figma, you can edit images, swap backgrounds, replace copy — everything is a real Figma layer, not a flat image.Where Max sees this going:
Eventual Well Copy workflow: internal copy tool → connects to Claude Code → connects to Figma. Build the campaign calendar in chat → generate briefs → generate copy → click "send to design" → emails get plopped into Figma. Designer's role becomes review and refinement, not building from scratch.
Same shift will hit brands directly — Klaviyo will likely build something like this natively.
Big-picture take: content production is becoming a commodity. The moat shifts to taste, analysis, and strategy. That's why Well Copy is repositioning as a retention agency and adding retention strategy calls — not just email performance reviews.Action items from this segment:
Post Claude Design / Claude Code + Figma workflow tutorial in Slack with prompts, assets, and HTML-to-design steps. (322s)
Create Claude Design system per brand using website URL. (424s)
---
ChatGPT Image Generation Update for Email Design (27:02–30:04)
Quick comparison demo. Max ran the same Happy Being prompt through the new ChatGPT image gen update — gave it brand guidelines, example emails, and asked for a "spring is here" email.
ChatGPT generated the full email in ~10 seconds. Quality was close to what his team would produce (some spacing/sizing nits — buttons too small, etc.).
Tradeoffs vs. Claude Design:
ChatGPT is faster and not credit-gated (covered under your standard plan vs. Claude credits which add up fast).
ChatGPT output is a flat image — you can't edit directly. You'd need to download, slice in Figma, then upload to Klaviyo. Claude Design gives you live editability.
Max plans to do a full comparison video across all the major AI design tools soon.Action item: Run Nano Banana e-commerce email test; include in the AI design comparison video. (1964s)

---
Q&A #1 — Aven: Rolling Out Claude Design With an Existing Design Team (19:17–27:02)
Question: Aven already delegated design to a team. How should he introduce Claude Design without spooking them about being replaced?
Max's answer:
Be honest. The framing isn't "AI replaces designers" — it's "designers who use AI become more valuable." A designer who can manage 20 brands instead of 6 is worth more, and pay scales with that capacity.
Pay for the tool yourself. Tell the team "experiment, don't worry about credits, spend the rest of the day messing around with this and watching tutorials."
Don't roll it out as a productivity mandate — roll it out as exploration. As soon as Max has a scalable system in place at Well Copy, he'll share it.
---
Q&A #2 — Biel: Converting One-Time Buyers to Subscribers (Spain Supplement Brand) (36:00–45:00)
Context: Biel runs a Spain-based supplement brand (3 single products at €29/mo + a 3-product bundle at €70/mo). Subscription culture in Spain is ~5 years behind the US — biggest subscription brand in the country only does $35–50M. Single products don't have positive unit economics, so they only run subscription on the bundle.
Question 1: Best way to convert one-time buyers to subscribers?
Max's answer:
The biggest lever is the post-purchase upsell page (AfterSell). This is where the customer is warmest — right after they buy. Test the hell out of subscription upsells here. Specifically test: 1x → subscription, 1x → bundle one-time, 1x → subscription bundle. Track which gives the best return.
Email's role is supporting, not primary. If someone bought a one-time product, they've already mentally decided "I'm trying it before I commit." Pushing subscription on day 4 is bad timing — they still have a 30-day supply.
Recommended sequence for one-time buyers:
Hard hit on the AfterSell post-purchase page.
7-day educational sequence about the product and how to use it.
Slow down to ~1 email/week until day 30–40.
Days 30–40 (when they're running out): subscription offer email — "Did you like it? Time to rebuy. Here's the subscription offer."
Email won't carry the weight the AfterSell page does — but the timing of the day 30–40 email captures real intent.Question 2: Best way to convert single-product buyers to the bundle?
Max's answer:
Nothing magic. Send 3–4 campaigns/week and consistently highlight the bundle. People who like your product will eventually buy the bundle on their own — especially during seasonal/promo sales where the bundle is featured.
Two specific tactics:
Add a "click here to swap to our bundle" quick action link in the billing reminder email.
Once a month, send a dedicated bundle-focused campaign.
Don't overthink it. Volume + consistent visibility wins.Action items from this segment:
Test AfterSell upsells: 1x → subscription, 1x → bundle, 1x → subscription bundle. (2330s)
Build 7-day education flow for 1x buyers; then weekly cadence until day 30–40 reorder push. (2450s)
Add bundle-swap quick action to billing reminder; send monthly bundle-highlight campaign. (2720s)
---
Q&A #3 — Aven: Surveys & Cancel Flow Insights for Subscription Churn (46:17–51:53)
Context: Aven is working a subscription brand with churn spiking at months 6–8 (unusually late). They've been running third-party Gather surveys (with AI but realistic-sounding) to understand churn reasons.
Question: Has Max tested surveys outside the cancel flow itself to win back churned subscribers?
Max's answer:
Most of the data Max needs comes from the Skio cancel flow itself (also passed into Klaviyo as profile properties — lets you build cancel-reason-specific email variants in Klaviyo's cancel flow).
Outside of that, Well Copy keeps it simple — sometimes just plain Google Forms for high 8-figure brands. Zembula and similar tools also have native survey functionality if you're already on those platforms.
Push back on long cancel flows. If the #1 reason is "too much product," you don't need a 10-email cancel sequence. Send 1–2 emails right away (educate on pause/skip/delay options), then maybe one more a few weeks later. After that, the regular 3–4x/week campaign cadence does the heavy lifting on win-backs naturally.
The cancel flow's job is fast education on flexibility — not aggressive convincing.
---
Q&A #4 — Adam: Failed Payment Recovery + Subscription Upsells (52:05–60:33)
Context: Adam runs a supplement brand with strong retention (~97% on first rebill across 7K subscribers) — but most of the churn is failed payments, not active cancellations.
Question 1: How does Well Copy handle failed payment recovery flows?
Max's answer:
Keep it simple but go heavy on volume. 15+ plain text emails minimum across the failed payment journey.
Build it in Klaviyo using the "payment failed" trigger with conditional splits on the count: payment failed = 1 → email 1, payment failed = 2 → email 2 (slightly more urgent), etc. Skio retries the card automatically — Klaviyo emails fire alongside each retry.
Add SMS or WhatsApp on top for additional touch.
Once a subscription is fully canceled because of repeated failures, hit them again with another wave of "update your card" emails.
All plain text — no designed HTML. Plain text outperforms here every time.Question 2: Anything special on Klaviyo vs. Skio's native failed payment emails?
Max's answer: Well Copy keeps Skio's native emails off and runs everything through Klaviyo. Cleaner attribution, more control over flow logic.
Question 3: Best place to upsell/cross-sell active subscribers?
Max's answer:
The billing reminder email is the most underused real estate in subscription email. Subscribers see this every month — most brands let it sit static.
Use Skio/Recharge/Loop quick action links so subscribers can add a one-time item to their next order without re-entering payment info.
Tactic: cross-sell based on what they already subscribe to (creatine subscribers → protein cross-sell). Build separate billing reminder flows by product if your subscription mix justifies it.
When you launch a new product or flavor — add a quick action link to the billing reminder for the next month so subscribers can swap into it in one click.Question 4: Optimal timing for billing reminder — 24 hours, 48 hours, 10 days?
Max's answer:
10 days lifts performance numbers but increases cancellations because subscribers have time to think about canceling.
24 hours feels urgent and forces faster decisions.
Well Copy's standard is 3 days out — best balance.Action items from this segment:
DM Max the Phoenix subscriptions failed-payment metrics + flows for review. (3384s)
DM Max the billing reminder email with quick actions for review. (3554s)

lessons.title: [April 17th] $100M Funnel + Breakdown
lessons.description:
Watch Call Recording >>
Summary below 👇

---
Opening & Housekeeping (0:00–7:00)
Heelys tangent that went for several minutes — legitimately ended with you deciding to buy a pair in NYC next month and record an Instagram series in Meta glasses frolicking around Central Park doing email teardowns. Travel logistics: quick stop in Vegas to establish Nevada residency via DMV, flying to Austin tonight to speak at an e-com event Monday (welcome flow vs. post-purchase "battle of the flows"), then Portugal for the team retreat (~15 people), then NYC for a month, then Europe summer tour (Barcelona, Marbella, Greece, probably Prague).
Austin BBQ recommendation landed: Terry Black's over Franklin's.

---
Mars Men Funnel Teardown — The Subscription Acquisition Playbook (7:00–23:00)
Walkthrough of the Mars Men funnel — men's testosterone supplement, subscription-only, scaled to $100M in 18 months after raising $28M. Founder is Zach Stuck (sold Homestead agency, built this in the background). Personal connection — meeting one of the founders this weekend.
Front-end offer. 50% off + $70 in free gifts (travel tin, testosterone e-book, month of a bladder workout app, Apple Watch raffle) + 90-day money-back guarantee. Guarantee likely hard to actually collect on — classic gray-hat subscription play.
Ethics flag. Mars Men ghosts subscribers, skips billing reminders, makes cancellation nearly impossible (email support only). Front-end acquisition is world-class. Retention mechanics are ethically questionable. Worth noting for anyone planning to copy the model — you're copying a machine that burns long-term trust for short-term LTV.
Ad strategy. 430 live ads. Top performer: "We made too much Mars Men, please help us empty our warehouse" — running since August, simple warehouse photo, highlights free gift. Max instructed his team to recreate this format across client brands. Heavy on static and AI statics (more than expected for this vertical, where video usually dominates).
Two main traffic destinations.
Quiz funnel (~50% of traffic). Health brands are the only category where quizzes still print. Regardless of answer path, the quiz concludes "you're fucked, testosterone declining." Reframes the buyer into a problem state. Max's client pitched copying the quiz for a seasoning brand — doesn't translate. Quizzes work when the category is problem/identity-driven (health, weight loss, skin), not product preference.Educational landing pages. Never the PDP. Headlines are the most tested asset — "Torch Stubborn Belly Fat," "Your Natural Testosterone Upgrade." Listicles ("10 Reasons Why…") everywhere. Advertorials still running. Pop-up fires ~2 seconds on every landing page.Pop-up offer = site offer. No extra discount layered in the pop-up. Just the 50% subscription offer repeated. CPG prediction: this stops working in ~12 months as customers wise up. Until then — reclaimed margin on pop-up opt-ins is the glory window for subscription CPG.
Email cadence. 5 emails day 1, 3 day 2, 3 day 3, 2 day 4. Insanity. Only works because subscription = first purchase is the entire game. Every day cold = lost forever. Meta compounds this — once a user clicks a Mars Men ad, their feed floods with competing testosterone brands. Drilling the prospect while attention is yours is the whole strategy.
Welcome flow. Immediate founder email → second email 2 hours later → daily thereafter for 7 days of product-usage education → regular campaigns.
SMS. Daily. Welcome SMS day 1. Images selective — only when they contribute to the sale (ingredients visual, us-vs-them, new product). 3x the cost of plain text.
Browse Abandon. Daily. Email 1, reminder, $10 extra off day 3, text-based last chance.
Key thesis. Inbox aggression is going to get worse across DTC. Even non-subscription brands will move this direction. Frequency is becoming king. Subscription brands doing this today are ahead of where non-sub brands will be in 12 months.

---
Q&A: SMS Images — When They're Worth the Cost (23:00–28:40)
Question (Aven): When to include images in SMS vs. keep plain?
Max's answer:
Decision framework is net profit, not ROAS. Images always drive more revenue, but cost 3x per message. Real example: plain SMS made $1K on $150 cost (8x ROI). Image SMS made $2.2K on $500 cost (4x ROI). ROI halved, but net profit nearly doubled. If the brand cares about net profit (most do), images win.
Qualifier: Images only when they contribute to the sale. Decoration gets zero. Legitimate uses: infographics, us-vs-them comparison tables, product reveals, new launches. Default ratio: 80% plain / 20% image.
Welcome flow = fine to use images for brand-setting infographics. Campaigns = sparingly, especially for large lists where send cost compounds.

---
Q&A: Climbn Electrolyte Brand — Pre-Launch Pop-Up & Funnel Diagnosis (28:40–40:00)
Question (Jacob): New to email. Desktop pop-up converting 8%, mobile at 0.9%. What's wrong?
Max's diagnosis:
Funnel issues layered on top of each other:
Conflicting offers. Site-wide 20% off banner competing with the 25% pop-up. When the pop-up offer looks barely better than what's already visible, it loses urgency.
Pre-launch intent problem. Product doesn't ship until May 1. Visitors are low-intent — nothing to buy yet, so why opt in? This is the biggest factor.
Mobile form is overdesigned. Busy background, too-small email field, too-small CTA button.
Mobile-specific trigger misfires. Exit-intent and scroll-depth triggers can't reliably track thumb behavior on mobile. Kill both. Use time delay only (3 seconds is fine).Strategic fix on positioning:
Remove the discount from the embedded waitlist form. Reframe embed as "Sign up for early access." Keep the real offer (discount + free gifts + early access) exclusive to the pop-up. Makes the pop-up feel special instead of redundant.
Quiz recommendation: skip it for now. Quizzes work in health when you can hit someone with "you're fucked." Electrolytes don't have a natural "you're deficient" hook strong enough to sustain a quiz. Possibly worth testing post-launch when the brand has legs.
Action items (Jacob): Kill exit/scroll triggers, 3s time delay, plain background test, bigger email field + CTA, rewrite embedded form as "early access" without discount, keep pop-up as the exclusive offer mechanism.

---
Q&A: Copy-What-Works Strategy (53:00–56:00)
Question (Shashi): Is it fine to just find top brands, copy what they do, test, and move to the next?
Max's answer:
That's literally the strategy. Full stop.

Q&A: Climbing Gifting Brand — Price Point & Product-Market Fit (40:00–52:30)
Question (Haadi): UK brand, £60K/month, breakeven on revenue (not profit — revenue). Climbing-themed gift product at a premium price point. What to do?
Max's diagnosis:
Brutal reality: the funnel is fine. The ads are fine. The offer is fine. The pop-up is fine. Nothing is broken.

Day 2: how to get the most from the product

net profit, not ROAS.

Images only when they contribute to the sale. Decoration gets zero. Legitimate uses: infographics, us-vs-them comparison tables, product reveals, new launches. Default ratio: 80% plain / 20% image.

lessons.title: [April 10th] Industry Updates + Q&A
lessons.description:
Watch Call Recording >>
Summary below 👇

---
Opening & Housekeeping (0:00–2:15)
Light opener — banter about Facebook being "for old people," jorts making a comeback, and back pain. Quick rally for Micheál's ongoing entrepreneur competition vote. Then straight into tooling updates and Q&A.

---
Tooling & AI Updates — Where the Industry Is Heading (2:15–14:00)
Max walked through what's coming and what Well Copy is building behind the scenes.
Klaviyo Composer (waitlist/beta): AI email creative feature built natively inside Klaviyo. Pulls from Shopify product images, helps create emails, audits flows, assists with segmentation. Max applied for the waitlist despite being Klaviyo's biggest referrer — they haven't given him access yet. Prediction: this is the direction the entire industry is moving.
Key thesis on AI email design: Pretty emails convert roughly the same as simple/messy emails on an email-by-email basis. Long-term, polished design helps brand equity and engagement rates. But speed is the real unlock — tools like Composer will compress design time dramatically, which matters more than aesthetic quality for most brands.
Manus (Meta-acquired AI platform): Max has been testing it. One-shot prompt with an example email and a brand website generated a converting email with AI-generated product imagery. Also using it to build a weekly automated DTC/e-com newsfeed pulled from his Twitter, Instagram, and industry sources. Not day-to-day chat material (Claude wins for that), but strong for bigger automated workflows. Connects directly to Klaviyo and Instagram.
Current Well Copy approach: Still designing in Figma. AI used only for image asset generation inside emails (backgrounds, product imagery). No full AI email generation yet — but will shift the moment it's usable and the team will hear first.
Internal tool build: Klaviyo now integrated with Well Copy's internal tool. Building out dashboards + AI chatbot for brand analysis — Flaunt-style. Will replace manual reporting work once shipped.
Custom Claude project (in progress): Max moved off ChatGPT entirely. Building an upgraded version of his "email marketing brain" — potentially shipped as a Claude-coded app for copy, calendars, strategy support.
Figma mix-and-match template library: Updated version dropped in chat. Tons more bridge sections, testimonial layouts, product sections to piece together full emails faster.
Action item: Save the mix-and-match templates.

---
Q&A: Shopify Transactional Emails in Klaviyo (14:00–17:15)
Question (Chelsea): Can only get "order delivered" working in Klaviyo — struggling with order confirmation migration and the required code snippets.
Max's answer:
Most brands leave order confirmation in Shopify by default — but it's possible to migrate fully. Requires direct communication with Shopify to turn off their native sends. May require Shopify Plus. Max confirmed Well Copy does this for select brands and that subscription brands especially migrate fully to control the post-purchase experience end-to-end.
Action item (Max): Confirm with team and update Chelsea in Slack.

---
Q&A: Trade Show Email Capture Strategy (17:15–25:22)
Question (Cade): Does hair-industry trade shows. QR code + giveaway (free product for a year) → 2,000+ sign-ups per show. Anything better?
Max's answer:
Giveaway is still the right mechanic — but tie the prize to your product (not Birkins, not trips). Product-tied giveaways filter for real intent. Monthly giveaways kill conversion because buyers wait to see if they won — announce winners ASAP.
The real upgrade: reframe the booth offer. The moment someone walks up to the booth is the warmest they will ever be. Two days is already too cold.
New pitch: "Buy now at X% off before the giveaway is announced. If you win, we'll refund your purchase and you still get the prize." Removes the wait-to-see downside, converts warm traffic immediately.
Hormozi principle: if you don't close them on the spot, you've probably lost them. Give them every reason to buy now, not later.
Action item (Cade): Update trade show messaging — add the "buy now + refund if you win" mechanic.

---
Q&A: Affiliate Tracking Without Discounts (25:22–29:45)
Question (Micheál): Wants to activate sponsored athletes as affiliates but refuses to allow discounts (brand positioning). Any way to track without codes?
Max's answer:
No. Links or codes are the only attribution mechanisms. Links break on organic mentions — someone sees an athlete post, Googles the brand, buys later, no attribution. That's the cost of the no-discount stance.
Broader thesis on where e-commerce is heading: Every platform will have its own storefront (Instagram Shop, TikTok Shop, eventually Twitter Shop). Technology always moves toward lowest friction. Websites become less central over time. Entire agency categories will emerge around platform-specific storefront optimization. Eventually, AI assistants will buy on our behalf directly from what we see.

---
Q&A: Cold Email for Wholesale / B2B (50:00–55:28)
Question (Micheál): Interested in cold emailing boxing gyms for wholesale hand-wrap placements. How to approach?
Max's answer:
Cold email is a completely different game than e-com email marketing. Two viable paths, nothing in between:
Path 1 — Volume automation. How Max scaled Well Copy from 10 to 30 clients. 120 domains, ~30 emails/day each, ~5 replies/day. Short, snappy, to the point. Requires significant setup (domain warming, deliverability infrastructure, list sourcing).
Path 2 — Manual hyper-personalization. Build a list of 50 ideal gyms. Find every employee's email, Instagram, LinkedIn. Hit them across every platform with an opener that is clearly not AI — pull a detail from their Google Maps photos (sign on the wall, equipment, something specific). Lead with that, then pitch.
For Micheál at his stage, path 2 is the right move. Response rates are high when the first line proves you're human.

---
Q&A: Free Audit Funnel Delivery (31:00–37:25)
Question (Mapa): Built an AI-powered personalized audit tool on Lovable — delivers a custom PDF via a tool called Recent, goal is getting people to book a consultation call. Worried about being too sales-y, especially for European audiences.
Max's answer:
Nobody wants to get on a call. You have to frame it as saving time, not "let's talk."
Two options:
Option 1 — Partial delivery. Deliver 1 pillar of the audit in the PDF. "Want the other 4 pillars? Book a call." Natural friction → opt-in.
Option 2 — Full delivery + bonus-gated call. Deliver the full PDF. Offer a 90-day roadmap, personal audit of additional assets, or a tailored implementation plan as call-only bonuses. This is how Hormozi's Scaling Roadmap funnel runs.
Referenced Max's own webinar funnel from the previous Tuesday — registration thank-you page offered a 15-minute call to apply the system directly instead of sitting through the 90-minute webinar. Quite a few call bookings came from that reframe alone.
Action item (Mapa): Draft the delivery email with either partial PDF + call CTA or full PDF + call-gated bonuses.

---
Campaign Philosophy — Max's Core Frameworks (41:30–46:00)
Max walked through sections of his internal training doc in progress.
Attribution reality check. Klaviyo's 5-day opens/clicks default makes email look like 40% of revenue. Switch to 1-day click attribution and that number collapses to 5–10%. The goal of email isn't direct-click conversion — it's frequency and staying top of mind. Max rarely buys directly from an email. He opens, absorbs, and purchases later when the need hits. Instant Hydration got his purchase this way. That's the real mechanism.
Graphic vs. text ratio. 75/25 graphic-to-text. Too much text = unsubscribes unless the value is undeniable.
Specificity sells. "How our product supports your overall health" dies. "How magnesium improves your REM sleep" wins. Never list all benefits. Pick one, go deep. General benefits emails convert poorly.
Discounts with a twist. Plain 10% off is dead. Change the framing — make it a credit, bundle it, add urgency, layer it into a theme. Something other than a flat percentage.
5 content pillars for campaigns: Educational, social proof, community/brand, product/collection highlights, sales. Even mix across the month.
Microtopics over macrotopics. "Why most green powders taste terrible" beats "The benefits of our green powder." Zero in.
Recurring themes. Weekly gets tired. Bi-weekly to monthly works. Well Copy's German car accessory brand runs "Build of the Week" (user-submitted customer cars) — top-performing email every time. Another brand runs monthly staff picks. A urology brand runs bi-weekly "Ask a Urologist." Recurring = anticipated = opened.
Segmentation. 90% of sends go to 90-day engaged. 1–2 sends per month to the entire list for big sales or product launches. Layered interest segments help (e.g., pre-workout campaign → engaged + pre-workout viewers). Targeted campaigns outside of regional use cases usually aren't worth the time.

---
Q&A: Recurring Theme Design — Templated or Fresh Each Time (46:15–49:30)
Question (Mapa): For recurring themed emails, use a template or design fresh every time?
Max's answer:
Always fresh. Templates dull the brand over time. "Build of the Week" runs weekly with completely different designs every send — keeps the subscriber on their toes.
For B2B / personal newsletters (Max's own), a consistent layout is fine — logo, photo, body, value, email inspiration section, footer. The meat is different each time, the container stays the same. Works because the value is in the writing, not the design.
For e-com: switch it up. Templates kill engagement.

---
Q&A: Clothing Brand Email Strategy (59:00–1:02:30)
Question (Toni): How does "specificity sells" translate for clothing brands where there's nothing to educate on?
Max's answer:
Clothing is the opposite playbook. Nobody cares about education — they buy because they saw it on a model and want to look like that. Strategy flips to pure visual volume.
Show as many products as possible per email. Max pulled examples — 15–17 product images in a single email. Supplements convert on focused single-product deep-dives. Clothing converts on options. More options = more chances something catches the eye.
Apply specific themes to product dumps. Not "bestsellers." Instead: "Monday office," "spring evening," "athleisure edits," "what to wear to a wedding." Theme the dump.
Occasional educational emails on material/quality work — founder plain-text emails about fabric, fit, construction rip for clothing. Toni confirmed his founder plain-text emails on material choice have been his best-performing format. Max's response: keep doing it. Plain text always rips. But cap at 50/50 — ideal ratio is 75% graphic / 25% text, otherwise plain text loses its pattern-interrupt power.

---
Closing (1:04:50–1:05:15)
Wrapped with the usual DM invitation. Everyone should DM Max something in the next week for direct help.

Build a list of 50 ideal gyms. Find every employee's email, Instagram, LinkedIn. Hit them across every platform with an opener that is clearly not AI — pull a detail from their Google Maps photos (sign on the wall, equipment, something specific). Lead with that, then pitch.
For Micheál at his stage, path 2 is the right move. Response rates are high when the first line proves you're human.
Q&A: Free Audit Funnel Delivery (
Question (Mapa):

Built an AI-powered personalized audit tool on Lovable — delivers a custom PDF via a tool called Recent, goal is getting people to book a consultation call. Worried about being too sales-y, especially for European audiences.
Max's answer:
Nobody wants to get on a call. You have to frame it as saving time, not "let's talk."
Two options:
Option 1 — Partial delivery.
Deliver 1 pillar of the audit in the PDF. "Want the other 4 pillars? Book a call." Natural friction → opt-in.
Option 2 — Full delivery + bonus-gated call.
Deliver the full PDF. Offer a 90-day roadmap, personal audit of additional assets, or a tailored implementation plan as call-only bonuses. This is how Hormozi's Scaling Roadmap funnel runs.

Referenced Max's own webinar funnel from the previous Tuesday — registration thank-you page offered a 15-minute call to apply the system directly instead of sitting through the 90-minute webinar. Quite a few call bookings came from that reframe alone.
Action item (Mapa):
Draft the delivery email with either partial PDF + call CTA or full PDF + call-gated bonuses.
Campaign Philosophy — Max's Core Frameworks (
Max walked through sections of his internal training doc in progress.
Attribution reality check.

Klaviyo's 5-day opens/clicks default makes email look like 40% of revenue. Switch to 1-day click attribution and that number collapses to 5–10%. The goal of email isn't direct-click conversion — it's frequency and staying top of mind. Max rarely buys directly from an email. He opens, absorbs, and purchases later when the need hits. Instant Hydration got his purchase this way. That's the real mechanism.
Graphic vs. text ratio.
75/25 graphic-to-text. Too much text = unsubscribes unless the value is undeniable.
Specificity sells.
"How our product supports your overall health" dies. "How magnesium improves your REM sleep" wins. Never list all benefits. Pick one, go deep. General benefits emails convert poorly.
Discounts with a twist.
Plain 10% off is dead. Change the framing — make it a credit, bundle it, add urgency, layer it into a theme. Something other than a flat percentage.
5 content pillars for campaigns:
Educational, social proof, community/brand, product/collection highlights, sales. Even mix across the month.
Microtopics over macrotopics.
"Why most green powders taste terrible" beats "The benefits of our green powder." Zero in.
Recurring themes.

Weekly gets tired. Bi-weekly to monthly works. Well Copy's German car accessory brand runs "Build of the Week" (user-submitted customer cars) — top-performing email every time. Another brand runs monthly staff picks. A urology brand runs bi-weekly "Ask a Urologist." Recurring = anticipated = opened.
Segmentation.

90% of sends go to 90-day engaged. 1–2 sends per month to the entire list for big sales or product launches. Layered interest segments help (e.g., pre-workout campaign → engaged + pre-workout viewers). Targeted campaigns outside of regional use cases usually aren't worth the time.
Q&A: Recurring Theme Design — Templated or Fresh Each Time (
Question (Mapa):
For recurring themed emails, use a template or design fresh every time?
Max's answer:
Always fresh. Templates dull the brand over time. "Build of the Week" runs weekly with completely different designs every send — keeps the subscriber on their toes.

For B2B / personal newsletters (Max's own), a consistent layout is fine — logo, photo, body, value, email inspiration section, footer. The meat is different each time, the container stays the same. Works because the value is in the writing, not the design.
For e-com: switch it up. Templates kill engagement.
Q&A: Clothing Brand Email Strategy (
Question (Toni):
How does "specificity sells" translate for clothing brands where there's nothing to educate on?
Max's answer:
Clothing is the opposite playbook. Nobody cares about education — they buy because they saw it on a model and want to look like that. Strategy flips to pure visual volume.
Show as many products as possible per email.

Max pulled examples — 15–17 product images in a single email. Supplements convert on focused single-product deep-dives. Clothing converts on options. More options = more chances something catches the eye.
Apply specific themes to product dumps.
Not "bestsellers." Instead: "Monday office," "spring evening," "athleisure edits," "what to wear to a wedding." Theme the dump.
Occasional educational emails on material/quality

work — founder plain-text emails about fabric, fit, construction rip for clothing. Toni confirmed his founder plain-text emails on material choice have been his best-performing format. Max's response: keep doing it. Plain text always rips. But cap at 50/50 — ideal ratio is 75% graphic / 25% text, otherwise plain text loses its pattern-interrupt power.
Closing (
Wrapped with the usual DM invitation. Everyone should DM Max something in the next week for direct help.

Summary below 👇

---
Opening & Housekeeping (0:00–3:15)
Light opener — Max joking about being cursed with Instagram perfectionism and never taking notes in school. Quick check-in with Micheál on his entrepreneur competition vote (daily voting mechanic tied to charity donations — making it tough to sustain engagement from supporters). Max committed to voting daily and rallied the group to do the same.

Pixel Picasso — Email of the Week Awards & Design Inspiration (3:15–16:00)
Max walked through the latest batch of Pixel Picasso candidates — the internal $100 bonus award for the most creative email design across ~130 client accounts. Full showcase of recent work including:
Calendar layout for an anniversary sale
Double urgency (time-limited + first 100 people) discount framing
Puzzle piece hero sections, Tinder-style swipe layouts, crossword puzzles with embedded discount codes
AI-generated "starter pack" and "cartoonified" product imagery
Netflix-style email with AI-generated movie posters featuring products
Photo galleries (especially strong for fashion brands)
