He acknowledged the tension — he loves the creative output, but the most creative emails often don't drive the most sales. Needs to re-gamify the award to balance creativity with conversion performance.
Mix & Match Templates: Max resurfaced the mix-and-match email section templates (hero, bridge, testimonial, product, photo gallery sections you combine to build full emails). Current version is outdated but a fully refreshed version is coming in the next couple weeks, exclusive to the community.
Action item: Post mix-and-match templates link in Slack/Skool.

---
Top 15 Performing Email Templates — March Pack (16:00–19:30)
Max walked through the monthly template pack — the 15 best-performing (not most creative) emails from the previous month, delivered as reusable templates.
Highlights:
AI image extender trick: extend product images so designs flow with one coherent image/color throughout rather than blocked sections
WhatsApp-style chat email template
Step-by-step sale instructions (add item → spend threshold → use code)
High-placement abandonment email with discount and dynamic section above the fold
Benefits email with us-vs-them section
"Are you a bot?" Google CAPTCHA-style creative email
Simple FAQ email layout
Review email with photo gallery
---
A/B Test Roundup — March Results (19:30–23:00)
Max reviewed the month's top A/B tests across client accounts:
Full-page vs. standard pop-up: Full page wins. Consistently. Always. Max has tested with Alia multiple times — good pop-ups increase overall site conversions.
Plain text vs. designed welcome email: Designed email got significantly higher click rates this round.
Mystery offer pop-up vs. standard discount: Mystery discount outperformed. "Mystery discount" also beat "mystery percent off" as copy framing.
Abandonment time delay — 30 min vs. 1 hour: 30 minutes won (0.3% vs. 0.1% placed order rate).
Hybrid plain text email: Plain text got more clicks, but hybrid (plain text layout with images inserted at top) drove more actual sales/conversions. Worth testing.
Discount placement — above hero vs. below hero: Above hero won. Always place discounts as high in the email as possible.
Mystery discount in abandonment flow: 6.7% click rate vs. 3.2% for a flat 15% off. 3.5% placed order rate vs. 2.4%. Mystery discount crushes in abandon cart/checkout.
Welcome offer test ($25 vs. 10% vs. free gift): $25 off won with 32 orders vs. 20 (10%) and 10 (free gift) — despite $25 and 10% being effectively the same dollar value on a ~$250 AOV. Free gift (which the brand had run for years) was the worst performer.
Pop-up X button — top right vs. top left (mobile): Moving the X to the top left increased conversions 25–50%. Can do natively in Alia; workaround needed in Klaviyo.
CTA copy — "Shop Now" vs. "Magic Button": Magic Button won (0.87% vs. 0.62% click rate).
Scratch-to-reveal pop-up: Beat standard pop-up (~6% vs. ~4%) for a brand that's been stuck under 6% for two years of weekly testing.
SMS with image vs. without: Image version drove more revenue ($2,300 more) but costs 3x per message. Factor in economics.
Mystery discount welcome email vs. flat 10% off: Mystery discount won again.
---
Q&A: Design-Heavy vs. Simple Emails — Finding the Balance (23:07–27:00)
Question (Aven): How do you find the line between design-heavy creative emails and simple emails that convert better?
Max's answer:
There's no number you can assign to it. It's brand representation and feel. Both approaches work — it depends on how the brand wants to be perceived.
Plain text rips. Design-heavy rips. What matters most for long-term list health is mixing it up.
Brands that stick to one template or one style see declining engagement over time. People crave newness. The thrill of "what's next?" keeps subscribers opening.
Pattern interrupts always pop — make an email look like a 1930s newspaper article, do something unexpected, keep the list on their toes.
When stuff gets stale, inject a pattern interrupt. It resets engagement.
Unsubscribes are higher and subscriber LTV is lower for brands that only do one style (all simple or all plain text).
---
Q&A: Day & Time Consistency for Sends (27:00–29:40)
Question: Does the "newness" principle apply to send day and time, or should those stay consistent?
Max's answer:
Lean toward consistency on day/time. Get the list to expect when emails are coming.
But it's contextual to the audience. Max shared an analysis across brands:
Home cleaning brand targeting moms → Sunday/Monday/Tuesday performed best (beginning-of-week planning behavior).
Performance supplement brand targeting busy entrepreneurs → Thursday/Friday/Saturday performed best (too busy Mon–Tue to even think about purchasing).
Max's newsletter: consistent Monday/Wednesday/Friday sends. People expect it.
You don't restrict yourself to only sending on your best days — you still send other days. But lean into what works.
Optional: run a recurring series on a specific day (e.g., Sunday email series) to build habitual engagement.
---
Q&A: Landing Page Pop-Up Conversion Tanked — Diagnosis (29:40–38:25)
Question (Mapa): Has a landing page with a quiz-style pop-up (5 options). Was converting well, then suddenly tanked last week. No changes made. Three theories: too many quiz options, incentive copy isn't enticing enough, or mobile design is off without an image.
Max's answer:
First question: Why did it drop? If nothing changed on the form, it's either (1) natural statistical variability from low traffic volume, (2) a change in traffic source/quality, or (3) something conflicting on the page.
Low traffic = high variability. At 12K visitors/month you'll see bigger swings. 500K visitor brands stay near the mean. Smaller volume means more randomness.
Traffic source matters. Mapa confirmed they recently added Google Ads. New traffic source = new audience behavior = old conversion benchmarks are invalid. Need to re-test from scratch.
Conflicting offers: Check if anything on the landing page undermines the pop-up offer (e.g., a bigger site-wide discount making the pop-up feel weak).
On the quiz itself: Fewer options = less cognitive load = higher conversion. 5 options is overwhelming. Best quiz question: something brain-dead simple. Max's favorite: "Who are you shopping for?" → Men / Women / Both. Zero thought required.
Images on mobile pop-ups: Generally don't help. Simple forms with minimal distractions convert best. Offer + opt-in, nothing else.Action item (Mapa): Rebuild the pop-up with 3 options max, no mobile image, simplified copy. Test against current version. Report back next week.

---
Max's Daily Schedule & Time Management Philosophy (39:26–44:00)
Mapa asked how Max does everything he does. Max broke down his daily structure:
4:30 AM wake-up.
5:00–9:00 AM: Deep work. No calls. No Slack. No email. Only needle-moving work — content, team trainings, webinar prep, business growth initiatives. This 4-hour block produces more output than most people's full workday.
9:00–11:00 AM: Calls.
11:00 AM–12:00 PM: Break.
12:00–3:00 PM: Internal calls, partner calls, business development.
2:00/3:00–5:00 PM: Deep work or content recording.Key philosophy — "Slack-a-mole": Most fires and Slack messages can wait. Max stopped responding to everything immediately and started batching communication into dedicated windows. Nothing exploded. Clients didn't leave. Mentorship members didn't quit. The quality of responses actually improved because he answers with full attention instead of reactive half-answers.

---
How Max Reviews Every Email Across 130 Clients (44:00–46:30)
2-hour time block every Friday (inside the 5–9 AM deep work window).
Executive assistant compiles all client emails into a review queue.
Max pulls up ~20 client Figma boards at a time, speed-runs through them, drops comments on anything off-standard or noteworthy.
Not reading every word — scanning for quality, best practices, and repeat mistakes.
If the same mistake appears multiple times, he DMs the team member directly on Slack.
Account managers handle pre-send approval, not Max. He's the quality overlay, not the bottleneck.
---
Team Management & Delegation — The 10-80-10 Rule (46:30–49:10)
Max broke down his delegation framework:
Clear owners for every department. Head of design, head of copy, head of Klaviyo tech, head of AI. Max leads sales and marketing.
The 10-80-10 Rule: Max does the first 10% (idea, direction, groundwork), the owner does the middle 80% (execution), Max does the final 10% (review, polish, sign-off).
Ownership has to feel like theirs. People don't perform when they're just "Max's execution guy." They perform when it's their department, their client, their baby. Attach bonuses to outcomes. Let them run it their way.
Max's biggest lesson: he used to breathe down account managers' throats and dictate how to do everything. They couldn't execute his way — and their way was perfectly fine. Once he let go, client satisfaction actually went up.
"Nobody's going to be as good as you at doing things your way." Stop trying to clone yourself. Let people own it.
---
Q&A: Seasonal Flow Updates (49:10–51:25)
Question (Tristan): Do you change flows seasonally? How high-leverage is it?
Max's answer:
Fashion brands: Yes, roughly quarterly. Mainly product image swaps as bestsellers shift by season. Account managers have an internal clock for this. Not a full strategy overhaul — just updating what's being featured.
Supplement/consumable brands: Probably not worth the time. Could you update messaging to "get shredded for summer"? Sure. Will it move the needle meaningfully? Probably not enough to justify the effort.
Rule of thumb: update seasonally when products/bestsellers actually change. Don't force seasonal updates on brands where the product stays the same year-round.
---
Q&A: Continuous A/B Testing in Flows (51:25–53:15)
Question (Tristan): Once flows hit a good performance level, what do you keep testing? Do you ever stop?
Max's answer:
Never stop testing. Ever. Always have something running.
Easiest ongoing test: take your best-performing campaigns each month and A/B test them as replacements for underperforming flow emails.
Example: A text-based founder story campaign crushed as a one-off send. Take that email, add the welcome discount, and A/B test it against welcome flow email #3.
Well Copy has an internal A/B test Slack channel with a constant stream of new ideas from across the team. The volume of test ideas is unlimited when you have multiple people contributing.
---
Q&A: Aligning Email Messaging with Ad Angles (53:15–54:35)
Question (Tristan): How much do you coordinate email messaging with what the brand's ad team is running?
Max's answer:
Not deeply integrated with ad teams in practice. No formal process of pulling top-spend ad angles monthly.
What they do: ask clients in their monthly campaign planning form — "Any specific angles working well right now that we should know about?"
Can also check the brand's Meta ad library to see what's running.
It's loose and informal, not a rigid system. Works well enough without overcomplicating it.
---
Q&A: AI Reporting & Analytics Tools (54:35–60:00)
Question (Tristan): How are you using AI for reporting? Spending too much time manually reviewing Klaviyo accounts.
Max's answer:
Honest answer: they aren't fully using AI for reporting yet. It's a priority but not built out.
Hyro: Not AI — it's clean dashboards and report generators. Good for high-level numbers, month-over-month changes, and client-facing reports. Well Copy uses it and leaves notes on dashboards.
The AI limitation with Klaviyo: AI can pull numbers via API (subject lines, preview text, campaign names, KPIs) but cannot read email creatives — can't analyze copy, angles, or design. That's the gap.
Flaunt AI: The most advanced tool Max has found. Connects to Shopify + Klaviyo + anything else. Chat-based interface — ask any question and it pulls the data.
Example: Max asked for 6-month LTV split by first-time subscription vs. one-time order, broken out by product. Found an underrepresented product with high LTV and low subscription take rate → actionable insight for the brand's acquisition funnel.
You can schedule recurring prompts (e.g., every Monday: "What KPIs changed drastically? What's breaking?").
~$100/brand to start, decreasing with volume.
Max is trying to either partner with Flaunt AI or build the functionality internally with his AI developer.
Bottom line: Nothing replaces getting your hands dirty in Klaviyo and clicking around. That's still the best way to find insights.
---
Q&A: Free Shipping Threshold Strategy (1:00:04–1:06:40)
Question (Guery): Brand doing $20K/month top line, losing ~$4,400/month bottom line. $89 shaving kit, $32 COGS, $58 CAC on Meta. Can't afford free shipping on the kit alone. Should they add a free shipping threshold? How do brands handle it?
Max's answer:
Free shipping thresholds exist to increase AOV. Set the threshold above your current AOV, strategically aligned with your product pricing.
Example: If AOV is $45 and cheapest product is $20, set threshold at $50. Customer needs to add a $20 item to qualify — effectively doubling the order.
Don't set it at or below your AOV. Set it above, at a point where the customer has to add at least one more product.
For Guery's economics: the moisturizer (launching soon) could be the bundle play that makes free shipping viable. Without it, the margins are too thin on the shaving kit alone.
Could A/B test: send some traffic to a free-shipping version of the product page and compare CAC. Maybe the conversion lift makes the math work.
Bigger picture reframe: Most big replenishable brands are not profitable on first purchase. They're negative for the first 2–3 orders and profit on the 4th+. The game is backend LTV, subscription take rate, and repeat purchase — not first-order profitability.
Referenced Jordan Menard's talk on making high CAC work through backend optimization.Action item (Guery): DM Max the P&L, landing pages, and full funnel for a detailed review and free-shipping threshold recommendations.

---
Q&A: What Separates Founders Who Scale vs. Plateau (1:07:33–1:12:40)
Question (Micheál): What's the fundamental difference between founders who plateau and those who keep scaling?
Max's answer (raw, unfiltered):
Referenced Comfort's founder on the Operators Podcast — the clip about needing irrational, almost delusional self-confidence.
Max's personal frame: "Every room I walk in, I genuinely believe I'm the most competent person there. The only reason anyone's ahead of me is time and experience. Give me that, and I'd be miles ahead."
It's identity. You live up to exactly what you think you are. The founders who scale have internalized that they figure shit out. Period.
The downside: down months feel like personal failure. It's stress. It's not for everybody.
"If you really wanted it, you'd have it." If you're not where you want to be, you either don't want it bad enough, or you haven't let enough time pass. Both are true simultaneously.
But also: not everyone wants that life. Define what you're optimizing for. Comfortable growth is valid. Hyper-scaling comes with lawsuits, mental health strain, and personal sacrifice.
The brands Max has seen scale fastest all share one trait: the founder breathes confidence and refuses to let slowness happen.
---
Q&A: Key Metric for Months 6–12 of a New Brand (1:12:41–1:15:17)
Question (Micheál): Six months in, scaling every month. What's the one metric to compound from month 6 to 12?
Max's answer:
Customer retention rate. Without question.
The brands that scaled fastest built community from day one. That community becomes a cushion when ads are tough and acquisition gets expensive.
Example: The Black Stuff (Irish brand) — one guy, scaled fast, had a Facebook group of superfans who just loved the product. Even with ads off, people kept coming back.
For a clothing brand like Micheál's: community + new styles consistently = repeat purchases. Give people something to look forward to and keep coming back for.
Build community everywhere — email, Instagram, Facebook groups, wherever your audience lives.
---
Q&A: Finding & Building Trust with Key Hires (1:18:18–1:22:30)
Question (Micheál): How do you find people like Jesrin and Michael that you actually trust to run parts of the business?
Max's answer:
It starts with organic content. Every single early hire came from Max's online network built through posting on Twitter for 4 years.
Started at 50 followers. Engaged with other accounts, posted daily, slowly built an audience. When he eventually posted job openings, his followers — people who'd been watching the journey — applied.
Trust is earned over time, not given upfront. Jesrin earned trust over 3 months of crushing everything before getting keys to the credit cards. Michael worked 6 months before becoming Director of Ops.
Other people in your network amplify your job posts. Your "boys" retweet it, it reaches their audience, and you get warm applicants who already know your story.
Advice for brand owners starting out: The #1 skill to learn is organic marketing. It's free. When you don't have money, you have time. Content is the leverage.
Referenced Brian Blum as a go-to for organic content strategy.
Best-performing webinar ads for Max right now: not custom creative — just his best organic content repurposed with a CTA in the description. Lowest CPA by far ($0.72 vs. $3.50 for designed static ads).
---
Q&A: Content Recording Cadence — Batching vs. Daily (1:23:41–1:26:00)
Question (Mapa): Do you record content every day or batch it on one dedicated content day?
Max's answer:
Recording content is Max's least favorite thing in the world. He loves strategizing content and coming up with ideas. Hates filming.
Tried monthly batching → despised the day, kept putting it off, never happened.
Tried weekly batching → resented the day, kept pushing it, content didn't get made.
What works: one video per day, first thing in the morning. Lowest possible barrier to entry. Knock it out before anything else so it can't get pushed.
The short-form agency he works with needs 3 videos/week — only takes 10 minutes to record — and he still hasn't recorded in a month and a half because he keeps avoiding the batch session.
Lesson: if you hate something, make it bite-sized and daily. Don't let it accumulate into a session you'll dread and dodge.
---
Closing (1:26:00–1:27:00)
Max wrapped with a reminder to keep posting in the community, keep asking questions, and announced he'll run another design-of-the-day poll in the community.
Action item: Post design-of-the-day poll in community.

Question (Mapa):

Has a landing page with a quiz-style pop-up (5 options). Was converting well, then suddenly tanked last week. No changes made. Three theories: too many quiz options, incentive copy isn't enticing enough, or mobile design is off without an image.
Max's answer:
First question: Why did it drop?
If nothing changed on the form, it's either (1) natural statistical variability from low traffic volume, (2) a change in traffic source/quality, or (3) something conflicting on the page.
Low traffic = high variability. At 12K visitors/month you'll see bigger swings. 500K visitor brands stay near the mean. Smaller volume means more randomness.
Traffic source matters.
Mapa confirmed they recently added Google Ads. New traffic source = new audience behavior = old conversion benchmarks are invalid. Need to re-test from scratch.
Conflicting offers:
Check if anything on the landing page undermines the pop-up offer (e.g., a bigger site-wide discount making the pop-up feel weak).
On the quiz itself:

Fewer options = less cognitive load = higher conversion. 5 options is overwhelming. Best quiz question: something brain-dead simple. Max's favorite: "Who are you shopping for?" → Men / Women / Both. Zero thought required.
Images on mobile pop-ups:
Generally don't help. Simple forms with minimal distractions convert best. Offer + opt-in, nothing else.
Action item (Mapa):
Rebuild the pop-up with 3 options max, no mobile image, simplified copy. Test against current version. Report back next week.
Max's Daily Schedule & Time Management Philosophy (
Mapa asked how Max does everything he does. Max broke down his daily structure:
AM wake-up.
AM:

Deep work. No calls. No Slack. No email. Only needle-moving work — content, team trainings, webinar prep, business growth initiatives. This 4-hour block produces more output than most people's full workday.
AM:
Calls.
AM–
PM:
Break.
PM:
Internal calls, partner calls, business development.
PM:
Deep work or content recording.
Key philosophy — "Slack-a-mole":

Most fires and Slack messages can wait. Max stopped responding to everything immediately and started batching communication into dedicated windows. Nothing exploded. Clients didn't leave. Mentorship members didn't quit. The quality of responses actually improved because he answers with full attention instead of reactive half-answers.
How Max Reviews Every Email Across 130 Clients (
2-hour time block every Friday
(inside the 5–9 AM deep work window).
Executive assistant compiles all client emails into a review queue.
Max pulls up ~20 client Figma boards at a time, speed-runs through them, drops comments on anything off-standard or noteworthy.
Not reading every word — scanning for quality, best practices, and repeat mistakes.
If the same mistake appears multiple times, he DMs the team member directly on Slack.
Account managers handle pre-send approval, not Max. He's the quality overlay, not the bottleneck.
Team Management & Delegation — The 10-80-10 Rule (
Max broke down his delegation framework:
Clear owners for every department.
Head of design, head of copy, head of Klaviyo tech, head of AI. Max leads sales and marketing.
The 10-80-10 Rule:
Max does the first 10% (idea, direction, groundwork), the owner does the middle 80% (execution), Max does the final 10% (review, polish, sign-off).
Ownership has to feel like theirs.
People don't perform when they're just "Max's execution guy." They perform when it's their department, their client, their baby. Attach bonuses to outcomes. Let them run it their way.

Max's biggest lesson: he used to breathe down account managers' throats and dictate how to do everything. They couldn't execute his way — and their way was perfectly fine. Once he let go, client satisfaction actually went up.
"Nobody's going to be as good as you at doing things your way."
Stop trying to clone yourself. Let people own it.
Q&A: Seasonal Flow Updates (
Question (Tristan):
Do you change flows seasonally? How high-leverage is it?
Max's answer:
Fashion brands:

Yes, roughly quarterly. Mainly product image swaps as bestsellers shift by season. Account managers have an internal clock for this. Not a full strategy overhaul — just updating what's being featured.
Supplement/consumable brands:
Probably not worth the time. Could you update messaging to "get shredded for summer"? Sure. Will it move the needle meaningfully? Probably not enough to justify the effort.
Rule of thumb: update seasonally when products/bestsellers actually change. Don't force seasonal updates on brands where the product stays the same year-round.
Q&A: Continuous A/B Testing in Flows (
Question (Tristan):
Once flows hit a good performance level, what do you keep testing? Do you ever stop?
Max's answer:
Never stop testing. Ever.
Always have something running.
Easiest ongoing test: take your best-performing campaigns each month and A/B test them as replacements for underperforming flow emails.
Example: A text-based founder story campaign crushed as a one-off send. Take that email, add the welcome discount, and A/B test it against welcome flow email #3.
Well Copy has an internal A/B test Slack channel with a constant stream of new ideas from across the team. The volume of test ideas is unlimited when you have multiple people contributing.
Q&A: Aligning Email Messaging with Ad Angles (
Question (Tristan):
How much do you coordinate email messaging with what the brand's ad team is running?
Max's answer:
Not deeply integrated with ad teams in practice. No formal process of pulling top-spend ad angles monthly.
What they do: ask clients in their monthly campaign planning form — "Any specific angles working well right now that we should know about?"
Can also check the brand's Meta ad library to see what's running.
It's loose and informal, not a rigid system. Works well enough without overcomplicating it.
Q&A: AI Reporting & Analytics Tools (
Question (Tristan):
How are you using AI for reporting? Spending too much time manually reviewing Klaviyo accounts.
Max's answer:
Honest answer: they aren't fully using AI for reporting yet.
It's a priority but not built out.
Hyro:
Not AI — it's clean dashboards and report generators. Good for high-level numbers, month-over-month changes, and client-facing reports. Well Copy uses it and leaves notes on dashboards.
The AI limitation with Klaviyo:
AI can pull numbers via API (subject lines, preview text, campaign names, KPIs) but
cannot read email creatives
— can't analyze copy, angles, or design. That's the gap.
Flaunt AI:
The most advanced tool Max has found. Connects to Shopify + Klaviyo + anything else. Chat-based interface — ask any question and it pulls the data.

Example: Max asked for 6-month LTV split by first-time subscription vs. one-time order, broken out by product. Found an underrepresented product with high LTV and low subscription take rate → actionable insight for the brand's acquisition funnel.
You can schedule recurring prompts (e.g., every Monday: "What KPIs changed drastically? What's breaking?").
~$100/brand to start, decreasing with volume.
Max is trying to either partner with Flaunt AI or build the functionality internally with his AI developer.
Bottom line:
Nothing replaces getting your hands dirty in Klaviyo and clicking around. That's still the best way to find insights.
Q&A: Free Shipping Threshold Strategy (
Question (Guery):

Brand doing $20K/month top line, losing ~$4,400/month bottom line. $89 shaving kit, $32 COGS, $58 CAC on Meta. Can't afford free shipping on the kit alone. Should they add a free shipping threshold? How do brands handle it?
Max's answer:
Free shipping thresholds exist to increase AOV. Set the threshold
above
your current AOV, strategically aligned with your product pricing.
Example: If AOV is $45 and cheapest product is $20, set threshold at $50. Customer needs to add a $20 item to qualify — effectively doubling the order.
Don't set it at or below your AOV. Set it above, at a point where the customer has to add at least one more product.
For Guery's economics: the moisturizer (launching soon) could be the bundle play that makes free shipping viable. Without it, the margins are too thin on the shaving kit alone.
Could A/B test: send some traffic to a free-shipping version of the product page and compare CAC. Maybe the conversion lift makes the math work.
Bigger picture reframe:

Most big replenishable brands are not profitable on first purchase. They're negative for the first 2–3 orders and profit on the 4th+. The game is backend LTV, subscription take rate, and repeat purchase — not first-order profitability.
Referenced Jordan Menard's talk on making high CAC work through backend optimization.
Action item (Guery):
DM Max the P&L, landing pages, and full funnel for a detailed review and free-shipping threshold recommendations.
Q&A: What Separates Founders Who Scale vs. Plateau (
Question (Micheál):
What's the fundamental difference between founders who plateau and those who keep scaling?
Max's answer (raw, unfiltered):
Referenced Comfort's founder on the Operators Podcast — the clip about needing irrational, almost delusional self-confidence.

Max's personal frame: "Every room I walk in, I genuinely believe I'm the most competent person there. The only reason anyone's ahead of me is time and experience. Give me that, and I'd be miles ahead."
It's identity.
You live up to exactly what you think you are. The founders who scale have internalized that they figure shit out. Period.
The downside: down months feel like personal failure. It's stress. It's not for everybody.
"If you really wanted it, you'd have it."
If you're not where you want to be, you either don't want it bad enough, or you haven't let enough time pass. Both are true simultaneously.
But also: not everyone wants that life. Define what you're optimizing for. Comfortable growth is valid. Hyper-scaling comes with lawsuits, mental health strain, and personal sacrifice.
The brands Max has seen scale fastest all share one trait: the founder breathes confidence and refuses to let slowness happen.
Q&A: Key Metric for Months 6–12 of a New Brand (
Question (Micheál):
Six months in, scaling every month. What's the one metric to compound from month 6 to 12?
Max's answer:
Customer retention rate.
Without question.
The brands that scaled fastest built community from day one. That community becomes a cushion when ads are tough and acquisition gets expensive.
Example: The Black Stuff (Irish brand) — one guy, scaled fast, had a Facebook group of superfans who just loved the product. Even with ads off, people kept coming back.
For a clothing brand like Micheál's: community + new styles consistently = repeat purchases. Give people something to look forward to and keep coming back for.
Build community everywhere — email, Instagram, Facebook groups, wherever your audience lives.
Q&A: Finding & Building Trust with Key Hires (
Question (Micheál):
How do you find people like Jesrin and Michael that you actually trust to run parts of the business?
Max's answer:
It starts with organic content.
Every single early hire came from Max's online network built through posting on Twitter for 4 years.
Started at 50 followers. Engaged with other accounts, posted daily, slowly built an audience. When he eventually posted job openings, his followers — people who'd been watching the journey — applied.

Trust is earned over time, not given upfront. Jesrin earned trust over 3 months of crushing everything before getting keys to the credit cards. Michael worked 6 months before becoming Director of Ops.
Other people in your network amplify your job posts. Your "boys" retweet it, it reaches their audience, and you get warm applicants who already know your story.
Advice for brand owners starting out:
The #1 skill to learn is organic marketing. It's free. When you don't have money, you have time. Content is the leverage.
Referenced Brian Blum as a go-to for organic content strategy.

Best-performing webinar ads for Max right now: not custom creative — just his best organic content repurposed with a CTA in the description. Lowest CPA by far ($0.72 vs. $3.50 for designed static ads).
Q&A: Content Recording Cadence — Batching vs. Daily (
Question (Mapa):
Do you record content every day or batch it on one dedicated content day?
Max's answer:
Recording content is Max's least favorite thing in the world.
He loves strategizing content and coming up with ideas. Hates filming.
Tried monthly batching → despised the day, kept putting it off, never happened.
Tried weekly batching → resented the day, kept pushing it, content didn't get made.
What works: one video per day, first thing in the morning.
Lowest possible barrier to entry. Knock it out before anything else so it can't get pushed.
The short-form agency he works with needs 3 videos/week — only takes 10 minutes to record — and he still hasn't recorded in a month and a half because he keeps avoiding the batch session.
Lesson: if you hate something, make it bite-sized and daily. Don't let it accumulate into a session you'll dread and dodge.
Closing (
Max wrapped with a reminder to keep posting in the community, keep asking questions, and announced he'll run another design-of-the-day poll in the community.
Action item:
Post design-of-the-day poll in community.

lessons.title: [March 27th] Full Q&A Session
lessons.description:
Watch Video Recording >>
Summary below 👇

---
Opening & Housekeeping (0:00–4:09)
Max called in from a cafe in Vegas (switching hotels after Shop Talk, the big ecom event). No prep today — straight Q&A format. Barbie sent out the live notification. Max mentioned he won a client $100K in a lottery at one of the Shop Talk events (snuck in pretending to be a brand owner). Light banter about gambling plans for the weekend.

---
Mobile vs. Desktop Email Design & File Size / Clipping (4:09–11:25)
Question: Should you design separate mobile and desktop versions of emails in Klaviyo? And do long emails or GIFs cause Gmail clipping?
Max's answer:
90% of opens are mobile. Don't bother designing a desktop version — the time investment isn't worth the ROI for 10% of your list. In an ideal world, yes, but practically, skip it.
Gmail clipping is rare. Klaviyo tells you right in the preview/test screen whether your email is at risk. Long emails are fine as long as the first one to two scrolls contain everything a buyer needs to make a purchase decision.
The real concern with large files isn't clipping — it's load time. Keep individual images under 2MB, ideally under 500KB–1MB. GIFs tend to run heavier, so be mindful, but just check Klaviyo's preview tool and you're good.
For fashion brands specifically, long emails with tons of product imagery tend to perform well because shoppers just want to see what the product looks like on people.
Tables (not images) are often what bloats email file size unexpectedly.
---
Campaign Revenue Split for a Fast-Growing Brand (12:02–18:37)
Question: A sunglasses brand doing ~€600K/month has almost all its email revenue coming from the welcome flow. How do you increase campaign revenue, and what's the right flow-to-campaign revenue split?
Max's answer:
Some brands legitimately run 90/10 flow-to-campaign splits. It's structural — depends on list size, product repurchase rate, and how fast the brand is growing.
The highest lever for campaign revenue is sending volume and list width. Send to the widest engaged segment possible, at minimum every other day, ideally daily for a brand this size with heavy traffic.
Content and angles won't double your campaign performance. 80% of what drives campaign revenue is just being in the inbox at the right time. Don't overthink creative — focus on frequency and reach.
Math reframe: If the welcome flow is doing €500K and campaigns are doing €57K, a 10% improvement on the welcome flow (~€50K) is the same dollar impact as doubling campaign performance. Go where the leverage is.
For product categories with low repeat purchase rates (sunglasses, golf carts, etc.), campaign revenue will naturally be lower. Don't benchmark against CPG brands. Create your own KPIs and compare against your own past performance.
Other big campaign revenue drivers — new product launches and sale events — are largely out of the email team's control.Action item: Aiberson to send Max a campaign review video + site URL via Slack/community for a deeper audit.

---
Sale Strategy for a Low-Repeat-Purchase Brand (18:37–23:02)
Question: For the same sunglasses brand — how many sales per month, and what kind of sale structure makes sense when repeat purchases are naturally low?
Max's answer:
Everything works. The question is what kind of brand do they want to be — always-on sale, two sales a month, or no sales at all. Each has tradeoffs.
For a brand with competitive pricing and select items already on sale (but not publicized): feature those sale items on a dedicated collection page, label it seasonally ("Spring Sale" not "Clearance"), and send a weekly email highlighting what's currently on sale.
On top of that, run two ~5-day sale events per month with rotating offers (20% off, buy-two-get-one, dollar-off, etc.). Never run the same offer consecutively.
Sale items should not be eligible for additional discounts during the broader sale events.
For fashion/accessories brands, the number one driver of repeat purchases is new styles launching. Push product drops as hard as possible.
---
Subscription Churn & Getting People on the Right Plan (23:12–31:25)
Question: A subscription brand (hair foils for stylists) just started focusing on subscriptions. What's the best advice for reducing churn and getting people to subscribe?
Max's answer:
The #1 reason people churn on subscriptions: they're on the wrong plan. Wrong quantity, wrong interval, wrong match to actual consumption. Nailing the plan fit on the front end has the biggest impact on long-term retention — not the free gifts or win-back offers after the fact.
Most subscription pages don't help buyers figure out what they need. Build a simple quiz or modulator ("How many of these do you use per week?") that recommends the right plan. People do what they're told — if you recommend a plan based on their answers, they'll take it and stick longer.
Referenced Grüns as an example of matching consumption to household size.
For non-CPG subscription products, expect lower retention benchmarks. A sensory activity box for kids is not going to retain like toothpaste. Adjust expectations by product category.
Standard best practices still apply: make sure subscribers know how to manage their subscription, send billing reminders, push "delay" instead of "cancel" in the cancellation flow.Action item: Cade to add Max to Recharge so Max can review cancellation reasons directly.

---
Founder-Led Brand vs. Luxury Brand Positioning (41:48–48:10)
Question: A founder (boxer/fight camp background) runs an underwear brand with long-term luxury aspirations. Currently all sales come from personal social media. Should email campaigns lean into the founder story or try to be more "faceless luxury"?
Max's answer:
Ask yourself honestly: are you forcing the luxury positioning right now, or is it authentic to where the brand actually is? If founder-led content is what's working and driving sales, lean into it.
You can always pivot later. This is a two-way door. Ridge Wallets and many others started scrappy and went premium over time.
Max shared his own parallel: Well Copy's long-term vision is "the Apple of email marketing," but right now, everything runs through his personal brand. The transition is happening slowly — sponsorships under the Well Copy name, slowly removing his face from emails, building the team as the public-facing identity.
For the competition (Entrepreneur of Impact), absolutely go full founder-led. Use what's working right now to win. Then use the funding and exposure to start the transition.
Don't box yourself into a rigid 10-year plan. Things change fast. Do what feels right now and pivot when the time comes.Action item: Micheal to send Max the Entrepreneur of Impact voting link; Max to post it in the community.

---
Guerrilla Marketing & ManyChat for Apparel (49:15–54:17)
Question: Any guerrilla marketing tactics or campaigns that get customers to post or engage socially?
Max's answer:
Street interview ads are crushing right now. Referenced a buddy who runs an agency (Street Talk) that exclusively produces street interview content for brands to use as ads.
Getting customers to post organically is nearly impossible unless you have an exceptionally strong community. People don't want to be seen publicly entering giveaways or promoting brands on their personal Instagram. "Your Instagram is your life profile now."
Even Max himself won't publicly comment on other email marketers' posts to grab a free resource — but he'd DM for it. That's why DM-based CTAs work better than public engagement asks.
For ManyChat: set up three automations — (1) Instagram bio CTA ("DM us [keyword] for [offer]"), (2) same CTA in every post caption, (3) auto-DM new followers with a free resource offer. Plus a weekly story post driving DMs.Action item: Max offered to help Micheal set up ManyChat via Slack.

---
Subscription Offer Structure for a Creatine Brand (54:17–1:01:02)
Question: What are the best subscription offers for a new creatine brand concerned about CAC?
Max's answer:
Don't overthink free gifts. Bundle what makes sense, but stickers and tumbler bottles don't move the needle meaningfully.
The real play: turn it into a challenge or protocol. "60-Day Creatine Protocol" or "90-Day Transformation Challenge." This forces daily consumption (which drives retention), creates differentiation, and builds in a testimonial/UGC engine (before-and-after photos).
Hormozi-style offer: if someone completes the full 90 days with proof of daily use, refund them 100%. Most people won't complete it, but the ones who do become your best customers and content creators.
Creatine is a brutally competitive category. Expect to lose money on the first purchase. The game is LTV, not first-order profitability. Every major creatine brand loses money for the first three months and makes it back on retention.
Ideal retention benchmarks for subscription: 100% first order → 80% second order → 50–60% third order.
Mindset shift: stop optimizing for first-purchase profitability. Optimize for getting people to stay.
---
Customer Surveys — Keep It Simple, or Just Call Them (1:01:22–1:13:17)
Question: How do you run customer surveys effectively? What questions, how many, and what format?
Max's answer:
Google Forms work fine — even for nine-figure brands. Don't overthink the tool. Just ask for feedback.
For small lists: keep it to ~5 multiple choice questions max, maybe one optional written response at the end. The more complex the survey, the fewer responses you'll get.
For large lists: you can afford a more complex survey because even a low response rate yields thousands of replies.
Segment your survey sends: repeat buyers (why do you buy?), recent customers (what got you engaged?), lapsed buyers at 120+ days (why'd you stop?). Offer a mystery discount for completing it.
The fastest, highest-quality feedback method: just call people. Referenced Josh Snow (nine-figure brand) personally dialing cart abandoners and asking "What stopped you from buying?" Raw, unfiltered, immediate feedback. Set aside 15 minutes a day to dial customers.
For in-email surveys, Zamo (caymo.com) lets people respond directly inside the email — increases response rates but is expensive. Not necessary for most brands.Action item: Gary to send Max the survey Google Doc for review.

---
High-Ticket Welcome Flow Strategy — Electric Motorbikes at €6K (1:04:44–1:09:55)
Question: For a €6K electric motorbike brand, should the welcome flow use urgency/discount expiration, or does the long decision cycle make that counterproductive? Also, how to handle stacking the welcome offer with a cart abandonment offer (free white glove delivery)?
Max's answer:
Still go aggressive with daily emails, 7–10 days. High-AOV buyers move faster than you'd expect. You only need one purchase from these people, so you can afford to push hard.
Use urgency on the welcome discount. Let it "expire" around day 8–9.
Then reactivate the same offer (different discount code) in the cart abandonment flow alongside the white glove delivery offer. Nobody gets mad about receiving a discount they thought expired. Use a different code so it feels fresh.
After the welcome flow ends, campaigns become your long-term follow-up. If you're sending 3–4x/week, people will convert from campaigns when they're ready. Don't overthink extending the welcome flow indefinitely.
Most welcome flow revenue comes from the first email anyway. The rest is incremental.Action item: Tristan to revise the welcome flow to 7–10 daily emails with urgency, then reactivate the offer in the cart abandonment flow with a new code.

---
Building a Campaign Calendar — Repeat Winners First (1:13:43–1:17:39)
Question: What's your thought process for building a campaign calendar, especially for a fashion/eyewear brand where product imagery drives purchases?
Max's answer:
Step one: repeat your winners. If an email generated 2x the revenue of any other send last month, why aren't you resending it monthly with a slight twist? Your list doesn't remember your emails. You could literally send the same email once a month and it would print.
Put your best-performing campaign content into your flows too.
Step two: steal inspiration externally. Every person on Max's 80-person team sends one email inspiration daily — brands they admire, angles they find interesting. Build an unlimited swipe file and pull from it constantly.
Step three: use AI tools (ChatGPT, the email marketing brain prompt) to brainstorm angles based on principles like micro-topics.
Max's problem isn't coming up with ideas — it's choosing what not to send. That's the position you want to be in.
---
Closing (1:17:00–1:17:39)
Max wrapped up, reminded everyone to message him freely in Slack or the community — "spam me, that's what we're here for." Weekend gambling update promised for next week's call.
Action item: Max to have his EA upload mentorship podcast episodes to Spotify.

Even Max himself won't publicly comment on other email marketers' posts to grab a free resource — but he'd DM for it. That's why DM-based CTAs work better than public engagement asks.

For ManyChat: set up three automations — (1) Instagram bio CTA ("DM us [keyword] for [offer]"), (2) same CTA in every post caption, (3) auto-DM new followers with a free resource offer. Plus a weekly story post driving DMs.
Action item: Max offered to help Micheal set up ManyChat via Slack.
Subscription Offer Structure for a Creatine Brand (
Question: What are the best subscription offers for a new creatine brand concerned about CAC?
Max's answer:
Don't overthink free gifts. Bundle what makes sense, but stickers and tumbler bottles don't move the needle meaningfully.

The real play: turn it into a challenge or protocol. "60-Day Creatine Protocol" or "90-Day Transformation Challenge." This forces daily consumption (which drives retention), creates differentiation, and builds in a testimonial/UGC engine (before-and-after photos).

Hormozi-style offer: if someone completes the full 90 days with proof of daily use, refund them 100%. Most people won't complete it, but the ones who do become your best customers and content creators.

Creatine is a brutally competitive category. Expect to lose money on the first purchase. The game is LTV, not first-order profitability. Every major creatine brand loses money for the first three months and makes it back on retention.
Ideal retention benchmarks for subscription: 100% first order → 80% second order → 50–60% third order.
Mindset shift: stop optimizing for first-purchase profitability. Optimize for getting people to stay.
Customer Surveys — Keep It Simple, or Just Call Them (
Question: How do you run customer surveys effectively? What questions, how many, and what format?
Max's answer:
Google Forms work fine — even for nine-figure brands. Don't overthink the tool. Just ask for feedback.
For small lists: keep it to ~5 multiple choice questions max, maybe one optional written response at the end. The more complex the survey, the fewer responses you'll get.
For large lists: you can afford a more complex survey because even a low response rate yields thousands of replies.
Segment your survey sends: repeat buyers (why do you buy?), recent customers (what got you engaged?), lapsed buyers at 120+ days (why'd you stop?). Offer a mystery discount for completing it.

The fastest, highest-quality feedback method: just call people. Referenced Josh Snow (nine-figure brand) personally dialing cart abandoners and asking "What stopped you from buying?" Raw, unfiltered, immediate feedback. Set aside 15 minutes a day to dial customers.
For in-email surveys, Zamo (
caymo.com
) lets people respond directly inside the email — increases response rates but is expensive. Not necessary for most brands.
Action item: Gary to send Max the survey Google Doc for review.
High-Ticket Welcome Flow Strategy — Electric Motorbikes at €6K (

Question: For a €6K electric motorbike brand, should the welcome flow use urgency/discount expiration, or does the long decision cycle make that counterproductive? Also, how to handle stacking the welcome offer with a cart abandonment offer (free white glove delivery)?
Max's answer:
Still go aggressive with daily emails, 7–10 days. High-AOV buyers move faster than you'd expect. You only need one purchase from these people, so you can afford to push hard.
Use urgency on the welcome discount. Let it "expire" around day 8–9.

Then reactivate the same offer (different discount code) in the cart abandonment flow alongside the white glove delivery offer. Nobody gets mad about receiving a discount they thought expired. Use a different code so it feels fresh.

After the welcome flow ends, campaigns become your long-term follow-up. If you're sending 3–4x/week, people will convert from campaigns when they're ready. Don't overthink extending the welcome flow indefinitely.
Most welcome flow revenue comes from the first email anyway. The rest is incremental.
Action item: Tristan to revise the welcome flow to 7–10 daily emails with urgency, then reactivate the offer in the cart abandonment flow with a new code.
Building a Campaign Calendar — Repeat Winners First (
Question: What's your thought process for building a campaign calendar, especially for a fashion/eyewear brand where product imagery drives purchases?
Max's answer:

Step one: repeat your winners. If an email generated 2x the revenue of any other send last month, why aren't you resending it monthly with a slight twist? Your list doesn't remember your emails. You could literally send the same email once a month and it would print.
Put your best-performing campaign content into your flows too.

Step two: steal inspiration externally. Every person on Max's 80-person team sends one email inspiration daily — brands they admire, angles they find interesting. Build an unlimited swipe file and pull from it constantly.
Step three: use AI tools (ChatGPT, the email marketing brain prompt) to brainstorm angles based on principles like micro-topics.
Max's problem isn't coming up with ideas — it's choosing what not to send. That's the position you want to be in.
Closing (
Max wrapped up, reminded everyone to message him freely in Slack or the community — "spam me, that's what we're here for." Weekend gambling update promised for next week's call.
Action item: Max to have his EA upload mentorship podcast episodes to Spotify.

lessons.title: [March 23rd] Email Philosophies + Q&A
lessons.description:
Watch Video Recording >>
Summary below 👇

---
Opening & Housekeeping (0:00–5:30) Max opened from a coffee shop between Airbnb transitions, riffing on the ethics of camping out in coffee shops for eight hours on one cold brew (verdict: probably unethical, but emails ain't gonna write themselves). Shout-out to White Monster Energy and nicotine pouches as unofficial sponsors. He announced updated trainings dropping soon — more conceptual and philosophical rather than step-by-step SOPs — built originally for the internal Well Copy team but being shared with the community. He also flagged that course content is being refreshed across the board.

---
Core Philosophy: High Levers First (5:30–12:00) Max walked through the internal training doc he's building for his team — the foundational philosophies that sit on top of the tactical course material.
The three pillars that matter above everything else:
Optimized pop-up form. Nothing else matters until this is dialed. Taking a pop-up from 10% to 12% is a 20% increase in list growth — stacked over a year, that's 20% more people to sell to. Max is currently building a study on customer cohort LTV and CAC tied to pop-up conversion rates.
Campaign volume. Three to four campaigns per week to a wide engaged list. You could send a blank email with a Shop Now button 3–4x/week and it would still make money. Being in inboxes drives revenue. No need for complex segmentation at this stage.
Core base flows. Three to five emails per flow. A blank abandoned cart email that says "check out now" will still convert — it's the timing and the reminder that does the work. Don't overthink it until the basics are live and running.Max's point: if you just execute these three things — even with bare-bones, plain-text emails — it's very hard not to generate meaningful revenue. Everything else is optimization on top of a functioning machine.

---
Levels of Email & SMS Marketing: 7-Figure vs. 8-Figure vs. 9-Figure (12:00–18:00) Max broke down how the strategy changes at each revenue tier:
7-figure brands:
Execute the basics. Pop-up form, 3 campaigns/week, base flows live with 3–5 emails each.
Don't over-send — at this traffic level, you can't replace the unsubscribes that come with higher volume.
If traffic is really low, 2/week is fine. Just keep growing.
No crazy flows needed. Build the machine, run it consistently, spend time on other areas of the business.8-figure brands:
Pop-up forms become even more critical — with 100K+ monthly site visitors, a 10% to 12% pop-up improvement = 2,000 extra subscribers/month. Weekly pop-up testing at minimum.
Increase to 5–7 campaigns/week. More traffic means you can absorb the extra unsubscribes from higher send volume.
Layer in product interest segments on top of the 120-day engaged list. Widen sends to the full list 1–3x/month — at this scale with a healthy domain, it won't tank deliverability.
Flow optimization: customize welcome flows by traffic source and quiz answers, split abandonment flows by product or collection.
Mindset: same basics, but more volume, smarter targeting.9-figure brands:
Hyper A/B testing. Stack 1% gains. Maintain quality at scale.
1–2 campaigns every single day. Flows split further.
The brands that crush aren't doing anything exotic — they're doing the basics at high quality and high volume.
Working with 9-figure brands is painful because the quality bar is so high — design branding, copy branding, approvals — it's a grind. But it's fundamentally about quality and staffing, not complexity.
---
General Flow Philosophies (18:00–19:20)
Why 3–5 emails per flow:
If a welcome flow is 8 emails long (one/day), by email 8 it's been a week — the lead is cold, they've moved on or bought from a competitor.
The back half of long flows almost never converts. Shortening creates tighter urgency and better revenue.
After the flow ends, they're receiving 3–4 campaigns/week anyway.
Exception: high-AOV brands can run longer flows due to longer consideration cycles.Key principles across all flows:
Send every day within flows. Do not delay — it kills conversion.
Include at least one text-based email in every flow.
Be aggressive with copy in flows. Flows are not the place to nurture. ("Place your order" > "Forgetting something?")
Segment abandonment flows by buyers vs. non-buyers — the one segmentation split that's always worth it.
Dynamic product sections as high up in the flow as possible.
Offer testing is the single highest-leverage optimization inside flows — it can literally double conversion rates. Subject line A/B tests and micro-copy changes can't get you a 2x. Offer changes can.Bonus flows Max mentioned (not in the standard course):
Espresso Shot Flow: Fires 10 minutes after someone clicks an email (or hits site multiple times recently) — quick punch offer for high-intent window shoppers.
Replenishment Reminder Flow: Uses Klaviyo's Expected Date of Next Order trigger. Works extremely well for consumables.
Sunset Flow: For sunsetting inactive profiles to save on Klaviyo costs. Not critical — manual suppression works too.
VIP Flow, Review Request Flow, and others.
---
One-Time Purchase / Service Business Email Strategy (19:22–27:30) Question (Mapa): Sells website-building services — one-time purchase, customer is done after that. Does she need campaigns? Should the welcome flow be super long?
Max's answer:
For one-time purchase businesses (mattresses, services, medical devices), be significantly more aggressive on the first purchase push. There's no long-term brand equity concern — every day the person doesn't buy, they're getting colder.
Hyper-sending works here: two texts/day, two emails/day once someone opts in. Go crazy.
Max's approach from his first 8-figure client ($900 medical device): built a 7-email daily welcome flow, then sent a campaign every single day testing new angles. When a campaign crushed, he moved it into the welcome flow — only putting proven winners in the flow.
Don't pre-build a 30-email welcome series and hope it works. Start small with proven angles, send campaigns to test new ones, then migrate winners into the flow over time. This is exactly how Max built his personal newsletter's 30-day onboarding sequence.
For the digital products question (selling smaller items to non-converters): start with a 3-email welcome flow, send campaigns, add winners over time. Test whether small products or the main service converts better.Action item: Build a 3-email welcome flow for the service + digital products. Add winners from campaigns over time.
Footer strategy: Don't be pushy in the email body — bring value, and list all products/services in the footer of every email. People naturally scroll to footers after getting value from the content. Some of Well Copy's best-performing e-commerce campaigns are pure value emails (e.g., creatine FAQs) where the selling happens organically through footer category buttons.Action item: Add product/service links to all email footers.

---
Aggressive vs. Emotional Copy in Abandonment Flows (27:33–31:05) Question (Aven): Working with a vegan brand — very mission-driven, non-confrontational customers. Can you still be aggressive, or does the approach change?
Max's answer:
"Aggressive" doesn't mean "buy now or die." It means making the customer feel like they were right there — one click away from completing the purchase.
Wording that works: "Your order's ready to ship," "You're one click away," "We have your order prepped." This positions the customer as being far along in the buying process, reducing perceived effort.
Wording that underperforms: "Forgetting something?" or "You left this behind" — implies the customer wasn't that close, which is psychologically deflating.
CTA wording matters: "Complete my order" or "Finish checkout" > "Go back to your cart." The first implies one step; the second implies multiple steps.
For emotional/mission-driven brands: you can absolutely layer in emotional copy (e.g., Butcher Box for Pets: "We want our dogs to lick their bowls clean"). Mix emotional messaging with direct CTAs.
Max's caveat: everything he teaches is a starting point — works for ~70% of cases. Always test brand by brand.Action item: A/B test direct/urgent copy vs. emotional copy in abandoned cart flows.

---
Subscription Brand Strategy (31:45–58:00) Question (Guery): Sells a grooming bundle for bald men (lather bar, exfoliator, moisturizer, oil). Wants to increase subscription rates. When do you send the subscription pitch?
Max's answer:
It is extremely difficult to convert a one-time buyer into a subscriber after the fact. Once someone's first purchase is one-time, that's their default mental model for the brand.
First-order subscription take rate is everything. Optimize the initial purchase experience to drive subscription from the start.
For repeat purchase timing: go into Shopify, find the re-buy window for each product, then fire a replenishment flow ~1 week before that window. Example: if average re-buy is 35 days, fire at day 30 with "You're probably running low — subscribe and save."
Keep the replenishment flow simple — 2 emails, product-specific (different timing per product based on consumption rate). Can be text-based.
Best-performing replenishment email example (9-figure toothpaste brand): a personal check-in from the VP, 21 days post-delivery. Founder-style message asking how the product is working, listing the benefits they should be experiencing, with a subtle CTA to reorder. Converts extremely well because it feels personal, not salesy.
80% of repeat orders come from campaigns, not flows. Sending campaigns 3x/week keeps you top of mind and drives the bulk of repeat purchases — replenishment flows are supplementary.For subscription-first brands specifically:
Exclude active subscribers from most campaigns. Only send subscribers 1–2 campaigns/month. Every extra email to an active subscriber increases cancellation risk.
Build a strong post-purchase onboarding flow focused on product education and sticking with the product to see benefits.
Optimize the billing reminder email.
Lead with subscription messaging everywhere — don't present it as an option alongside one-time purchase. Make subscribe the default.Action items:
Analyze Shopify re-buy windows per product; build product-specific replenishment flows (2 emails, fire ~1 week before average re-order date).
Exclude active subscribers from standard campaign sends.
---
CRO & Product Page Feedback (39:36–43:10) Question (Guery): Can you look at my product page for CRO?
Max's answer:
Above the fold on mobile needs a clear CTA button — that was missing.
Simplify product selection: don't make the customer choose between multiple products. Direct them toward one thing (the bundle). Individual products can exist on the store, but the primary path should be bundle-first.
Referenced The Black Stuff (a client scaling hard with a similar vibe) and IMA Health as gold-standard product page examples for subscription optimization.
Max's BOGO reframing example: The Black Stuff was already offering buy one get one free + 15% off. Confusing. They dropped the 15% and reframed as "You've got 99% off" (the second bar). Giving away less but framing it better — conversion skyrocketed.
The lesson: test and reframe your offers relentlessly. Offer framing is everything.Action item: Optimize product page — add mobile CTA above fold; simplify to bundle-first experience.

---
Welcome Flow Priorities & Fashion Brand Emails (49:30–54:55) Question (Brandon): Has 7–8 emails per flow. If trimming to 3–5, which email types matter most?
Max's answer:
Every flow needs: an intro email, filler emails, and a last-chance urgency email. The filler content depends entirely on the brand.
Social proof / customer transformations — almost always worth including.
Founder story — works well for brands where authenticity and origin matter.
FAQs — great for consumables and competitive niches, not needed for fashion.
"How we're different" — strong for competitive categories like jewelry.
Best-performing filler emails vary wildly. Example: Gains & Bulk's top performer is "Our creatine isn't cheap" — explains pricing rationale.For fashion/luxury streetwear specifically:
Customers only care about how it looks. Don't do FAQ emails, "what's inside," or how-it-works content.
Just show a massive amount of product imagery — people wearing the items, styled shots. That's what drives fashion purchases.
Look at Lululemon, Alo, Gymshark — their emails are basically walls of photos, and it works because it lets the customer imagine themselves in the product.
Mix in fit notes (sizing, how it fits) and social proof where relevant.
Authenticity messaging can work well for resellers (Louis, Gucci boutiques) where legitimacy concerns exist.Action items:
Audit existing flows; trim to 3–5 emails.
For fashion brands: design emails heavy on product imagery with fit notes.
---
Transactional Emails in Klaviyo (43:12–46:45) Question (Chelsea): How to move Shopify transactional emails (order confirmation, shipping) into Klaviyo?
Max's answer:
Turn off transactional emails in Shopify.
In Klaviyo, create flows using the same triggers (e.g., Shopify Placed Order metric for order confirmation). Klaviyo has pre-built templates that dynamically pull all order data.
Critical step: apply for transactional status on these emails in Klaviyo. Check the transactional checkbox — once approved, the email is guaranteed to go to the primary inbox (legal requirement for inbox providers).
The catch: transactional emails cannot contain any selling (no "shop now," no cross-sells). If you sell in it, it loses transactional status.
For shipping/delivery notifications: some brands use Wonderment, which integrates with Klaviyo. One email + one text per shipping event (carrier pickup, shipped, out for delivery, delivered). Mark all as transactional.
Don't forget to disable the Shopify versions to avoid double-sending.Action item: Migrate transactional emails to Klaviyo; disable Shopify defaults; mark as transactional; test.

---
Subject Lines & Inbox Placement (46:46–49:20) Question: Do subject lines affect spam/promotions placement? Emojis seem to help land in primary sometimes.
Max's answer:
It's largely a guessing game. Inbox placement isn't binary — a brand might land 20% primary, 70% promotions, 10% spam on any given send. It fluctuates.
Known triggers that can push toward spam/promotions: emojis, all-caps, words like "free," "sale," "99% off."
Max's mental model: think like Gmail. If you were an inbox provider trying to separate promotional content from personal content, what signals would you use? That's your guide.
He hasn't cracked a reliable formula and doesn't know anyone who has. Focus on maintaining good deliverability and domain reputation — some emails will hit primary, some won't.
---
Vote-For-Me Competition Email Strategy (59:23–1:01:45) Question (Micheál): Running a 10–14 day vote-for-me competition (one free vote/day). How to incorporate it into emails without losing the selling function?
Max's answer:
Send one dedicated kickoff email when the competition starts — full focus on "vote for me."
After that, continue normal email cadence but add a thin banner at the top or a slice above the footer in every email linking to the vote page.
Don't make the vote the focus of every email — just keep it persistently visible without being distracting.
Optional: offer an incentive for proof of voting.Action item: Build kickoff email + persistent vote banner in all sends for the competition duration.
Micheál also shared that his Meta ads account got hacked through a former agency that still had access — account has been down 4+ days. Max offered to connect him with a Meta contact.
Action item (Max): Check with Meta contact re: Micheál's hacked ads account.

---
Flow Benchmarks & Offer Framing Wins (1:03:46–1:10:00) Question: What are good conversion rate benchmarks for flows?
Max's answer:
Rough benchmarks: Cart Abandon ~4%, Checkout Abandon ~8%, Welcome Flow ~10%.
But it varies massively by brand size, traffic quality, ad strategy, and whether visitors are coming in warm or cold. Smaller brands will have a harder time hitting these numbers.
Better approach: test against yourself, not industry benchmarks. Post your numbers and email screenshots in the community for review.Offer framing win — Micheál's case study:
Same emails, same offer — just changed the wording and directed to one product page instead of multiple. Welcome flow went from ~1% to 28% conversion. Maintained.
Lesson for everyone: if 90% of your sales come from one product/bundle, make everything point there. Don't scatter attention across the catalog.The Black Stuff reframe recap:
Dropped a 15% off pop-up offer. Reframed the existing BOGO as "You've got 99% off." Actually giving away less — conversion skyrocketed. Framing is everything.Action items:
Post flow metrics + sample emails in the community for review.
DM Max with: product split (% of sales per product), current offer/code, welcome flow link for personalized feedback.
