Max's BOGO reframing example: The Black Stuff was already offering buy one get one free + 15% off. Confusing. They dropped the 15% and reframed as "You've got 99% off" (the second bar). Giving away
less
but framing it better — conversion skyrocketed.
The lesson: test and reframe your offers relentlessly. Offer framing is everything.
Action item:
Optimize product page — add mobile CTA above fold; simplify to bundle-first experience.
Welcome Flow Priorities & Fashion Brand Emails (
Question (Brandon):
Has 7–8 emails per flow. If trimming to 3–5, which email types matter most?
Max's answer:
Every flow needs: an intro email, filler emails, and a last-chance urgency email. The filler content depends entirely on the brand.
Social proof / customer transformations — almost always worth including.
Founder story — works well for brands where authenticity and origin matter.
FAQs — great for consumables and competitive niches, not needed for fashion.
"How we're different" — strong for competitive categories like jewelry.
Best-performing filler emails vary wildly. Example: Gains & Bulk's top performer is "Our creatine isn't cheap" — explains pricing rationale.
For fashion/luxury streetwear specifically:
Customers only care about how it looks. Don't do FAQ emails, "what's inside," or how-it-works content.
Just show a massive amount of product imagery — people wearing the items, styled shots. That's what drives fashion purchases.
Look at Lululemon, Alo, Gymshark — their emails are basically walls of photos, and it works because it lets the customer imagine themselves in the product.
Mix in fit notes (sizing, how it fits) and social proof where relevant.
Authenticity messaging can work well for resellers (Louis, Gucci boutiques) where legitimacy concerns exist.
Action items:
Audit existing flows; trim to 3–5 emails.
For fashion brands: design emails heavy on product imagery with fit notes.
Transactional Emails in Klaviyo (
Question (Chelsea):
How to move Shopify transactional emails (order confirmation, shipping) into Klaviyo?
Max's answer:
Turn off transactional emails in Shopify.
In Klaviyo, create flows using the same triggers (e.g., Shopify Placed Order metric for order confirmation). Klaviyo has pre-built templates that dynamically pull all order data.

Critical step: apply for transactional status on these emails in Klaviyo. Check the transactional checkbox — once approved, the email is guaranteed to go to the primary inbox (legal requirement for inbox providers).
The catch: transactional emails cannot contain any selling (no "shop now," no cross-sells). If you sell in it, it loses transactional status.

For shipping/delivery notifications: some brands use Wonderment, which integrates with Klaviyo. One email + one text per shipping event (carrier pickup, shipped, out for delivery, delivered). Mark all as transactional.
Don't forget to disable the Shopify versions to avoid double-sending.
Action item:
Migrate transactional emails to Klaviyo; disable Shopify defaults; mark as transactional; test.
Subject Lines & Inbox Placement (
Question:
Do subject lines affect spam/promotions placement? Emojis seem to help land in primary sometimes.
Max's answer:
It's largely a guessing game. Inbox placement isn't binary — a brand might land 20% primary, 70% promotions, 10% spam on any given send. It fluctuates.
Known triggers that can push toward spam/promotions: emojis, all-caps, words like "free," "sale," "99% off."
Max's mental model: think like Gmail. If you were an inbox provider trying to separate promotional content from personal content, what signals would you use? That's your guide.
He hasn't cracked a reliable formula and doesn't know anyone who has. Focus on maintaining good deliverability and domain reputation — some emails will hit primary, some won't.
Vote-For-Me Competition Email Strategy (
Question (Micheál):
Running a 10–14 day vote-for-me competition (one free vote/day). How to incorporate it into emails without losing the selling function?
Max's answer:
Send one dedicated kickoff email when the competition starts — full focus on "vote for me."
After that, continue normal email cadence but add a thin banner at the top or a slice above the footer in every email linking to the vote page.
Don't make the vote the focus of every email — just keep it persistently visible without being distracting.
Optional: offer an incentive for proof of voting.
Action item:
Build kickoff email + persistent vote banner in all sends for the competition duration.
Micheál also shared that his Meta ads account got hacked through a former agency that still had access — account has been down 4+ days. Max offered to connect him with a Meta contact.
Action item (Max):
Check with Meta contact re: Micheál's hacked ads account.
Flow Benchmarks & Offer Framing Wins (
Question:
What are good conversion rate benchmarks for flows?
Max's answer:
Rough benchmarks: Cart Abandon ~4%, Checkout Abandon ~8%, Welcome Flow ~10%.
But it varies massively by brand size, traffic quality, ad strategy, and whether visitors are coming in warm or cold. Smaller brands will have a harder time hitting these numbers.
Better approach: test against yourself, not industry benchmarks. Post your numbers and email screenshots in the community for review.
Offer framing win — Micheál's case study:
Same emails, same offer — just changed the wording and directed to one product page instead of multiple. Welcome flow went from ~1% to 28% conversion. Maintained.
Lesson for everyone: if 90% of your sales come from one product/bundle, make everything point there. Don't scatter attention across the catalog.
The Black Stuff reframe recap:
Dropped a 15% off pop-up offer. Reframed the existing BOGO as "You've got 99% off." Actually giving away
less
— conversion skyrocketed. Framing is everything.
Action items:
Post flow metrics + sample emails in the community for review.
DM Max with: product split (% of sales per product), current offer/code, welcome flow link for personalized feedback.

lessons.title: [March 9th] Best Performing Emails + Q&A
lessons.description:
Watch Video Recording >>
Summary below 👇

---
Opening & Housekeeping (0:00–4:25)
Max opened with some banter about his Airbnb situation (nailing the Well Copy sign into the wall, then getting kicked out for construction). He then laid out the format question: he's testing whether to combine the consulting/mentorship group with the Email Marketerz Skool community on one call, or keep them separate with two calls per week. He committed to sending a survey to decide.
Max reminded everyone to post actively in the Skool community — A/B tests, wins, email designs, questions — and that his DMs are open for anything, with the rule that email marketing questions should go in the community first so everyone benefits. Agency-specific questions can stay in DMs.
The lead strategist for the mentorship/consulting program introduced himself, and Max mentioned a live event/webinar happening March 18th.

---
Store Credit Email Deep-Dive (6:48–19:00)
Question: One brand implemented the store credit concept in the welcome flow but it's converting lower than expected. Struggling with how much store credit to give relative to the AOV.
Max's answer:
He cited a client doing over $1M/month who increased email revenue 156% in 30 days and went from ~15% to 48% of total revenue from email, largely by sending the store credit email six times in a month.
For a brand with a $35 AOV and an 11% mystery discount welcome offer: A/B test a small store credit amount ($3.72 with a $25 minimum order threshold) versus a larger amount ($7.42 with a $70+ threshold) to see if you can push AOV higher.
Send the store credit email as a campaign to all non-buyers on the list, not just in the flow — thousands of people already on the list won't get the new flow email otherwise.
Set up a 3-email store credit sequence with a 72-hour expiry: Day 1 announcement, Day 2 reminder, Day 3 last chance.
Put it in both the welcome flow (after a 2-week delay past the main offer) and the win-back flow (90 days of no purchase).
Max's philosophy: if something works, don't do it once a quarter — do it once a month. Stop being precious about "overusing" tactics that print money.Max then covered two other high-performing email concepts:
"Your order might be on us" — randomly refunding 3 orders placed within 24 hours. Doesn't feel like a sale, builds goodwill, drives massive volume. Follow up with the winning order numbers, then hit non-winners with a discount. Some brands run this monthly as an "order lottery."
First 100 people get X discount — urgency-based, ripped every time, and Max caught his own team not repeating it enough.
Tiered store credit & framing — higher credit with higher thresholds. Max referenced a well-known brand that frames everything as "store credit" instead of "% off" because it consistently converts better after extensive A/B testing.Action item raised: Consult a lawyer about order-lottery compliance (potential state lottery board issues, especially in certain states). Exclude restricted states as needed.

---
Multi-Country Targeting & Waitlist Setup (21:23–29:00)
Question: A brand sells in Germany, Netherlands, and UK using country-specific subdomains. Normally they segment via those domains. But for a new product launch, the client wants one single waitlist URL promoted through social/influencers. How do you segment signups by country from a single opt-in?
Max's answer:
Build a blank landing page in Shopify.
Create full-page pop-up forms in Klaviyo, one per country, each targeted by visitor location (Klaviyo's "show to visitors in certain locations" setting).
Set each pop-up to fire immediately on that specific URL only.
Remove the X/close button so the pop-up essentially is the landing page.
Duplicate for each country. The URL stays the same but visitors see the correct country-targeted form based on Klaviyo's location detection.
Alternatively, could do this with Alia if more design customization is needed.
Caveat: VPN users would break the location targeting, but it's generally reliable.Max also mentioned that Well Copy charges significantly more (essentially doubles the price) for multi-country work due to translation coordination and technical complexity.

---
Gmail Promotions Tab Annotations (29:52–31:30)
Question: How do you get those coupon codes and countdown timers that show up in Gmail's promotions tab preview (outside the email)?
Max's answer:
He doesn't currently do this. A lot of what you see there is actually Google Ads (Performance Max), not native email features.
There is an HTML-based method to do it natively, but Max hasn't cracked it and doesn't know anyone who has reliably. Open call: if anyone in the group knows, share it.
---
HTML vs. Figma-Sliced Email Design (31:32–34:30)
Question: Are you using HTML uploads or still slicing from Figma?
Max's answer:
Straight Figma slicing. 80/20 approach — HTML-coded designs are harder to manage in Klaviyo (can't preview them easily, always have to go back to the source file).
For some brands (especially older audiences or deliverability-challenged brands), Max will A/B test image-based emails vs. mixing in Klaviyo native text blocks. Sometimes the text-heavy version wins on deliverability, but usually the plain image approach performs better.
For marketplace brands with tons of rotating SKUs, he uses Klaviyo's dynamic product blocks in flows — set to show in-stock best sellers from the last 24 hours — instead of static product images. Sometimes that outperforms hand-picked products.
---
Subject Lines & Spam/Deliverability (34:34–37:15)
Question: How important are subject lines in triggering spam, and how do you track it?
Max's answer:
Highly brand-dependent. Some brands can send all-caps alarm-emoji subject lines and land in primary. Others are just cooked regardless.
Max doesn't obsess over it. If flow open rates are around 20%, yeah, you're in trouble and need a full warm-up. Otherwise, just keep sending to your engaged list and your reputation improves over time.
For brands with suspected deliverability issues, he uses GlockApps — send a test email to their seed list, it tells you where you're landing (inbox, spam, promotions) and flags blacklists or missing DNS records.
Max committed to creating a GlockApps training in the Skool community.
---
SaaS Onboarding Email Strategy (37:26–46:45)
Question: A team is launching an AI content-creation software ($97/month), switching from Kajabi to ActiveCampaign. Wanted guidance on onboarding email strategy — was thinking 4–6 emails with case studies to fire people up.
Max's answer:
The #1 reason SaaS users cancel: they get overwhelmed, don't learn the product, don't use it. So the goal isn't "get pumped" — it's consumption.
Max referenced work he's doing with a major platform right now: the strategy there is a 30-day onboarding course teaching people how to use the product, with emails summarizing each lesson.
Recommended a 7–14 day daily email sequence, each email covering one feature or use case. Essentially a crash course broken into daily tutorials.
For each email: record a 5–10 minute Loom, transcribe it, turn the transcription into a written summary, then send the email with both the video link (thumbnail) and the written version.
After the onboarding sequence, transition to a weekly newsletter for all subscribers with value-driven content — how other users are winning, strategies, tips. This serves retention by keeping people engaged and seeing the product's value.
On billing reminders: probably not legally required for SaaS (unlike e-com subscriptions). But you do need to send receipts.
Unlike e-com subscriptions (where the advice is often to go quiet so people forget), for SaaS you should keep emailing — because if they stop using the product, they cancel. Ongoing communication = ongoing engagement = retention.
---
Cart & Checkout Abandonment for High-AOV Products (47:57–55:40)
Question: Working with a bed/mattress brand (~€1,000 AOV). Flows are underperforming — cart had ~300 entries last month with almost no conversions. Timing was 1 hour trigger, then Day 1/Day 2/Day 3 emails. What's the right approach for high-AOV, long-consideration products?
Max's answer:
He referenced a $2,000 office chair client: 8-email abandonment flow, one email per day, discount offered at the end. Heavily educational — pain messaging, product differentiation, USPs.
Big lever for high-AOV: push people to call the support/sales team. Once you get someone on the phone, the close rate jumps. Max started including CTAs in every abandonment email to contact support.
On the giveaway pop-up (€1,000/month giveaway entry): Max isn't a fan of giveaways for lead gen because people sign up and then buy elsewhere before the drawing. Better approach: find out what the brand already gives buyers (free shipping, consultations, bonuses) and make that the pop-up offer instead.
One attendee suggested: "What if ordering in the first 24 hours doubles your giveaway entries?" Max loved it — creates urgency to buy now rather than wait.
He cited another brand doing a similar mechanic: free product + giveaway entry, with every dollar spent earning additional entries, making the free entry nearly worthless by comparison.
Subject line tip: use "Your order's ready to ship" — consistently one of the highest-performing abandonment subject lines.
The updated timing (30 min trigger for cart, 15 min for checkout, then tighter follow-ups at 3 hours) got Max's approval.
Max asked the person to post or DM the actual abandonment creatives for review.
---
Attribution Tangent (55:40–59:30)
Came up organically from the cart/phone-sales question.
Max's take:
Email revenue attribution (5-day opens, 5-day clicks in Klaviyo) is largely a joke. Someone opens an email, clicks a Meta ad 4 days later and buys — email gets the credit.
The higher you go in e-com, the less people care about Klaviyo attribution numbers. Nine-figure brands don't take it seriously as a primary metric.
It's a useful directional indicator, but not a gospel metric. Max is trying to talk about it less and less.
The real question is: is the email system functioning as a cohesive part of the overall marketing machine? Compare your numbers to your own past performance, not other brands.
---
Browse Abandonment: General vs. Product-Specific (59:34–1:01:20)
Question: When do you decide to build product-specific browse abandonment flows with tailored USPs vs. keeping it general/dynamic?
Max's answer:
Default: start with a general browse abandonment flow, optimize the hell out of it.
Product-specific versions yield maybe a 25% increase at most — not worth it for smaller brands.
Makes sense for 8–9 figure brands, or brands where 2–3 products represent a disproportionate share of revenue and those products are meaningfully different from each other.
If the general flow is underperforming badly, try product-specific as a diagnostic move.
Can also use conditional splits within flows as a middle ground.
---
Retention & Suppression Strategy (1:01:22–1:05:00)
Question: For brands with very low returning customer rate, what do you focus on in email? When do you suppress?
Max's answer:
80–90% of customer retention is product and positioning, not email. Some products just don't have natural repeat purchase cycles and no email flow is going to change that.
AG1's retention is insane because they sell a daily ritual, not a supplement. Creatine brands that position as "add to your morning coffee every day" crush brands that position as "take before the gym." It's consumption frequency driven by product messaging.
What email can do: stay top of mind, cross-sell, and test offer structures. But don't expect to 2x retention with email tactics alone.
Suppression benchmark: 180 days of combined email inactivity + site inactivity + no purchases. Unsuppress for major events like BFCM.

lessons.title: August 4th: Scaling, Hiring & Agency Growth
lessons.description:
Call Summary — Referral Client Acquisition, Scaling Playbook, Hiring, Firing & Raising Prices
Doc Featured On Call >>

---
Opening (0:00–12:00)
Tristan called in from Prague surviving the heat. Ben joined from his bedroom on a Starbucks coffee buzz, having spent the morning wrestling Claude into producing the scaling document for the call. Marlon introduced himself properly — previously in-house for a brand for three years, helped generate over £10M in revenue, and now looking to build his own agency. Cyril confirmed he'd landed his first client and was building out a full flow setup for a subscription brand switching from one-time purchase to a heavily discounted subscribe-and-save model.
Charlie dropped in from Malaysia with a story about accidentally flying for free after a system error said his flight was cancelled — airline refunded all his points, he got on the flight anyway, made it to Kuala Lumpur, and came out ahead. He then dropped some useful acquisition sauce that opened the main Q&A.

---
Charlie's Referral Acquisition Strategy (12:00–25:00)
Charlie shared a client acquisition method his agency has been using that's been highly effective — paying referral fees to people in their network and even cold contacts who send them qualified leads.
How it works:
Reach out to ecom brand owners, operators, and founders in the niche — people who are likely to know other brands at a similar level
Offer a flat $1,000 for every lead they refer that closes as a client
Send a short cold DM on Twitter, LinkedIn, or Discord ecom communities introducing yourself, sharing a case study or deck, and proposing the deal
Most people ignore it, but enough reply that the volume works
From six leads generated this way, three converted — a strong hit rate for warm-ish referralsWhy it works:
These people are already plugged into a network of brands doing similar revenue
The referrer is essentially becoming a commission-based salesman with almost zero effort required
The $1K fee is roughly in line with or below what agency owners would pay in CAC through paid ads anyway
Referred clients come in warmer — the referrer often pre-sells you before you even get on a call, meaning you're sometimes jumping straight to pricing
Even when nothing closes right away, you stay in people's minds — when they hear of a brand needing email help, your name comes upTristan's version:
Already uses a 15% off next invoice incentive for existing clients who refer. Charlie's approach — paying external people who aren't clients — was new to him and something he planned to take further. The external version taps a much wider pool of people.
Key targeting note:
Aim at people doing over £100K/month in revenue — they tend to know other people doing similar numbers. Spending time on people doing £10K/month doesn't generate the right referral quality.

---
The Scaling Playbook — Hiring, Firing & Letting Go (25:00–72:00)
Ben presented a document compiled from a 10-minute voice note from Max plus transcripts from three of Max's YouTube interviews on growing an agency.
The four stages of agency scale:
Solo (£3–10K/month): one person doing everything, maybe occasional Upwork freelancers
First team (£30K/month): cold email running, first hires in place, founder still leads on everything
Letting go (£150K/month): delegating sales calls and fulfillment, real management layer emerging

Hire ahead of the pain — bring people in and train them before you're already overwhelmed. Have spare capacity ready before the next client signs, not after. The aviation analogy: planes rarely fly at 100% engine capacity — that's how you burn out the engines. Always keep 10–15% headroom.

---
Who to hire when you're small:
The mistake most small agencies make is trying to attract experienced hires they can't yet afford or compete for. The move at this stage is to hire for hunger, not experience.
Traits to look for: moldable, coachable, wants to learn, willing to grow, and crucially — has that dog mentality where they want to win. Someone who says they eventually want to start their own agency is often the best hire — entrepreneurial mindset means they'll take real ownership of the work.
Ben's own example:
When Ben joined Well Copy, he had no email marketing background and no ecom experience. He'd never done appointment setting before. He got hired because he was competent, confident, moldable, and Max felt he could be a reliable representation of the brand without needing constant monitoring.
Tristan's example:
His new designer didn't come from a big impressive agency background. He came from a smaller UK agency where there was no growth and no opportunity. He joined Tristan's team because he could learn more, try more things, and wasn't stuck doing the same thing every day. That kind of person brings drive.

---
Where to source different roles:
Designers and commoditised roles: LinkedIn job posts targeting talent hubs like Buenos Aires, Argentina. Also Upwork. Argentina in particular produces a high density of strong, affordable remote designers.
Senior/niche roles (account managers, Klaviyo experts): recruiters who head hunt people already employed. The best account managers aren't browsing job boards.
Contract roles (copywriters): personal brand and social posts. People who want flexible project-based work self-select here. Max gets so many copywriter DMs that when Well Copy needs one, the first step is going to the Instagram search bar and typing "copywriter" — every conversation where that word has appeared surfaces immediately.

---
Staff up in stages, not all at once:
1–5 clients: do everything yourself, part-time contractors for copy and design, paid per piece
5–20 clients: build the core roles — copywriter, designer, account manager, Klaviyo technician. Founder still on every client call.
20+ clients: promote a strategist from within to own oversight. Start stepping back.Rule of thumb: move a contractor to full-time around 8–10 clients, once the margin genuinely supports it. Don't rush it.
The pod model:
One copywriter, one designer, one account manager, one Klaviyo technician, working the same accounts every time. One pod handles 6–8 accounts comfortably. At 15–20 clients, you'll usually have 2–3 pods running under a strategist. This structure creates consistency, keeps brand knowledge concentrated, and means clients build relationships with one team rather than getting passed around.
The pricing floor that makes pods work:
$1,000/month retainers kill your margins. At that rate, staffing a single role is already 50% of revenue. $3,000/month is the floor. At 10 clients, that's $30,000 in revenue — enough to properly staff a pod and keep healthy margins.

---
Training is what actually frees up your time — not just hiring:
The hire alone changes nothing. The investment is the training period. Expect months before it pays off.
Max's system for early-stage hires:
Morning check-in: walk through the day's agenda together, coach through problems before they hit
Evening clock-out message: quick check on what's done, what's open, what needs reviewThis hand-holding tapers naturally over time as the person learns your systems and standards. The investment upfront means you eventually don't need to check in at all.

First couple of weeks — a call every day, 20 minutes each. Then twice a week. Then it stopped entirely. Started with homework, documents to read, fathom recordings of sales calls to watch and write notes on. Max's goal was to understand exactly where Ben's psychology was with sales before putting him on any calls.

---

The classic mistake: handing a new account manager eight clients on day one. They're overwhelmed before they've learned your systems, and quality slips on every account simultaneously.

---

100% of Well Copy's last 30 hires came from internal team referrals. A £1–2K referral bonus scaled by how difficult the role is to fill. The rule: A-players know other A-players. Land a couple and recruiting starts doing itself.
When Well Copy is hiring, the COO puts out a message on Slack with a Google Sheet where people can drop names and emails — no need for CVs, just a name, contact, and suggested role. The DMs and network do the rest.

---

The single belief that keeps most agency owners stuck in fulfillment the longest.
Max example: an account manager once wrote a full client strategy and email sequence with no oversight during a busy week. The expected outcome was worse results. The client's actual reply: "These are my favorite emails you've sent yet."

The 10/80/10 rule (from Daniel Martell's Buy Back Your Time):
10%: you set the direction, the brief, the standard — the part only you can define
80%: they own it completely. No hovering. They take real pride in it because it's actually theirs.
10%: you polish. Final review and adjustments. Not a rebuild — just finishing touches.

---

Non-negotiable weekly all-hands touch point. When it was floated as biweekly, the team pushed back. Keep it weekly.

The founder sets the emotional tone — energy cascades top down. Show up stressed, the team absorbs it. Show up locked in, they mirror it.
Direct, personal appreciation outperforms generic praise every time.Well Copy's Friday coffee date:

Q&A (72:00–94:00)
Contractor vs employee structure across Europe (Marlon, Rinse):
Well Copy runs entirely on contractor agreements — no PAYE, no payroll via a tax office. Everyone receives a fixed monthly payment direct to their bank account and manages their own tax obligations. Ben sends a Slack message of what he's owed and gets paid — no formal monthly invoice in his case. On the UK legality of exclusive contractor arrangements:
Ben and Tristan both landed on the view that a contractor agreement that specifies full-time hours and exclusivity is still legally a contractor agreement — not an employment contract — if it's written that way. The film industry was cited as an example where people work exclusively for one production for months without being classified as employees. However, both acknowledged it's worth verifying with a professional depending on the jurisdiction.
Handling unqualified prospects — brands doing sub-£25K/month (Tristan):
Getting an influx of smaller brands booking calls from content growth. Options discussed:
Some members said they'll still hop on a call and try to pitch a standalone flow build (1.5–3K) rather than a retainer
The problem: brands at this level tend to be the most demanding, have the highest expectations, and are the hardest to close even when the ROI is obvious. Cyril shared a first-hand example of a client who had massive expectations, couldn't sustain even a modest retainer, and disappeared after one month — despite the ROI being clear
Ben's perspective: set a hard baseline for the brand size you'll actually take calls with, based on where you've historically closed clients. Yes, that thins the calendar initially — use that as the push to improve the quality of your outreach and content to attract better-fit brands. Time spent chasing small brands who won't close is time not spent on something actually useful
The meme analogy: brand doing 5K/month sends a five paragraph email about synergy. Brand doing 500K/month says "send Stripe link."Raising prices on an existing client (Rinse):
Rinse has a client doing roughly £5M/year in revenue, generating £80–90K/month attributed to email, paying £1,500/month — a 25X revenue ROI for the client and a wildly underpriced retainer.
Tristan's approach (which he has successfully used across all existing clients):
Prepare as if it's a sales call — review the numbers, pull the ROI data, have it ready to present
Frame the increase around the agency's own growth: "When we started, I was a smaller team, less experienced. The team has grown, margins have changed, our quality has increased — so our pricing has to reflect that"
Anchor the new price against what new clients are currently charged, then offer the existing client a loyalty discount below that — makes them feel they're still getting a deal
If you want to sweeten it, add a small value increase (a few more emails per month, a guaranteed number of A/B tests, etc.)
The result: Tristan went through all of his existing clients, raised every single retainer, and lost none of themBen's additional framing:
If the cash flow risk feels too high, don't raise existing clients straight away — set the new price floor for every new client going forward. Then when you're building towards capacity, you have natural leverage: "We've been charging all new clients this amount. You've been grandfathered on the original rate, but we need to align things now." You can still offer a loyalty discount on top of that to soften the conversation. And realistically, clients who are getting a 25X revenue ROI know they're underpaying you. They're not surprised when the conversation finally comes.

---
Closing (~94:00)
Tristan wrapped up. Ben thanked everyone for bearing with the last-minute document scramble. Topic suggestions for next week to be sent via DM. August design challenge reminder — post one email design per week to qualify for a private call with Max at the end of the month.

lessons.title: July 28th: Social Proof, DM Strategy & Q&A
lessons.description:
Call Summary — Using Social Proof to Generate Leads, DM Pipeline Management & Outreach Strategy
Doc Featured On Call >>

---
Opening (0:00–8:00)
Tristan joined with his brace off and arm slowly rebuilding muscle. Ben called in from his bedroom after missing a flight in Spain and having to rebook — ended up flying with a different airline, arriving hours late. Light catch-up before diving in.
A few members introduced themselves as new joiners — Danny (agency owner, joined the previous night) and Marlon (brand-side currently, exploring building an agency). Max was also on the call briefly but had mic issues throughout.

---
Social Proof as a Lead Generation Tool (8:00–35:00)
Ben presented a resource compiled from Well Copy's internal approach and Max's content strategy — how to use social proof across a sales pipeline.
Why social proof matters:
Every email agency is making the same promise. The only way to credibly differentiate is to show someone else vouching for you. Social proof does two jobs: it builds immediate authority (combined portfolio numbers) and it builds personal trust (individual client stories).
Well Copy's macro numbers:
300+ brands worked with, £250M+ generated for clients, 41% average attributed revenue across the client base. These headline numbers establish authority before any individual case study is even needed.

---
The four types of social proof:
1. Written and video testimonials
Ask clients to write a testimonial framed around before and after — what they were struggling with before and what's changed since. The more specific the numbers, the better.
The more powerful subtype: selfie video testimonials. Just a client holding their phone, talking for 30–60 seconds. Extremely hard to fake, immediately authentic. These are tough to get because most clients don't enjoy being on camera — expect to follow up multiple times. But when you land one, it's worth the effort significantly more than a written version.
What makes a good testimonial:
A specific revenue number or percentage increase
A clear before and after
Full name and role (especially if they're at a notable brand)
One quotable line that can be pulled out and used standalone
Their brand name if it carries weight in the niche2. Raw client love
Screenshots of Slack messages, DMs, and reactions from clients responding to your work. A client saying "these designs are sick, can't wait to see them go out" or "that A/B test just crushed" — these are immediate, unprompted, and impossible to fake. Screenshot everything as it comes in and build a swipe file.
These often carry more weight than polished case studies because they show how it actually feels to work with you, not just the numbers. Ben noted that some agencies have run these Slack screenshots as Meta ad creatives and found them highly effective — the raw, conversation-style format cuts through.
3. Hard revenue proof
Screenshots of Klaviyo dashboards, campaign revenue stats, flow performance numbers. When posting these:
Lead with one headline number — don't overwhelm
Add context (brand size, timeline, what was built)
Reframe the number as what's possible, not a flex — "here's what brands like yours are seeing"
End with a low-friction CTA (DM a keyword or book a call)4. Case studies
The full transformation story — where the brand was, what was built, where they ended up, ideally with a client quote. Worth building a dedicated section on your website and potentially a YouTube video if the result is strong enough.

---
Team and culture content:
A fifth form of proof that often gets overlooked — showing the team, the energy, and how the work environment feels. Clients aren't just buying results, they're trusting a group of people with their brand. Seeing that those people are happy, skilled, and enthusiastic de-risks the relationship. Max's team Zoom in costumes, OperaX's London team skit videos — this stuff builds trust that no dashboard screenshot can.

---
Recycling and milking your proof:
Don't feel the need to constantly generate new proof. New people are following you every week — they've never seen the screenshot you posted two months ago. Post your best performing proof repeatedly on stories. Build an Instagram highlights section with just testimonials and results — it does the heavy lifting every time someone visits your profile after seeing your content.
On rewriting testimonials: if a client left a good but boring review, use the numbers and reframe them in a way that's more scannable and compelling. Not fabricating anything — just presenting what they actually said in a way that lands harder.

---
Two CTA styles for stories:
Direct to book a call: best when the proof is strong enough to stand alone. Someone sees a dashboard screenshot or a powerful testimonial and they're ready to take action.
Slide up with a keyword: starts a DM conversation. Works with ManyChat automation to instantly deliver a lead magnet and then flow into a qualifying conversation. Best when you want to warm people up before putting them in front of the closer.
---
DM Pipeline — How Well Copy Manages Inbound (35:00–50:00)
Ben walked through the exact process used to manage the Instagram DM pipeline at Well Copy.
How the flow works end to end:
Max posts content or a story with a "DM me X for [free resource]" CTA
ManyChat automation fires instantly — delivers the resource, then follows up with a question like "how's email performing for you at the moment?" at the end of the flow
Any message that's a normal reply (not a trigger) lands as unread in the Instagram inbox — ManyChat ignores it
Ben opens Meta Business Suite, filters to unread messages, and scrolls through to identify actual brand owners vs noise (SaaS people, designers, marketers, etc.)

Danny's approach — Claude-powered hyper-personalisation at scale:

Buy 3–4 domains (all redirect to your main site)

Tristan wrapped up. Topic suggestions for next week to go to Tristan or Ben via DM. Everyone encouraged to post questions in the community feed between calls for faster responses.

A few members introduced themselves as new joiners — Danny (agency owner, joined the previous night) and Marlon (brand-side currently, exploring building an agency). Max was also on the call briefly but had mic issues throughout.

Ben presented a resource compiled from Well Copy's internal approach and Max's content strategy — how to use social proof across a sales pipeline.
Why social proof matters:

Every email agency is making the same promise. The only way to credibly differentiate is to show someone else vouching for you. Social proof does two jobs: it builds immediate authority (combined portfolio numbers) and it builds personal trust (individual client stories).
Well Copy's macro numbers:

300+ brands worked with, £250M+ generated for clients, 41% average attributed revenue across the client base. These headline numbers establish authority before any individual case study is even needed.
The four types of social proof:
1. Written and video testimonials
Ask clients to write a testimonial framed around before and after — what they were struggling with before and what's changed since. The more specific the numbers, the better.

The more powerful subtype: selfie video testimonials. Just a client holding their phone, talking for 30–60 seconds. Extremely hard to fake, immediately authentic. These are tough to get because most clients don't enjoy being on camera — expect to follow up multiple times. But when you land one, it's worth the effort significantly more than a written version.
What makes a good testimonial:
A specific revenue number or percentage increase
A clear before and after
Full name and role (especially if they're at a notable brand)
One quotable line that can be pulled out and used standalone
Their brand name if it carries weight in the niche
2. Raw client love

Screenshots of Slack messages, DMs, and reactions from clients responding to your work. A client saying "these designs are sick, can't wait to see them go out" or "that A/B test just crushed" — these are immediate, unprompted, and impossible to fake. Screenshot everything as it comes in and build a swipe file.

These often carry more weight than polished case studies because they show how it actually feels to work with you, not just the numbers. Ben noted that some agencies have run these Slack screenshots as Meta ad creatives and found them highly effective — the raw, conversation-style format cuts through.
3. Hard revenue proof
Screenshots of Klaviyo dashboards, campaign revenue stats, flow performance numbers. When posting these:
Lead with one headline number — don't overwhelm
Add context (brand size, timeline, what was built)
Reframe the number as what's possible, not a flex — "here's what brands like yours are seeing"
End with a low-friction CTA (DM a keyword or book a call)
4. Case studies

The full transformation story — where the brand was, what was built, where they ended up, ideally with a client quote. Worth building a dedicated section on your website and potentially a YouTube video if the result is strong enough.
Team and culture content:

A fifth form of proof that often gets overlooked — showing the team, the energy, and how the work environment feels. Clients aren't just buying results, they're trusting a group of people with their brand. Seeing that those people are happy, skilled, and enthusiastic de-risks the relationship. Max's team Zoom in costumes, OperaX's London team skit videos — this stuff builds trust that no dashboard screenshot can.
Recycling and milking your proof:

Don't feel the need to constantly generate new proof. New people are following you every week — they've never seen the screenshot you posted two months ago. Post your best performing proof repeatedly on stories. Build an Instagram highlights section with just testimonials and results — it does the heavy lifting every time someone visits your profile after seeing your content.

On rewriting testimonials: if a client left a good but boring review, use the numbers and reframe them in a way that's more scannable and compelling. Not fabricating anything — just presenting what they actually said in a way that lands harder.
Two CTA styles for stories:
Direct to book a call:
best when the proof is strong enough to stand alone. Someone sees a dashboard screenshot or a powerful testimonial and they're ready to take action.
Slide up with a keyword:

starts a DM conversation. Works with ManyChat automation to instantly deliver a lead magnet and then flow into a qualifying conversation. Best when you want to warm people up before putting them in front of the closer.

lessons.title: July 21st: Bad Clients, Client Reporting, Open Q&A
lessons.description:
Call Summary — Client Reporting, Identifying & Handling Bad Clients, Relationship Building & Open Q&A


---
Opening (0:00–5:00)
Tristan opened with a health update — brace off the arm, starting to regain movement, though the muscle loss from weeks of not using it is noticeable. The format for today was deliberately lighter: open Q&A and discussion rather than a structured resource doc, as requested by the group after last week's session.

---
Client Reporting — What Actually Works (5:00–18:00)
Chad from Holo Socks joined the call and opened a discussion on reporting — not because he was unhappy with his agency, but out of curiosity about what's actually worth reporting versus what's noise.
Tristan's approach:
Weekly reporting is not standard once a relationship is established. Flow performance week over week doesn't tell you much in isolation — a Q1 week and a Q4 week are completely different contexts.
Quick wins go to Slack as they happen — ad hoc wins, A/B test results, campaigns that popped. These are more valuable than structured weekly reports.
Monthly reporting uses Hyros' template covering flow vs campaign split, first-time vs repeat buyer breakdown, and list growth.
Bi-weekly calls focus on reviewing the last 14–30 days of campaigns, identifying what made the most revenue per recipient, why certain things worked, and how to apply those learnings to flows going forward.Jeremy's approach:
Weekly reporting felt redundant — clients never responded to the Hyros reports, and he suspects most weren't even reading them.
More effective: plain English updates in calls, explaining what's actually happened and why, rather than handing over a spreadsheet for the client to interpret themselves.
Quick wins communicated conversationally are more impactful than formal reports. Monthly reporting is an area Jeremy acknowledges he's gotten lazy on and wants to improve — specifically around adding an expert interpretation layer rather than just dumping data.Chad's takeaway:
As a brand-side head of retention, he doesn't need to see every campaign's performance — he already knows what's working. What he values most is ad hoc wins that come out of nowhere (a flash sale that ripped on a Tuesday, for example). That's a bigger signal of an agency that's actively in the account than a formatted weekly report.
On pop-up reporting:
Chad's agency doesn't manage the pop-up — he handles that himself via Alia, which provides its own insights and is always running some kind of A/B test. Makes it easy for him to always have something to share with the agency.
On division of responsibility:
Chad handles strategy and approvals, leads all A/B testing on the flow side (subject line testing in campaigns feels pointless to him — you can't reuse a winner), and flags new ideas and product launches. The agency handles calendar planning 60 days out plus copy, design, and implementation.

---
Identifying & Handling Bad Clients (18:00–48:00)
Tristan opened the discussion by distinguishing between two types of difficult clients:
High-maintenance but manageable: lots of revisions, but they respect your authority and the retainer makes it worth it
Genuinely toxic: rude, disrespectful, pays late, wants to rewrite everything, doesn't trust your expertiseThe challenge of identifying them early:
Almost impossible to spot before you start working together. A one-call close gives you 15–30 minutes with someone who's on their best behaviour. Most agencies at a growth stage can't afford to turn away a decent retainer on a gut feeling. You take the client and figure it out as you go.
Common types of bad clients:
The non-responder — short replies, slow turnaround on approvals, causes internal bottlenecks
The revision-maxer — never satisfied with anything but keeps you on anyway as an execution arm
The stress-transferrer — struggling with other parts of their business (social agency, ads, whatever) and taking that out on their email teamJeremy's experience:
Had a client who kept him on for over a year despite never being happy with the work — essentially treating the agency as a cheap execution resource. Also flagged the emotional challenge of not taking client negativity personally, particularly when it's clearly coming from external pressure in their business rather than anything the email agency has done.
Ben's framing:
The root issue is when clients treat the agency like an employee rather than a hired expert. The remedy is setting that dynamic correctly from the start — in the sales process and in the onboarding. Daniel at Well Copy sets the tone through nonchalance and quiet authority during the discovery call, not through a script. That tonality signals from day one that this is a partnership of equals, not a service provider taking orders.
Ben also shared a specific example of a $7–10M/month brand that reached out wanting to sign immediately, skipping the vetting process. When Ben explained that Well Copy also needed to assess fit from their side, the prospect got offended and said he didn't have time for a 30-minute call. Max's response: screw that guy. Being in a position of strength means you can walk away from disrespectful leads regardless of their revenue. The theory: acting with that same self-respect from day one — even with an empty pipeline — would likely produce the same growth rate, just with better clients.
On having the direct conversation:
Ben raised having actually said to a difficult client that the communication wasn't working and that there needed to be more trust. He was calm and professional about it. The relationship continued for another two months before naturally ending. The conclusion: hard conversation is better than slow resentment, but timing matters — it's much easier to have it when your pipeline is healthy and you're not coming from a place of scarcity.
Tristan's approach to difficult clients:
When a client says "what am I paying you for?" when you push back on a last-minute request: "You're not the only one paying me. If I drop everything for you right now, what are the other brands paying me for?" Framing yourself as a shared resource removes the dynamic where they feel entitled to 100% of your immediate attention.
On saying no:
Tristan acknowledged always defaulting to saying yes and figuring it out — and that this removes your authority over time. If a client throws a last-minute request and you always deliver, they learn that last-minute requests get delivered. If you say no once, they get burned, and they're unlikely to do it again. The short-term discomfort of one missed campaign is worth the long-term benefit of a client who respects your process.
The price increase as a client exit strategy:
Raise your rates. If they can't afford it, they're gone — and you didn't have to have an awkward conversation. If they say yes, you at least get compensated properly for the difficulty.
Protecting your reputation:
If a client is forcing decisions you fundamentally disagree with and your agency's name is on the output, that's a reason to walk away regardless of the revenue. Bad results from decisions you didn't endorse will follow you.
On onboarding as prevention:
A lot of problematic client behaviour stems from anxiety — not knowing what's happening, not having visibility into the process. The clients least likely to spiral are the ones who've been over-communicated with from day one. Respond to messages within minutes even if just to say when the real answer is coming. Give them a clear roadmap from the moment they sign. Deliver early wins in the first week. If they never have space to doubt you, they're much less likely to become difficult.

---
Client Gifting & Relationship Building (48:00–57:00)
On gifting clients:
Tristan raised the idea of sending gifts — he did it once for a client who was in hospital after an accident. Mixed opinions on whether it drives retention, but general consensus it's a nice thing to do and costs very little relative to retainer value.
Jeremy: heard of agencies sending a personalised gift (e.g. a football shirt if a client mentioned a team) at key moments like birthdays or milestones. The ROI potential is significant — £80 can buy another year of retention.
Ben's perspective — the best restaurants in the world hire people specifically to do pre-research on guests during reservation confirmation calls, then personalise the experience based on what they learn. The email agency equivalent: when a client mentions something personal on a call, note it, and bring it up or reference it later. Doesn't have to be a physical gift — just demonstrating that you were actually listening goes a long way. The principle is: if you know they love a specific thing, act on that knowledge at the right moment.
On meeting clients in person:
Every member on the call who had met a client in person said those were their strongest and longest-lasting relationships. The consensus: don't wait until you've hit some milestone of closeness before suggesting it — meeting in person fast-tracks the relationship to a different level of trust and warmth almost immediately.
Tristan's suggestion: if you share a city with a prospect, offering to grab a coffee or co-work during onboarding is a strong differentiator. "Come to my co-working space and we'll nail your brand together" signals a level of investment in the relationship that very few agencies offer.
Rinse mentioned taking it even further — two of his clients are worked with face to face at their offices on specific days of the week. One of those client relationships resulted in him being invited on a team trip.

---
Q&A — Open Discussion (57:00–80:20)
Mahad — first client going quiet (8 days no response):
Eight days without contact is a long time. Group recommended:
Keep building the flows anyway — don't let the work stall
Send a voice note to break through the noise of text-based messages
If the silence is blocking you from getting approval on important flow decisions, that warrants a phone call
Sending daily screenshot updates is fine, but if they're not replying to questions you specifically need answered, escalate the communication channel
Using a meme (e.g. someone talking to a wall) as a lighthearted nudge can work well depending on the relationshipMeta lead form vs website pop-up for email collection:
Mahad asked whether running lead forms on Meta (collecting emails in-platform rather than driving to the website) is a viable strategy.
Jeremy and Ben both confirmed: lead form traffic converts very poorly as an email list source. These subscribers typically have very low intent — they clicked something, maybe without fully understanding what they were signing up for. Open rates tank, conversion rates are negligible, and the list quality is genuinely bad. The biggest brands don't do it this way. Drive traffic to the website and capture email there through a properly optimised pop-up — the friction is intentional and filters for real interest.
Noah — Client Ascension review:
Noah joined Client Ascension roughly nine months ago and confirmed he's 10x'd his investment. Key benefits he highlighted:
The wins channel showing people in the same niche closing big deals — primarily useful for mindset
Upwork as a client acquisition channel — some members are closing $10K deals per month purely from Upwork
Live calls with founders running 7–8 figure businesses who answer questions in real time
Community connection — DMing other students at different stages and getting specific, actionable adviceBen's take on the value of communities generally: it's never about the 99% you already know. It's about the 1% you're missing — that one specific thing you haven't been able to figure out that, once unlocked, lets you build with momentum on everything else you already have.
Olivia — time management across a job, freelance clients, and a new product patent:
No silver bullet answer. Tristan admitted he doesn't have a perfect system. Ben referenced the Sam Ovens "warm-up" productivity framework — mapping out the year at a high level and then reducing each day to three core needle-moving tasks rather than a sprawling to-do list. Worth looking up on YouTube for the full breakdown.
Rinse — team update and the Dutch econ mafia:
Rinse recently hired a designer (Michelle, remote) and a new account manager/copywriter with Klaviyo experience — a meaningful upgrade from a previous copywriter who had no email marketing background and made account-level work harder than it needed to be. Also onboarded a designer. Now working with two clients face to face at their offices.
On the Dutch econ community being disproportionately active in email/ecom — Rinse's explanation: early exposure to dropshipping through Dutch course creators in the mid-2010s, compounded by the Netherlands being one of the most digitally advanced consumer markets in Europe (high online shopping adoption, high subscription comfort). Small country, everyone knows each other, so the network effects are strong.
Sales call volume check-in:
Tristan asked the group transparently how many sales calls they're actually booking per week. Matthias: five per week when he's doing cold calls, one to two when he isn't — and he acknowledged his inputs are inconsistent because client fulfilment eats his time. The conclusion from the group: it's not a strategy problem for most people — it's a consistency of inputs problem.
Q4 planning — topic requested for future sessions:
Two specific areas flagged for future docs or call topics:
Internal workload planning for Q4 — how agencies manage the volume spike operationally
When to start Q4 conversations with clients — specifically for smaller brands who haven't thought about it yet, how involved the email agency gets in Black Friday strategy, and whether scope increases should come with a price increaseBen's recommendation: start pushing Q4 conversations hard in Q3. By the second half of Q4, the window for getting new clients is basically closed — everyone's locked in with their existing agencies and too busy to onboard anyone new. The time to land Q4 clients is now.

---
Closing (~80:20)
Tristan wrapped up and invited topic suggestions for future calls and docs — anything to send through to Ben or Tristan via DM. The Q4 planning topic is now in the pipeline for a future session.
