Chad handles strategy and approvals, leads all A/B testing on the flow side (subject line testing in campaigns feels pointless to him — you can't reuse a winner), and flags new ideas and product launches. The agency handles calendar planning 60 days out plus copy, design, and implementation.
Identifying & Handling Bad Clients (18:00–48:00)
Tristan opened the discussion by distinguishing between two types of difficult clients:
High-maintenance but manageable:
lots of revisions, but they respect your authority and the retainer makes it worth it
Genuinely toxic:
rude, disrespectful, pays late, wants to rewrite everything, doesn't trust your expertise
The challenge of identifying them early:

Almost impossible to spot before you start working together. A one-call close gives you 15–30 minutes with someone who's on their best behaviour. Most agencies at a growth stage can't afford to turn away a decent retainer on a gut feeling. You take the client and figure it out as you go.
Common types of bad clients:
The non-responder — short replies, slow turnaround on approvals, causes internal bottlenecks
The revision-maxer — never satisfied with anything but keeps you on anyway as an execution arm
The stress-transferrer — struggling with other parts of their business (social agency, ads, whatever) and taking that out on their email team
Jeremy's experience:

Had a client who kept him on for over a year despite never being happy with the work — essentially treating the agency as a cheap execution resource. Also flagged the emotional challenge of not taking client negativity personally, particularly when it's clearly coming from external pressure in their business rather than anything the email agency has done.
Ben's framing:

The root issue is when clients treat the agency like an employee rather than a hired expert. The remedy is setting that dynamic correctly from the start — in the sales process and in the onboarding. Daniel at Well Copy sets the tone through nonchalance and quiet authority during the discovery call, not through a script. That tonality signals from day one that this is a partnership of equals, not a service provider taking orders.

Ben also shared a specific example of a $7–10M/month brand that reached out wanting to sign immediately, skipping the vetting process. When Ben explained that Well Copy also needed to assess fit from their side, the prospect got offended and said he didn't have time for a 30-minute call. Max's response: screw that guy. Being in a position of strength means you can walk away from disrespectful leads regardless of their revenue. The theory: acting with that same self-respect from day one — even with an empty pipeline — would likely produce the same growth rate, just with better clients.
On having the direct conversation:

Ben raised having actually said to a difficult client that the communication wasn't working and that there needed to be more trust. He was calm and professional about it. The relationship continued for another two months before naturally ending. The conclusion: hard conversation is better than slow resentment, but timing matters — it's much easier to have it when your pipeline is healthy and you're not coming from a place of scarcity.
Tristan's approach to difficult clients:

When a client says "what am I paying you for?" when you push back on a last-minute request: "You're not the only one paying me. If I drop everything for you right now, what are the other brands paying me for?" Framing yourself as a shared resource removes the dynamic where they feel entitled to 100% of your immediate attention.
On saying no:

Tristan acknowledged always defaulting to saying yes and figuring it out — and that this removes your authority over time. If a client throws a last-minute request and you always deliver, they learn that last-minute requests get delivered. If you say no once, they get burned, and they're unlikely to do it again. The short-term discomfort of one missed campaign is worth the long-term benefit of a client who respects your process.
The price increase as a client exit strategy:
Raise your rates. If they can't afford it, they're gone — and you didn't have to have an awkward conversation. If they say yes, you at least get compensated properly for the difficulty.
Protecting your reputation:

If a client is forcing decisions you fundamentally disagree with and your agency's name is on the output, that's a reason to walk away regardless of the revenue. Bad results from decisions you didn't endorse will follow you.
On onboarding as prevention:

A lot of problematic client behaviour stems from anxiety — not knowing what's happening, not having visibility into the process. The clients least likely to spiral are the ones who've been over-communicated with from day one. Respond to messages within minutes even if just to say when the real answer is coming. Give them a clear roadmap from the moment they sign. Deliver early wins in the first week. If they never have space to doubt you, they're much less likely to become difficult.
Client Gifting & Relationship Building (48:00–57:00)
On gifting clients:

Tristan raised the idea of sending gifts — he did it once for a client who was in hospital after an accident. Mixed opinions on whether it drives retention, but general consensus it's a nice thing to do and costs very little relative to retainer value.

Jeremy: heard of agencies sending a personalised gift (e.g. a football shirt if a client mentioned a team) at key moments like birthdays or milestones. The ROI potential is significant — £80 can buy another year of retention.

Ben's perspective — the best restaurants in the world hire people specifically to do pre-research on guests during reservation confirmation calls, then personalise the experience based on what they learn. The email agency equivalent: when a client mentions something personal on a call, note it, and bring it up or reference it later. Doesn't have to be a physical gift — just demonstrating that you were actually listening goes a long way. The principle is: if you know they love a specific thing, act on that knowledge at the right moment.
On meeting clients in person:

Every member on the call who had met a client in person said those were their strongest and longest-lasting relationships. The consensus: don't wait until you've hit some milestone of closeness before suggesting it — meeting in person fast-tracks the relationship to a different level of trust and warmth almost immediately.

Tristan's suggestion: if you share a city with a prospect, offering to grab a coffee or co-work during onboarding is a strong differentiator. "Come to my co-working space and we'll nail your brand together" signals a level of investment in the relationship that very few agencies offer.

Rinse mentioned taking it even further — two of his clients are worked with face to face at their offices on specific days of the week. One of those client relationships resulted in him being invited on a team trip.
Q&A — Open Discussion (57:00–80:20)
Mahad — first client going quiet (8 days no response):
Eight days without contact is a long time. Group recommended:
Keep building the flows anyway — don't let the work stall
Send a voice note to break through the noise of text-based messages
If the silence is blocking you from getting approval on important flow decisions, that warrants a phone call
Sending daily screenshot updates is fine, but if they're not replying to questions you specifically need answered, escalate the communication channel
Using a meme (e.g. someone talking to a wall) as a lighthearted nudge can work well depending on the relationship
Meta lead form vs website pop-up for email collection:
Mahad asked whether running lead forms on Meta (collecting emails in-platform rather than driving to the website) is a viable strategy.

Jeremy and Ben both confirmed: lead form traffic converts very poorly as an email list source. These subscribers typically have very low intent — they clicked something, maybe without fully understanding what they were signing up for. Open rates tank, conversion rates are negligible, and the list quality is genuinely bad. The biggest brands don't do it this way. Drive traffic to the website and capture email there through a properly optimised pop-up — the friction is intentional and filters for real interest.
Noah — Client Ascension review:
Noah joined Client Ascension roughly nine months ago and confirmed he's 10x'd his investment. Key benefits he highlighted:
The wins channel showing people in the same niche closing big deals — primarily useful for mindset
Upwork as a client acquisition channel — some members are closing $10K deals per month purely from Upwork
Live calls with founders running 7–8 figure businesses who answer questions in real time
Community connection — DMing other students at different stages and getting specific, actionable advice

Ben's take on the value of communities generally: it's never about the 99% you already know. It's about the 1% you're missing — that one specific thing you haven't been able to figure out that, once unlocked, lets you build with momentum on everything else you already have.
Olivia — time management across a job, freelance clients, and a new product patent:

No silver bullet answer. Tristan admitted he doesn't have a perfect system. Ben referenced the Sam Ovens "warm-up" productivity framework — mapping out the year at a high level and then reducing each day to three core needle-moving tasks rather than a sprawling to-do list. Worth looking up on YouTube for the full breakdown.
Rinse — team update and the Dutch econ mafia:

Rinse recently hired a designer (Michelle, remote) and a new account manager/copywriter with Klaviyo experience — a meaningful upgrade from a previous copywriter who had no email marketing background and made account-level work harder than it needed to be. Also onboarded a designer. Now working with two clients face to face at their offices.

On the Dutch econ community being disproportionately active in email/ecom — Rinse's explanation: early exposure to dropshipping through Dutch course creators in the mid-2010s, compounded by the Netherlands being one of the most digitally advanced consumer markets in Europe (high online shopping adoption, high subscription comfort). Small country, everyone knows each other, so the network effects are strong.
Sales call volume check-in:

Tristan asked the group transparently how many sales calls they're actually booking per week. Matthias: five per week when he's doing cold calls, one to two when he isn't — and he acknowledged his inputs are inconsistent because client fulfilment eats his time. The conclusion from the group: it's not a strategy problem for most people — it's a consistency of inputs problem.
Q4 planning — topic requested for future sessions:
Two specific areas flagged for future docs or call topics:
Internal workload planning for Q4 — how agencies manage the volume spike operationally

When to start Q4 conversations with clients — specifically for smaller brands who haven't thought about it yet, how involved the email agency gets in Black Friday strategy, and whether scope increases should come with a price increase

Ben's recommendation: start pushing Q4 conversations hard in Q3. By the second half of Q4, the window for getting new clients is basically closed — everyone's locked in with their existing agencies and too busy to onboard anyone new. The time to land Q4 clients is now.
Closing (~80:20)
Tristan wrapped up and invited topic suggestions for future calls and docs — anything to send through to Ben or Tristan via DM. The Q4 planning topic is now in the pipeline for a future session.

lessons.title: July 14th: Sales, Calls & Closing Framework
lessons.description:
Call Summary — Well Copy Sales Process, Discovery Call Framework, Objection Handling & Closing Mechanics
Playbook - https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QlgeRxFnEb6dqvsk_2qp0bK1aoJlmOrOL4Y9LLPHras/edit?usp=sharing

---
Opening (0:00–8:00)
Tristan opened with an update on his arm recovery — now out of the cast and into a brace with some movement returning. The group discussed managing client revision cycles, particularly on first email designs.
Key takeaway from the discussion: frame the revision process in onboarding from day one. Let clients know upfront that early feedback rounds are normal and collaborative, not a sign of failure. If they aren't able to give specific, actionable feedback ("make it more modern" tells you nothing), coach them on how to communicate what they actually want. Setting this expectation early means either you exceed it by getting it right first time, or you manage it cleanly when revisions are needed.
Jeremy shared an example of a fashion client who gave zero comments across two emails, requested a phone call instead of leaving written feedback, and ended the relationship after one week — having paid for half the month because of the time already invested in strategy and auditing. Sometimes a client who can't communicate what they want is a bullet dodged.

---
Context on the Resource (8:00–12:00)
The main content for today's call came from a document Ben put together using Claude — compiled from Well Copy's internal sales training materials plus the transcripts of every closed deal so far this month (seven closes in the first half of July). The document covers the full sales process end-to-end.
Well Copy runs a two-call close framework as a fallback, but always tries for a one-call close. The discovery call is the deal — not a warm-up before a separate sales call. How you run it sets the tone for everything that follows.

---
Sales Mindset & Foundations (12:00–22:00)
Low attachment to outcome.
Even if your pipeline is thin, act like it isn't. Detachment from the outcome is what allows you to diagnose the business properly instead of chasing the deal. The close becomes a side effect of successfully identifying real problems — not the goal in itself.
The doctor analogy.
Daniel, Well Copy's head strategist, runs calls like a doctor, not a salesman. A doctor doesn't pitch. They listen, ask questions, identify what's wrong, and prescribe a solution. The patient doesn't argue with a diagnosis — they trust the expertise. When a prospect pushes back, you're not defending your agency, you're calmly helping them realise what they already told you was a problem.
Don't introduce the agency first.
One of the worst ways to open a sales call is by talking about your company. Start with their business. You earn the right to pitch by demonstrating you understand their situation first. Daniel never explains Well Copy in the first half of the call — he builds the full picture of their business and uses everything he learns to shape the transition into the pitch.
Talk less than the prospect.
Use recording tools like Fathom to track talk time. If you're talking more than the prospect, you're doing it wrong. Ask open-ended questions, let them ramble, and sit with silence — people often fill it with more useful information than they were planning to share.

---
Discovery Call Structure (22:00–38:00)
The first 60 seconds.
Build quick, genuine rapport — crack a joke, make them laugh, break the ice. Then immediately set the frame with one sentence:
"Just want to get to know you a little better, see if we'd be a good fit, and if we are, I'll show you exactly what a partnership would look like."
This removes defensiveness. The prospect physically has to agree to it, which drops their guard. They know they're not being sold to immediately. Get to the first real business question within two minutes — don't let rapport-building drag on.
The question stack — always in this order:
Anchor question: "Give me a thousand-foot view of the business." Can't be answered yes or no. Opens up everything and lets them reveal what matters most.
Decision maker check: Confirm they're the decision maker. If someone else is involved, they need to be on the next call.
Acquisition and funnel: What's driving revenue — wholesale, Amazon, TikTok Shop, Shopify, organic? What's their channel split?
Current email and SMS setup: Are they on Klaviyo? What flows do they have? Who built them? How many campaigns per week? Have they worked with an agency before?
Key numbers: AOV, CAC, LTV, attribution window, subscription vs one-time purchase split, channel traffic split. These are non-negotiable — you can't map ROI, qualify the brand, or build a proposal without them.On the six key numbers:
If a prospect is cagey about sharing revenue figures, that's a red flag. You're exploring a long-term growth partnership — if they won't be transparent with you now, they won't be easy to work with later. Get these numbers or end the call.
Always ask for the attribution window when they tell you their email percentage. A 7-day attribution window inflates the number dramatically. Well Copy typically uses a 5-day default. Knowing their window tells you how much of their headline figure is real.

---
Uncovering Real Pain (38:00–48:00)
Make the prospect state the problems themselves.
Don't tell them what's wrong with their setup. Ask questions that lead them to say it themselves. When they name the problem, they can't walk it back later during objection handling — they already committed to it being real.
Techniques:
"When you say you're not happy with that, what do you mean exactly?"
"Why can't you keep doing it that way?"
"What's the actual impact of that on the business?"
Keep asking why — this is sometimes called Socratic reasoning. Keep going until the root problem is fully exposed.This also prevents them from going to evaluate other agencies after the call. If they told you it's a serious problem, they can't then say "actually it's fine" — you can reference exactly what they said and ask what's changed.
Swap your instinct to point out a problem for a question. Let them discover it. Review your recordings and check whether you managed to do this — it's a hard skill that only improves with repetition.

---
Handling Common Objections (48:00–58:00)
The most frequent objections and how to handle them — note that none of these responses argue with the prospect. They give a number, reframe the question, or ask something back.
"Is email even effective?"
Your agency averages 41% of revenue from email and SMS combined. Pull up screenshots if needed. Don't get defensive — give the number and move on with confidence.
"Will I get offloaded to interns?"
Everyone on the team has two-plus years of experience. If your designers produce high-quality, brand-led work, lean into that — show what your emails actually look like. Brand owners respond strongly to "we focus 80% on value and education, 20% on discounts."
"You'll send too many emails and annoy my list."
Unsubscribes don't hurt your business — they help your deliverability. More emails means more revenue. You can also lean into the expertise angle: explain segmentation, send-time optimisation, and engagement-based targeting — show them there's a whole world of list management they haven't discovered yet.
The "if you're so confident, why not do a rev share?" objection:
Month-to-month contracts are the guarantee. If they're not getting results, they can leave. That's more honest and cleaner than a rev share built on attribution numbers that neither side can fully trust.
When a prospect tries to blame your agency for what a past agency did:
Don't defend the agency space — join their side. "Has that happened to you before? I'm sorry you got burned that way." Then, when appropriate, flip it: "Our entire model is built around client retention. You think we could hit a million in MRR with clients churning every month? Our reputation is our asset." Let them answer their own question.
"We already have an in-house team."
Don't compete with the team — position above it. Frame yourself as a strategic layer above execution that also frees up their team's time for other priorities. You're not replacing them, you're adding to them.
"Can I write the copy or do the design to reduce the price?"
Hard pass. The framing: "I can only confidently tell you we'll deliver results if I control all the variables. If copy or design comes back via someone else, I can't put my agency's name behind the output or guarantee the outcomes I've been describing." Hold firm without being aggressive about it.

---
Trust Building (58:00–65:00)
Always ask about past agencies.
Most brands who are shopping for email help already believe email works — they've just been burned. Understanding exactly what went wrong with previous agencies gives you the material to differentiate without directly trash-talking anyone.
Common failures brands have experienced: being handed off to junior team members, poor design quality, no reporting, inactive account managers, email lists being stolen. When one of these comes up, note the specific failure and address it later in the call to make sure you're demonstrating you don't fit that pattern.
This question is also useful content research — what agencies are doing wrong is exactly what you can speak about across your content and website.

---
Transitioning to the Pitch (65:00–72:00)
Once you've diagnosed the business and earned conviction, transition using the ACE framework:
Analyze (Days 1–7): Deep understanding of the brand, competition, current setup. Quick wins — pop-up form rebuild, initial campaign calendar ready on the kickoff call.
Create (Days 7–40): Build out core flows, launch initial campaigns.
Elevate (Ongoing): Heavy A/B testing, 3–4 campaigns per week, near-daily communication, ongoing optimisation.On decks: Daniel sometimes presents the package visually, sometimes goes off the dome. The more calls you do, the more natural the free-ball approach becomes. Tristan uses a Miro board showing the three core pillars — pop-ups, campaigns, flows — as a visual anchor for the pitch.
Never give the price until they're convicted.
Handle as many objections as you can before naming a number. A useful temperature check before transitioning: "On a scale of 1 to 10, where 1 is you think I have no idea what I'm doing and 10 is you're fully convinced — where are you?" If they give anything below 10, ask why. This usually surfaces the last remaining objection and gives you a clean path into price.
Pre-price checkpoint questions:
"Is this exactly what you're looking for to scale?"
"Any hesitations in our ability to get these results?"
If they answer both without asking about price: "I guess it just comes down to price then."
---
Revenue Projections & Attribution (72:00–78:00)
On giving revenue projections:
Well Copy is careful not to guarantee specific numbers. What they do instead is anchor on their benchmarks — 30% is the minimum baseline, most brands land between 41–50%. Apply that to the prospect's current revenue figure and show them the gap. "You're at 15%, we set 30% as a floor — that alone doubles your email revenue. That's an additional £X per month."
The framing is: this isn't a cost, it's a return. Help them see it as a mechanism, not a line item.
On the attribution argument:
Attribution across ecommerce is genuinely messy — no one really knows the true incremental number, and being honest about that builds more trust than defending a perfect-sounding stat. Reframe it around the mechanisms: email captures traffic that's already been paid for through ads and converts it rather than letting it leave. The halo effect of email (keeping the brand top of mind so someone buys in-store or via a different channel) is real even if it never gets attributed.
For prospects who are already strong on acquisition, shift the conversation to LTV and repeat purchase rate — the side of the business email genuinely owns.

---
Closing Mechanics (78:00–85:00)
The end of a good discovery call is administrative. The selling already happened. What's left is locking in next steps cleanly.
If pushing to an audit:
Request Klaviyo analyst access on the call — tell them exactly how to add you
Book the follow-up call before hanging up. Never say "I'll send an email when the audit's ready." Get a specific time and date confirmed on the call.
Confirm time zones
Note anything they asked for specifically (case studies, data on a specific metric) and confirm it'll be in the follow-upBook a meeting from a meeting. Every time, without exception.
Buyer types to know:
Ballin' Brian ($500K–$3M/month): Cares about legacy and prestige. Wants an A-player agency on his team, not a vendor. Speak to results and reputation.
Struggling Sam ($50K–$100K/month): Plateaued and time-capped. Obsessed with the product, needs trust before spending. Still feels like the business could collapse — fill them with confidence and stability.
Marketing Marvin (in-house head of marketing): Has a budget to spend and needs to prove himself internally. Often an easier close because it's not his business — he's less protective and just needs systemisation.De-qualifying:
After 14 days without a response or a reason, move on. Same principle as email list drop-off after day one — interest fades fast. Prospects who keep rescheduling without communication are showing you exactly what the client relationship will look like. Don't chase for discounts either — if someone is asking for money off, never reduce price without reducing deliverables. It devalues the service.
On brands under $50K/month:
Well Copy's internal close rate on this segment is around 3–3.5% — not worth taking calls with at scale. Default on the booking form is effectively to make these leads fight for their slot. Matthew calls and qualifies them; if they don't respond, the call gets cancelled. The exception is pre-launch brands with significant budget who are looking for a standalone flow build.

---
Pre-Call & Post-Call Process (85:00–95:00)
Pre-call nurturing:
Speed to lead is critical. Well Copy has a team member (Matthew) whose primary job is to call leads within minutes of booking. That pre-call conversation sets expectations, confirms what the call will cover, and dramatically improves both show-up rates and close rates.
For smaller operations: even calling within an hour of someone booking in makes a meaningful difference. The psychological effect of having already spoken to someone before the call removes uncertainty, builds familiarity, and gets them more committed to showing up.
Post-booking VSL idea (raised by Tristan):
Redirect leads to a short video after booking — thank them, run through a couple of case studies, and answer common FAQs. Warms them up to the agency before they arrive on the call. An extension of this is the Hormozi "sandwich close" — send the full pitch as a recording pre-call so by the time they arrive they've already processed the process, and the call becomes a qualification and fit conversation rather than a full pitch.
No-call close approach (Aussie agency example):
One agency owner runs ads driving leads to WhatsApp. He sends a voice note requesting Klaviyo access and a voice note back to confirm they're real. Runs a full Loom audit, sends it with a price at the end, and closes without ever getting on a call. High conviction, no objection handling — works for him but relies on very warm, pre-qualified leads and serious authority.
Post-call follow-up:
Send the call recording so the prospect has an accurate record of what was discussed — useful if they need to present the partnership internally. Include a breakdown of where you think you can help and what the next steps are. If it went very well, send the contract for review immediately. If it went to an audit, send what you need from them and confirm the next call time.

---
Q&A (Throughout)
Attribution objection from prospects:
Three approaches: (1) your benchmark data shows real brands generating 40-50% — apply that to their numbers, (2) shift the focus to LTV and repeat purchase mechanics rather than raw attribution percentage, (3) be honest that attribution is imperfect across the entire ecommerce ecosystem and that doing the right things consistently is what produces results regardless.
Client rewriting copy / excessive revisions:
Offer an A/B test — run their version against yours and let the data decide. If they say no to that, they're prioritising pride over results. In that case, you weigh up whether keeping them happy as a client is worth accepting lower results. If they're a long-term client who's otherwise good, sometimes you just let it be their quirk.
Format feedback for future agency calls:
Suggestion from the group to run more open free-conversation calls alongside structured resource-based sessions — a rotating format. More icebreakers to get quieter members talking, topic-seeded discussions rather than 50-page documents, and more direct engagement with people who haven't spoken. Ben and Tristan to explore.

---
Closing (~95:00)
Tristan and Ben wrapped up. Topic and resource suggestions for future calls to be sent directly to Ben or Tristan via DM.

Swap your instinct to point out a problem for a question.
Let them discover it. Review your recordings and check whether you managed to do this — it's a hard skill that only improves with repetition.
Handling Common Objections (
The most frequent objections and how to handle them — note that none of these responses argue with the prospect. They give a number, reframe the question, or ask something back.
"Is email even effective?"
Your agency averages 41% of revenue from email and SMS combined. Pull up screenshots if needed. Don't get defensive — give the number and move on with confidence.
"Will I get offloaded to interns?"

Everyone on the team has two-plus years of experience. If your designers produce high-quality, brand-led work, lean into that — show what your emails actually look like. Brand owners respond strongly to "we focus 80% on value and education, 20% on discounts."
"You'll send too many emails and annoy my list."

Unsubscribes don't hurt your business — they help your deliverability. More emails means more revenue. You can also lean into the expertise angle: explain segmentation, send-time optimisation, and engagement-based targeting — show them there's a whole world of list management they haven't discovered yet.
The "if you're so confident, why not do a rev share?" objection:

Month-to-month contracts are the guarantee. If they're not getting results, they can leave. That's more honest and cleaner than a rev share built on attribution numbers that neither side can fully trust.
When a prospect tries to blame your agency for what a past agency did:

Don't defend the agency space — join their side. "Has that happened to you before? I'm sorry you got burned that way." Then, when appropriate, flip it: "Our entire model is built around client retention. You think we could hit a million in MRR with clients churning every month? Our reputation is our asset." Let them answer their own question.
"We already have an in-house team."

Don't compete with the team — position above it. Frame yourself as a strategic layer above execution that also frees up their team's time for other priorities. You're not replacing them, you're adding to them.
"Can I write the copy or do the design to reduce the price?"

Hard pass. The framing: "I can only confidently tell you we'll deliver results if I control all the variables. If copy or design comes back via someone else, I can't put my agency's name behind the output or guarantee the outcomes I've been describing." Hold firm without being aggressive about it.
Trust Building (
Always ask about past agencies.

Most brands who are shopping for email help already believe email works — they've just been burned. Understanding exactly what went wrong with previous agencies gives you the material to differentiate without directly trash-talking anyone.

Common failures brands have experienced: being handed off to junior team members, poor design quality, no reporting, inactive account managers, email lists being stolen. When one of these comes up, note the specific failure and address it later in the call to make sure you're demonstrating you don't fit that pattern.
This question is also useful content research — what agencies are doing wrong is exactly what you can speak about across your content and website.
Transitioning to the Pitch (
Once you've diagnosed the business and earned conviction, transition using the ACE framework:
Analyze (Days 1–7):
Deep understanding of the brand, competition, current setup. Quick wins — pop-up form rebuild, initial campaign calendar ready on the kickoff call.
Create (Days 7–40):
Build out core flows, launch initial campaigns.
Elevate (Ongoing):
Heavy A/B testing, 3–4 campaigns per week, near-daily communication, ongoing optimisation.
On decks:

Daniel sometimes presents the package visually, sometimes goes off the dome. The more calls you do, the more natural the free-ball approach becomes. Tristan uses a Miro board showing the three core pillars — pop-ups, campaigns, flows — as a visual anchor for the pitch.
Never give the price until they're convicted.

Handle as many objections as you can before naming a number. A useful temperature check before transitioning: "On a scale of 1 to 10, where 1 is you think I have no idea what I'm doing and 10 is you're fully convinced — where are you?" If they give anything below 10, ask why. This usually surfaces the last remaining objection and gives you a clean path into price.
Pre-price checkpoint questions:
"Is this exactly what you're looking for to scale?"
"Any hesitations in our ability to get these results?"
If they answer both without asking about price: "I guess it just comes down to price then."
Revenue Projections & Attribution (
On giving revenue projections:

Well Copy is careful not to guarantee specific numbers. What they do instead is anchor on their benchmarks — 30% is the minimum baseline, most brands land between 41–50%. Apply that to the prospect's current revenue figure and show them the gap. "You're at 15%, we set 30% as a floor — that alone doubles your email revenue. That's an additional £X per month."
The framing is: this isn't a cost, it's a return. Help them see it as a mechanism, not a line item.
On the attribution argument:

Attribution across ecommerce is genuinely messy — no one really knows the true incremental number, and being honest about that builds more trust than defending a perfect-sounding stat. Reframe it around the mechanisms: email captures traffic that's already been paid for through ads and converts it rather than letting it leave. The halo effect of email (keeping the brand top of mind so someone buys in-store or via a different channel) is real even if it never gets attributed.
For prospects who are already strong on acquisition, shift the conversation to LTV and repeat purchase rate — the side of the business email genuinely owns.
Closing Mechanics (
The end of a good discovery call is administrative.
The selling already happened. What's left is locking in next steps cleanly.
If pushing to an audit:
Request Klaviyo analyst access on the call — tell them exactly how to add you
Book the follow-up call before hanging up. Never say "I'll send an email when the audit's ready." Get a specific time and date confirmed on the call.
Confirm time zones
Note anything they asked for specifically (case studies, data on a specific metric) and confirm it'll be in the follow-up
Book a meeting from a meeting.
Every time, without exception.
Buyer types to know:
Ballin' Brian ($500K–$3M/month):
Cares about legacy and prestige. Wants an A-player agency on his team, not a vendor. Speak to results and reputation.
Struggling Sam ($50K–$100K/month):
Plateaued and time-capped. Obsessed with the product, needs trust before spending. Still feels like the business could collapse — fill them with confidence and stability.
Marketing Marvin (in-house head of marketing):
Has a budget to spend and needs to prove himself internally. Often an easier close because it's not his business — he's less protective and just needs systemisation.
De-qualifying:

After 14 days without a response or a reason, move on. Same principle as email list drop-off after day one — interest fades fast. Prospects who keep rescheduling without communication are showing you exactly what the client relationship will look like. Don't chase for discounts either — if someone is asking for money off, never reduce price without reducing deliverables. It devalues the service.
On brands under $50K/month:

Well Copy's internal close rate on this segment is around 3–3.5% — not worth taking calls with at scale. Default on the booking form is effectively to make these leads fight for their slot. Matthew calls and qualifies them; if they don't respond, the call gets cancelled. The exception is pre-launch brands with significant budget who are looking for a standalone flow build.
Pre-Call & Post-Call Process (
Pre-call nurturing:

Speed to lead is critical. Well Copy has a team member (Matthew) whose primary job is to call leads within minutes of booking. That pre-call conversation sets expectations, confirms what the call will cover, and dramatically improves both show-up rates and close rates.

For smaller operations: even calling within an hour of someone booking in makes a meaningful difference. The psychological effect of having already spoken to someone before the call removes uncertainty, builds familiarity, and gets them more committed to showing up.
Post-booking VSL idea (raised by Tristan):

Redirect leads to a short video after booking — thank them, run through a couple of case studies, and answer common FAQs. Warms them up to the agency before they arrive on the call. An extension of this is the Hormozi "sandwich close" — send the full pitch as a recording pre-call so by the time they arrive they've already processed the process, and the call becomes a qualification and fit conversation rather than a full pitch.
No-call close approach (Aussie agency example):

One agency owner runs ads driving leads to WhatsApp. He sends a voice note requesting Klaviyo access and a voice note back to confirm they're real. Runs a full Loom audit, sends it with a price at the end, and closes without ever getting on a call. High conviction, no objection handling — works for him but relies on very warm, pre-qualified leads and serious authority.
Post-call follow-up:

Send the call recording so the prospect has an accurate record of what was discussed — useful if they need to present the partnership internally. Include a breakdown of where you think you can help and what the next steps are. If it went very well, send the contract for review immediately. If it went to an audit, send what you need from them and confirm the next call time.
Q&A (Throughout)
Attribution objection from prospects:

Three approaches: (1) your benchmark data shows real brands generating 40-50% — apply that to their numbers, (2) shift the focus to LTV and repeat purchase mechanics rather than raw attribution percentage, (3) be honest that attribution is imperfect across the entire ecommerce ecosystem and that doing the right things consistently is what produces results regardless.
Client rewriting copy / excessive revisions:

Offer an A/B test — run their version against yours and let the data decide. If they say no to that, they're prioritising pride over results. In that case, you weigh up whether keeping them happy as a client is worth accepting lower results. If they're a long-term client who's otherwise good, sometimes you just let it be their quirk.
Format feedback for future agency calls:

Suggestion from the group to run more open free-conversation calls alongside structured resource-based sessions — a rotating format. More icebreakers to get quieter members talking, topic-seeded discussions rather than 50-page documents, and more direct engagement with people who haven't spoken. Ben and Tristan to explore.
Closing (~
Tristan and Ben wrapped up. Topic and resource suggestions for future calls to be sent directly to Ben or Tristan via DM.

lessons.title: July 7th: Well Copy Agency Operations + Q&A
lessons.description:
Call Summary — Pricing Models, Client Reporting, Hiring, IG to Booked Calls, Production Process & Mindset

---
Opening (0:00–5:00)
Tristan joined fresh off a rough week with Wi-Fi issues and his ongoing arm recovery — now out of the cast and into a brace with some movement returning. Ben co-hosted alongside him.
The session format was different from usual — instead of one focused topic plus Q&A, Tristan and Ben walked through a large doc Max produced by dictating his honest opinions on commonly asked agency questions into Whisper Flow, which was then transcribed. The group worked through it point by point, adding commentary and real-world context throughout.

---
Pricing (5:00–20:00)
Well Copy's pricing structure:
All pricing is done on a per-email basis — no complicated performance-based models, no ambiguity. Three core tiers:
Entry tier: 12 emails/month — ~$5K/month. Suited to smaller brands.
Mid tier: 20 emails/month — most popular. Typically split 15 campaigns, 5 flow emails.
Top tier: 30+ emails/month — ~$10K/month. Fully custom for larger brands.
Enterprise: Brands doing 5M+/month can be on close to $20K/month for high volume.Why flat per-email pricing:
No fluff, no re-pricing based on brand size — what you pay is what you get. Removes all ambiguity for both sides and makes the value proposition clean. You're not buying strategy in theory, you're buying a defined set of deliverables.
Setup fee:
Well Copy charges a one-time setup fee on top of the first month — typically around $1–2K. This covers onboarding, systems integration, and kickoff. It also has psychological weight — both sides have skin in the game from day one, which filters out uncommitted brands.
Flow builds as standalone projects:
For brands not yet ready for monthly management (e.g. pre-launch brands or those under 50K/month), Well Copy offers one-time flow builds averaging around $12K for a two-month project. Payment is typically split across the project period rather than taken upfront in full.
Why they don't do campaigns-only retainers with a separate flow build fee:
Bundling everything into a single package — campaigns, flow management, ongoing optimisation — means the team can fix and iterate without having to re-consult the client every time. It's cleaner, faster, and produces better output. Brands just get everything taken care of.
Minimum revenue requirement:
Well Copy generally won't take brands onto monthly management if they're doing under $50K/month. Below that, the ROI maths rarely make sense for the client, and the agency doesn't want to take money from a brand that isn't going to get enough back.
Minimum contract terms:
Month-to-month. There's also a 14-day money-back guarantee — if within the first two weeks the brand just isn't feeling it, they can pull out for a full refund.
On the "per email sounds expensive" objection:
It's a real pushback — clients can do the maths and it looks like a lot per email in isolation. The answer is reputation, results, and team depth. Well Copy is one of the fastest growing email agencies in North America. If a brand has a problem with the price, they can be pointed toward smaller agencies — but if they want Well Copy, that's what it costs.

---
Rev Shares & Bonuses (20:00–25:00)
Max's position: don't do rev shares or performance bonuses.
Why:
Klaviyo attribution makes it almost impossible to track "real" incremental revenue accurately — both sides will end up arguing about the numbers
Month-to-month contracts are the guarantee. If the client isn't getting results, they can leave. That's more honest than a complicated revenue share that obscures what's actually being earnedOn bonuses:
One community member (Dan) uses a bonus structure where he sets a revenue target for the client, won't charge extra to hit it, but takes a bonus if they do. Interesting approach but requires tight tracking and trust on both sides.
General consensus:
Guarantees and bonuses can be good early on to build trust and win clients, but at scale they tend to attract brands with the wrong mindset — people looking for a guarantee rather than committing to the process. Month-to-month is the better long-term model.

---
Client Reporting (25:00–33:00)
Monthly reporting:
Use Hyros' auto-generated monthly report as the base — it's professionally formatted out of the box and looks polished without needing to build anything from scratch. Clients feel in safe hands when they receive something that looks credible and data-rich.
Key principle:
Don't overwhelm clients with every metric. Pick one meaningful insight per report — the thing that actually matters most this month — and lead with that. If revenue is looking good, show that. If there's a clear explanation for a dip, surface it clearly.
Live example from Max:
A client was unhappy with their email revenue. Max dug into Hyros and found the drop was caused by the pop-up discount code being revealed in the pop-up itself rather than gated in the welcome email — killing attribution. Being able to identify and explain that clearly turned an angry client into a reassured one.
Quarterly roadmaps for retention:
At the end of each quarter, present a before and after — how things looked entering the quarter versus now — and map out the next three months. Clients who can see clear progress and a defined plan are far less likely to churn.
On communication (Ben's Uber analogy):
Consistent, visible communication is more valuable than a perfectly polished report. A client who can track progress throughout the month — even via quick Slack messages or Loom updates — will stay far longer than one who gets a great report but hears nothing in between. Even if you're behind on something, just sending an update saying when the next one is coming is enough to maintain trust.
On client retention specifically:
A common churn pattern is brands doing really well and then thinking they can bring it in-house or find someone cheaper — because they don't see what's happening behind the scenes every day. Always keep clients focused on the bigger picture: what's next, what still needs building, why they're only just getting started. There always needs to be a "next phase" to work towards.

---
Getting the Most Out of Hires (33:00–42:00)
Most people hire someone and expect results immediately — the reality is the first month costs you more time than it saves, because you're training as well as doing. That's the investment. Be prepared for it.
Max's system for the first month:
Morning check-in: Ask two things — what are your tasks today, and what questions do you have? Sets accountability and gives the hire a safe space to flag confusion before it becomes a problem.
End of day check-in: How did it go, any questions that came up, set the plan for tomorrow. Closes the loop.Five minutes at the start and end of each day — low time cost, high impact. Don't stop these check-ins just because a month has passed if the outputs aren't where they need to be yet. Be direct about it — "this isn't where I need it to be, here's what needs to improve."
For agencies you're working with rather than individual hires:
Same idea, adjusted cadence. Weekly check-ins (start and end of week) rather than daily — you don't want to appear like you're micromanaging an agency. The principle is the same: accountability, clarity, and a clear feedback loop.

---
Finding Insights (42:00–47:00)
There's no universal dashboard or silver bullet for finding what's broken in an account — every brand is different and what's a red flag in one account can be totally normal in another.
The job is to develop the habit of actively digging. Assign it as an explicit responsibility for whoever owns the account — not a nice-to-have, but a core part of the role.
Where to start when digging:
Send time performance
Buyer type splits (first-time vs returning)
AI-assisted pattern spotting
Chase whatever looks off from thereThe best account managers are the ones who go looking for problems proactively rather than waiting for a client to flag something.

---
Turning Instagram Followers into Booked Calls (47:00–60:00)
Getting followers and likes is one thing — converting them into actual conversations and calls is a completely different skill.
Core principle:
Every CTA should drive people to the DMs, not a link. Don't say "click the link in bio to book a call." Say "got questions about this? shoot me a DM." That opens a real conversation you can then steer.
When to use ManyChat automation:
If you're small and your DM volume is manageable, handle it manually. Every interaction is a potential lead and personalisation dramatically increases close rates.
When volume gets too high to manage manually, automate — but only what needs automating.Well Copy's ManyChat setup:
New follower automation: sends one opening DM framed as a question ("are you a brand or an agency?"). The people who reply are the ones worth prioritising.
Free guide flows: when someone opts into a guide, the flow ends with a follow-up question an hour later — "let me know if you're struggling with anything in email, the real me will reply." Opens conversation without being salesy.
For brands vs agencies: different conversation paths from the start. Brands get qualified. Agencies get pointed to the community.On DMs converting to sales:
About 25% of Well Copy's actual sales have involved DM conversations at some point in the nurturing process. Speed to lead matters significantly — replying within 5–10 minutes of someone following or engaging dramatically increases the likelihood of them showing up to a call and closing.
Ben's approach in the DMs:
Never lead with the sale. Lead with curiosity — ask what they sell, have a look at their store, use tools like SimilarWeb to qualify traffic before even getting into email. If they start to naturally identify as a potential client, then you can introduce the idea of a discovery call. Don't jump straight to price — direct people to a quick chat with the team.
For smaller accounts:
Don't rely on automation if you don't need to. Every comment, story view, and share is an opportunity to start a conversation. The more personal the outreach, the better the conversion rate.

---
Case Studies (60:00–63:00)
Most people aren't going to read a long case study or watch a full testimonial video — the reality is they're mostly there for social proof, not education.
What actually matters:
Having plenty of testimonials that exist and are visible
Highlighting the key numbers clearly: increase in email revenue percentage, total revenue attributed to email, increase in repeat purchase rate
Testimonial videos are great to have on the site but don't stress about them being in-depth — their job is to be there, not to be consumed in fullKeep it simple. More case studies with clean numbers beats fewer elaborate ones every time.

---
Mindset & Charging More (63:00–70:00)
If you're under $50K/month in revenue, one thing matters more than anything else: getting clients. Not optimising your current clients' accounts, not building better systems — getting clients.
The single most important mindset shift:
Charge more. 95% of your current problems can be solved by raising prices. Higher prices mean:
You can be more selective about who you work with
You attract easier brands with bigger budgets
You have more resource to hire better people
You make more money with fewer clientsAction items:
Set a $3K floor today. If any client is below that, raise it before doing anything else.
Block 6 hours a day for client acquisition until you're past $50K/month. Nothing else takes priority.
If client delivery work is blocking you from having time to get new clients, you're underpriced — which brings it back to charging more.
---
Productivity (70:00–75:00)
Max's approach is protecting the first four hours of the day for deep, uninterrupted work. When he was based in California, that meant being up at 4:30am. Now in Europe, he blocks 2–6pm as deep work — uncancellable on his calendar.
The principle isn't about the specific time — it's about finding the window where you can work without clients pinging you, employees asking questions, or fires to put out, and protecting that time ruthlessly.
Get caffeinated, turn on focus mode, and use that window exclusively for needle-moving work. Everything else can happen around it.
Max's day-in-the-life vlogs on his YouTube channel give a more detailed look at how this plays out practically.

---
Goal Setting & Production Process (75:00–82:00)
Goal setting:
Set quarterly goals, not yearly. Too much changes in 12 months for annual goals to stay relevant. Pick 2 north star goals for the quarter — revenue target, number of clients, a key system to build — and reverse engineer your daily inputs from there.
Example: if the goal is to add $10K in monthly revenue this quarter, work backwards — how many clients at what price, how many calls needed to close that many clients, how many leads to generate that many calls, what daily activity produces that lead volume. Suddenly a big goal becomes a daily number of actions.
Production process — onboarding:
Before the kickoff call, the internal team has already been briefed by sales, reviewed the client's account, and outlined initial flow strategy
Kickoff call: go through the completed onboarding form, align on priorities, and come prepared with an initial campaign calendar or flow strategy ready to present — this makes an immediate strong impression
Within the first 3 days: rebuild the pop-up form. Fast, visible, impactful — sets the tone
Days 7–10: first campaign or flow presented to client
Day ~14: first campaigns launched
Weekly calls for the first month, then bi-weeklyMonthly campaign cadence:
15th–20th: Send the monthly planning form to the client — upcoming sales, product launches, key events
20th–23rd: Build the full campaign calendar and share for approval
10-day rule: Aim to have each email reviewed and approved 10 days before its send date. Absolute floor is 3–5 days. Ceiling is 14–21 days.Why the 10-day rule matters:
Sending too close to deployment means clients often don't leave comments — not because they're happy, but because they don't want to create pressure to deploy late. Give them space to actually review properly.
Production chain:
Account manager writes the brief → copywriter produces copy (or AM writes it themselves) → designer builds the email → AM reviews and sends to client → client revisions go back to AM → small fixes handled by AM directly, larger ones escalated to copywriter or designer.

---
Closing (~82:00)
Tristan wrapped up and invited questions and topic suggestions for next week's session. Format feedback from the group: the multi-topic doc format worked well — suggestion to mix it up going forward, alternating between deep dives and broader Q&A sessions depending on what's been submitted.
Tristan confirmed he's setting up a WhatsApp group for agency owners in the community — send your number via DM to get added. Aiden's document on following up with engaged followers is also being circulated — DM Tristan to get a copy.

Getting followers and likes is one thing — converting them into actual conversations and calls is a completely different skill.
Core principle:

Every CTA should drive people to the DMs, not a link. Don't say "click the link in bio to book a call." Say "got questions about this? shoot me a DM." That opens a real conversation you can then steer.
When to use ManyChat automation:
If you're small and your DM volume is manageable, handle it manually. Every interaction is a potential lead and personalisation dramatically increases close rates.
When volume gets too high to manage manually, automate — but only what needs automating.
Well Copy's ManyChat setup:
New follower automation: sends one opening DM framed as a question ("are you a brand or an agency?"). The people who reply are the ones worth prioritising.

Free guide flows: when someone opts into a guide, the flow ends with a follow-up question an hour later — "let me know if you're struggling with anything in email, the real me will reply." Opens conversation without being salesy.
For brands vs agencies: different conversation paths from the start. Brands get qualified. Agencies get pointed to the community.
On DMs converting to sales:

About 25% of Well Copy's actual sales have involved DM conversations at some point in the nurturing process. Speed to lead matters significantly — replying within 5–10 minutes of someone following or engaging dramatically increases the likelihood of them showing up to a call and closing.
Ben's approach in the DMs:

Never lead with the sale. Lead with curiosity — ask what they sell, have a look at their store, use tools like SimilarWeb to qualify traffic before even getting into email. If they start to naturally identify as a potential client, then you can introduce the idea of a discovery call. Don't jump straight to price — direct people to a quick chat with the team.
For smaller accounts:
Don't rely on automation if you don't need to. Every comment, story view, and share is an opportunity to start a conversation. The more personal the outreach, the better the conversion rate.
Case Studies (60:00–63:00)
Most people aren't going to read a long case study or watch a full testimonial video — the reality is they're mostly there for social proof, not education.
What actually matters:
Having plenty of testimonials that exist and are visible
Highlighting the key numbers clearly: increase in email revenue percentage, total revenue attributed to email, increase in repeat purchase rate
Testimonial videos are great to have on the site but don't stress about them being in-depth — their job is to be there, not to be consumed in full
Keep it simple. More case studies with clean numbers beats fewer elaborate ones every time.
Mindset & Charging More (63:00–70:00)
If you're under $50K/month in revenue, one thing matters more than anything else: getting clients. Not optimising your current clients' accounts, not building better systems — getting clients.
The single most important mindset shift:
Charge more. 95% of your current problems can be solved by raising prices. Higher prices mean:
You can be more selective about who you work with
You attract easier brands with bigger budgets
You have more resource to hire better people
You make more money with fewer clients
Action items:
Set a $3K floor today. If any client is below that, raise it before doing anything else.
Block 6 hours a day for client acquisition until you're past $50K/month. Nothing else takes priority.
If client delivery work is blocking you from having time to get new clients, you're underpriced — which brings it back to charging more.
Productivity (70:00–75:00)

Max's approach is protecting the first four hours of the day for deep, uninterrupted work. When he was based in California, that meant being up at 4:30am. Now in Europe, he blocks 2–6pm as deep work — uncancellable on his calendar.

The principle isn't about the specific time — it's about finding the window where you can work without clients pinging you, employees asking questions, or fires to put out, and protecting that time ruthlessly.
Get caffeinated, turn on focus mode, and use that window exclusively for needle-moving work. Everything else can happen around it.
Max's day-in-the-life vlogs on his YouTube channel give a more detailed look at how this plays out practically.
Goal Setting & Production Process (75:00–82:00)
Goal setting:

Set quarterly goals, not yearly. Too much changes in 12 months for annual goals to stay relevant. Pick 2 north star goals for the quarter — revenue target, number of clients, a key system to build — and reverse engineer your daily inputs from there.

Example: if the goal is to add $10K in monthly revenue this quarter, work backwards — how many clients at what price, how many calls needed to close that many clients, how many leads to generate that many calls, what daily activity produces that lead volume. Suddenly a big goal becomes a daily number of actions.
Production process — onboarding:
Before the kickoff call, the internal team has already been briefed by sales, reviewed the client's account, and outlined initial flow strategy

Kickoff call: go through the completed onboarding form, align on priorities, and come prepared with an initial campaign calendar or flow strategy ready to present — this makes an immediate strong impression
Within the first 3 days: rebuild the pop-up form. Fast, visible, impactful — sets the tone
Days 7–10: first campaign or flow presented to client
Day ~14: first campaigns launched
Weekly calls for the first month, then bi-weekly
Monthly campaign cadence:
15th–20th:
Send the monthly planning form to the client — upcoming sales, product launches, key events
20th–23rd:
Build the full campaign calendar and share for approval
10-day rule:
Aim to have each email reviewed and approved 10 days before its send date. Absolute floor is 3–5 days. Ceiling is 14–21 days.
Why the 10-day rule matters:

Sending too close to deployment means clients often don't leave comments — not because they're happy, but because they don't want to create pressure to deploy late. Give them space to actually review properly.
Production chain:

Account manager writes the brief → copywriter produces copy (or AM writes it themselves) → designer builds the email → AM reviews and sends to client → client revisions go back to AM → small fixes handled by AM directly, larger ones escalated to copywriter or designer.
Closing (~82:00)

Tristan wrapped up and invited questions and topic suggestions for next week's session. Format feedback from the group: the multi-topic doc format worked well — suggestion to mix it up going forward, alternating between deep dives and broader Q&A sessions depending on what's been submitted.

Tristan confirmed he's setting up a WhatsApp group for agency owners in the community — send your number via DM to get added. Aiden's document on following up with engaged followers is also being circulated — DM Tristan to get a copy.

lessons.title: June 30th: Open Q&A, Flow Review & Klaviyo Audit
lessons.description:
Call Summary — Cold Calling, Community Introductions, Live Welcome Flow & Klaviyo Audit, Pricing Objections & Instagram Strategy

---
Opening Catch-Up (0:00–3:30)
Tristan caught up with Matthias, Robert, and Fito. Discussion touched on one-off flow build projects versus ongoing retainers, and Fito shared he'd just signed a new client through cold calling rather than Instagram.
Cold calling flagged as heavily underused in the space — most people default to hiding behind Instagram DMs rather than picking up the phone
Tristan noted that recorded cold calls make excellent content due to the immediate, bold nature of the action, but very few people in the community actually do it
A friend running a UGC agency accidentally FaceTimed a prospect on Instagram, ended up in a 10-minute conversation, and booked a Google Meet off the back of it
Tristan planning to test cold-calling via Instagram FaceTime this week
Numbers for outreach sourced via Apollo.io
---
Mahad's First Client Win (3:30–6:00)
Mahad landed his first client after roughly two weeks of consistent outreach. Now has account access and is learning from real data for the first time, navigating some early imposter syndrome.
Group reassurance: two weeks is genuinely fast — it's fundamentally a volume game, and confidence builds quickly once real revenue movement is visible
Noted that attributed revenue figures can appear inflated, which may also help build early confidence as a new operator
---
Open Q&A Announcement & Round of Introductions (6:00–8:00)
No resource doc from Max this week — fully open Q&A format. Tristan proposed a fresh round of introductions given the number of new faces in the community.
Idea pitched to Max for a future session: a breakdown of key KPI benchmarks to look at inside Hyros. Max liked it but is saving it for a first-day call topic since it's broadly relevant to everyone in the community.

---
Round of Introductions (8:00–22:00)
Tristan — Runs Drive Media. 18 months to 2 years in the space, started with cold email as a service and freelancing before launching his own agency.
Jeremy — ~3 years in email. Came from a drop shipping background that didn't work out — under-resourced idea, more work than expected. Worked at a large US agency before going independent recently.
Robert — ~3 years in the space. Started in ads for small businesses; a client asked about email, he didn't know anything, went home and self-taught overnight from content found on Twitter. First client a few months later. 90% of clients now based in Poland/Europe, with some US brands.
Matthias — Based in Hamburg, Germany. Started as a copywriter in 2023, pivoted to focus on email in 2024 after a rough first year. Found Max via YouTube early on and joined the original Skool community from day one. Quit his 9-5 in 2025 and now works exclusively with German brands.
Brooke — Brand owner, not agency. Runs Mosquito Beads, a natural mosquito repellent brand. Completely new to email marketing — didn't know what a flow was 2–3 months ago. First month in the community, first call attended.
Ben — Started as a social media content creator in 2020, built a large following, moved into talent management before pivoting to organic content agency work for brands. Spent a year in Canada running a cookie business via Shopify, which is where his e-commerce experience began. Found Max through networking and joined Well Copy — sales team by day, managing community retention for the Skool group in his own time.
Mahad — Based in Virginia, US. Background in software engineering, found it unfulfilling. Got into email after discovering a young YouTube creator making money in email design. Drawn in by the creative side. Three months into the community.
Aaron — Based in Minneapolis, Minnesota. Previously worked at Wells Fargo in corporate banking after a finance degree. Spent 2025 learning copywriting without finding a strong niche, then landed an opportunity writing plain-text emails for a small brand. Found Max, joined the community in February 2026. Quit his job in late April after replacing his income, and is on track for his first $10K month — credits the community's responsiveness as the biggest factor in his fast progress.
Final intro (clothing brand) — ~7 years in e-commerce. Started a reselling brand at 17, scaled it to a meaningful size with staff and overhead, then had the brand's Google Ads account hacked during Q4 and lost everything. That experience deepened his understanding of e-commerce fundamentals. Pivoted into service-based work, landed on email specifically, and eventually sold the original brand. Currently helping a friend's clothing brand while building out service work.
---
Brooke's Welcome Flow Review — Live (22:00–32:00)
Brooke shared her draft welcome flow for Mosquito Beads (single product, two sizes, plus bundles including a "most loved" 4-pack).
Email 1 feedback:
Discount code (OUTSIDE15) was too obviously static — recommended making it look dynamic (e.g. a hyphen plus random characters) so future urgency/expiry messaging doesn't look fake
CTA button needed more padding from the box above it and could extend further from the background
Keep the hero section above the fold — don't push it down with excess image height
Add "use code" in front of the discount code itself, since it wasn't immediately obvious it was a codeEmail 2 feedback (conditional split — opens if clicked, repeats if not):
Stronger setup overall, code placement cleaner with "use code" already included
Minor adjustment to the 15% callout placementStructural notes:
No time delay built in between email 1 and email 2 on the conditional pass branch — should add at least 30 minutes to an hour
Non-open branch currently delayed a full day — recommend tightening to same-day, ideally 5–6 hours later, since subscribers already expect an email after opting in
Resend email correctly used a different subject line from the original — confirmed best practice, never resend with the identical subject line
Final email was a long-form, text-based founder email — feedback was to A/B test a shorter version rather than assume it's too long
Reminder that most people scan rather than read emails — keep crucial information unmissable regardless of length. Claude recommended for tightening copy efficiently
Confirmed the flow should filter out anyone who has already placed an order since entering itGeneral welcome flow aggressiveness discussion:
Standard approach: deliver incentive immediately, follow up 1–2 hours later or same day, then daily for roughly a week — extending further for high-ticket products, stopping sooner (~7 days) for low-ticket
Jeremy referenced a welcome series breakdown he'd done on a popular US creator-led coffee brand — they send a follow-up roughly 30–60 minutes after signup but never mention the discount code in it, flagged as a missed opportunity
Resending the welcome email to non-openers isn't common practice in the group. Resending sale/campaign emails to non-openers is standard and effective, but resending the identical welcome email was seen as risky for first impressions — most felt it's unnecessary since a well-structured flow already has 5–7 follow-ups regardless
---
Brooke's Klaviyo Deliverability Audit — Live (32:00–46:00)
Brooke's account showed an overall deliverability score flagged as "poor," making her hesitant to send.
Context: the email list was inherited from previous brand owners with little to no sales history, and Brooke had attempted to resurrect this old, cold list — negatively impacting deliverability.
Live walkthrough:
Email attributed revenue sitting around 34–35% — solid on its own, with the caveat that more context is always needed
Located the deliverability score in the analytics navigation
A recent send to a 30-day engaged segment performed reasonably (~40% open rate)
Root issue diagnosed: a recent campaign sent to the old inherited D2C list performed poorly and likely damaged sender reputation
Drilling into the deliverability tab for a specific recent send: Apple inbox performance was fine, but Hotmail and Outlook showed very low open rates, dragging overall deliverability downRecommended fix:
Create a segment specifically targeting Hotmail/Outlook profiles and exclude them from sends going forward
Segment built live: filter "what someone has done" → received email → at least once over all time → add second condition using "inbox provider" property → equals → Hotmail/Outlook
Stick with the 30-day engaged segment as the primary send list and exclude the Hotmail/Outlook segment from all campaigns until the list is cleaned up over time
---
Pricing & Sales Objection Handling (46:00–56:00)
Question: A prospective client (fashion niche outreach, ~£70K/month, strong ROAS on ads already, zero email marketing) is hesitant about pricing and wants a tangible, defensible answer on expected return before committing.
Ben's framing:
Anchor the conversation around ROI and urgency — if a brand is doing zero through email, that alone is the opportunity. Reference industry benchmarks (e.g. "30% is our baseline minimum, most of our brands run 45–50% of revenue through email") to highlight how much is being left on the table
Email also extends the lifespan of paid ads, since ad creative fatigues over time — retention infrastructure lets a brand run ads longer before returns declineOn attribution accuracy:
A brand going from 0% to 35% attributed revenue doesn't mean total sales increase by 35% — attribution isn't true incremental revenue
Practical method to produce a more conservative, defensible figure for skeptical clients: subtract welcome flow email 1 revenue from total email-attributed revenue, since most of that revenue would have converted regardless given the high intent of new sign-ups. Roughly 80% of total attributed revenue suggested as a closer approximation to true impact
For especially price-sensitive clients, a results guarantee (e.g. ROI guaranteed within 60 days) based on this adjusted figure was suggested as an optionMatthias's honest take: nobody actually knows true incremental email revenue with certainty. The only way to know for sure would require a genuine control-group split test — one cohort with no email, one with full email marketing — something nobody in the space has properly run. Customer lifetime value as an alternative metric is also imperfect, since LTV is influenced by many variables outside of email.
Group consensus: regardless of exact attribution accuracy, the core sales argument holds — a brand running ads with zero retention infrastructure is leaving revenue on the table, and that's the most honest, defensible framing to lead with.

---
Instagram Content Strategy Discussion (56:00–67:00)
Jeremy — One week into posting on Instagram after years of being unable to due to a previous employer's restrictions. Posted twice in a single day — more than the past three years combined. Currently at 60 followers, focused on consistency while figuring out format.
Tristan — Follow-up on his previous viral reel: roughly doubled his follower count and generated a wave of inbound brand DMs. Intentionally turning the format into a recurring content pillar, already repeated successfully once. Also posted a story offering free redesigns, which generated a strong batch of brand owner DMs — using this as both a content engine and lead source over the coming weeks.
Discussion on Tristan's reel format being copied by others in the space, potentially including Max — general consensus this is a good sign, since proven formats are meant to be reused and adapted
Why the format works (Tristan's take): it appeals to a broad, non-niche audience (satisfying to watch fast-paced design transformations with music) while simultaneously demonstrating skill and credibility — a mix of entertainment and education outperforms purely educational talking-head contentBen's algorithm breakdown:
Platforms want maximum time-on-app to serve more ads — understanding that goal makes content strategy easier
Every post generates data regardless of performance. A flop simply means the algorithm matched it to the wrong audience, not that the content failed
Content gets tested with a small audience first; based on engagement signals (watch time most important, followed by comments, likes, shares), it gets pushed to wider audiences if it performs well
Compared this to a "credit score" for an account — each post adds data refining who the algorithm shows future content to
Broader, more generic content early on casts a wider net and generates more signal data, allowing future content to be niched down over time
Dramatic content pivots too early or too often can spook the algorithm's existing read on the audience — consistency and incremental refinement perform better than sudden shifts
Final recommendation: once something performs, double down rather than reinvent. Export the transcript, feed it to Claude, analyse audience drop-off points from analytics, and systematically refine the same proven formatClosing note from Tristan: sheer posting volume matters as much as format — referenced a community member generating consistent results by posting extremely high volumes daily, where most individual posts underperform but the occasional outlier drives meaningful follower growth.

---
Closing (~67:00–69:10)
Tristan had to jump off. Brief exchange on building connections from content engagement (following up with people who engage with posts) — Tristan offered to share a relevant document via DM before wrapping the call.

---

lessons.title: June 23rd: Team Structure, Hiring & Scaling + Q&A
lessons.description:
Call Summary — Team Structure, Hiring & Scaling, Instagram Outreach & Client Management

---
Opening & Context (0:00–5:00)
Tristan opened the call fresh off a serious climbing accident — a fall of roughly 35 metres after a roping error, resulting in an open fracture and reconstructive elbow surgery. Despite this, he managed to keep clients on track by being ahead of schedule, and had understanding clients who told him to take his time.
The call focus: how to build and scale a lean email marketing agency team — moving from a one-man band to a structured team capable of handling 20–30 clients.

---
Core Team Structure (5:00–23:00)
Max's recommended lean starting structure — four roles:
1. The Business Owner (you)
Focus: sales, growth, new business, and quality oversight
Should not be in the weeds of daily execution, client back-and-forth, or delivery
Priority activities: content creation, outreach, sales calls — things that actually move the needle2. Account Manager — most important hire
Responsibilities: writing copy, planning campaign calendars, daily client communication, revisions, quality control
Hardest to find — the best ones are already employed at other agencies
Recommended approach: use a recruiter or headhunter to poach from competing agencies
Risk: people with this skillset often have entrepreneurial ambitions and may leave after a few months3. Designer
Takes copy and a brief, produces finished email designs — very focused, execution-heavy role
Critical for brand-focused clients who care about look and feel
