lessons.title: June 16th: Client Communication, Compensation, Ops
lessons.description:
Call Summary — Client Communication, Payment Structures, Team Operations & Client Acquisition

---
Context & Introductions (0:00–10:00)
Tristan (the usual host) was absent — he had a mountain climbing accident and was in the hospital. A team member filled in. First-time attendees included Brandon (6-client retail/luxury streetwear agency, all clients from referrals) and Ben (has his own brand, newer to the program). Mahat shared that outreach is in the "trenches" phase — manual, personalized, no automation yet.

---
Client Communication Framework (10:00–30:00)
Main topic of the session, based on an internal training doc and a Lido Hamosi video (link shared in chat — no sound available on the call).
Core principle: if you don't tell clients what you're doing, they'll assume you're doing nothing. From the client's perspective, they've paid for an invisible service, often upfront, often to someone younger — doubt accumulates silently until they leave.
The recommended communication cadence:
Monthly deep-dive report (done before the 7th, after 5-day attribution window closes)
Weekly breakdown every Monday — KPIs, progress, what's planned
Daily Slack response within 30 minutes; all comments addressed by end of day
Random updates 3x/week minimum — Klaviyo screenshots, A/B test wins, flow performance — these are considered the most important because they signal you're in the account every day, not just at reporting time
Meeting recaps after every call, with action items visible to the clientThe slide deck showed two report examples — one bad (stats with no insights), one better-but-not-great (some observations but still thin). No great example was available.

---
What Makes a Report Great (30:00–38:00)
Open floor discussion after the presentation.
Paul: the basic numbers are something the client can pull themselves. What makes a report great is the human layer — insights, learnings, and what you're going to do differently because of them.
Ben: reemphasize that you're the expert. Present the results and the roadmap for the next 30/60/90 days together. Following through on that roadmap builds trust faster than any metric.
Robert: switched to an observation → insight → action structure after clients complained about long reports with no clear takeaways. Also: some clients (especially in Poland, he noted) explicitly don't want frequent communication — but even those clients benefit from it. A client who goes quiet and then leaves was almost always a communication breakdown in disguise. Lost a client once to a cheaper agency, communication was the real gap.
Tony: trust reduces the need for heavy reporting. Weekly calls are overkill for most clients — they're busy. A clear monthly summary with thoughtful commentary is usually enough. The goal is to get time off their plate, not add to it.
Mezraim: smaller clients tend to want more frequent touchpoints; bigger clients want metrics and movement. A content calendar sent weekly (with a preview of what's going out and a 48-hour window for changes) works well for smaller clients. Month-over-month Klaviyo screenshots — showing the arrow going up — keep reporting lightweight but meaningful.
---
Payment Structures: Retainer vs. Performance-Based (38:00–52:00)
Brandon opened this by sharing his first client deal — 10% of attributed revenue on a rolling 30-day window. It worked financially, but became unmanageable: monthly calls turned into 30-minute line-item disputes over which campaign drove which purchase.
The group consensus: retainers are the right structure. Predictable for both sides, no attribution fights.
Robert: still has two performance-based clients from early on, making good money, but wants to convert them. Noted that bigger brands tend to prefer flat retainers because it's more predictable for their own budgeting.
Preferred hybrid: flat retainer as the base, with a milestone bonus on top (e.g., hit $X in attributed revenue and you earn a $1K bonus). Gives the client upside alignment without tying your base income to attribution chaos.
Robert's firing story: had an early client that was low-paying, demanding, and wanted weekly calls — nothing to report after a week with a 5-day attribution window. Ended it after a year (should have done it sooner). Initiated the "renegotiation" conversation directly; the client countered two weeks later by ending the partnership themselves, having quietly shopped alternatives. Lesson: set terms on the onboarding call, don't let the client dictate the rhythm of the relationship. Reference the April 21st recording on client onboarding.
On renegotiating rates: if you've worked together long-term and haven't raised rates, being direct and open works. If it's early (1–2 months in), don't renegotiate — let the results speak first. Three to five months is a better window.
---
Team Structure: Who Handles Email Slicing & Uploading (52:00–60:00)
Robert asked who handles slicing and uploading emails into Klaviyo, and what people pay for it, after a bad experience with a hired Klaviyo tech.
Tony: designer handles slicing and uploading — $50/email all-in (design + slice + upload + subject line + audience selection). That rate reflects offshore, lower cost-of-living market.
Messerim and Ben: both still handling it themselves at this stage, which makes sense while the volume is low.
Ben: once demand gets high enough — 3–4 campaigns a week across multiple brands — slicing becomes a bottleneck. At that point, train your designer via a Loom recording. If you have an account manager pulling metrics and writing reports, they can also be trained on it.
Paul: Max's team hires from the Philippines. There are recruiting agencies they use for offshore Klaviyo talent. Salaries are typically in the hundreds, not thousands. Robert to follow up with Max directly for an intro.
Also mentioned: Adam has a tool that handles slicing and uploading — worth exploring if you want a software solution rather than a person.
---
Client Acquisition & Outreach (60:00–70:00)
Messerim asked about everyone's approach to getting clients.
Messerim: getting ready to build out an Instantly sequence. Goes by industry, revenue, and location. Targets under $1M revenue / mid-market. Lead-in tactic: "I'd love to give you a free breakdown of your flows" — no commitment ask, then uses Loom to record a walkthrough with a few Figma visuals. Biggest unlock: name the prospect's competitor. It creates FOMO, signals industry knowledge, and makes them more likely to take a 10-minute call. Has a pitch deck (uses Pitch.com). Currently still has a nine-to-five in B2B sales.
Matthias: does cold calling and cold email. Cold email less effective this year — heavier on calling now. Targets 5 booked meetings per week. Did 350 cold calls in one week (Messerim noted he does 200–250 per day in SaaS). Tool mentioned: Nooks (N-O-O-K-S) — a parallel dialer that fires 5 calls simultaneously, letting you hit 200–300 dials in 20–30 minutes. Matthias noted that for a German-language market, burning through leads that fast isn't viable — personalization matters more when your total addressable market is small.
Paul: Max grew through organic social after cold outreach in the early days. His content approach: download all publicly available info on a brand (Meta Ads Library, their mailing list, ad angles, funnel structure), then dissect it on camera. That's YouTube/Instagram content that simultaneously demonstrates expertise. Sales calls have come in from people who watched those videos and assumed Max had inside access to their brand. All public sources.
On social media hesitation: Mezraim said he's shy about putting himself on camera. The group pushed back — he's articulate and likable on the call. Common blocker is imposter syndrome, plus for people still at a nine-to-five, a concern about being seen freelancing. Messerim confirmed his company actually values it (they see it as proof of sales ability). Agreed to start an Instagram page.
---
Closing
Call ran ~9 minutes over. Tristan expected back next week. Thursday call with Max — he'll bring one email topic and then open Q&A.

Also mentioned: Adam has a tool that handles slicing and uploading — worth exploring if you want a software solution rather than a person.
Client Acquisition & Outreach (60:00–70:00)
Messerim asked about everyone's approach to getting clients.

Messerim: getting ready to build out an Instantly sequence. Goes by industry, revenue, and location. Targets under $1M revenue / mid-market. Lead-in tactic: "I'd love to give you a free breakdown of your flows" — no commitment ask, then uses Loom to record a walkthrough with a few Figma visuals. Biggest unlock: name the prospect's competitor. It creates FOMO, signals industry knowledge, and makes them more likely to take a 10-minute call. Has a pitch deck (uses
Pitch.com
). Currently still has a nine-to-five in B2B sales.

Matthias: does cold calling and cold email. Cold email less effective this year — heavier on calling now. Targets 5 booked meetings per week. Did 350 cold calls in one week (Messerim noted he does 200–250 per day in SaaS). Tool mentioned: Nooks (N-O-O-K-S) — a parallel dialer that fires 5 calls simultaneously, letting you hit 200–300 dials in 20–30 minutes. Matthias noted that for a German-language market, burning through leads that fast isn't viable — personalization matters more when your total addressable market is small.

Paul: Max grew through organic social after cold outreach in the early days. His content approach: download all publicly available info on a brand (Meta Ads Library, their mailing list, ad angles, funnel structure), then dissect it on camera. That's YouTube/Instagram content that simultaneously demonstrates expertise. Sales calls have come in from people who watched those videos and assumed Max had inside access to their brand. All public sources.

On social media hesitation: Mezraim said he's shy about putting himself on camera. The group pushed back — he's articulate and likable on the call. Common blocker is imposter syndrome, plus for people still at a nine-to-five, a concern about being seen freelancing. Messerim confirmed his company actually values it (they see it as proof of sales ability). Agreed to start an Instagram page.
Closing
Call ran ~9 minutes over. Tristan expected back next week. Thursday call with Max — he'll bring one email topic and then open Q&A.

lessons.title: June 2nd: Early-Stage , Sales Tactics, Pricing
lessons.description:
---
Call Summary — Early-Stage Focus, Sales Tactics, Pricing Models & Brand Owner Perspective
When to Prioritize Email vs. Ads (0:00–15:00) Aaron shared his situation — ~$1K/month revenue from Meta, 20% email attribution. The group's consensus was unanimous: don't over-invest in email at this stage.
Tyler's logic: at low traffic volumes, you won't have enough people entering flows or building your list for email to move the needle. His main brand scaled to seven figures before they touched Klaviyo seriously.
Charlie agreed: email becomes high-leverage at $10K–$100K/month+. Before that, acquisition is the whole game.
The 20% attribution Aaron has is actually fine — the issue is scale, not performance.
Practical takeaway: keep learning Klaviyo on the calls, but spend the majority of time dialing in Meta ads.
---
Transactional Email Warning (15:00–18:00) One participant flagged a risk in Aaron's setup — piggybacking marketing content (discounts, offers) onto transactional-style emails to exploit higher open rates.
If Klaviyo detects marketing content inside transactional-status messages, it can disable those messages and flag the account.
Aaron clarified he hadn't applied for transactional status on those flows — the risk is lower, but the warning stands. Everyone on the list had consented to marketing, which helps.
---
Aaron's 33-Brand Model (18:00–28:00) Aaron explained his business structure — invested in or co-founded 33 clothing brands, using one (Pokemon-inspired, acknowledged gray market) as a live testing ground for ad and email strategies before rolling learnings across the portfolio.
The group initially pushed back, assuming he was spreading himself thin.
Aaron clarified: only one brand is running paid ads. Learnings get systematized and handed to his team, who implement across the others. It's closer to an Alex Hormozi "gym launch for clothing brands" model.
Charlie's counterpoint stood: every brand will respond differently to ads — angles and avatars don't port cleanly. The testing methodology (stair-step offer tests, weeding out what doesn't work) is solid practice, but assuming one system will transfer universally is risky.
---
Sales Call Strategy (28:00–42:00) Discussion triggered by a member prepping for a sales call the next day — should he build assets beforehand?
Tristan's recommendation: treat the first call as pure discovery. Diagnose the brand, see if it's a fit, pitch an audit at the end. Second call is where you walk through findings and close.
If the brand has basically nothing set up in Klaviyo, you can attempt to close on call one — no point in a second call if there's nothing new to uncover.
Playing devil's advocate: if you really want the client and have low call volume, designing one email (e.g., a reimagined welcome flow email) beforehand gives you a backup asset if confidence is needed.
On case studies: only surface them if the prospect asks. Speaking with authority and correctly diagnosing their situation usually does more than leading with results. If they're asking for case studies, there's usually a deeper, unstated objection — handing over a case study won't close it.
---
Handling the "Do You Have Experience in My Industry?" Objection (42:00–52:00) Tristan shared a live situation — warm referral, agreed on pricing, but the prospect came back last-minute asking for email examples from his specific niche.
Charlie's take as a brand owner: just back yourself. The fundamentals of email — system, structure, sequencing — are transferable across niches. You change the copy and design, not the system. Saying that directly to a prospect signals confidence, not laziness.
One member's tactic: design one email for the prospect's brand on your own time, present it as "here's exactly what I'd do for you." Turns the objection into a demonstration.
Tristan's read: the prospect probably doesn't realize that a dialed-in email operator can apply the same playbook across niches — he's never built it himself, so he doesn't understand it works that way.
---
Hiro Analytics Interlude (52:00–55:00) Brief sidebar on Hiro pricing.
The $250/month freelancer plan was discontinued at the end of last year — new signups are quoted $500/month for 10 clients.
Those already on $250 are grandfathered. 30-day free trial is available.
Referral mechanic: once on a paid plan, a referred friend gets a free month and so do you.
---
Agency Pricing: Flat Retainer vs. Rev Share (55:00–75:00) Charlie opened a broader challenge to the flat retainer / email-volume-based pricing model most members use.
As a brand owner, per-send pricing feels transactional and makes it easy for a client to calculate cost-per-email — which invites pushback, especially at scale (his brand sends daily).
His preference: rev share plus retainer, with the rev share percentage declining as revenue scales and the retainer rising to compensate. Incentivizes the agency to perform, not just execute.
Counter from Tristan and Elton: Klaviyo over-attributes heavily. Performance-based pricing built on Klaviyo numbers creates a different problem — the agency looks like it's extracting margin it didn't earn, especially when the brand scales for external reasons (Meta performance, TikTok virality, seasonality).
Curtis shared a firsthand example: paid an Amazon agency on rev share, noticed his Amazon revenue correlated directly with his own Meta spend — not the agency's work. When the agency started claiming the results, the relationship broke down. He eventually hired internally for less.
---
Attribution & How to Frame It (75:00–83:00) The attribution mess came up repeatedly as the core blocker to performance pricing.
Klaviyo over-attributes by design (last-click, 5-day window). Triple Whale is more accurate but still not clean. Meta over-attributes. Google over-attributes. Every platform does.
Elton flagged this from experience — realizing how much Klaviyo inflated his numbers made him question his own results and eventually stop charging on percentage.
Tristan's reframe: email is part of an ecosystem. A sale attributed to email is still a real sale. Someone opened an email and bought — that happened, even if other channels assisted. The role of email in reducing CAC (cheap retargeting vs. paid acquisition) is what makes the attribution debate mostly academic for clients who understand the funnel.
Charlie's example: months where Meta ROAS was break-even, email kept the brand profitable. Without email, they'd have been negative.
How to handle it in a sales conversation: don't over-explain the attribution problem. Acknowledge it exists everywhere (Meta, Google, Klaviyo) and pivot to the principle — the customer saw multiple touchpoints before buying, email is one of the cheapest ways to be in that mix.
---
Bonus Structures as a Middle Ground (83:00–88:00) One member (referencing a call with Dan) surfaced a tactic that bridges flat retainer and performance pricing.
Pitch the retainer as standard, then add an optional milestone bonus — e.g., "if we hit $600K in Q4 attributable revenue vs. your $300K last year, we earn a $1K bonus."
Charlie was receptive: it signals confidence, aligns incentives without locking in a percentage, and feels like upside rather than a baked-in margin extraction.
Tristan flagged this as something he wants to test — particularly powerful in Q4 when brands are already targeting big numbers.
---
Unlimited Sends vs. Scoped Volume (88:00–98:00) Charlie challenged the idea of capping email volume per retainer.
When Meta is performing and scaling hard, you want your email team sending aggressively — daily campaigns, more touchpoints. A send cap limits your ability to capitalize on momentum.
Elton's current model: unlimited sends, one flat price. He attributes long client retention to this — clients feel like they're getting everything, not negotiating for extras.
Tristan's counter: in practice, he does scope 12–16 emails/month but doesn't hold clients rigidly to it. Sale week? He sends the extra emails without charging. Clients notice, and it builds goodwill.
The risk Charlie flagged: some clients will take advantage of unlimited scope. It's a balance.
---
Small Agency Positioning (98:00 –End) Charlie closed with advice on agency positioning, framing it from the brand owner perspective.
Brands at scale want internal teams, not agencies. If you can present as a small, plugged-in operator who responds fast and feels like part of the team, you win over the agency model.
Max's advice to Tristan (referenced): stop trying to look like a big agency when you're not. Lean into the small agency identity — it's a feature, not a liability.
Authority in sales: don't drop price under pressure. Confidence in your rate signals quality. Clients who push for discounts often end up being more difficult, and the discount sets the wrong tone for the relationship from day one.
Charlie's own experience with Max's mentorship: attribution went from 20% to 50% even though they weren't on frequent calls. Results are what matter — not hours logged or call frequency.

lessons.title: May 26th: Agency KPI Tracking & Targets
lessons.description:
Call Summary — Agency Metrics, Pricing, Pop-Ups & Fulfillment Discussion
Max's Executive Business Health Dashboard Walkthrough (4:00–18:00) Tristan ran through Max's agency-wide KPI tracker as the anchor for the session — macro-level internal reporting most members aren't doing in this detail.
Financial benchmarks Max calls out in the doc:
Gross profit margin: 60–80% at scale. Higher if you're below scale.
Net profit margin: 40% target at scale. Max defines "at scale" as ~$20–30K/mo+.
Minimum retainer: $3K/mo. Anything below is a rule Max says shouldn't be broken.Francis added context from a podcast Max appeared on: Max said in practice he fluctuates between 30–40% net profit, averaging ~35%. Some agencies operate as low as 20–25% depending on the work mix. Francis is at 26% currently — pinned it on a few grandfathered sub-$3K clients.
Tristan's own situation: ~75% net profit but pre-scale (solo). Acknowledged the margin hit that comes with scaling — "part of the game."
Pod structure (Max's setup): 7 clients per pod = 1 AM + 1 copywriter + 1 designer + Klaviyo tech (sometimes doubled by the copywriter). Pricing tiers based on campaign volume: 12, 16, 20, 24+ emails/month.
Sales metrics Max tracks:
Show rate target: 80%
Close rate target: 20% (Tristan flagged this as a useful sign — if your close rate is way above this on inbound, you're likely underpricing. Hormozi-style logic.)
Booked vs. scheduled vs. taken — three separate counts.Churn:
Target: <5%/mo
Tracking churned $, churned MRR %, average client lifespan in months, LTV
Most small operators on the call aren't tracking churn — not enough volume for it to matter yet, but at scale it's the canary.Labor: FT count, PT count, total monthly salaries, revenue per employee.
Action item for everyone: Copy the sheet, strip out what doesn't apply, start tracking month-over-month even if it's mostly in your head right now. Holds you accountable to growth.

---
Hiro for Reporting (18:00–24:00) Jeremy is on Hyro — uses the small agency plan ($250/mo for 5 clients, $500/mo for 10). He swaps clients in and out as needed. Doesn't send raw Hyro reports to clients the way Max does — he pulls screenshots into his own deck with plain-language commentary on why numbers matter.
Tristan just signed up after the demo call but got quoted the $500 / 10-client plan (they didn't surface the smaller tier — likely because he said he had 5 clients, ceiling-pushing tactic). He'll Slack them to downgrade. 30-day free trial is gettable just by asking on the demo. Referral mechanic: refer a friend and you both get an extra month free.
Why Tristan's switching: Hyro pulls Klaviyo data directly, white-labels to agency colors/logo, and you can send clients a live web link to a dashboard instead of static screenshots. Saves time on monthly reporting and looks more professional.
Dan's pushback (came up later but relevant here): "Isn't sharing all the analytics waking up sleeping dogs?" He only shares wins in reporting — when clients see click rate / flow performance themselves, they start optimizing for the wrong things and asking why specific numbers aren't higher. Robert agreed — uses Hyro internally for the team, not client-facing.
Tristan acknowledged the tension — he hasn't actually used it for client reporting yet, so he'll learn whether transparency backfires.

---
Milestone Bonuses Instead of Performance Fees (24:00–28:00) Dan dropped a tactic he's been using to lift retainers without going to a performance fee structure (which a lot of brands resist):
Set a milestone tied to a launch, sale, or growth target (e.g., "last year you did $300K in Q4, if we hit $600K we get a $1K bonus").
Especially powerful in Q4 — brands are already aiming high, you tie your incentive to it.
He shares the bonus with his team → keeps them invested in execution.
Win-win-win — agency, client, and team are all aligned on the same number.Frame: brands that hate performance fees love this because it's optional upside, not baked into the retainer.

---
Setup Fees vs. Bundling First Month (28:00–34:00) Niccolò asked: setup fee for flows separate, or bundled into a higher first month?
Matthias (Well Copy team): separate setup fee is the cleanest — easier to account for the extra work.
Dan: Charges higher first month for flows but only when he knows the client will stick around long-term. If he's confident on retention, he'd rather absorb on the front end and get them locked in. If retention's a question mark, charge separately. Always customizes per client.
Jeremy's pricing model: ~$325 per email for flows. Don't tell the client the per-email number — that's internal napkin math. Helps you scale price to what they actually want (e.g., 8 emails per flow vs. 3 emails per flow). Lets you flex to budget — "$4K budget? You get 3 emails per flow. Full build-out? $8–9K."
Dan's two-call structure (came up in detail here):
First call = audit call. No price, no pitch. Just ask questions, get a feel for the client, sometimes get Klaviyo access for a deeper look. Frame: "I'm not here to pitch anything — we're just figuring out if we can help each other." Builds massive trust.
Second call = proposal. Walk through what you found in the audit, pitch the strategy mapped to their brand specifically (not generic), give the price.The personalization moat: Matthias mentioned his team adds brand-specific examples into the Miro/strategy doc — niche-specific email mockups, founder-led variant suggestions, etc. He said no client has ever not commented on how personalized it feels. Differentiates from generic "we'll send 3 campaigns/week" pitches.
Dan: "I'm not good at closing — it's the audit that closes them."

---
Onboarding Meeting / Kickoff Structure (34:00–37:00) Francis asked about a separate kickoff call. Both Dan and Francis run a 3-call structure:
Qualification / discovery call
Audit walkthrough + proposal
Kickoff (after they say yes) — runs through the onboarding form, deeper access, team introsDan keeps the kickoff to ~20–25 mins. Onboarding form + flagging anything that stands out. The deep flow strategy doc gets built and shared after the kickoff, not on the call.

---
Capacity & Hiring on the Spot (37:00–39:00) Francis asked Dan: what happens if you're at capacity and a new client comes in?
Dan: He doesn't really turn down clients. He flexes deliverable timelines (e.g., "month 1 we focus on your highest-traffic country, months 2 and 3 we expand to the others"), and hires on the spot if needed. The audit gives him enough signal on workload to set realistic expectations on the proposal call.

---
Alia Pop-ups: Submit Rate vs. Profit (39:00–55:00) Dan opened a deep critique of Alia after a recent client experience. His core issue: Alia optimizes for submit rate, not profit.
Specific complaints:
They show 5 different pop-ups within ~60 seconds if you close one — aggressive, brand-damaging.
Pop-ups trigger at 2–4 seconds — before a visitor has seen anything.
He found a 40% gap between Alia's "unique visitors" count and Shopify's. When he pressed Alia's success manager, the only answer was "we don't calculate exact Shopify visits, we have our own tracking." Translation: black box.
Pop-ups still display to people already on the email list — the "thank you page for existing subscribers" workaround they suggested is, in Dan's words, garbage. You're showing fresh offers to people who already opted in.Tristan's counter: Better-looking pop-up builds, more creative micro-commitments (slider quizzes, scratch-to-win, etc.), and Alia manages the A/B tests for you in a Slack channel. Suggestions come from them, you approve/decline. He still controls the tests, but doesn't run them.
Robert's compared: A client on free trial — Alia got ~8% submit rate, same as Klaviyo. Ended the trial.
Dan's take on timing — biggest contrarian point of the call:
Most agencies (himself previously included) trigger pop-ups under 15 seconds.
He now triggers at 30 seconds minimum, excluded from checkout pages.
Logic: if a visitor is buying quickly, they're high-intent and would have bought at full price. Showing them a discount under 10 seconds is just margin destruction.
Adjusts based on AOV / LTV — replenishment / low-AOV beauty brands can trigger faster because LTV is built into the model.
KPI he optimizes for: total brand profit, factoring AOV, LTV, and conversion rate — not submit rate.Tristan acknowledged he's been operating "binary" on timing (under 15 seconds across the board) and is going to test longer delays.
Premium brand example: Tristan has a client who keeps asking him to test scratch-to-win. He's refused — "the founder hates them, they look tacky, this is a premium brand." Submit rate would probably go up. Brand integrity matters more.
On Prism (Alia's new feature — traffic-source-based pop-up variants): Nobody has serious experience yet. Tristan is testing it on a small client. Skepticism on whether changing the hero image per source moves the needle meaningfully.

---
Reporting Philosophy: Share Wins Only (55:00–1:00:00) Dan and Robert aligned on a contrarian reporting stance vs. Hyro/Tristan's approach:
Don't share full dashboards with clients. Use Hyro internally for the team, share wins externally.
Frame weak points as "what we're focusing on next month" rather than as losses.
Monthly meetings are about business growth, not email metrics. Dan barely talks Klaviyo numbers — he talks how the client can grow the business overall (he has an ecom background from selling his own brands).
Campaign calendar = the real touchpoint. Sharing the upcoming month's calendar, flagging which past campaigns worked and which to retire, gives clients more confidence than data dumps.
Q1 reporting trap: If you've trained clients to focus on click rate / conversion rate, Q1 and post-BFCM months will look terrible — even though it's seasonal and normal. Better to never anchor them on those numbers in the first place.
---
Meetings Cadence — Avoiding Micromanagement (1:00:00–1:03:00) Robert and Dan both pushed hard against weekly client meetings:
Weekly = micromanagement red flag. Robert has had clients turn into painful relationships every single time.
Dan sets expectations on sales call #2: monthly strategy meeting, Slack for everything else, jump on a call only if something specific needs it. Clients agree because expectations are clear.
Dan's framing: "Clients only want frequent meetings if they don't trust you. Handle trust on the sales call and in your reporting, and you won't need them."
---
Close Rate, Pricing, and Charging More (1:03:00–1:09:00) Tristan asked Dan directly: your close rate is ~90% — Max's doc says 20% is the target for cold inbound, so are you underpricing?
Dan's honest answer: Yes, probably — but it's a strategic choice.
Close rate is high because leads come from Twitter/X, affiliates, or referrals — all warm.
He hits ~$3K/mo per retainer, has ~$1K in COGS per client, healthy profit.
He's choosing case studies, referrals, and milestone bonuses over squeezing first-month price up by $1–2K.
"I make enough profit for me to live how I want to live, I get nice people, I get referrals — why risk it?"Tristan's situation: Average retainer ~£1.5K, knows it's too low, working to get to £2–3K. Most leads are referrals or hyper-personalized DMs (essentially warm). Has been increasing prices recently.
Francis: Mostly inbound, ~5 active clients, prices per email internally (£185/campaign as benchmark — translates to ~£1.5K at 8 campaigns, ~£2.9K at 16). Doesn't share per-email pricing with the client.
Dan's pricing logic floor: Minimum 2.5x your COGS. If your designer + copywriter cost ~€1K per client, charge €2.5K+ minimum. Everything above is profit.

---
In-House Designers vs. Outsourcing to Ahmed (1:09:00–1:20:00) Tristan is using Ahmed (~$35/email, Middle Eastern team) short-term while looking for an in-house designer. Posted on LinkedIn, got applicants but no one strong enough — most were from regions he felt wouldn't culturally match his premium client base.
Dan's setup: 2 full-time designers in the Philippines, ~$1K–$1.4K/mo each. He pays well above local minimum. Math: with 5–6 clients per designer, the per-client cost is ~$200/mo for unlimited design.
Key Dan insight on team management — he changed his entire model:
Used to run a team of 11 with heavy SOPs, "kept dialed in"

content.text: Call Summary — Agency Metrics, Pricing, Pop-Ups & Fulfillment Discussion
Max's Executive Business Health Dashboard Walkthrough (
) Tristan ran through Max's agency-wide KPI tracker as the anchor for the session — macro-level internal reporting most members aren't doing in this detail.
Financial benchmarks Max calls out in the doc:
Gross profit margin:
60–80% at scale. Higher if you're below scale.
Net profit margin:
40% target at scale. Max defines "at scale" as ~$20–30K/mo+.
Minimum retainer:
$3K/mo. Anything below is a rule Max says shouldn't be broken.
Francis added context from a podcast Max appeared on:

Max said in practice he fluctuates between 30–40% net profit, averaging ~35%. Some agencies operate as low as 20–25% depending on the work mix. Francis is at 26% currently — pinned it on a few grandfathered sub-$3K clients.
Tristan's own situation:
~75% net profit but pre-scale (solo). Acknowledged the margin hit that comes with scaling — "part of the game."
Pod structure (Max's setup):
7 clients per pod = 1 AM + 1 copywriter + 1 designer + Klaviyo tech (sometimes doubled by the copywriter). Pricing tiers based on campaign volume: 12, 16, 20, 24+ emails/month.
Sales metrics Max tracks:
Show rate target: 80%
Close rate target: 20% (Tristan flagged this as a useful sign — if your close rate is way above this on inbound, you're likely underpricing. Hormozi-style logic.)
Booked vs. scheduled vs. taken — three separate counts.
Churn:
Target: <5%/mo
Tracking churned $, churned MRR %, average client lifespan in months, LTV
Most small operators on the call aren't tracking churn — not enough volume for it to matter yet, but at scale it's the canary.
Labor:
FT count, PT count, total monthly salaries, revenue per employee.
Action item for everyone:
Copy the sheet, strip out what doesn't apply, start tracking month-over-month even if it's mostly in your head right now. Holds you accountable to growth.
Hiro for Reporting (

) Jeremy is on Hyro — uses the small agency plan ($250/mo for 5 clients, $500/mo for 10). He swaps clients in and out as needed. Doesn't send raw Hyro reports to clients the way Max does — he pulls screenshots into his own deck with plain-language commentary on
why
numbers matter.

Tristan just signed up after the demo call but got quoted the $500 / 10-client plan (they didn't surface the smaller tier — likely because he said he had 5 clients, ceiling-pushing tactic). He'll Slack them to downgrade. 30-day free trial is gettable just by asking on the demo. Referral mechanic: refer a friend and you both get an extra month free.
Why Tristan's switching:

Hyro pulls Klaviyo data directly, white-labels to agency colors/logo, and you can send clients a live web link to a dashboard instead of static screenshots. Saves time on monthly reporting and looks more professional.
Dan's pushback

(came up later but relevant here): "Isn't sharing all the analytics waking up sleeping dogs?" He only shares wins in reporting — when clients see click rate / flow performance themselves, they start optimizing for the wrong things and asking why specific numbers aren't higher. Robert agreed — uses Hyro internally for the team, not client-facing.
Tristan acknowledged the tension
— he hasn't actually used it for client reporting yet, so he'll learn whether transparency backfires.
Milestone Bonuses Instead of Performance Fees (
) Dan dropped a tactic he's been using to lift retainers without going to a performance fee structure (which a lot of brands resist):
Set a milestone tied to a launch, sale, or growth target (e.g., "last year you did $300K in Q4, if we hit $600K we get a $1K bonus").
Especially powerful in Q4 — brands are already aiming high, you tie your incentive to it.
He shares the bonus with his team → keeps them invested in execution.
Win-win-win — agency, client, and team are all aligned on the same number.
Frame: brands that hate performance fees love this because it's optional upside, not baked into the retainer.
Setup Fees vs. Bundling First Month (
) Niccolò asked: setup fee for flows separate, or bundled into a higher first month?
Matthias (Well Copy team): separate setup fee is the cleanest
— easier to account for the extra work.
Dan:

Charges higher first month for flows but only when he knows the client will stick around long-term. If he's confident on retention, he'd rather absorb on the front end and get them locked in. If retention's a question mark, charge separately. Always customizes per client.
Jeremy's pricing model:

~$325 per email for flows. Don't tell the client the per-email number — that's internal napkin math. Helps you scale price to what they actually want (e.g., 8 emails per flow vs. 3 emails per flow). Lets you flex to budget — "$4K budget? You get 3 emails per flow. Full build-out? $8–9K."
Dan's two-call structure
(came up in detail here):
First call = audit call.

No price, no pitch. Just ask questions, get a feel for the client, sometimes get Klaviyo access for a deeper look. Frame: "I'm not here to pitch anything — we're just figuring out if we can help each other." Builds massive trust.
Second call = proposal.
Walk through what you found in the audit, pitch the strategy mapped to their brand specifically (not generic), give the price.
The personalization moat:
Matthias mentioned his team adds brand-specific examples into the Miro/strategy doc — niche-specific email mockups, founder-led variant suggestions, etc. He said no client has ever
not
commented on how personalized it feels. Differentiates from generic "we'll send 3 campaigns/week" pitches.
Dan: "I'm not good at closing — it's the audit that closes them."
Onboarding Meeting / Kickoff Structure (
) Francis asked about a separate kickoff call. Both Dan and Francis run a 3-call structure:
Qualification / discovery call
Audit walkthrough + proposal
Kickoff (after they say yes) — runs through the onboarding form, deeper access, team intros
Dan keeps the kickoff to ~20–25 mins. Onboarding form + flagging anything that stands out. The deep flow strategy doc gets built and shared
after
the kickoff, not on the call.
Capacity & Hiring on the Spot (
) Francis asked Dan: what happens if you're at capacity and a new client comes in?

Dan: He doesn't really turn down clients. He flexes deliverable timelines (e.g., "month 1 we focus on your highest-traffic country, months 2 and 3 we expand to the others"), and hires on the spot if needed. The audit gives him enough signal on workload to set realistic expectations on the proposal call.
Alia Pop-ups: Submit Rate vs. Profit (
) Dan opened a deep critique of Alia after a recent client experience.
His core issue: Alia optimizes for submit rate, not profit.
Specific complaints:
They show
5 different pop-ups within ~60 seconds
if you close one — aggressive, brand-damaging.
Pop-ups trigger at
2–4 seconds
— before a visitor has seen anything.
He found a
40% gap between Alia's "unique visitors" count and Shopify's
. When he pressed Alia's success manager, the only answer was "we don't calculate exact Shopify visits, we have our own tracking." Translation: black box.
Pop-ups still display to people
already on the email list
— the "thank you page for existing subscribers" workaround they suggested is, in Dan's words, garbage. You're showing fresh offers to people who already opted in.
Tristan's counter:
Better-looking pop-up builds, more creative micro-commitments (slider quizzes, scratch-to-win, etc.), and
Alia manages the A/B tests for you
in a Slack channel. Suggestions come from them, you approve/decline. He still controls the tests, but doesn't run them.
Robert's compared:
A client on free trial — Alia got ~8% submit rate, same as Klaviyo. Ended the trial.
Dan's take on timing — biggest contrarian point of the call:
Most agencies (himself previously included) trigger pop-ups under 15 seconds.
He now triggers at
30 seconds minimum
, excluded from checkout pages.
Logic: if a visitor is buying quickly, they're high-intent and would have bought at full price. Showing them a discount under 10 seconds is just margin destruction.
Adjusts based on AOV / LTV — replenishment / low-AOV beauty brands can trigger faster because LTV is built into the model.
KPI he optimizes for:
total brand profit
, factoring AOV, LTV, and conversion rate — not submit rate.
Tristan acknowledged he's been operating "binary" on timing
(under 15 seconds across the board) and is going to test longer delays.
Premium brand example:

Tristan has a client who keeps asking him to test scratch-to-win. He's refused — "the founder hates them, they look tacky, this is a premium brand." Submit rate would probably go up. Brand integrity matters more.
On Prism (Alia's new feature — traffic-source-based pop-up variants):
Nobody has serious experience yet. Tristan is testing it on a small client. Skepticism on whether changing the hero image per source moves the needle meaningfully.
Reporting Philosophy: Share Wins Only (
) Dan and Robert aligned on a contrarian reporting stance vs. Hyro/Tristan's approach:
Don't share full dashboards with clients.
Use Hyro internally for the team, share wins externally.
Frame weak points as "what we're focusing on next month"
rather than as losses.
Monthly meetings are about business growth, not email metrics.
Dan barely talks Klaviyo numbers — he talks how the client can grow the business overall (he has an ecom background from selling his own brands).
Campaign calendar = the real touchpoint.
Sharing the upcoming month's calendar, flagging which past campaigns worked and which to retire, gives clients more confidence than data dumps.
Q1 reporting trap:

If you've trained clients to focus on click rate / conversion rate, Q1 and post-BFCM months will look terrible — even though it's seasonal and normal. Better to never anchor them on those numbers in the first place.
Meetings Cadence — Avoiding Micromanagement (
) Robert and Dan both pushed hard against weekly client meetings:
Weekly = micromanagement red flag.
Robert has had clients turn into painful relationships every single time.
Dan sets expectations on sales call #2:
monthly strategy meeting, Slack for everything else, jump on a call only if something specific needs it. Clients agree because expectations are clear.
Dan's framing:
"Clients only want frequent meetings if they don't trust you. Handle trust on the sales call and in your reporting, and you won't need them."

) Tristan asked Dan directly: your close rate is ~90% — Max's doc says 20% is the target for cold inbound, so are you underpricing?
Dan's honest answer: Yes, probably — but it's a strategic choice.
Close rate is high because leads come from Twitter/X, affiliates, or referrals — all warm.
He hits ~$3K/mo per retainer, has ~$1K in COGS per client, healthy profit.
He's choosing case studies, referrals, and milestone bonuses over squeezing first-month price up by $1–2K.
"I make enough profit for me to live how I want to live, I get nice people, I get referrals — why risk it?"
Tristan's situation:
Average retainer ~£1.5K, knows it's too low, working to get to £2–3K. Most leads are referrals or hyper-personalized DMs (essentially warm). Has been increasing prices recently.

Mostly inbound, ~5 active clients, prices per email internally (£185/campaign as benchmark — translates to ~£1.5K at 8 campaigns, ~£2.9K at 16). Doesn't share per-email pricing with the client.

Minimum 2.5x your COGS. If your designer + copywriter cost ~€1K per client, charge €2.5K+ minimum. Everything above is profit.

Dan's setup:
2 full-time designers in the Philippines, ~$1K–$1.4K/mo each. He pays well above local minimum.

with 5–6 clients per designer, the per-client cost is ~$200/mo for unlimited design.

lessons.title: May 19th: Organic Content Masterclass
lessons.description:
Watch Video Recording >>
Summary below 👇

---
Opening & Housekeeping (0:00–2:42) Tristan opened with a small group already on the call (Jeremy, Matthias) before the bulk of attendees joined. Niccolo introduced himself — 5 years in email marketing, mostly service and course businesses in health and wellness, transitioning into ecommerce, just signed his first ecom client around 10 days ago. He's there to learn fast from people already operating in the space.
Quick side conversation before the main topic kicked off:
Jeremy flagged a new ecom client (~14 emails/month, half-dropshipping) where the team started behind on deliverables, the designer rushed early creative, and the client wasn't happy with the design quality.
Matthias and Jeremy agreed that one week of prep before the first campaign is the new minimum when onboarding a new account — especially when transitioning off another agency where you don't have access to the previous Figma file or design assets.
Consensus: dropshipping brands are budget-conscious, fickle on design, and churn faster. Plan accordingly on retainer structure and expectations.
---
Max's Content Strategy Walkthrough (3:16–18:24) Tristan ran through Max's content strategy doc as the anchor for the session. The doc maps how Max grew Well Copy from $0 to current scale through content, with distinct phases tied to revenue milestones.
Revenue tier → acquisition channel mapping:
$0–$10K/mo: Freelancer/in-house copywriter. No acquisition funnel — just getting reps in.
$10K–$35K/mo: Cold email (likely a List Kit / Client Ascension-style setup — 30+ inboxes, mass scraping).
$35K+/mo: YouTube, Instagram, Twitter, eventually newsletter. Cold email died around early 2024 from saturation, and the content engine took over.Phase 1 — Twitter (audience building):
Build the initial audience by networking with peers at a similar level — not chasing big accounts.
Farm accounts under 500 followers, become friends, engage daily on each other's tweets.
Reciprocity drives early engagement, which the algorithm then amplifies.
2–3 posts/day, 2 lives + 1 value tweet.
The goal is audience, not clients. Twitter is better for networking and driving traffic to other platforms than for direct deal flow.Phase 2 — YouTube (omnipresence + intent capture):
YouTube won't push fresh accounts cold, so Max used the Twitter audience to drive initial views.
People searching his name on YouTube signaled to the algorithm that there was real demand.
High watch-through rates pushed the algorithm further in his favor.
He had a monopoly — no one else was doing email marketing on YouTube at the time.
September 2024: closed 12 deals from YouTube alone. None of those were polished — they were Loom-style walkthroughs over Gamma docs.Phase 3 — Instagram (volume + virality):
6 months of daily posting, averaging 200 views per video, before one video blew up and brought in 5 deals.
Instagram is a pure volume game — keep posting high-quality content, eventually one hits.
Even at 200 views, you don't know who's watching quietly. Volume + consistency wins.
Max's winning angle: brand redesigns for big names (Lululemon, Gymshark, Aloe). Hits both normies (interested in design) and ICPs (interested in capability).
~50% of booked calls now come from Instagram.Phase 4 — Newsletter (the connector):
Lead magnets pull people off YouTube/Instagram into the newsletter.
Welcome sequence drives book-a-call conversion.
~18K subscribers, 30–50 signups/day, and most booked calls now come from the newsletter or people who are subscribed to it.
10 lead magnets total — the "value firehose" approach.
---
Platform-Specific Content Tactics (18:24–27:23)
YouTube — make straight tutorials.
People come to YouTube to be educated, not entertained. Lead with the answer.
Make a list of every objection and FAQ you've ever heard on a sales call → that's your content calendar.
No editing required. Loom + Gamma doc + good thumbnail is enough.
Max's 12-deal month off YouTube was entirely unedited content.
~30 min prep, ~20 min film, asset lives forever.Instagram — entertain while you educate.
People aren't searching Instagram for "how to build a cart abandon flow." They're scrolling.
You need content that hits normies (so the algorithm pushes it wide) AND demonstrates expertise (so ICPs convert).
Max's winning angles:
Big brand teardowns + redesigns ("21-year-old vs. billion-dollar company" hook — now copied widely, still ripping).
Psychology of marketing — how brands manipulate consumers.
AI demos — still has wow factor.
Banging marketing breakdowns — screen-record a good email in your inbox, green-screen, explain why it works. Easiest content to make, still effective.
Over time the algorithm learns your niche and pushes content to the right people.
---
Delegation & Outsourcing Content (18:24–22:52) Aven asked when Max started delegating content production. Tristan's read:
Max is fully removed from fulfillment and spends his day on sales + marketing, so he keeps content close.
He still films a video daily on his phone, edits rough.
The polished videos that pop up are batch-filmed monthly with a content agency as backup for days he can't film.
For personal brand-led acquisition, the founder needs to stay in the content. Outsourcing the writing or filming loses authenticity, which is the whole point.
Twitter ghostwriting could work if it's pure value content — but at that point, you could whisper-flow into Claude and write it yourself in less time.
---
Behind the Scenes — How Brand Owners Actually Find You (26:13–29:26) Tyler (a brand owner in the community) shared his perspective:
Found Max on YouTube in 2024, watched 70–80% of his videos.
The content that converted him was direct, value-first tutorials — not pitchy.
"Don't pitch yourself for the first 20 minutes and then mention it at the end. Lead with the value. Pitch at the end."
On the "too young to be credible" objection: proven authority overrides age every time. If you sound confident and the information is good, age doesn't come up.
---
Audit Funnel + LinkedIn for Smaller Brands (37:24–48:04)
Tristan made a sharp point that pivoted the discussion: Max's strategy of redesigning Gymshark/Lululemon goes viral. But for smaller agencies, the same tactic works differently — instead of going viral, you do public redesigns/audits of brands you actually want to work with. They see it, they reach out.
Aidan confirmed: he signed a client off a public redesign post.
Aven added: this overlaps with the audit funnel — flag something specific in their account, prove competency, build trust. Clients who come through this path rarely ask for case studies because you've already proven the work.
LinkedIn dynamics:
Higher quality ICP than other platforms (C-suite, founders, operators).
Front-facing profile matters most early on — no revenue claims, no "We'll make you $100K in 30 days" bios.
Build through recommendations, then post a mix of value, visual, and personal content.
The corporate stigma is fading. Authenticity wins on LinkedIn too now.Aidan's results so far on the new content strategy: ~10 meetings booked in 3 weeks of consistent Instagram posting (3–5 posts/day, raw talking head, ~1 hour/day production). Mix of quality — some brokies, some 7-figure brands. No closes yet but pitching one this Thursday after an audit.

---
YouTube Mental Block (33:14–35:14) Tristan opened up about his own mental block on YouTube — wants to start, hasn't. The group's advice:
You don't need 30-minute videos. A focused 5-minute walkthrough on how to build a high-converting pop-up form is enough.
Niche topics rip on YouTube. Jeremy mentioned a 5-minute Loom from 2 years ago on a Squarespace sign-up form that still gets views and comments.
Niccolo's warning: he burned out doing daily IG + 3x/week YouTube + editor + lights. Started too big. Max's Loom-style approach is more sustainable.
---
Onboarding a Designer Hire (48:04–54:05) Tristan asked the group for tips on onboarding his new part-time designer hire. Jeremy (who's prepping to hire his second full-time designer) shared his playbook:
Day 1: welcome letter with letterhead. Sounds small, drives buy-in even for contractors.
Set hard expectations on revisions — 24 hours? 3 hours? Get the standard in writing day one.
Google Drive structure — clear folders for briefs, design assets, brand guidelines.
Loom walkthroughs of your project management system (Airtable, ClickUp, whatever you use).On sharing copy with designers:
Jeremy uses an A-spot / B-spot / C-spot framework — A-spot is hero, B-spot is mid-email, C-spot is below. Tells the designer where the major sections live without locking them into rigid wireframes.
Above-A-spot notes for banners, GIFs, etc.
Let a good designer make design decisions on the copy. If they need handholding, you hired the wrong designer.Niccolo's add: match your handholding to their skill level. Trying to micromanage an expert burns them out. Trying to set free a junior loses them.
Side benefit Jeremy flagged: the SOPs you build for internal designers double as lead magnets later. Run them through Claude, polish, ship as a client-facing resource. "Email design best practices" doc writes itself.

---
Retention After Flow Builds (55:00–58:00) Matthias asked Tristan to share what Max said about retaining clients after one-off flow builds — and clients who churn after their account is "optimized."
Max's read (relayed by Tristan):
Only ~10% of one-off flow build clients convert to retainer, even with high-quality fulfillment.
They don't have a systemized handoff for this — it's just the nature of the offer.
Workaround: stop selling flow builds separately. Bundle them into the retainer from day one so the client is already roped in.For clients who churn after the account is "optimized":
Often a communication problem, not a value problem. You're doing the work — they don't see it.
Niccolo's framing: "Make their life so easy that if you took yourself out of the picture, they'd be lost."
Tristan: brands that are going to scale recognize the value of agency fulfillment (cross-account data, testing volume, time off the founder's plate). Brands that don't recognize that aren't worth fighting for.

The corporate stigma is fading. Authenticity wins on LinkedIn too now.
Aidan's results so far on the new content strategy:

~10 meetings booked in 3 weeks of consistent Instagram posting (3–5 posts/day, raw talking head, ~1 hour/day production). Mix of quality — some brokies, some 7-figure brands. No closes yet but pitching one this Thursday after an audit.
YouTube Mental Block (
) Tristan opened up about his own mental block on YouTube — wants to start, hasn't. The group's advice:
You don't need 30-minute videos.
A focused 5-minute walkthrough on how to build a high-converting pop-up form is enough.
Niche topics rip on YouTube. Jeremy mentioned a 5-minute Loom from 2 years ago on a Squarespace sign-up form that still gets views and comments.
Niccolo's warning: he burned out doing daily IG + 3x/week YouTube + editor + lights.
Started too big.
Max's Loom-style approach is more sustainable.
Onboarding a Designer Hire (
) Tristan asked the group for tips on onboarding his new part-time designer hire. Jeremy (who's prepping to hire his second full-time designer) shared his playbook:
Day 1: welcome letter with letterhead.
Sounds small, drives buy-in even for contractors.
Set hard expectations on revisions
— 24 hours? 3 hours? Get the standard in writing day one.
Google Drive structure
— clear folders for briefs, design assets, brand guidelines.
Loom walkthroughs of your project management system
(Airtable, ClickUp, whatever you use).
On sharing copy with designers:
Jeremy uses an
A-spot / B-spot / C-spot framework
— A-spot is hero, B-spot is mid-email, C-spot is below. Tells the designer where the major sections live without locking them into rigid wireframes.
Above-A-spot notes for banners, GIFs, etc.
Let a good designer make design decisions on the copy. If they need handholding, you hired the wrong designer.
Niccolo's add:
match your handholding to their skill level.
Trying to micromanage an expert burns them out. Trying to set free a junior loses them.
Side benefit Jeremy flagged:
the SOPs you build for internal designers double as lead magnets later.
Run them through Claude, polish, ship as a client-facing resource. "Email design best practices" doc writes itself.
Retention After Flow Builds (
) Matthias asked Tristan to share what Max said about retaining clients after one-off flow builds — and clients who churn after their account is "optimized."
Max's read (relayed by Tristan):
Only ~10% of one-off flow build clients convert to retainer
, even with high-quality fulfillment.
They don't have a systemized handoff for this — it's just the nature of the offer.
Workaround: stop selling flow builds separately. Bundle them into the retainer from day one so the client is already roped in.
For clients who churn after the account is "optimized":
Often a communication problem, not a value problem. You're doing the work — they don't see it.
Niccolo's framing:
"Make their life so easy that if you took yourself out of the picture, they'd be lost."

Tristan: brands that are going to scale recognize the value of agency fulfillment (cross-account data, testing volume, time off the founder's plate). Brands that don't recognize that aren't worth fighting for.

lessons.title: May 12th: Sales Process Masterclass
lessons.description:
VIEW RECORDING — 76 mins
Summary below 👇

---
Opening & Intros (0:00–6:10)
Tristan (ThriveTribe Media) led the call this week — not Max. Matthias opened with a compliment on Tristan's comic-style email, which went out that day. Tristan's own read: cool for list retention, probably won't be a big money-maker, but it maps out problem-solution and tells the brand story well.
Tristan in London (planning to move there), Jeremy in Portland, Maine, Matthias in Hamburg, Nikko in Orange County, Marielet in the Philippines (brand new — less than a week in, already watching recordings and implementing). Toni and Jan also present.

---
Pre-Call Warm-Up Sequence — The Part Before Phase 1 (6:10–9:35)
Tristan flagged this as the most important piece before diving into the phases. After a prospect books on Calendly, they hit an internal confirmation page and receive a short sequence of reminder emails linking to case studies, videos, and proof assets. Purpose: decrease no-shows, warm the prospect, and put them in a better buying state before the intro call even happens.
Mapa asked whether Max intentionally spaces the booking window out (e.g., minimum 4 days) to give the email sequence time to work — unknown. Jeremy shared that he started doing something similar a couple months ago — manually sending an intro deck with case studies after someone books. No automation yet (low volume), but he thinks it helps answer early questions and showcase design/results before the call starts.

---
Phase 1: Intro Call — Discovery & Qualification (9:35–18:00)
Three pillars of discovery: (1) learn about the brand — product, niche, customer, stage of scale; (2) what triggered the call — what's broken, what's working, what partnership might solve; (3) current email/SMS setup — starting from scratch, underbuilt, past agency experience.
Tristan's personal move: asks "what motivated you to book this call?" right after rapport — lets the prospect do the talking and reveal pain. Jeremy co-signed hard — best sales calls are when the prospect talks 80%+ of the time. Let them fork themselves into the close. Tristan added: sit with the silence after they answer — they'll keep talking and open up more pain points you can use later for objection handling.
After discovery, the closer does a live light audit — screen-sharing in Klaviyo, looking at pop-ups, flows, surface-level stuff. Not deep, but enough to make the prospect feel seen. Two outcomes from here: (1) prospect is qualified, in pain, ready — move straight into pricing on the call, or (2) they need more proof — transition to a full deep audit (Phase 2).
Tristan also highlighted that Max sets the working tone during the intro call — how revisions work, where design feedback happens, Slack communication cadence. Positions the agency's process as a USP early.
Pricing discussion sidebar (15:17–20:50): Jeremy raised the awkward moment when prospects ask for price during discovery. Tristan's stance: only drop price when you're closing, not during discovery — if you drop too early, they haven't grasped full value yet. His deflection: "I don't know your problems yet, so I don't want to give you a generic price — let me understand your pain points first." Frames it as building a bespoke solution. Mapa shared her method: she calculates business size by asking AOV and monthly order count (sneaky math without asking revenue directly), then walks through the solution before asking the prospect to confirm "yes, this is exactly what I need" before ever mentioning price. Uses the Hormozi closer framework. If they don't confirm, she doesn't even go to price — just moves on. Breakthrough for her was calculating business size without asking for it, and getting the verbal yes before the number drops.

---
Phase 2: The Full Audit (20:50–30:00)
Deep audit — not surface level. Covers revenue attribution, cancellation data (subscription brands), flow architecture, segmentation logic, campaign performance. Max does these as Loom recordings sent to the prospect to watch on their own time. Tristan's take: Max only does Looms because he doesn't have time for live calls — if you have the time, always present audits live on a call. Live = you can push value, objection handle in real time, and actually close. Sending a PDF or Loom cold = prospect watches, isn't that interested, moves on. You lose control.
Audit structure covers three buckets:
List growth — simplify pop-up, add micro-commit, mystery discount testing, SMS capture, offer testing (biggest lever). Flows — identify what's missing, highlight critical flows (cart abandoned vs. checkout abandoned), subscription flows (billing reminders, campaign targeting for subscribers), underbuilt flows (welcome with only one email, short browse abandonment), buyer vs. non-buyer splits, turning off smart sending, adding text-based post-purchase. Campaigns — segmentation (whole list vs. engaged), buyer vs. non-buyer targeting, creative/copy quality (8/10 brands have massive text blocks — replace with infographics), SMS strategy, deliverability health.
Audit presentation best practices: Be blunt — if email sucks, say it sucks before you even start the walkthrough. Bring comparisons — pull up a client's Klaviyo account where you're crushing it as social proof. Use specific numbers — "this could add 10K" not "you could make more money." Explain the strategy behind recommendations — founders respect understanding the why (e.g., explaining commitment bias behind micro-commits makes you look like a real strategist, not just someone reading a checklist).
After the audit, transition into a high-level roadmap: quick wins in 7 days, what happens at 30/60/90 days. Lets them visualize working with you.

---
Phase 3: Closing & Pricing Framework (30:00–42:00)
Structure: ask what they thought of the audit → what stuck out → iron out scope/communication details → temperature check before pricing. Tristan's temperature check: "On a scale of 1–10, how do you feel about the system we discussed?" If they don't say 10, ask why — usually "I don't know the price yet," which is a perfect bridge into pricing.
Max's pricing tiers (per email volume):
Bronze: 12 emails/mo — $5,000/mo
Silver: 16 emails/mo — $5,600/mo
Gold: 20 emails/mo — $6,200/mo
Platinum/Custom: 24+ emails/mo — $6,800/moAdd-ons: SMS ($200 extra), $1,000 setup fee, $4,000 minimum investment, 60-day agreement, 14-day money-back guarantee, can upgrade/downgrade anytime.
Group discussion on volume-based pricing: Matthias noted Max previously used flat fees with unlimited emails — this tiered model is relatively new. His concern: it makes it feel like you're being paid per email, which is transactional and commoditizes the service ("then go to Fiverr for $50/email"). Jeremy echoed this — clients automatically do the math ($5K ÷ 12 = $416/email) even though you're delivering strategy, reporting, everything else. Tristan doesn't use volume pricing — he prices flat and says "I'm your email/SMS partner, we do whatever it takes." Downside: high-scope clients can eat your margin. Jan advocated for rev share — 10% of email revenue or a minimum retainer (e.g., $2.5K + 5% with a ceiling). Lets the client see aligned incentives. When revenue spikes (like BFCM), the bill spikes too — and that becomes leverage to lock in a higher flat rate ("if you're paying me 12K, you're making 120K — let's lock at 5–6K flat"). Mapa's point: this doc is internal — Max's team isn't just showing these tiers cold. They're wrapping pricing in value after the audit explains how every issue gets fixed and how the email volume maps to expected revenue.
Setup fees: Tristan charges a setup fee to cover full flow builds, then campaign retainer is separate. Jeremy doesn't charge a setup fee — just dedicates month 1–2 of the retainer to building core flows before starting campaigns. His old agency didn't charge setup fees either — they front-loaded pricing in months 1–3, then dropped it after flow work was done.
Unlimited revisions: Mapa called this a game changer — "unlimited revisions within 24 hours" sounds incredible to clients but never actually burns you. If they request 30 revisions in a month, they just end up only sending one email. No downside. Jeremy agreed. On SMS pricing: Jeremy just includes unlimited SMS at no extra charge — it's 160 characters, minimal effort, and helps push clients over the line. Tristan same. Jan pushed back: even if it's easy work, you're still allocating mental capacity and process bandwidth — charge for everything, because higher revenue = better talent, better clients, more growth. Undercharging is overgiving.

---
Objection Handling (42:00–48:00)
Max's framework: every objection answered with an ultra-specific case study. "Already worked with an agency" → case study of taking over from another agency and driving X revenue. "My niche doesn't work with email" → case study of a non-email niche hitting 20–45% of total store revenue. "Nobody gets our brand voice right" → case study of nailing a complicated brand voice by studying ad creative and customer responses. "I'm too busy to manage another vendor" → case study of a founder who went fully hands-off and email still killed it. "How do I know you'll deliver?" → 95% client retention, $200M+ generated, 207+ brands. "What if it doesn't work?" → 14-day money-back guarantee + can exit after 60 days.
Tristan's takeaway: Max's closer has the luxury of a massive case study library for every objection. At smaller scale, you may not have that depth — you'll need to lean harder on explaining service delivery and strategy instead of just stacking proof.
Other closing best practices: BAMFAM — Book A Meeting From A Meeting. Never let a prospect leave a call without the next call booked. If you're auditing, book the audit presentation call before you hang up. If you close, book the onboarding call right then. Once it goes to email/WhatsApp, momentum dies.

---
AI Threat to Email Agencies (50:00–1:04:00)
Jan opened this up — he's hearing from friends with 7–8 figure stores firing their email agencies and having AI agents handle everything. His buddy running an agency for 7–8 figure brands is cutting to just a designer and a QA person for the chatbot. Jan's take: there's still time, but the window is closing — push hard now, get as many clients as possible, invest the cash in whatever comes next. Don't assume email agencies survive five years.
Tristan's pushback: AI email design isn't good enough yet. Flows built by AI would all look and read the same — sloppy, generic. He believes taste is the differentiator — knowing what's good vs. bad design and copy. AI can't judge taste yet. Jeremy agreed — big brands aren't switching to AI. Only smaller, founder-led, price-sensitive brands are trying to DIY with AI.
Toni's angle: the real differentiator isn't the emails themselves — every agency does the same tactical stuff. It's knowing the why behind it, understanding LTV, AOV, reading the data, and diagnosing the business. If you're the one who surfaces the real pain points and strategic gaps, you're irreplaceable. AI can execute, but it can't think at that level yet.
Tristan brought up Max's advice from a 1:1 call: leverage being a small founder-led agency. Brands want to work with someone who's personally in the strategy, talking to designers, in the weeds. That's Max's weakness at scale — everyone thinks they're working with him, but he's not in service delivery anymore. While you're small enough to offer that, capitalize on it.
Jan's synthesis: business splits into two lanes — transactional (AI-friendly, commoditized) and soulful (relationship-driven, high-touch). The soulful path is where you want to be. He shared his old approach from the bigger agency: when a client's business dipped, he'd check in on their personal life — know their kids' birthdays, know when someone's wife is struggling, send gifts. That level of care is the moat.
Matthias grounded it: we can only talk about what AI can and can't do today. Predicting 1–2 years out is guesswork that just makes you anxious. Focus on now.

---
Nikko — New Member, Just Signed First E-Com Client (1:05:00–1:13:30)
Nikko joined the community two days ago and signed his first e-commerce email client yesterday — full flow build-out + campaigns, tech fee + 10% performance. He's transitioning from B2B cold email lead gen (using Instantly/Apollo) where sales cycles are brutal (90-day close cycles), infrastructure is expensive ($2,500+ just in domains for 3–5K emails/day before warmup, lead lists, etc.), and client churn is fast if results don't come quick. Saw e-com email as higher margin, faster results, more demand.
He asked for general operational advice — day-to-day, design tools, mistakes people wish they'd avoided. Group consensus: go through the classroom content in the Skool community — it gets you 80% of the way there. Use the templates. Max gives away everything you need to start. Specific technical questions → post in the community group and someone will answer fast, or use Claude.
Nikko admitted he told the client he's new to Klaviyo but knows copywriting and email strategy — didn't lie about experience level. Group respected the honesty + confidence combo.

---
Closing & Logistics (1:13:30–1:15:55)
Jan announced a Barcelona meetup with Max and Tristan, early June (5th or 6th) — open invite to anyone in Europe. 90% locked in. Mapa shared LinkedIn connections with the group as a last goodbye — emotional sign-off, said she'll rejoin the community when she needs it again. Group exchanged LinkedIn info in chat.

---
Key Takeaways:
Pre-call warm-up sequences between booking and showing are underutilized — most people in the group aren't doing it yet
Live audit presentations close better than Looms/PDFs sent cold — Max only does Looms because of time constraints at scale
Volume-based pricing risks feeling transactional — the group is split between flat fee, rev share, and tiered approaches
Unlimited revisions is a low-risk, high-perception value add — clients rarely abuse it
BAMFAM (Book A Meeting From A Meeting) — never let a prospect leave without the next call scheduled
AI is coming for commoditized email work, but taste, strategy, and founder-level relationships are the moat for now
Being a small, founder-led agency is a competitive advantage while you can still be in every client relationship — use it before you outgrow it

lessons.title: May 5th: Client Reporting Masterclass
lessons.description:
Call Recording >>
Full summary below 👇

---
Main Topic: Well Copy’s Client Reporting System
Tristan walked through the reporting framework you shared with the group, and everyone viewed it as one of the strongest agency systems they’d seen. The biggest takeaway was that your reporting system is not just about analytics — it’s designed to constantly reinforce client confidence, reduce buyer’s remorse, improve retention, and keep clients emotionally connected to the agency.
The framework was broken into four layers:

---
1. Daily Reporting (Slack Communication)
Your team sends updates in Slack every business day to keep clients in the loop in real time. The purpose is less about “formal reporting” and more about maintaining visibility and reinforcing activity.
