lessons.title: April 28th: Hiring Processes + Design
lessons.description:
Call Recording >>
Full Summary Below 👇

---
Main Topic: Well Copy’s Hiring Process for Designers
The session began with Tristan walking the group through the hiring process you shared for Well Copy’s design team. The group viewed the system as straightforward, practical, and scalable.
Main hiring sources discussed:
LinkedIn job posts (viewed as the best channel for long-term/full-time hires)
Upwork and Twitter/X were viewed more as freelancer ecosystems rather than long-term team-building channelsThe consensus:
LinkedIn attracts more stable, career-oriented people
Twitter and Upwork attract more entrepreneurial/freelance personalities who may churn faster
---
Geographic Hiring Strategy
The group discussed Well Copy’s international hiring structure in detail.
Philippines
Typical pay discussed:
~$500–$750/monthAdvantages:
Lower cost
Easier to scale headcount quicklyDisadvantages:
Significant quality drop at lower price ranges
Less refined design taste compared to premium marketsSouth America & Europe
Areas mentioned:
Argentina / Buenos Aires
Portugal
Serbia
Other European countriesAdvantages:
Higher design quality
Better aesthetic taste
Stronger branding instinctsTradeoff:
Often 2–3x the cost of Philippines-based hiresThe general opinion:
Higher-level ecommerce design work increasingly requires strong “taste,” not just technical execution.

---
Trial Projects & Hiring Philosophy
The group liked your paid trial project system.
Key reasons discussed:
Incentivizes quality effort
Mirrors the real working relationship
Helps test:
Communication
Turnaround speed
Interpretation of copy
Attention to detail
ReliabilitySeveral members noted they previously used unpaid trials but saw the logic behind paid tests because they produce more realistic work quality and improve candidate experience.
Matthias suggested one optimization:
Potentially sending the trial project before doing multiple interview calls to reduce wasted time on poor candidates.
---
AI Design & Claude Design Discussion
A massive portion of the call revolved around AI design tools, especially Anthropic’s Claude Design workflows.
The core theme:
AI is powerful, but human taste is still the differentiator.

---
Aven’s Perspective on AI + Designers
Aven explained that he does not want to replace designers outright. Instead:
AI should augment designers
Skilled designers should supervise AI
Human taste remains criticalHis process involved:
Feeding AI:
Brand guidelines
Product images
Tone of voice
Existing designs
Copy directionThen using AI to generate initial design concepts before designers refine them.
The group strongly agreed that:
AI still needs human oversight
Bugs/errors happen
AI lacks nuanced taste
Human iteration remains necessaryOne major point:
As AI becomes commoditized, “taste” becomes even more valuable.

---
Claude Design Workflow Discussion
The group dug deep into practical AI workflows.
Topics covered:
Exporting Claude HTML into Figma
Using HTML-to-Figma plugins
Potential future automation into Klaviyo
AI-assisted slicing workflowsA major pain point:
Claude Design usage limits and credit consumption.
Several people mentioned:
Burning through credits extremely quickly
Heavy iteration costs
AI still being slower than experienced human designers in many casesThe consensus:
AI is promising, but not yet operationally mature enough to fully replace high-level designers.

---
Copywriting → Design Workflow Systems
The next major discussion centered around how agencies should hand off copy to designers.

---
Toni’s “Copy Directly in Figma” Workflow
Toni shared a workflow where:
Copy is written directly inside Figma
Sections are wireframed visually
Notes and image references are embedded inside the design file
Designers build from that structureBenefits discussed:
Faster production
Less ambiguity
Fewer revisions
Designers spend less time interpreting intentHowever, Toni emphasized:
Designers are still encouraged to improve layouts creatively
The structure is guidance, not limitationThis sparked discussion about balancing:
Operational speed
vs.
Creative freedom
---
Counterpoint: Too Much Structure Can Hurt Creativity
Bipul shared that his agency actually tested this system extensively and found:
It reduced designer creativity
Designers subconsciously followed the wireframe too rigidly
Google Docs ultimately produced better design outcomesEspecially difficult:
Multi-language brands
High-volume translation workflowsTheir conclusion:
Loose structure sometimes creates stronger creative results.

---
Internal AI Dashboard / Well Copy Software Discussion
One of the most interesting sections of the call was Bipul referencing the custom Well Copy internal dashboard discussed on a prior Max call and podcast.
The group tried to reverse-engineer what it likely does.
Features they believed it includes:
Client profile management
Campaign ideation
Monthly planning
AI-assisted strategy generation
Copywriting prompts
Brand knowledge storage
SOP integrations
Dashboard-based workflow managementThe assumption:
The system likely combines:
GPT/Claude APIs
Internal SOP documents
Strategy libraries
Brand data
Automated prompts…into a centralized operating system for the agency.
The group was extremely interested in how this operationally works and requested future breakdowns on:
Concept creation systems
AI workflow structure
Internal campaign systems
---
Agency Differentiation Discussion
A major section focused on:
“How do small agencies actually stand out?”

---
Tristan’s Take: Small Agencies Win By Being Small
Tristan shared advice you gave him directly:
The best advantage a small agency has is being small.
Key points:
Clients love founder access
Founder-to-founder relationships are powerful
Trying to appear “bigger than you are” often backfires
Authenticity scales trust faster than fake corporate positioningThis resonated heavily with the group.

---
Aven’s Perspective: Foundational Excellence
Aven emphasized:
There is no secret differentiator.
The real edge comes from:
Being likable
Being a strong communicator
Listening well
Remembering details
Delivering quickly
Being reliable
Doing the basics exceptionally wellHe repeatedly stressed:
Most agency owners fail because they are inconsistent with fundamentals.

---
Relationship-Based Retention
Multiple attendees discussed how relationship quality directly impacts retention.
Themes:
Becoming genuine friends with clients
Traveling together
Dinners/drinks
Human connection beyond “vendor status”Biel specifically emphasized:
Once clients trust you deeply, referrals become much easier
Strong client ecosystems can create chain referrals across multiple brandsThis aligned closely with Well Copy’s relationship-heavy philosophy.

---
Bipul’s Agency Philosophy
Bipul delivered one of the strongest philosophical sections of the call.
His core rule:
He refuses to work with bad people regardless of money.
He said:
Team burnout often comes from bad clients
Caring about client businesses deeply is the real retention lever
Many agencies simply “do tasks” without genuine ownershipHe contrasted this with experiences onboarding brands from other large agencies where:
Flows were extremely poor
Campaign quality was weak
Clients were neglected despite paying large retainersHis agency’s philosophy:
Care deeply
Maintain ownership mentality
Treat clients like real partners
Fire employees who only “check tasks”This section strongly echoed many of Well Copy’s internal values.

---
Content & Personal Brand Discussion
The group discussed how content helps agencies stand out.
Consensus:
Content:
Builds trust
Warms outbound leads
Increases authority
Multiplies outreach effectivenessMultiple people referenced your content specifically:
Funnel breakdowns
Instagram content
Community positioning
Educational systemsImportant insight:
Even when content doesn’t directly create inbound leads, it dramatically improves outbound conversion rates because prospects already trust the sender.

---
Pricing, Retainers & Revenue Share
The group then moved into pricing structures and retainers.

---
Tristan Doubled His Pricing
One notable moment:
Tristan shared that he doubled one client’s retainer from ~£800/month to ~£1,600/month.
The client’s reaction:
“You were way too cheap.”
Key lesson:
Strong relationships + proven ROI make pricing increases much easier.

---
Revenue Share Debate
Large discussion around:
Rev share models
Attribution problems
Flat retainers
Hybrid structuresMost attendees were skeptical of pure rev share because:
Attribution is messy
Klaviyo overattributes
Subscription brands distort metrics heavily
It creates endless disputesKey insight:
Even if email attribution rises, total store revenue may stay flat because email simply touched more customers who would have purchased anyway.

---
Attribution Settings Discussion
The call ended with a deep conversation around Klaviyo attribution windows.
Topics:
5-day open attribution
3-day open attribution
1-day click attribution
Subscription brand distortionsAven’s recommendation:
3-day open
1-day clickEspecially for non-subscription brands.
However, others argued:
Keeping default settings makes benchmarking easier across brands and historical data.
A major concern raised:
Agencies sharing inflated attribution screenshots publicly without context.
The group debated whether:
Attribution numbers are “dishonest”
or
Attribution still reflects real influence because customers did engage with emails before purchasingThe final consensus:
Attribution should be treated as:
A directional benchmark
Not absolute truthAnd:
Integrity/transparency with clients matters more than maximizing attributed revenue screenshots.

This section strongly echoed many of Well Copy’s internal values.
Content & Personal Brand Discussion
The group discussed how content helps agencies stand out.
Consensus:
Content:
Builds trust
Warms outbound leads
Increases authority
Multiplies outreach effectiveness
Multiple people referenced your content specifically:
Funnel breakdowns
Instagram content
Community positioning
Educational systems
Important insight:
Even when content doesn’t directly create inbound leads, it dramatically improves outbound conversion rates because prospects already trust the sender.
Pricing, Retainers & Revenue Share
The group then moved into pricing structures and retainers.
Tristan Doubled His Pricing
One notable moment:
Tristan shared that he doubled one client’s retainer from ~£800/month to ~£1,600/month.
The client’s reaction:
“You were way too cheap.”
Key lesson:
Strong relationships + proven ROI make pricing increases much easier.
Revenue Share Debate
Large discussion around:
Rev share models
Attribution problems
Flat retainers
Hybrid structures
Most attendees were skeptical of pure rev share because:
Attribution is messy
Klaviyo overattributes
Subscription brands distort metrics heavily
It creates endless disputes
Key insight:
Even if email attribution rises, total store revenue may stay flat because email simply touched more customers who would have purchased anyway.
Attribution Settings Discussion
The call ended with a deep conversation around Klaviyo attribution windows.
Topics:
5-day open attribution
3-day open attribution
1-day click attribution
Subscription brand distortions
Aven’s recommendation:
3-day open
1-day click
Especially for non-subscription brands.
However, others argued:
Keeping default settings makes benchmarking easier across brands and historical data.
A major concern raised:
Agencies sharing inflated attribution screenshots publicly without context.

Attribution numbers are “dishonest”
or
Attribution still reflects real influence because customers did engage with emails before purchasing

Attribution should be treated as:
A directional benchmark
Not absolute truth
And:
Integrity/transparency with clients matters more than maximizing attributed revenue screenshots.

lessons.title: April 21st: Client Onboarding
lessons.description:
Call Recording >>
Summary below 👇

---
Opening & Housekeeping (0:00–6:00) Tristan opened the call with Matthias (joining from Albania), Mapa, Jan, Adam, Francis, Aiberson, and Toni. Mapa raised a concern about the recordings: because agency owners discuss internal process — commission structures, team management, referral payouts — it's not ideal for the raw recordings to be visible to anyone who might bring clients into the community. Tristan agreed to share recordings via private link only and flagged that Max already runs anonymized summaries for the community at large. Mapa also asked if the link could be shared directly so members can revisit without needing the recording.

---
Max's Onboarding Form Walkthrough (2:30–10:07) Tristan ran through Max's client onboarding form as the anchor for the session. Key points he called out:
Frictionless tech access. Loom videos embedded directly in the form for granting Klaviyo access, Klaviyo app collaborator access, and Shopify collaborator access. Low friction = higher completion.
Brand & positioning section. Standard brand story, positioning, product, ICP, competitors, best sellers.
Customer objections mapped to responses. Example: "price too high → we emphasize value / 30-day returns." Tristan called this out as something worth stealing if you don't already do it.
Do's and don'ts for copy AND design. Both explicit. Hard constraints upfront prevent rework later.
Email examples the client likes. Reference point for design direction.
Wider marketing context. Ad strategy, review platforms, discount history, content calendar. Gives the email team the full picture, not just email-in-a-silo.
Partnership goals + previous agency experience. "What did you like about previous partners? What could they have done better?" — the gold question. Sets expectations and reveals the client's real friction points.
Kickoff call booking embedded at the end. Tristan flagged he personally books the kickoff on the back of the sales call to prevent drop-off, but Max's flow is: close → form → kickoff booking inside the form.Matthias flagged the one gap: expectation-setting (communication cadence, turnaround times, revision rules) isn't in the form. Likely covered in the kickoff call — Tristan asked Max to share kickoff call structure for next week.
Action item: Tristan to get Max's kickoff call structure + agenda to share next session.

---
Tristan's Onboarding Process (10:07–11:02) For comparison, Tristan walked through his own stack:
Close on sales call
Onboarding email with Stripe link + communication guidelines
Typeform-hosted onboarding form
E-signature fires as separate email
Kickoff call booked on the back of the sales callAdmitted his expectation-setting is weak — no strict process around asset deadlines, approval windows, or turnaround commitments. Called this a gap.

---
Onboarding Timelines & Expectation Setting (12:38–16:25) Question (Matthias): How do you set expectations on onboarding timelines and communication?
Jan's answer:
Be upfront that onboarding timelines only start once you have all the info. If the client is dragging on assets, the clock hasn't started.
Jan's most recent client: told them onboarding would take 45 days. Longer than most, but it let him find a better designer, run a proper customer survey (500+ responses), and do deep research before putting work in front of the client.
His reasoning: he was mentally drained, didn't want to grind, wanted to do great work. Client agreed. Result: client is blown away by the emails because they're built off survey data, not assumptions.
The mindset shift: two years ago he would have called this lazy. Now he's optimizing for quality and enjoyment, not speed.Tristan's addition: If you know you can't thoroughly onboard a client in the timeline they want, tell them upfront. Over-promising and missing creates a pissed-off client — that's worse than setting a longer timeline.

---
Customer Surveys as Part of Onboarding (16:25–23:00) Jan's system:
Surveys every new client as part of onboarding. Framing: "Fill this out to enter a giveaway."
Success page after survey submission = 20% off + still in the giveaway. Turns a research exercise into a revenue event.
Generated $2K for his most recent client from existing customers alone (no ad spend).
Why it works: most founders who've run a brand for 2–3 years still don't know their customer as deeply as they think. Surveys surface the actual language customers use, their real objections, and why they buy.
Real example: for one client (soccer gear brand), 80% of reviews showed moms were buying for their kids. The brand was marketing to athletes. Jan recommended a full repositioning to moms — but the client has investors pushing otherwise. Jan's position: "Give me the data and we do email my way. If my way doesn't work, we go back to yours."Adam's system:
Running surveys for every client. Uses discount incentive for older customers instead of giveaway.
Recent result: 8% open rate, 4% reply rate on a survey campaign. Huge deliverability boost.
Also drives goodwill — clients love seeing 5,000+ survey responses even when revenue is quiet.Jan on deliverability: If the brand has customer support on the same email address as Klaviyo, asking people to reply drives major sender reputation gains. If they don't, stick to form-based surveys.
Action item: Anyone not running a survey at onboarding — start. It doubles as revenue, research, and a deliverability boost.

---
Claude Design — First Impressions (24:10–28:52) Question (Tristan): Has anyone played with Claude Design yet?
Mapa's take:
"Almost in love, almost in hate." Creates beautiful output but doesn't understand strategy, function, customer experience — treats design as pure aesthetics.
Built a 60-page PDF in one evening that would have taken her designer a full week. Designer now finishes it in one day instead of starting from scratch.
Required ~2 hours of brand kit setup with iterative feedback and screenshots to get the style dialed. After that setup, every subsequent design is fast.
Verdict: designer role isn't going away, but output speed is transformed.Tristan's take:
Tested it for email design. Everything he got out still looked AI-generated. Not client-ready yet.
Loaded a full Figma file and told it to learn best practices — got better but still needed manual corrections (e.g., buttons in the hero section above the fold).
Open question whether it's a skill issue (prompting) or a model limitation.Workflow note: Claude Design connects with Figma. Mapa uses Illustrator (exports PDFs), but Figma export should be editable. Worth testing for the email team.

---
Case Study Approval & Contract Language (29:18–32:51) Question (Matthias): How do you get a client to approve releasing a case study with KPIs?
Tristan: In the contract from day one. Never had an issue.
Mapa's approach (more polished):
Contract language is written warmly: "We love the work we do and because we're so proud of it, we want to share it."
Client has a 2-week approval window to request edits. No response = implied approval.
For sensitive clients: never publish revenue figures. Use conversion rates, percentage lifts, and blur the brand name.
If the brand has a strict NDA, this doesn't work — but that's rare outside of enterprise.Aiberson: Similar contract language, only had one pushback from a client with a lot of competitors.

---
Pricing — Raising Rates on Existing Clients (33:34–41:09) Tristan's situation: Currently charging ~£1–1.5K (~$2K). Max told him on a call he should be doubling prices. Stuck on how to raise rates on clients he's already working with without adding more value.
Adam's experience:
Had to raise prices from 2K because he had a full team and wasn't profitable. Framed it honestly: "I have more designers, here's the ROI you're getting, here's what I need to pay the team." Most clients understood.
The one painful negotiation took 3 calls and he hit every objection he'd ever heard on one call. Still closed it.
The ROI framing is key: if you know client COGS, you can show them what they're actually pocketing from email vs. what they're paying you.Jan's framework (the meat of the section):
Q4 is the natural lever — every year he uses the Q4 playbook as the reason to increase prices. "Here's extra value for free, but if you want the premium version, it's +X."
Long-term: move to profit share / revenue share instead of flat-fee increases.
His structure:
New smaller clients: ~$2.5K flat + 5% of email-attributed revenue
Bigger brands ($70K+/mo): $4K onboarding fee, then 10% of email-attributed revenue OR minimum $1.7–2K floor
Uses Klaviyo's native attribution. Doesn't mess with custom AI attribution — his old agency did $10M+ on Klaviyo attribution alone.
Frames it as "I win if you win." If the client pushes back on price after a few months, he caps it: "OK, we'll lock at $5K" — client feels like they're getting $7K of perceived value for $5K.
On objections: "If someone's hostile about it, work with someone else. No ego, no arguing, just move on." Scarcity mindset kills negotiations — he's confident he can replace any client within days.Tristan's concern: Heard horror stories about rev share disputes over attribution. Jan's counter: he's never had the issue, and even if a client leaves early, rev share months usually out-earn what flat fee would've brought for the full year.

---
Revenue Share Structure & Ethics (46:27–53:27) Question (Aiberson): What percentage do you use on rev share?
Aiberson: 1% on a multi-brand, low-margin account. Works for him.
Toni's framework:
Uses rev share almost exclusively with small brands (under $50K/month) who can't afford flat fee.
Structures: 10%, 15%, or 20% depending on situation.
Acts as more than an email guy — business partner energy. Works on offers, branding, social strategy, keeps founders accountable.
Self-regulates: when a client's big promo month would have generated an uncomfortable rev share payout, he voluntarily capped it to protect the relationship. "I don't want to stitch money from them."Mapa's warning (the most important point of the section):
Email doesn't live in isolation — it lives inside their full P&L.
Know the client's margin before proposing any rev share. If margin is under 20% and you're taking 20% of revenue, you're taking more than their profit.
Never go above 10% of their margin. Proposing bad math signals you don't understand their business.Francis's add: Cap the rev share. "15% up to $5K, then it stops." Protects client margins and keeps the upside uncapped for scale, not bleeding.
Toni's philosophy: Calculate where it hurts the client before you calculate what you want to take. If the value you're giving isn't worth the money, you're sneaking.

---
Charging New Clients the New Price First (53:27–54:57) Matthias's practical advice to Tristan: Before raising rates on existing clients, prove the new price works with new clients.
Test the new price on every incoming sales call.
If they pay it — your pricing is validated, your mindset shifts, and justifying the raise to existing clients is easier.
If they don't — it's a data problem, not an ego problem.Tristan's diagnostic: His close rate is well above 40%. Hormozi's rule: if your close rate is above 30–40%, you're under-pricing. Not everyone should be able to afford you.
Action item: Tristan to charge the new price on every new sales call going forward and report back.

---
Finding Closers (56:00–58:11) Question (Jan): Where do you find closers (not for email marketing — for another project)?
Tristan: Discord communities for online money/closer networks. He's in several with lots of closer applicants. Offered to post listings for Jan.
Mapa: LinkedIn outreach campaigns. Her team runs parallel campaigns — some for clients, some for teammates. Separate pipeline tab in Fondo for "potential closer" leads.

---
LTV & AOV Calculation (58:27–1:01:23) Question (Toni): How do you calculate LTV and AOV in a spreadsheet to drive them higher?
Francis: Angus Cairn has a YouTube video with a downloadable dashboard — export your list, plug it in, it calculates everything. Francis shared the video links.
Mapa's add:
Request viewer access to Shopify for every client — email lives in the full ecosystem.
Use a Shopify Partners account so you're not consuming one of their paid seats. Free viewer access.
Warning: Shopify analytics numbers aren't fully accurate — they miss B2B purchases, upsell revenue, post-purchase upsells. Always calculate manually if you want a real picture.Adam: Every Well Copy client onboarding includes Shopify collaborator access. Essential for identifying best sellers, tracking CVR movement with pop-up changes, and understanding upsell-driven AOV (which Shopify often doesn't report accurately).
Action item: Anyone not pulling Shopify viewer access at onboarding — add it. You can't optimize what you can't see.

---
Closing (1:02:15–1:03:00) Tristan's Wi-Fi gave out twice across the call (traveling, bad Airbnb connection). Wrapped by asking for DMs with agenda items for next week and confirming he'll push Max for the kickoff call structure.

This video and doc covers the retention frameworks behind 20+ nine-figure ecom brands, pulled straight from Thomas Lalas and his book Retention Economics. The stuff that moves a brand from one bad month away from disaster to genuinely bulletproof.
I cover the full retention system from acquisition to win-back...
Why brands generating record revenue still can't pay their bills and what the P&L actually shows
Payback period and the RCM Pyramid: the four tiers every brand sits in (Rust, Bronze, Silver, Gold)
The three dimensions of a subscription offer and why misalignment guarantees churn

lessons.title: AI Just Changed Email Marketing Forever
lessons.description:
Link To In-Depth Summary Document >>
Max sat down with Chase Dimond — one of the most respected names in ecommerce email — to cut through everything that's changed, everything that hasn't, and exactly where the game is heading next. Between them: 300+ brands and $250M in email revenue. This is the conversation.
What actually changed in 2026: Apple Mail categorization defaulting to promo, Apple Intelligence summarizing emails before they're opened, and full Gmail/Yahoo enforcement of SPF, DKIM, and DMARC — and what each one means for your program right now
The honest AI assessment: where AI genuinely adds leverage in email (voice of customer mining, subject line variants, editing, data analysis) and where handing it full ownership of copy reliably produces worse results than writing it yourself
The 10-80-10 framework: you do the first 10% (brief, data, criteria), AI does the middle 80% (drafting, variants, self-check), you do the last 10% (judgment call on what's actually good)
Welcome flow, abandonment, and post-purchase non-negotiables: the specific structures, splits, and sequencing decisions that separate programs leaking revenue from programs compounding it
The replenishment data play: how Chase used Shopify cohort data to discover a beverage brand's peak repurchase window was Days 22 to 28 while they were sending on Day 30 — and how to run the same analysis on your own list
Where the agency model is heading by 2028: smaller teams, fewer accounts, revenue share over flat retainers, and fractional retention leadership instead of vendor relationshipsThe companion doc includes the full 90-day audit checklist across infrastructure, flows, campaigns, and metrics — everything in one place to find where your program is bleeding most.
